This is going to be the short version: I find myself trying to force myself to have fun with this. There's some good in it, but so much holds it back.The machines and combat are fun. Gathering thousands of items is not. Having to wait for dialogue and animations to finish before continuing any task is not. Invisible walls, Aloy's personality, and the quests are not.Full review:Aloy:I feel uncomfortable writing this part, because I looked it up to see if others had the same feel. However, most people attempting to get their point across sounded sexist and most people who responded gave weak reasoning. Aloy for the first 20+ hours of the game will be incredibly mean to all the guys she encounters (new, old friends, companions) and seems like a misandrist. Telling them to go away, they can't help, they won't understand, they're stupid, etc. Even to people who have consistently helped her in the first game or those who are loyal and useful. She excuses this by saying if she doesn't do her job alone, all of life might end. Okay, world ending is a good reason. However, I noticed this was almost exclusively towards the guys which felt awkward. There's a cutscene about 18~ hours in where she finds out a gal from the first game is in the area and perks up and immediately wants to go hang out with her. This gal wants to hunt and look for her guy friend and Aloy is instantly gleeful, wanting to tag along. What happened to that end of the world timer? There's quite a few examples of this flip-flop behavior. Saying she won't wait for any guy and no one will tell her what to do, but then saying "Oh okay I'll go the opposite direction and listen to you. No rush :))" to gals.I've seen some people defend this by saying that Aloy has been an outcast since birth and she has to grow to accept comrades. However, I don't remember her acting like this so heavily towards many in the first game and she had people helping her then.I think part of what bothers me is this sort of anti-men rhetoric adheres to some anti-lesbian stereotypes. It's hinted at pretty heavily that Aloy is queer and a common stereotype about lesbians is that they're "just men haters". It's a negative, harmful lgbt trope and if Aloy was pretty consistent towards her "I'm not going to listen to anyone because I have an important, timed job to do" towards /everyone/ it wouldn't be an issue. Having powerful, queer women in games is a great thing and something we need more of, but seeing a clear difference in behavior towards the sexes is a problem. Puzzles:Aloy also does not stop speaking. Starting the game, the game asks if you'd like more of an "Explorer" or "Guided" feel to the game. Guided will show you immediately where the next points are in a Skyrim-esque style while explorer encourages you to solve puzzles. However, often times Aloy will spoil the puzzle immediately when entering a new area or the puzzle. "There's a ledge up there, if I can climb that I can get in" before you even see a ledge. "I can ride those machines to get across this gap" .. Didn't even scan them yet. If the game allowed some time before giving hints this wouldn't be an issue, but it's immediate. This takes away from some of the actual adventuring. Exploration:For the most part exploring is fine. I did find a few invisible walls that blocked off quest areas or places that it felt I should solve some puzzle to get into. I glided off a mountain towards an area that looked neat, Aloy made a comment about it being a quest objective. Well cool, I'm overhead so I'll just go right in- Nope. Game pops up a "You can't go in here" message. Why though? :/Climbing feels very slow and some of the ways it will try to guide you lead to dead ends just to mess with you.Some of the gathering points for flora are inside walls, rocks, terrain that's inaccessible. It feels very.. randomly generated?Machines:Designs of machines are cool, but I wouldn't say there's as many as the game leads on. Separating things like "Frostfang" and "Firefang" to two different machines is silly when they don't do that for other variants.Hunting machine parts in stealth is extremely slow. Have a high tear weapon, shoot once, see them get alerted and spin around for a few moments until the alert wears off then shoot again.  Yawn.However going loud will most likely risk you getting 1-2 shot almost always. Currently I have fully upgraded very rare armor and found some machines that will get me to 10/460 health in one shot. This being said, loud is still more fun imo.Sound/Music is unremarkable and forgettable. Aloy has to start over with all of her weapons and gear even though this is a direct continuation of the first game. She gives some vague "Had a run in with a machine" reason. The story being a direct continuation will make some of it hard to swallow. You're expected to know all of the old friends that pop up, everything she went through, the secret twists of HZD going in.Overall some of the game is tolerable, but it just feels like a slog.

I included a bunch of links to my Horizon blog posts and also some content from them for this summary. I also link to other media for more details.Horizon Forbidden West was one of the most visually impressive titles on the PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5. Two years later, the same sentiment repeats on the PC. Despite no fancy raytracing features, Guerrila's Decima Engine still produces a stunning game world and character rendering. I gushed enough about the visuals when I wrote my  and  reviews. The PC version is essentially the PS5 version, with a slightly higher level of detail in the distance and some PC-specific improvements, as . The most significant benefit of this PC version is the "unlimited" performance. Now that Horizon Forbidden West has been kicked out of the bird's nest, it can finally spread its wings and soar above and beyond the limits of console hardware. And soar it does. Horizon Forbidden West performs admirably. The YouTube channel eTeknix did enormous work . Nixxes did an excellent job making the game scalable, and Guerilla's initial work optimizing for the weaker consoles also paid off immensely. Even my former 3060 would have been enough to enjoy the Forbidden West with some help from DLSS upscaling.Speaking of hardware and performance, here's what I measured on my system. It is a Ryzen 7600 with 32GB of DDR5 6000 MT/s memory and an AMD Radeon 7900 XT. The Windows installation ran the game off a Samsung 980 Pro, while Linux had to make do with a Samsung 970 Evo.In 1440p with the Very High graphics preset, Windows achieved 101/86 avg/min fps, and my Fedora 39 managed 102/55 avg/min fps. I have more numbers and thoughts on  if you are interested.One aspect that deserves proper kudos is the game launch, which is one of the fastest I've ever seen. Until now, I considered  to be exemplary in this aspect. However, Horizon Forbidden West takes it to a whole new level. The game allows you to skip every intro movie and logo on launch with a single press of the Escape button. Immediately after, the main screen shows up, and you can continue with the last saved state by pressing Space. Thanks to these insanely short loading times, you're back in the game, ready to play in just a few seconds. This holds true for both Windows and Linux, adding to the convenience and smoothness of the gaming experience.The game is still Horizon, with a much deeper skill tree and combat options. The world is much bigger, too big for my liking, but traversal and combat are so fun that it almost does not matter. While the story is not as mindblowing as the first game - how could it be - it is a continuation of the events of Zero Dawn. It gets more science fictiony, but still stays true to the lore. You will not be running around shooting lasers from your eyes if that's what you're afraid of.My personal highlights in the Forbidden West are the relic ruins and the depiction of quest conversations. The latter are on a different level and the best I have seen so far. Gone are the times when awkward camera cuts jump from face to face, depending on who is talking. Guerrilla's tech is so immersive that I actively sought out all side quests I could find, even after I beat the game, just to experience the conversation and the quests. And that is saying something because I rarely get back into a game after the credits roll.The second highlight, the relic ruins, are like prepper stashes in Far Cry 5 crossed with Tomb Raider tombs. These are small puzzle areas where Aloy can spend some cozy time exercising her brain cells on environmental puzzles. There's the exact right amount of such ruins to be a welcome distraction without becoming overwhelming and a chore.I finished this game on the PS4 Pro, about half of the base game on the PS5, beat the Burning Shores expansion on the PS5, and now I'm back at it on the PC in all its visual glory at higher than 30 fps.It's a great game that runs close to flawlessly on PC.I hope this was informative.Thank you for reading.

TL,DR: Forbidden West is a game of two halves, the first one, gameplay, is just as sublime as the first game. Hunting machines is always fun, and the multiple different weapons one can use to solve the same problem makes this game infinitely better. The second one, the story, is underwhelming. There’s plenty of factors that play into this, but the main two are the lack of a true antagonist and pacing. You can do the entirety of act 2 at your leisure, neither of the antagonists will pose problems to Alloy like the eclipse/ Hades did in the last game, and the story focus every dramatic bit to its final act, leaving the pacing quite unbalanced. This is a game one should buy if they played the first one, and probably get on a sale. 7/10 GameplayVery little has changed from HZD, thus I’ll be short. It is still one of the most satisfying games to play. Hunting machines are as fun as ever, although some machine combos can get frustrating at times. The biggest annoyance is with the exploration and puzzles, Forbidden west puzzles have one solution, yet three different solutions that look plausible without the focus. This made me give up on environmental puzzles for the entirety of the game, as I rather not keep looking this beautiful graphics through the focus. Performance:Game runs fine, didn’t drop out of 60 FPS once with a 7800XT + R5 5600X 32 GB RAM on ultra, 3440x1440 (21:9). One of the best optimized ports I’ve come across, and just as impressive graphically as the first game. Story (this will contain spoilers) The premise of Forbidden west is that despite our victory in the previous game, the lack of Gaia has made its subfunctions lose control, and create essentially a blight in the land, with infertile soil, hostile climate conditions that will end life on planet. Alloy, as the clone of Sobeck, is the only person who can access the old zero dawn facilities to find a Gaia backup and reboot the terraforming system. If this sounds familiar, it’s because this is Mass Effect Andromeda. It goes far beyond than only the premise, plenty of plot points match, Beta another Sobeck clone acts as the Ryder twin, who also gets herself kidnapped at the end of act 2 and arguably, a similar ending. This is hardly the first time the Horizon games have done this, HZD has its fair share of similar elements to Dragon Age on the current earth narrative, from the end of act 1 to Sylens being what amounts to discount Solas. Once more this meant that, personally, I was not caught by surprise by quite a few of the plot points, removing a sizable part of its impact. That said, this is a good take on that narrative. A lot has to do with Alloy being a much better character than Ryder, and so is her journey. A competent person who needs to learn to share the burden is a far more endearing journey than nepotism places you in a bad spot. One empathizes with Alloy’s journey, her challenges and the weight of her knowledge. Her character has evolved to become far more cunning than when we last saw her and it is somewhat of a joy to play as her. This game had the challenge of making you interested in the current world, as the first one rode on the Zero Dawn project. And it sort of rises to the occasion, most of the new tribes are interesting, and the narrative has a rather clever angle of culture being defined by how they interact with the old-world ruins or data. The problems of this narrative stem all from a core issue: the lack of a true antagonist. Neither Sylens nor the Zeniths rise to the occasion, as both are missing from the entirety of act II, and with no subordinates to deal with. This impacts both the pacing, as everything is dumped on the player in the last act, and the themes of the narrative. The narrative seems to be about how one must learn to share the burden and accept the different cultures if you go by Alloy, she is running away from her friends, not accepting any help, trying to barge through the gates of a diplomatic mission, and she ends saving the Tenakth and shouting for the winds for help against nemesis. But there’s no such thing as a foil to challenge that, the Zeniths fall as they have no allies, but they are barely present, and Tilda’s obsession with Elizabeth is hardly aligned with the story. Regala could’ve worked if Hekaro was a questionable leader, but as he is mostly a bland okay leader, her goal of returning to war is just shortsighted and clearly wrong. Finally, Sylens is the most disappointing, as he ends up doing the same thing as the last game, Regala’s rebels are the eclipse from the last game, but not as connected to the story because there’s no Hades. It is not like it was easy to avoid this, as it stems from last game twist, Sylens threat level in taking Hades is too vague. In HZD, the issue with the twist was how predictable it was (coming from Inquisition), but now, it seems they borrowed a great twist with no plans to follow up with it. The companions are another part that doesn’t quite work. As they spend most of the time in the base and said base is not required to access the open world, like a Ship or Camp, you barely interact with them. Their individual missions don’t push the story in exploring the main theme or branch of it.The exception to this is Beta. Here both her and Alloy hold themselves to an impossible standard, Alloy to Elizabeth and Beta to Alloy, which they see as a perfect role model. This leads to Alloy to throw all her frustration onto Beta, who herself cannot gain a once of confidence, and is ball of nerves, due to her past experience with the Zeniths. Their dynamic essentially worsen the problem, while Varl tries, but fails to help. When it reaches the boiling point, their growth comes from the shared experience it becomes one of the best moments in the narrative. The Burning Shores: (8/10)The DLC fixes most of the problems discussed above. Londra is a clear antagonist and Seyka, present in the whole narrative, is a character that gets development. She is actually the centre of the emotional core, as it is her sister missing. Alloy’s challenge of interacting with someone, whom she clearly has feelings towards, and the knowledge of what’s to come is certainly an interesting idea. While thematically it doesn’t go much beyond cult bad, it is a narrative that flows much better. It brings, however, a point regarding Alloy. The Horizon games must either make her a character in which the player has more input, akin to Sheppard/Geralt, or make her more into Nathan Drake. So I got this while it was on sale because I've heard so many good things about the Horizon series. I can tell (even with only 16 hours in) the story seems to be well thought out and a main driving force behind the game which I love, but (at least for the PC) the controls feel beyond clunky if using M/KB. With only 82% of people reaching even the first small area and being one who passed the embassy, here are some of my thoughts. . . First I'll mention some gameplay things. The weapon wheel isn't too bad, but to needing to 'quick craft' arrows mid fight is tedious over anything. The berry mechanic is worse, with being able to hold 10 on you for quick use (Q) but 20 more than once you use those ten you need to HOLD (Q) to restock - it feels like a lazy mechanic implemented in an attempt to make the game more difficult. Then once you get the glider movement can become more complicated, if you jump off anything you can also rappel to and attempt to glide the double jump input makes the game think you're trying to rappel back to the same ledge instead of gliding. Then we have jumping - there are places I'm obviously NOT meant to reach by jumping (ledges and stuff to climb instead) but with a little determination and luck you can skip the long climbing animations and jump along some trees. Most important, go into your options and switch pick-up to auto with no animations - you'll thank me.Next my issue with the game is the graphics. I have a decent setup with an 11th gen Intel i7-11700 @ 2.5GHz, 32 GB RAM and a 3060 TI yet cannot run this game at 1440. If I try I get fps between the range of 15-20 depending on how low or high the graphics are set and how much is happening - so I tried running it at 1080. While this is a lot better at medium graphics (45-55 FPS) going to anything higher results in the fps dropping to 35-45 with drops to under 20 during super busy times. While I get I don't have a top of the line PC I have no issues running other high demanding games at 1440 with much more stable frame rates. According to my Nvidia performance overlay my GPU and CPU don't even reach 70% utilization while running at 1080, in 1440 the GPU is constantly at 100%Last complaint I have is the animations - for ***** sake the animations. I get you want to have the character model do some cool movements when preforming actions but they are WAY too time consuming to the point of frustrating. Before I had auto collect on picking up loot took up I feel way too much time - it's quicker to loot in Fallout 3. Then when you climb and use the rappel you constantly try to preform this cool launch-rappel up move - while awesome to watch a couple of times seeing this animation happen again and again becomes tediously annoying. It feel far faster to rappel up entire buildings in the Batman games then it takes to rappel up once in this game. At 16 hours of game play I want to say at least 3 of those have been spent watching the same animations during times where you're unable to control anything - it feels like when you replay a boss multiple times and have to watch the same cut scene again and again: there's a reason most games have skip features for cut scenes.Overall I do enjoy the game play, I do enjoy the story, but the poor optimization for both the graphics and controls for PC make it less fun than I expected or hoped. If I had not spent more than two hours attempting to fix the graphical issues I listed above I would have refunded this game - the entertaining mechanics are just outweighed too much by the poor quality of life things in this game. In conclusion I give Horizon Forbidden West Complete Edition for PC a 5.8/10: enjoyable, likely more so with a top of the line PC and PS controller (which should not be needed to make a game enjoyable); graphics and animations could be optimized better. I bought this on sale for $45 USD and feel the price tag was too high, I would recommend this game if you could snag it for the $25 USD price range (if you have the top-end PC and controller and price doesn't matter I'd snag it for no more than $35).

Horizon Zero Dawn was an excellent game, but some aspects of it have aged more poorly than others. However, Forbidden West takes everything excellent about Zero Dawn and makes it even better, while improving on so many things that have aged poorly from before. I highly recommend you play the first game first before playing Forbidden West, it's still a great game but you can definitely see and feel the age.Character interactions and conversations feel much more alive, more realistic, and immersive. Side quests are way better and more varied, mainly because these NPCs are so much more interesting or likable.Combat is more fluid, more punchy, and more fast, the archery itself feels better. Although it might be due to the hitboxes being more generous when shooting arrows, they almost feel like they home in on a particular weakpoint you are aiming at.The skill tree is... man, where do I even start? In the first game, it was a decent skill tree with plenty of game changing abilities, but in Forbidden West there are so many skills and so much improvement it is dizzying. There are playstyle defining "ultimate" abilities, and they are so fun!The open world is still full of a lot of map icons and stuff to check out, so if you're tired of that then it hasn't really gotten that much better than the first game. However, you will stumble upon "unknown" things that are question marks on the map, and they will reveal themselves when you get closer, and this is such an excellent way of improving this tired Ubisoft-style trope. You can still easily navigate the world with waypoints or fast travel, but as before there are fast travel packs which are a limited resource and more often than not I want to walk around on foot because the world is breathtaking. You can even climb on more surfaces that are less obviously climbable, but we still get some yellow paint objects. You can ping with the Focus to see where you can climb on natural geometry.Speaking of map icons and the huge open world. There's A LOT to do in Forbidden West, a lot more than even in Zero Dawn. I love this in open world games, personally, but it's up to you whether or not this is all padding or worthwhile content. I feel like any excuse to explore the world, the cultures, the ruins, and the machines is a good excuse to me. If you're a completionist, you'll have A LOT on your plate with this game.Speaking of breathtaking, the graphics are truly "next gen", at least in my eyes. The first game was the same way, and it visually holds up, but it's even better now in Forbidden West. I appreciate this commitment to color and visual style while still hammering home the graphical fidelity, and it all runs pretty damn good from what I can tell. There's a few odd little graphical glitches, such as flickering shadows for specific details on characters, especially indoors, but it's not that big of a deal.The music is great, and it's full of motifs, which is something I love. The only problem is that the sound overall is kind of low or strangely mixed, where it feels like the music is too loud but the sounds are too quiet.There is now swimming, you can dive and it's actually pretty terrifying for me as a thalasaphobe. You have to worry about water machines and drowning, which is scary, but I love that now there are even mechanics for swimming, such as grabbing an object and boosting yourself forward to swim faster. There is real attention to detail in how you navigate the world in general, on foot or even when swimming, such as wall jumping and other such climbing abilities.There's tons of loot to find and to upgrade ( or to buy ), it's far better than in the first game in how fun it is, but sadly the upgrades don't change how your stuff looks which annoys me a lot. But this is how it often is.Look, I could go on and on. This review was already going on long enough. So do yourself a favor and play the first game, and then this game, you will not regret it. Did I mention the story is tense, compelling, and amazing? Hm?

First off, about the port itself: How Guerilla and Nixxes managed to make a game that looks this good run this well is some sort of miracle. Incredibly short loading times, no significant frame drops apart from a few cutscenes and spots in DLC, massive amount of graphical, QoL and accessibility settings you can tweak. $60 for a full game with DLC included and 0 microtransactions. Absolute masterclass in optimization and porting in general from Nixxes. Worth every penny.Now about the actual game: In general, it's a pretty solid game. It is no masterpiece, but it'll keep you entertained from start to finish with a few drawbacks here and there. And it's definitely not a soulless, "industry plant" type of game as many will try to convince you it is. Anyone that actually played the game can tell that it had a lot of love and passion put into it. Just like Zero Dawn, this game is structured like a typical Ubisoft open world game, yet still manages to be a unique and memorable experience with a decent amount of replay value. Two general complaints I have are that the early game is pretty rough and does no justice to how good the mid and late game are, as well that the game can feel pretty "bloated" with the amount of side content it has but some may find that as a positive.Gameplay/combat: A clear step up from Zero Dawn. Both melee and ranged combat have been vastly improved, machines and human enemies are more interesting, their AI has been improved. Gear upgrade system is improved, although it can be pretty grindy in the late game. Weapon variety is much greater which lets you have more freedom in how you approach combat encounters, but it makes it almost impossible to make a permanent loadout. I also didn't like that Aloy now stumbles when you spam dodge roll and that when you get knocked down it takes forever to get back up, which can ruin the flow of the combat.Story, characters and dialogue: Story is significantly weaker than in Zero Dawn. It's still a serviceable story, but nowhere near as engaging and satisfying as in Zero Dawn. After you finish the main story, the whole game just feels like an awkward setup for the next game. DLC is even worse when it comes to the story: Writers tried to sell a lame villain as a charismatic one, as well as tried to sell you a very forced and unconvincing love story crammed into a few hours of DLC's main questline. Another important issue that the side quests and errands are still uninspired and repetitive, but there is some other interesting and rewarding side content. Main cast is great and go through some great character development - apart from Aloy, the main heroine herself. Aloy in Forbidden West goes through fake and forced development just to end up being the same character she was at the end of Zero Dawn. There is still a massive amount of dialogue the game, but it is better written and acted than in Zero Dawn, with much better facial animations that help in sharing the emotions that characters go through. Visuals, worldbuilding and soundtrack: Visuals in Forbidden West are second to none. By far the most impressive looking game yet. A perfect mix of realistic, high fidelity visuals and a low fantasy/Sci-Fi artstyle. Maybe a bit too detailed even, making it hard to know what to focus your sight on, and making it easy to miss points of interest if you don't constantly check your map/radar/focus. But exactly those detailed visuals are what make the game come to life and make the worldbuilding so intriguing. They help make each biome and each tribe believable. From each tribe's unique aesthetic, to their behavior, their lore... truly wonderful work by the devs in this department. Soundtrack is beautiful as well, it's no masterpiece but it's memorable.Traversal, climbing and exploration: Traversal is even better than in Zero Dawn, especially in the late game and DLC, thanks to some new tools, but they somehow made the climbing worse. Climbing can be janky, inconsistent and often frustrating thanks to mostly poorly placed climbing spots and unresponsiveness from Aloy. Exploration is better thanks to new tools, and your exploration is better rewarded, although there is a bit too much scanning and looting involved. A common complaint here is that Aloy talks too much while exploring and doing puzzles, which can be annoying and even insulting but I don't mind it that much since I want to get through puzzles and other tedious tasks as quickly as possible. Collectibles are, IMO, a lot less interesting than in Zero Dawn, but still worth the time.And for the end - for those that say that they made Aloy ugly in Forbidden West: You should go see a doctor and check your eyes... or maybe go outside and look at some real women for a change :D

Beautiful HorizonsGuerrilla Games has knocked it out of the park with a dazzling, polished, and thought provoking sequel.  The massive open world utilizes some of the highest quality assets ever seen in this art form.  With its beautiful and ranging color palette to its precise and detailed particle effects that flutter around in the most organic ways, slowing down for a moment and just taking it all in is truly a remarkable experience.  The character models have extremely high polygon counts with fluid animation which means conversations will have you thinking it’s a pre-rendered cutscene.  Horizon Forbidden West is undoubtedly, one of the best looking games of all time. Combat is intuitive, with many ways to go about each encounter and a skill system to back up your favorite ways to play.  I’m a sucker for slow motion in video games, and this probably has the best use of it I can think of since Max Payne.  It’s super satisfying to watch your arrow tear off a piece of armor from a robot, and then as you go to loot you can see each and every arrow that you hit it with still lodged into the frames of these creatures.  Truly marvelous stuff, and it all ties together to give you one of the most immersive experiences you can have in this industry.The PC version was handled by Sony’s in house porting studio, Nixxes, and they have once again proven why they are the kings of porting.  Excellent utilization of hardware, with impressive frame times and no stutters.  This makes the upcoming Steam release of Ghosts of Tsushima something to be excited about.  In a world of unoptimized games, it’s a real treat to have a team like Nixxes handling this.   Ultimately it makes the experience exactly what Guerrilla intended, which is why it’s worth mentioning. All in all, Horizon Forbidden West is a game that deserves your time.  If you enjoyed things like Witcher 3, Red Dead Redemption 2, Hogwarts Legacy, Cyberpunk, and Starfield then you’ll feel right at home with this title.  Or if you’ve never taken the plunge into an open world RPG, this might be what makes you interested in the genre moving forward.  A masterclass AAA game in every sense.10/10

An overall really good game that is held back by itself. Pros: First, the game runs great and the visuals are fantastic. Nixxes did a good job on the port. I did really like the story and the companions. The story didn't have as much mystery as the first, but was solid all around. If felt like a good sequel with how people are dealing with the new reality. The companions where more involved and felt more rounded out. The side quest where also better in HFW. The combat was improved from the first game and I like the new weapons. Fighting big robot dinos is still great fun.Cons: The first downside of the game is that it's too long. I feel like this game would be great instead of good if it was a little shorter and the pacing was tighter in the mid game. There is just too much stuff going on, too many cauldrons, ruins, rebel camps, collectibles, etc. The DLC is a good example of better pacing where the story moves along nice and there is side content to do, but not overwhelming amount. The climbing is super annoying, the difference between a climbable wall and non climbable wall is just if the dev designated it. On top of the the climbing mechanics are still wonky and Aloy just doesn't do what you want her to often. Melee combat still feels bad. Enemies get a shield, but you don't and enemies have poise but you don't. it is a little better than HZD, but not much. My final and biggest gripe is the gear upgrade system is just bad. I found it annoying at first, but it turned to just a pain. There are a lot of weapons now and unfortunately they all require similar monster parts and a lot of them. On top of that monster parts have rng drop rate now. But wait theres more, several monsters have limited spawn locations too. It just makes for a system that becomes frustrating instead of fun and punishes you for trying out more weapons and armor. In the end I installed a cheat mod to just upgrade everything I had with out cost so I could play around with builds and loadouts. It made the game more fun.  With that said it's still an 8/10 game that I enjoyed and I hope they improve further with Horizon 3.

The game world is absolutely enormous with some of the most beautiful scenery ever created in a AAA game.The main story is epic in scope, and there is so much side content you almost despair of getting it done. It's also mostly quality stuff, with very little fetchit and pizza delivery.The cut scenes are wonderfully produced, with some of the best mocap I've ever seen, and the music is uniformly great.The gameplay is rather different from that of Zero Dawn. The developers seem to want to ensure that Aloy doesn't get overpowered, so she rarely one-shots anything. Instead, the player needs to chip away at a machine's health by hitting weak spots and removing components. Some content creators have made freakish builds that do tremendous damage, but such builds aren't very practical and, in my opinion, go against the spirit of the developers' design ideas.There is a new emphasis on melee fighting which has caused some controversy. I don't care much for it, but I acknowledge that it's one of those things you'll probably enjoy if you get good at it.Upgrading weapons and outfits requires a much bigger commitment than in Zero Dawn. Prepare to spend a long time fighting a lot of big machines to max out a legendary item.On my system (i7 13700k, rtx 4070ti, 32gb ram, 2tb m.2 nvme drive), the game's performance has been excellent. The port to pc has, in my experience, been trouble free with very rare exceptions involving shader compilations. Just be aware that this is a huge game with stellar production values, and this demands relatively serious hardware.Aloy does not look exactly the same way she did in Zero Dawn, but this is because her face is more detailed. No one is conspiring to make her any less pretty than she was. In my opinion, she is still a very attractive video game character. She remains extremely athletic and does not have an excess ounce of fat anywhere on her person, in spite of what people think they're seeing.The game is not perfect, but I have enjoyed it quite a lot.

So, first of all I have to tell you that Horizon Zero Dawn is my most favorite game. So I was eagerly awaiting the release of Forbidden West on PCs. However, the reviews on release on PS left me with mixed feelings. One of the key points that the reviews said was that the story and the secrets of the world already had been told in HZD so the big moment of "Wow!" was missing in HFW. I don't agree, as in my opinion a new story unfolds which also left me almost speechless when introduced and I wanted to see how this new theme develops and ends. So storywise HFW definitly adds new, refreshing content to the already amazing universe of Horizon. When starting the game, travelling the world, fighting the first machines the unique Horizon-feeling immediately kicks in. Nevertheless, I found a couple things that I really didn't like about HFW.First of all the developers added a gameplay feature that wasn't present in HZD, or at least not that much. The game always points you in the right direction to proceed and to solve puzzles. That's not bad per se, but it does it in an annoyingly fast way. For example you enter a big room and even before you had a chance to get an overview about what is going on there your companion says or Aloy mumbles to herself: "Oh, look, there's a hatch!" or "Oh, I can climb up there!". So in the end you almost never get that rewarding feeling that you found a solution yourself because the game already told you what to do next by way too fast. So it also feels like the game wants to rush you through the story.I also didn't like the character development of Aloy at the beginning of the game. In HZD she was a humble, nice person. At the beginning of HFW she acts more in a Bruce Willis Die Hard kind of way, like "Oh, come on, I already beat every threat, every machine in HZD, so why are you annoying with this quest, you mere mortal?" Although this character development seems sort of relatable it fortunately becomes less dominant after Aloy has her first conversation with Gaia.Finally I didn't like the woke propaganda that really destroyed my immersion at times. In HZD relations and sexuality were not present at all or at least not that much that I can remember it. But in HFW and even worse in Burning Shores suddenly every second NPC talks to you about their homosexual relationship. Don't get me wrong, I have no issues with someone being gay, lesbian or whatever, neither in real life nor in games. I also have no issues with GLBTQ-related topics presented in games. But if suddenly 90% of all NPCs who you interact with seem to be either gay or lesbians then that's too much in my opinion.So in the end HFW left me with mixed feelings. I still enjoyed travelling and exploring the world and the story, but unfortunately the game simply isn't as good as HZD anymore.

END-GAME UPDATE: This game follows in the footsteps of its predecessor in terms of great storytelling. Horizon will surely be a movie franchise someday, and it's well-deserved. On top of that, gameplay is top-notch -- even better than Zero Dawn -- and the graphics and scenery are otherworldy from start to finish. It was a pleasure to play this. The only minor criticisms I can muster are the rough start I mentioned in the original post and a sense of urgency in the plot that prevented me from feeling like I could take part in frivolity like the in-game board game, Strike. (Would Aloy really be playing games, engaging in hunting challenges, or participating in arena death matches when the end of the world -- that only she can prevent -- is mere weeks away?) Hopefully, the DLC plays out more casually so that I can see what Strike is like.TL;DR: Play Zero Dawn and Forbidden West ASAP. It'll be a great 1-4 months of entertainment, depending on how fast you like to play.MID-GAME UPDATE: Aloy starts to feel adequately powerful against enemies around level 25 if you're just coming off playing the previous game. It was a bit of a slog, but once you get there, this game is amazing. The plot, how the mission structure weaves with the plot, the combat variety -- everything is incredibly fun for the most part. And the graphics are killer. Other than the rough start, this is everything I hoped the sequel would be.ORIGINAL POST:There is a tremendous amount of work that went into this game, BUT I cannot applaud the game without expressing the immense amount of disappointment that there is nothing that carries over from the previous game. And that is just plain lazy. No weapons, no overrides, no armor, no 750 health bar -- nothing. All the work done in the previous game is undone, and then you get thrown into missions like "Thirst for the Hunt" to take down a thunderjaw without the Banuk bow or stormslinger you worked so hard to get. I beat Redmaw in Zero Dawn in less than a minute and should have kicked the crap out of the Forbidden West Thirst for the Hunt thunderjaw, but instead I had to waste 45 minutes of my life hacking away at it and failing until I finally got lucky enough to beat it. That's no way to treat fans of your game.I'm thankful to have this game on PC, and I will surely hack away and yell out loud about other missions that grossly understate the character level one should have when Aloy's gear is hopelessly gone -- BUT I hope developers will use the frustration I've felt to inform their decisions about future games and gear that should carry over. Developers, please help your fans love your game. Please don't take our stormslingers et al away. Thank you for listening.

Late game health doesn't matter because you'll get stunlocked when fighting groups and just die anyway, even with max health and potions. An entire skill tree is added for using your spear but it feels like a trap since you'll get one hit, maybe a single combo if your lucky, before getting knocked down. Hit boxes are triggering too. I've looked at my replays and most enemy attacks have an extra foot of reach than they appear to, and some weapons actually slow down as they get close to the enemy so it can dodge out of the way. Did almost every quest on hard difficulty for 95% of the time. I'd give it a 6/10 (2 out of those 6 points are for the exceptional visuals) . My recommendation is to get this on at least a 50% sale and also only if you get a lot of enjoyment out of the visuals in a game or if you somewhat enjoyed games like AC Valhalla.Spoiler warning but the Story isn't interesting or exciting anyway.Positives: The graphics are excellent except for the yellow filter. Almost every Dialogue has some of the best animations I've seen in any game.The DLC boss fight against Horus was the best thing in the whole game.Running/walking animations look really good and change depending on the terrain.Very well optimized performance and lots of settings.The world looks very beautiful and has many different biomes.Many different cool looking machines you can fight and override.Sylens is a great character. R.I.P Lance Reddick.Mid:Lots of different kinds of weapons and traps but the only really useful ones are the spear, hunter bows, sharp shoot bows and throwing spears the rest isn't worth the effort.You can override flying machines but flying feels on rails, is slow and you can't fight on them. The barrel rolls are useless. Exploring is nice because of the visuals and you can dive/fly anywhere but there is nothing interesting to find.You can upgrade weapons and armors but it's a tedious grind.Stealth works but is nothing special and Aloys head peaks out of every bush and enemies still don't see her, it looks ridiculous. Moreover the game doesn't show how much damage you'll do from melee stealth attacks.You can do combos with the spear and it has some cool animations but it's overall extremely surface level and melee is almost completely useless against machines.There is a glider like in the new Zelda games but it's way worse and restrictive. You can level up a lot and you'll get enough skill points to get all skills and nodes. Sadly there is only a hand full of useful nodes and skills and after about only 30h you'll have them unlocked making the leveling underwhelming for a majority of the game and without any consequence.Negatives:Combat should be one of the best in gaming in theory, there are many different options, you can shoot weak spots and for some attacks it's better to dodge and others to slide away but it gets completely ruined by being attacked from out of sight with no indication and then flung around the area like a rag doll (multiple times when you are unlucky). Machines just spam their attacks endlessly sometimes and human enemies can parry melee attacks without any warning and sometimes take half your health with those parries. Many attacks are aoe and dodging or sliding away hardly makes you avoid them also multiple enemies can attack all at ones and pile up on you without damaging each other (it looks like they should) making it impossible to avoid their attacks. Aim assist only works for about 60% of shots and either doesn't work or targets enemy armor doing very low damage same as in Horizon 1. You'll also get stuck a lot on the terrain even on the highest fov setting the camera has lots of issues. Additionally you can't even aim up properly there was a mod in Horizon 1 to fix that but not for this it seems. Quests are literal quantity over quality there are zero memorable quests. None of them are thought provoking or interesting in any way, they are repetitive and writing is boring. Dialogue is only nice to look at without any substance. The Main Story is just a massive filler episode there is nothing interesting happening the only memorable thing was the Horus fight in the DLC and the extremely underwhelming ending. It turns out the main bad guys aren't even a threat for Earth and actually want to leave because the real threat will show up in Horizon 3. The vast majority of clothing and armor looks overdesigned, impractical, out of place and makes the setting way less believable. Many hairstyles are just goofy looking especially the Quen (their whole design is ridiculous) and no one in their right mind would make the effort to get those cuts trying to survive in a world dominated by dino machines making the whole setting even less believable.Aloy and most other characters are just boring. Aloy only shows very mild emotions and is inhumanly stoic. She  never makes a mistake and never shows any sign of doubt, struggle or weakness. Visually she is pretty and her hair is nice but like many others said, her face looks too bloated, no lean human on such a fitness level would have such cheeks. The DEI infestation only hurts the game. Every LGBTQ character (and there are many) always clearly states that they are special in that way making the setting even less believable.Climbing is very below average and there is lots of climbing in this game. Horizon Forbidden West is another gift from PlayStation to the PC gaming community. It was one of my favorite games back in 2020 and now that it's on Steam I got the chance to play it once again. Thanks, PlayStation! And what a journey this is, as you continue from where the last game ended in the flesh and bones of Aloy, The Champion of Meridian. She still doesn't like that name tho.The story continues the attempt to save the world after what felt like a nice ending to the first game. This time, you're looking for a mysterious signal sent by, presumably, HADES, the evil AI which unleashed hell earlier, in Zero Dawn. I won't go into detail, but the story progression carries you around a beautiful map with a lot of activities to complete. You will get lost in the world, searching for secrets and various loot locations - similar with what we got in Marvel's Spider-Man Remastered. Great game, btw!The gameplay is more of the same, with the much needed additions in mind. The action is still fast-paced and I love that. You won't get bored around the Forbidden West and the variety of machines in the wild will surely keep you on your toes at all times. Is that a herd of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mech kongoroos?! I hate those beasts! And you're also fighting human opponents which are pretty easy to beat - except of the few boss-like figures that you'll face from time to time. You can ride machines, the Tallnecks still serve the role of Far Cry towers. I love the variety of weapons, I like to jump around on platforms and overall, I feel like the gameplay is pretty solid. Control wise, I used both a DualSense and a Xbox Series controller. The one from Sony is the way to go thanks to the full support via USB cable - you get the adaptive triggers, as well as the fine vibrations.Visually, Horizon Forbidden West is an eye candy game. I really love the vibrant colors of the environment and the lights from the machines add a sprinkle of life in the fields. Especially at night, you can feel pretty nervous when out of the sudden, a growing red light is approaching you. I play on a pretty beefy PC (R7 7700X + RX 7900 XTX) and the optimization is top notch. At 1440p I manage to easily get 100FPS+ with all details maxed out. When turning FSR 2 on Quality, I got closer to a solid 120FPS, whilst setting the tech on Balanced gave me over 144FPS and the V-Sync kicked in. I prefer to keep FSR disabled tho, as my GPU is powerful enough to handle the game on its own. On the NVIDIA side we get DLSS 3 (with Frame Generation) and the performance is good as well. I ran the game for a bit on a RTX 4070 Ti Super and got very good results. In the future, the game will also get FSR 3 and the affiliated Frame Generation alternative.Overall, the game is a blast and the Complete Edition package is a very nice bonus. At 60 bucks (euros, whatever) you get a 2-year old ex-exclusive with a story DLC worth over 6 hours of gameplay. Not bad, not bad at all! Horizon Forbidden West is one of the better Nixxes PC port, being in the same category as Spider-Man for me. An essential game for PlayStation fans and a very nice recommendation for a casual story-driven experience where you get to explore a beautifully crafted world.

Forbidden West was a surprise hit for me. I expected it to be like most sandbox games: A completely generic experience that is still ever so slightly more fun than banging two bricks together. Instead I got a fantastic combat system with a pretty okay story (Which is still pretty far above what we usually get in Sandbox games).The biggest strength the game has is in the machines and how involved the whole combat system gets. A lack of enemy variety is one of the big peeves that appears in almost every combat focused game I play, but Horizon has a very healthy amount of enemies with different subtypes and tactics. Apart from looking very cool, they encourage different approaches and it never stops being fun analyzing a new enemy and planning how you're gonna deal with it. A healthy amount of different weapons and such ensures you'll get a LOT of bang for your buck in the longterm. I also really like how each elemental debuff does its own unique thing, so it isn't just rock paper scissors.The exploration is somewhat middling, on the other hand. Its fair to point out that i'm simply not the target audience for this, but a lot of the puzzles are too simple or you "solve" them and then still have 5 minutes of execution to do before youre down. Block pushing is boring, no matter the setdressing. Way too many locations are also simply locked behind gear, i.e. you can't open the burgercave until you got the ketchupcannon, so the game expects you to tediously backtrack at some point. The extra sad part: its so rarely worth it, since you get 1-2 chests of mediocre things as a reward.As I said, the Story is okay. The main quest kept my interest enough that I actually watched the cutscenes and listened to what people are saying, which these days is very rare in sandbox games. You DO feel that the first game got a free ride on the whole "Why robots?" mystery, and now that we know it struggles more to keep the intrigue going. Sidequests range from boring to decent, there are a few with interesting hooks but also a lot that are basically just an excuse to go fight something, which I rarely mind.Overall this beats out most other openworld options quite handily, and its sad we got the whole Elden Ring rivalry, since I think both games are strong in very individual, noteworthy ways.

First, a tech issue. I had to apparently set the game to compatibility mode for Windows 8 in order for this game to function without crashing between ten minutes to an hour (or sometimes instantly) due to some memory leak error issue. Just wanted to mention that in case my review catches some Google searches.Once again my review is roughly three years late, given I am playing the PC release. Some grander spoilers may already be known just through cultural osmosis, but I won't spend too much time talking about the story. It takes place somewhat immediately after the first game, within a few months. Aloy takes off almost immediately during the victory party from the first game as she's become privy to new information in short order: The terraforming system of the planet has gone haywire and the environment is becoming as deranged as the machines from the first game. It is Aloy's job to figure out why.To wit, this game is very heavy on the "As You Know" ways of storytelling. "As you know' is in quoted verbatim by a character shortly after the prologue sequence. There's a lot of that as you explore dialog trees with your companions. I urge any players to just go ahead and play the first game. The general gameplay loop is very similar and beyond some janky face animations, Zero Dawn is a fine game on its own.Meanwhile its sequel improves upon many aspects. Everything that worked, still works. The game is largely stealth-reliant as you hide in tall grass and snipe out some machine parts before they begin to notice you. Though many outfits in this game heavily rely on "lower health" statuses, a lot of them based around having half to thirty percent health which caters to folks that prefer the hack and slash melee. They'll do well here, with the right armor you will get a hefty dose of damage reduction. Frankly, I prefer to sneak around in the shadows and have half a machine's health half gone before they're even fully alerted. There's tricks for that as well, as the outfits in FW are significantly more nuanced. There's a late-game armor that adds more than one bonus to Concentration (slowing down time to give you a proper aim) and I have great joy sniping parts from the distance before a machine can turn towards me properly.Speaking of equipment, that is expanded on greatly here. For good and for ill. It runs into the Sniper Elite issue of some sequels adding all manner of tools but other than laying down mines against vehicles, nothing really beats just sniping someone through a window. The same problem presents itself here. I still utilize the tripwire weapons to essentially protect myself from patrols as I begin my sniping spree, but the game introduces too many weapons that I haven't wasted much time trying to learn. We have some melee slicers that require timing to function. We get something that's essentially a machinegun (the projectiles are just wood instead), with a power move that lets you lay down the entire set of 30 shots within just a couple of seconds. In theory it's great damage but a large majority of machines seem to be far too agile for it to have been any use. Even the human enemies come with helmets you must snipe off first, making it impossible to go full stealth archer and pick off sentries before moving into the camps.All these extra tools and nothing really compares to my trusty Hunter's Bow. Ammunition is cheap to produce, it aims quickly, has an ever-useful 2-3 arrow knock power, and does sufficient damage even on Hard difficulty. All in all, it just does what I need it to do and rarely find myself switching to any other weapon except to lay down some tripwires, and occasionally switching to the Sharpshooter bow for the very rare exception. Yet, I don't feel that it bloats the game too much as I'm sure many players will find some joy in trying to master the more fickle weaponry. And hey, they gave us six slots instead of four to encourage that very thing. So, kudos.I needn't waste too much time on this fact but the game continues to be gorgeous. I'm an absolute sucker for weather conditions so all the rain, snow, and sandstorms throughout the game's various biomes just gives me a sense of comfort and immersion that I usually have to mod into my other open world games.The map being dotted with icons is not the typical and tired Ubi-like fare. Most of the map icons are just sites for machines to assist you in your hunts when upgrading your gear, and generally just give you something to run into as you're traversing the world. You run into the occasional collection quest, like black boxes from Old World jets. They tend to lead to something tangible, like a new weapon, outfit, or some cosmetic face paint. It's usually something more concrete than "here's seven more old world watches to sell to a vendor".Speaking of vendoring. There's a couple of aspects that I don't care fore, which kind of ties into the gear expansion. There's more on the ground to grab as there's a whole food mechanic I've yet to bother engaging with because I can't be bothered. I've picked up more peppers and basil than I care to say. Maybe it'll all be there for me in a NG+. Secondly I'm getting rather tired of picking up watches and gold ingots out of treasure chests. It turns into something akin to busywork. Imagine if they just replaced all junk items with the game's main currency (metal shards), literally nothing would be lost in translation. It's just several extra buttons to press in a menu when you visit a town.Still, I find the gameplay loop here comforting. I like running around and finding the Tallnecks to open my map up. I enjoy the very well paced power creep over time. I have eventually noticed that machines I used to be scared of in the first few hours, become barely a challenge at all a few hours later as their health drops halfway just because I shot off a couple of their tusks. So even with a goal in mind, I like veering off the path when I see a new machine icon because it inevitably has something I need to upgrade my weapon or outfit proper. Meeting new machines is intimidating but with the game's new 'job' system, you can make a custom quest and help you track where specific machines are, go get the items, and upgrade. It's a useful tool so you don't spend any time alt-tabbing, wondering where the hell a Clawstrider is. The game itself has a function to just tell you!Sometimes I write reviews where it's two paragraphs of good followed by seven of bad with me just stating "the game is good though, trust me". That problem is not present here. I nitpick a bit about equipment I'm not familiar with and don't use and the ever-present annoyance of menu busywork when selling trash items. That's almost completely it in terms of nitpicks, as I continue to enjoy every other aspect of the game.And if you liked the first, you will like this one as well.

(no spoilers) well after beating the main game and the dlc now i have to say this is a great second game in the Horizon catalogue! I think that Guerilla did a great job improving on the really enjoyable fundamentals they established in HZD. For example you still override Tallnecks in HFW but each one is an entirely new puzzle compared to HZD where they were much more straight forward overall. Really fun. There's a ton of new weapons, and a ton of variations which can be overwhelming for newer players I'm sure. Just remember you don't have to use every weapon-- they're all just there to give you different playstyles. That being said, i really enjoyed a lot of the different weapons once I got a feel for using them. Hard and ultra hard the machines have a ton of HP so it's really helpful to keep a nice boltcaster on you compared to lower difficulties where the hunter bow is pretty reliable. The machine catalogue is improved a lot as well. It's done really well IMO. Guerilla added a ton of new heavy weight machines that are really deadly and fun to fight. Getting 1 shot by Apex dudes isnt fun but it encourages you to really tailor your armor and kit for every occasion on higher difficulty which is really fun to me. This game plays similar to Monster Hunter in some ways to me, except the pacing is so much more enjoyable to me. The meals and crafting on the fly is fun and I enjoy going on long jaunts just hunting different machines and playing around different shelters in the game. So fun to me. There's a few aspects of the game that I didn't always love but all in all, this is still one of the finest crafted franchises on the market. The story is superb. The gameplay is visceral and breath taking at the same time. My biggest sad point about the series is unfortunate loss of Lance Reddick, a prolific voice actor whose character has provided so much to the series that I'm not only saddened by his passing for his family and friends, but also for the impact it will have on the third game eventually. I know Guerilla will work it because they're proven to me they are a high quality game developer. They have a nice shrine in game dedicated to Mr. Reddick as well. Great game. If you enjoyed anything about HZD, I think it's clear you will like this game. But also if you had reservations about HZD, I believe the gameplay is changed and the overall pacing is improved in a great way in this installment and I recommend it to anyone on the fence as well.  ** worth mentioning ** I had a handful of crashes in my first 20-25 hours that said i was having graphics issues that were actually fixed by grabbing a really simple "cpu anti-stutter" mod on nexus that seemed to fix my issue which I have seen with a number of playstation ports on PC. Hope that helps for anyone having troubles.

=====Edit after first completion of main story and all side content:It was a fantastic game and pretty different than I originally thought. The enemies for one ended up being very different than I had assumed. The world building with multiple different landscapes with different tribes and cultures was fascinating to play through and it made me explore on foot quite a bit just because of its beauty as well as the fun of simply traversing the landscape (I kind of want to go mountain climbing and horseback riding now ngl). The DLC added on the this by introducing new machines and characters who most likely will play a large role in the third game. I have a feeling the third game is going to be a monster. If the first game let you explore a handful of dystopian future states of the Union and the second game let you pretty much do the entirety of the US than I kind of expect the third game to open up the world in this same exponential way and I am all for that with open arms.=====Story - The story from what I can tell assumes you did everything in the first game, side missions and errands alike so even if the game doesn't use the save from the first game the early missions feel like you're getting rewarded for all you did in Zero Dawn which is nice. The good guys are all you're old people and the bad guy is obvious from the start though I'm a bit early into my play so lets see what happens I guess.Graphics - It's a pretty decent presentation, I'm running this on an old 2070 build and it looks amazing.Gameplay - More tools/skills to use and different machines to kill make the game a step forward from the first game play wise. In the first game you're learning how to kill things, in this game you're perfecting how to kill them.My thoughts - Replayed the first game to get ready for this one and so far I'm not disappointed. They fine tuned some things here and there but mostly everything works the way it did in the first game. The only thing I would warn is that the very first mission is very linear which scared me a bit but after finishing it and getting to the open world the game is beautiful; the new tools you get to traverse the world and the more in-depth platforming Alloy can do makes getting around a bit more fun also. I'm not super far into the game (in fact I'm way at the beginning) because I'm the type to hit every corner of the map but I'm enjoying this a lot. The only slightly annoying thing to me right now is probably the skill system, they have so many little things to choose from I've just been stacking points and buying skills I think might help me here and there making my Alloys skill set a bit erratic, other than that though I love everything about this game and plan to dedicate a few sleepless nights to exploring every nook and cranny.

Over the past two weeks I have played 112 hours of this game. In that time I have spent 80 hours at my full time job. It's good. Ultra Hard is life.---Horizon Forbidden West is a more than worthy successor to its masterpiece of a predecessor. It grows upon the first in almost every way as you explore its vast and jaw-droppingly beautiful world. It's a game to get lost in, a flow state to be absorbed by in your entirety. A truly monumental achievement in gaming.However, there are a few details that simply must be mentioned. As spectacular as HFW is, and despite all the ways it improves upon Zero Dawn, I still do consider Zero Dawn to be the true masterpiece between the two. Forbidden West gets oh so close, and yet a couple tiny details hold it back. Foremost among those, there are moments where it feels as though the near perfection of the mechanical movement of the first game has slipped just enough to be noticeable. Getting stuck in an awkward to leave climbing state in the middle of a fight or the literally less than 5 times I've had my player or an enemy clip into something irreversibly are not *major* problems, but they're the kind of moments that stick with you.The world also suffers without the mystery that built the first. It feels like there is a smaller density of findable lore, and frankly I understand why. The first game was magical with this creeping realization of the horrifying truth of the end of the world, but that question is now answered, and it's not quite as captivating without it.And yet, all of that is OK. Not exceeding a masterpiece is hardly a bar for recommendation, especially when this comes so very close to it. The massively improved inventory system, the fantastic spear combat overhaul, and the phenomenal world itself are huge strides forward. The core activities continue to feel satisfying and the machine combat remains the finest system in any RPG.I absolutely recommend Forbidden West. And please. Play it on Ultra Hard or at least turn off enemy health bars. The game is so much better for it.

This game look's but plays nothing like Horizon Zero Dawn. So far, I find that the cons outweigh the pros by a lot. Short version, its a 15 hour game ( the story feels like it could be a DLC) with about 20 hours of fetch quest/walking. The graphics are stunning and the world is beautiful. The new Machines look cool and intimidating. Dont let the pretty graphics fool you though once that wears off its downhill fast.The combat has been changed completely for the worst.The fun of Zero Dawn is gone. The choice of play style is gone. You can no longer choose to be the savy hunter, the reckless hunter or the silent ninja. They sell you the illusion of choices in the skill tree but force you to play a certain way.Combat is purposely broken. You cannot dodge during an attack anymore, you have to dodge before the enemy attack mechanic begins. For example, a robot begins his attack from 20 feet away,if you don't anticipate the attack and dodge before its cast, all of sudden in a blink of an eye they teleport right in front of you. You get the WTF moment, asking yourself how did this thing get across the map like that. It completely brakes the immersion.The Devs obviously know the enemy combat is flawed. The Ai is mid at best, they try their best to hide it by taking away the dodge and  during story mission "boss"  fights they surround them with smaller robots and humans, that way you cant pick it apart piece by piece, dodge by dodge. Artificially creating a challenge and pushing you to play how they want.Alot of Weapon's have 1 element tied to it, you need to have many bows if you want to cover every element. Making it a complete mess and constant juggling. All bows have a 3-5 stage upgrade path adding a grind element for all bows.  The Trait skill tree UI is a total disaster.The game feels like a walking simulator. Traveling to undiscovered areas is horrific, mounts are purposely scarce. I kid you not, if you play 1 hour, you will spend at least 30 out of the 60 minutes going from point A to point B/ fetching something and back to point A.  At the end  of the quest you get 1 decent "boss fight" Then its rinse and repeat. Small (Spoiler) Flying doesnt happen to almost end game. I could sit here and keep adding to the list of flaws but im gonna cut it off here. I love Zero Dawn but Forbidden West take's 2  steps forward and 3 steps back.If you liked Zero Dawn give it a try at around $10-20. But certainly wait for that price drop.

Forbidden West is a good game, but not great.  It's also not better than the first in pretty much any way.  The story is interesting, but really only when they are talking about the main plot. Most of the time you are engaging with the primitives who think the machines are gods, but since you know the truth, it just makes all their dialogue and story arcs uninteresting and meaningless.  Their sidequests are all magic voodoo nonsense and it makes them all seem like irrelevant ignorant characters since Aloy is one of the few who actually know the truth and how the world actually operates through the AI systems.Besides the story the combat feels way more aggressive than the first one, it feels less about hunting a machine, than just outright beating it to death with your spear, or shooting dozens of arrows at it.  Which overall makes the combat less fun because the hunting aspect of the first one made for some very tense fights of guerrilla hit and run trap tactics which seem to have all been removed since the second you attack a machine the entire group is attacking you.  The RPG mechanics are just too apparent in this game which was the problem with games like assassins creed Odyssey where you shove a sword into someones head and they only take 30 damage because of their level.  There's too much information to remember and account for during a fight now, and when I stab something in stealth, it should die.Also Aloy's dialogue and the way she talks is just absolutely annoying in this game.  I understand she has the weight of saving the world on her shoulders, no different than the last game, but I swear all her lines are spoken as though she's constantly letting out a huge sigh.  That she's just so constantly depressed.  Again, I get it, but its just really annoying because all her conversations she comes across as passive aggressive, somewhat arrogant, and depressing.Overall its a good game, but I keep finding myself skipping cut scenes depending on what's happening, or just meleeing everything to death because it seems easier than stealth or long range fights.

Turn off 'double tap to roll' in the menu. I don't know why this is an option and then why it's defaulted to on -.-. I saw a video of developers flexing a new 'crowd' system and, it very much shows. Towns feel much more fleshed out.Less HUD. I found ZD, although good, had so much going on on the screen that didn't need it, such-as XP taking a whole corner etc. Forbidden West does away with all of that to further immersion and compliment, maybe even flex how good looking their game is. Less icons everywhere too, they rely on subtle visual cues to recognise plants that can be picked up, and again it adds to the immersion and is less hand holding.Obvious graphic enhancements. The world is beautiful and even more varied, and reflective of the existence of the old world. Honestly, one of the best looking games released in the past few years.Leads me on to optimisation. ZD, although great looking, did have it's performance issues.. FW however, has released in one of the most stable states I've seen lately. I have 35+ hours and no noticeable frame drops (i9 9900k, 2080ti)This one is preference, but I found the music for the map menu in ZD an odd choice, and it got irritating fast. They listened and fixed this, there's no map music now and I'm not sad about it.Free flowing climbing. They fixed the issue of being stuck and feeling frustrated bc Aloy won't climb/grab a ledge that looks climb-able, or having to jank your way out of a river.  Now think assassins creed style with a touch of ZD but minus the frustrations.Inventory management highly improved thanks to the stash. Love the stash, thank u.Upgrading skills feels more like an upgrade than it did in ZD. Especially with relic buildings.AI has been noticeably improved, I understand the balance between realism and fun, but FW gets it right.Much more cinematic, enhanced animations/mocap and improved voice acting. Think Uncharted and think Uncharted 2 to Uncharted 4 in terms of the scale of improvement. Ashly Burch also does a great job as Aloy.Can be a little over bearing with all the different ways of approaching combat. Lots of skills to remember. I rarely used my specials as a result but not really needed.Aloy does talk a lot, can be seen as hand holdy but I personally didn't mind it. It was sometimes useful and/or reflective of my own thoughts. And I've heard worse. I have 64 hours in the first game. A combination of story mystery and an exciting dance with my enemies is what drove my to complete it. The combat system was simple, fun and rewarding. The weaknesses were that, while the lore was interesting, the character writing was complete ass. I was having an ok time with this one, and at first I thought it was promising that the character writing had improved. Instead of being questionable cariacatures waiting for some God to save them, the characters seemed to have some of their own agency and motivations this time, taking action instead of waiting for Aloy to do everything and worshipping her. What makes a world believable to me is good characters who act and have personality and desires and hardships, and in the first game Aloy was the only one with ANY of those things, but in this one they do a lot more to boost Varl and friends. Unfortunately these writing improvements do not extend past the core cast. You'll still be talking to various empty characters with the exact same problem. "Ahh, Aloy, red haired champion, Help us! My tribe are a peaceful people, but we will be destroyed because we keep camping in enemy territory because we really need these seeds/this bird/something. You're the only one who can save us." The acting is wooden and completely uninspired. Not a single joke or interesting comment to be found. Nothing that makes me feel like this is a living survivor-scavenger world and not just a bunch of people cosplaying as native americans. As with the first game I might've survived the poor writing it the worldbuilding was there and if the combat was fine. The worldbuilding is OK but now it's far less of the game than it was before. The cat's out of the bag - we already know what Zero Dawn was, and this game is about fighting some other group who are, again, apparent cariacatures, this time of 21st century elite fortune 50 members. Blah blah, capitalism bad, I get it, but the outcome of the world speaks that way better than some evil hi tech people showing up. It's just not that inspiring, even if taking them down is an exciting thought. But to take them down you have to interact with aforementioned wider world, which is not a good time. The combat is soooo much worse. For starters, the upgrade system is INCOMPREHENSIBLE. Not only are you offered a ridiculous skill tree where you can't figure out what's useful, you also only have weapon choices that make no sense. In the first game you have the normal bow with fire arrows, and then the War bow which has the other elemental types, and then the Precision bow which can pull off good headshots. Now you have to buy a bow for EACH element, by the way they all come with poison arrows instead of normal arrows, and you don't get electric bows anymore, and the precision bow is useless! You can't headshot most enemies anymore, it just bounces off them!  The human combat has not been improved, they still launch at you and knock you over. It's not fun. And the MACHINE combat? Oh boy! I bet the studio thought they were doing great when they added sudden AOE attacks to every single machine so when you dodge them, you get knocked back anyway. The elemental machine types where they explode upon canister hit? That would've been GREAT in the FIRST game, where you have access to all those elements, but in THIS game you have to deal with the confusing weapon system and the lack of electric arrows, and surprise surprise most machines are electric type. You also have to shoot specific parts of machines to get upgrade parts. Shooting parts off machines is a great idea, but if you haven't found the specific machine yet, you're gonna have to run around the map to get them.  And even if you find the machine you need, and manage to access its part (the hippos have teeth that are a nightmare to get out)... As soon as you attack ANY machine, you are being obliterated by EVERYTHING in a fifteen mile radius. As soon as you get aggroed, you are NOT ESCAPING until either you destroy everything or you die. Me trying to get a tracker burrower item only to be attacked by some rams three fields away. Why? Why does it have to be so complicated? Why are there hundreds of markers on my map, and why are none of these activities actually fun? My theory is that the studio was soooo big and the game rushed sooo much that none of them ever interacted with each other. The overworld designers had nothing to do with the story writers or the side mission creators. The combat designers had nothing to do with whoever took their weapons and decided they needed to be waaaaay more complicated. Someone just added a skill tree in retroactively with a bunch of abilities that were useless, and made some things in the base game harder to compensate. Have you noticed it's way harder to get medicine now too?
