The graphics and artistry is what stands out in Forbidden West. The world and everything in it looks superb, with even greater Detail than Zero Dawn. The tribes again have a distinct identity and all look interesting imo. Everything is just a step up. And that is the biggest positive about the game. If you just like roaming, or stumbling across the setpieces and loot, all with cool robo dinosaurs, then this is the game for you. It ultimately was what managed to keep me in game for as long as it did.You also still get some of the background that fleshed out the world of Zero Dawn so nicely. All the datapoints of various kinds giving you more details on the history of the game world.They noticeably tried to add mechanics. And once you actually get to use them, they are fun more often than not. Underwater challenges with focus on just stealth are just one example.The new different focus modes, while I hate the noise, of ping vs scan are neat and the ping went into my muscle memory now.Also, it ran really well for me, none of the early issues like agressive pop in.They probably looked at Zero Dawn and decided to make the sequel bigger and better. But instead of "keeping and expanding on what worked, getting rid of what didn't work" like reviewer SkillUp found, they did the opposite imo. Yes, Zero Dawn's combat was leaner, simpler. But that is what made it so good. I hope you like the sound of Aloy grunting in pain and the feeling of being stunned in a game. Because oh boy, it will be the main thing you experience.Why? Because they took the combat and gear system of Zero Dawn and freakin ruined it. Totaled it. Ran it into a tree at 250 Kph.Combat as in aiming and firing still feels nice. But your inventory and loadout is a mess of way too many ammo types. Not only more elements, but also upgraded versions and different ammo for each weapon type. Elements are now THE factor in combat. Yet the elemental effects are spread so weirdly across weapons it is impossible to get a well rounded loadout.Zero Dawn's machine encounters played kind of like a soulslike. You go in, you learn the patterns and if you time dodges and attacks correffctly you win them. And if you mess up timing you quickly die. It was insanely satisfying and what made Zero Dawn so good.Not in Forbidden West.Every machine is a bullet sponge, more so on harder difficulties. But they hit like a truck. Every move and attack cheaply seeks you and knocks you down instead of being reasonably dodgable. Even the lowest enemy now is aggressive and closing in like the Scorchers from the Zero Dawn DLC.Dodging is now effectively patched out of the game. You stumble after dodge three, the range is useless and you WILL get hit anyways. Slides, which are meant to replace dodges, are stupidly hard to pull of and needs like three different inputs at once to not end up slow crouching after each slide. So you spend most of the combat grunting on the floor, locked down and waiting for Aloy to get up, just before getting knocked down again. Either stunlocked or just normally hit. Regardless, it is extremely frustrating.All in all, combat went from possibly *the* strongest feature to a chore, even after switching to easy difficulty. The only difference between difficulties is that on very hard you die in stunlock, on easy you don't because it is physically impossible to take enough damage to die in combat if you have half a braincell left.And then the gear system, oh boi! It is one of the most soul crushing, joy sucking affairs I have ever encountered in a game. Gear isn't obtained and ready to use like in Forbidden West, minus coils and weaves. Now, you have to craft upgrades with machine parts if the gear is supposed to stay viable. Or just be so to begin with. And you have to shoot those machine parts off the machine on everything except Easy, which usually takes multiple hits, before you dispatch of the machine. With how bad combat now is, that makes upgrades which, again, are required to use weapons meaningfully for longer one of the worst experiences I had in any game, period. With ressouce gathering aspects and generally. Bad studio, bad! No gold star for you! :(And Melee is even worse. They added a load of skill tree locked combos, which are convoluted, hard to pull off, yet utterly useless. I will not finish this paragraph because melee wasn't either.Then there is the new mechanics. All of them are locked behind the story. So you have to backtrack a ton to locations you explore, only to stand in front of an obstacle that says "hey, come back in 15 hours when you are graciously awarded the tool to get in here". And one of the coolest things, the flight ability? Locked behind the story, just before the final story arc. Which takes all impact away from what you now can explore with this new skill, as cool as it may be.Finally, the story. It is one of the storys of all time. Everything that actually makes sense in terms of what happened in HZD with Hades and Sylens, combined with the threat to the ecosystem shown in the trailer would have made for a decent and long enough story, rooted in the universe. I would have been happy to be done with the game in 30 hours that way instead of the hours I now put in. Instead, they phone in an antagonist group. Which, while tangentially named in Zero Dawn lore, is just weird, cliche and a sci-fi buzzword-fest. It feels like it was just randomly duct-taped onto the setting of Aloy the Nora who had to turn from outcast trying to enter the clan into the unlikely saviour to unearth the truth and stop the ancient looming threat. The new story just feels cheap and didn't manage to create emotional investment past the early story beats where you think it is just about chasing down Sylens.All in all, the story often was the thing that made me facepalm and making me concider just stopping the game entirely and to never get back to it.Oh, and the ending is just one lazy sequel bait so there is no feeling of conclusion or satisfaction whatsoever.The DLC is fine. The new area looks nice, you get a new mode of transportation and a few more open world activities and collectibles. It flashes out one of the new tribes in a way I enjoyed, but the antagonist is part of the bad story of the base game. Which drags the experience down again. The combat too doesn't improve and the main new machine enemy manages to highlight the new flaws of combat even more drastically. It feels like they wanted to make a second Horizon game and forgot a lot of what made Zero Dawn great - like it's lean, flexible combat - while they were busy making it bigger because "bigger is better, right"? Most new or reworked systems feel janky and not thought through. And the story is a major letdown compared to both Zero Dawn and it's DLC. I will likely not replay the game and right now, I lack the motication to even finish the DLC.It still is an okay game, and definitely a Horizon game. But it can't live up to how almost perfect Zero Dawn was. Which is why I tend to feel let down so often while playing and ultimately quit halfway through the DLC.

La nuova avventura di aloy è maestosa da tutti i punti di vista, un mondo incredibile, con una storia non banale e personaggi carismatici, comparto tecnico che lascia a bocca aperta e gameplay divertente ma non innovativo!- Graficamente è fantastico e gira anche incredibilmente, nixxes e guerrilla hanno fatto un lavoro incredibile con forbidden west, tuttavia ogni tanto ho incontrato dei glitch grafici sui tessuti dei vestiti e pop-in dei personaggi, mentre lato bug non ho riscontrato niente, il che se si pensa che è un gioco che dura più di 70 ore ed è open world è un ottimo traguardo.- La storia parte lentamente ma dopo le prime ore inizia a prendere piede, per poi diventare molto interessante già da metà e chiudersi in un cliffhanger dalle conseguenze intriganti. Ogni volta che pensavo che un evento si sarebbe svolto in una determinata maniera, il gioco mi stupiva e arrivava un twist inaspettato, Bravo Guerrilla- Tra lo skill tree, un buon numero di macchine nuove da combattere e le nuove armi nell'arsenale sicuramente c'è tanta carne al fuoco, tuttavia almeno per me si riduceva al solito "equipaggia l'arco, colpisci punti deboli, usa le debolezze elementali", ma se la cerchi, la varietà c'è.L'unico vero "peccato" di questo sequel è che non innova in nulla, nel bene o nel male prende horizon zero dawn e lo migliora ed espande in tutte le caratteristiche, ma anche solo così vale ogni centesimo e vi divertirà un sacco. Ci vediamo nell'ovest proibito!Aloy's new adventure is majestic from every perspective: an incredible world, a compelling story with charismatic characters, breathtaking technical aspects, and enjoyable gameplay, though not innovative!Graphically fantastic and incredibly smooth, Nixxes and Guerrilla have done an incredible job with Forbidden West. However, I encountered occasional graphical glitches on clothing textures and character pop-ins. Regarding bugs, I didn't encounter anything, which is impressive considering the game's length of over 70 hours in an open world setting.The story starts slowly but gains momentum after the first few hours, becoming very interesting halfway through and ending with an intriguing cliffhanger. Every time I thought an event would unfold in a certain way, the game surprised me with an unexpected twist. Well done, Guerrilla.Between the skill tree, a good number of new machines to fight, and new weapons in the arsenal, there's certainly a lot to explore. However, for me, it often boiled down to the usual "equip the bow, target weak points, exploit elemental weaknesses." But if you look for it, there's variety. The only real "flaw" of this sequel is that it doesn't innovate in anything; for better or worse, it takes Horizon Zero Dawn and improves and expands on all its features. Even so, it's worth every penny and will provide plenty of fun. See you in the Forbidden West!

I don't see myself coming back to do NG+...I always said I would for Zero Dawn, but realistically my backlog is big and there are a ton of fantastic games I haven't played yet so will be honest with myself on this one.The only quests I didn't finish were the melee pits, machine strike, hunting grounds, and the last few arena matches. I just didn't feel like grinding them. I collected all collectibles and did all of the other side quests. This game, like alot of open world games, suffers from pacing issues if you do the side quests as they become available. I personally combated this by mainlining the main story until logical stopping points and then went back to do some of the side quests. As soon as I started to feel a drag, I would jump back into the main story. My only other critique of the game would be that grinding to upgrade weapons doesn't feel great in the base game. Lots of farming difficult machines and relying on random rolls for said machine to drop the part you need. All-in-all, I spent probably 2 hours farming for the weapons I was using, but never expanded my horizons weapons-wise because I didn't want to farm to upgrade others to the max level. The DLC weapons have a much better balance as far as upgrading and I hope they carry the DLC upgrade balance into the next game.Nixxes has done a great job of hitting some low hanging fruit with their initial patches (primarily allowing certain key rebinds), but the one change I think they could / should make is a way to recompile shaders after entering the DLC area. Without recompiling, I was getting 30 FPS max. Once recompiling, I was back to my normal 60+ except in the heaviest of areas / situations. If you suffer FPS issues once entering the DLC area, look up the issue on reddit and look for any comment re: recompiling shaders. In short, check your 'base' CPU usage while sitting on the main menu of the game (close everything else on your computer). Mine was around 2%. Then, manually roll back your GPU drivers, then re-update your drivers to the latest, and then let the game sit on the main menu for 20 or so minutes. Monitor you CPU usage - mine jumped to around 60% after a minute or so of sitting and then stayed at 60% for about 20 minutes after which it dropped back to 2%. Apparently the game only compiles shaders for the non-DLC map initially and doesn't ever compile the DLC shaders unless you force the game to after you've unlocked the DLC area.

I definitely recommend HFW for anyone who has played the first game, Zero Dawn and liked that game. If you liked that game, you will like this one. I wouldn't say that this is objectively better than ZD in every way, but it did a lot of good things. The gameplay and combat in the game is enjoyable just like ZD and in some ways feels more fleshed out than the first game. There are more weapon options, more elemental attacks, melee combat has been improved, and some things like traversal has been improved over the first game, with new options like flying mounts and underwater traversal with interactable objects there. I liked the story generally and also appreciated some of the new characters and liked how some older characters from ZD also played a large part. The graphics as usual were amazing, looking more stunning than the first game, which is a high bar to clear. All while generally having great performance that exceeded my expectations at times. Finally I thought the DLC area was fun and had a good story and hands down the best final boss of the entire franchise. Despite the gameplay generally being better, I wouldn't say it was without fault. I didn't like some of the choices they made such as making it easy for enemies to stunlock you or forcing your character to stumble if trying to evade too much. It felt like they were punishing you for playing a certain way. While I generally appreciated the variety of weapons and elemental ammo, I did feel like it was a bit overwhelming trying to understand what was good or necessary to use and what could be ignored. It felt like the game was meant to be min/maxed which is not necessary in a singleplayer game. While I had no problems with the story, it definitely didn't reach the same levels that the story in ZD did, which is understandable for a sequel. The performance was also generally good but I did have noticeable frame drops in certain areas and as the game progressed, which forced me to reduce the graphics quality. Finally, I didn't think the grinding for weapon upgrades was fun, especially with the number of weapons and the fact that you find more powerful weapons as the game progresses. Those gripes mean that I won't hold this game as high as I do with ZD, but I still definitely enjoyed the game and will come back to it often. It may not be as great as the first game but is still a worthy successor.

Okay, so I just have to write this Review now and get a few things of my chest, even though I am not YET finished (so far ~123 hours in and I think I am on the last mission in the Maingame, did so far all the available Side Missions/Errands and all Side Activities, after that the Burning Shores DLC will follow).Usually I only write a Review after I fully completed/finished a Game, but I also think that I have seen the most of what there is to see. I will of course still finish it and maybe get even a few more nice surprises that don't make it into the Review.Also let me preface that I really regret not writing a Review for Horizon: Zero Dawn, because I really loved it. Played it once with DLC on the highest difficulty, 138.8 hours of pure fun and immersion and almost got all the Achievements in one Playthrough. Let me tell you, this Game is worth it...Now let's talk about Horizon: Forbidden West. First off: This Game hates Men. I had to write it now because a few hours before writing this Review, I read the Review of a Steam User called "Sumatris" (just wanted to Credit this person here because he/she described exactly my thoughts and I suggest giving his/her review a read).And yes, I agreed with everything, except that I don't want to downvote the Game because of the issues.In the last 4-6 hours of playing it became so apparent that this Game really is misandrist. Or the writers are. Or Sweet Baby is?!I don't have a problem that there are more Gay relationships in the Game than heterosexual ones. (They are really on the nose with this one.)I also don't have a problem that they had a Trans Character in the Game. Sure, go on and represent. (I don't really care about anyones sexuality and I also don't want to start a big discussion here...)But I do have a problem with every single man (apart from 1-2) is portrayed as evil, stupid, weak and what have you.You really do feel that the writers just wanted to push one "political" agenda instead of making the world more believable.As I said, you should read the review of Sumatris, those are exactly my thoughts regarding this topic.But let's get away from that. If you can look past what I just wrote, you will still LOVE this Game.Everything else is nearly perfect.This is how a PC Port should be, in over 120 hours I maybe had a handful of bugs, nothing Gamebreaking at all. Apart from very minor frame drops here and there it runs perfectly fluid. Put it on an SSD and you almost have no loading times as well, it's almost instant, doesn't matter if you start the Game up or Fast Travel.For those who want to know here my specs:- Intel Core i5-13600K- MSI GeForce RTX 3060 Ti VENTUS 2X OCV1 LHR- G.Skill DIMM 32 GB DDR5-5200 Kit- GIGABYTE Z790 GAMING X AXThis Game looks absolutely stunningly beautiful at ALL times. Actually, there is, but it would be too much for this review on Steam.And the Gameplay, yes, it differs a little from Zero Dawn regarding Weapon Usage but it is still awesome and fun.The Mainquests are great and interesting, I still want to see everything the game/lore has to offer (even though the man hating went a bit overboard here).Sidequests, Errands and Activities are also not just simple Fetch Quests or boring side content, they are almost all interesting and fun to do. For some of the hunting challenges the Game expects you to use everything in your arsenal, which is fair but in the Arena everything is thrown out of the Window. I don't want to spoil here, let me just tell you, I searched the Internet and the Arena on higher difficulty is complete BS, I did it for the rewards in Story (!!!) Mode.I experimented a bit with other difficulties but I have to admit, I wanted a fair and more balanced experience for the rest of the Game, so I put it grudgingly on Normal and will finish it on that difficulty.So yeah, I could go on and on and on about this Game. But it's too much. (This is probably why I was too lazy to write a review for Zero Dawn as well.)What I can tell you is, if you can turn a blind eye to the misandrist writing and the "wokeness" - as it will probably be called as well - then you will love this Game.What a gorgeous and immersive experience!Just go get it, we all know we want a Bloodborne Remake as well!(...)Addendum:Okay, so I finally finished everything Horizon FW has to offer including everything in the Burning Shores DLC.So quick Addendum. Sure, the story is fine, but didn't have the same gut-punches as it's predecessor.It probably adds a few too many distractions (in terms of collectables, the in-game game "Machine Strike", machine races and the arena).  I mean... you're on a mission (in story terms on a limited timeframe - which does not affect the game), but you're encouraged to do a bunch of stuff that would needlessly waste time... it doesn't quite gel for me.  I skipped over most of these distractions.  It meant I finished the game without full completion on the skill tree (skill points come from quests/jobs as well as levels), but not having those skills didn't impede my progress as generally-speaking I'd expect most people's gameplay to only require small portions of some of the trees while focusing on two or three.Our protagonist is certainly more confident than I recall from the first game and maybe talks too much (often to provide directions and hints to the player), but she's still very well-drawn as a character.   I was sad to finish ZD, just as I'm sad that I'm leaving Aloy behind having finished FW.The combat is still decent, graphics are very good and the gameplay smooth.  Climbing is definitely better than the first game (I'd expect some difficulty if I wanted to back and re-play ZD now) in that there are more handholds and they can be made visible.This is a very good game, rather than an excellent game in terms of story.Gripes...  Nothing serious.  The crafting/upgrade mechanic and part farming can get a little tedious (particularly when you need an apex version of a particular, powerful enemy to spawn) and I'm yet to understand for what purpose one would need single a machine CPU when upgrading armour or why you'd specifically need rabbit skins to upgrade the capacity of a pouch or quiver... but it's part of the deal with these sort of games.  The requirements exist as a barrier... it's just something that takes you out of the story a bit.Also... I reckon there's too many different weapons and armour in the game.  To obtain and upgrade them all would require more grinding than I'm up for.Overall, if you enjoyed ZD, I can't imagine you wouldn't like FW.  Why haven't you bought it already?

Horizon Forbidden West is nothing short of a masterpiece, offering a truly unforgettable gaming experience. Building upon the foundation laid by its predecessor, this sequel takes everything to new heights, immersing players in a world teeming with life, danger, and wonder.From the moment I stepped into the vast, beautifully crafted landscapes, I was captivated not just by the technical brilliance but by the intricate world design. The machine animals, each with their own ecological role, create a living, breathing world that feels as real as it is mysterious. The people of this post-apocalyptic Earth, blissfully unaware of the civilizations that came before, add depth and intrigue to the story, making every interaction meaningful. Aloy, no longer just the savior of humanity, becomes a traveling vagabond, a wandering hero who learns the songs of the Utaru and the war chants of the Tenakth, a deadly warrior with a heart of pure selflessness. The machines themselves are a highlight, transforming each encounter into a strategic puzzle. Whether you’re scanning enemies to find their elemental weaknesses or setting up traps to take down a towering Thunderjaw, the variety of combat styles keeps the gameplay fresh and exhilarating. The thrill of using elemental effects to slowly weaken a machine before unleashing a devastating attack is immensely satisfying, and the option to take a stealthier approach adds even more depth to the gameplay. Every battle feels unique, and the satisfaction of outsmarting a machine can’t be overstated.Horizon Forbidden West excels in so many areas: the upgraded skill tree offers a wealth of options to tailor Aloy’s abilities to your playstyle, the vast array of weapons and armor enhances your combat strategy, and the new gear upgrading system makes you feel more powerful as you progress. The sheer number of new machines, each more inventive and deadly than the last, keeps you on your toes, while the story is nothing short of epic, with character development that tugs at your heartstrings and moments of triumph that make you cheer.Exploration is a joy in this game, with the world of Forbidden West offering countless opportunities to get lost in its beauty. Whether you're climbing to the highest peaks, diving into underwater ruins, or soaring through the skies, every corner of this world is filled with secrets waiting to be discovered.In conclusion, Horizon Forbidden West is a breathtaking achievement in gaming. The care and effort poured into every aspect of the game are evident, from the stunning visuals to the deep, engaging story. Whether you're looking to blow off steam by battling colossal machines or lose yourself in a richly detailed world for hundreds of hours, this game delivers on every front. I cannot recommend it highly enough—if you're even remotely interested in action-adventure games, this is one you absolutely must play. And if you ever feel like taking on a mechanical T-Rex with a bow and arrow isn’t for you, well, there's always knitting lmao! ;D

I enjoyed the first game, however, this one has a few issues at launch.  The biggest one is that it is almost unplayable with a controller on PC.  There are missing controller button icons, so you can't tell what button should active the current action.  There also isn't the normal hold ring for any buttons, so opening chests and doors have no way of knowing how long to hold for.  Using a controller, there isn't a way to pry open doors, highlight enemy paths, or select all items from a container.  Using a mouse and keyboard, the game displays all the key/mouse icons.  I'm a little surprised that controller support for all text is missing at launch and some actions cannot be done.Other issues at launch: jumping while crafting arrows, spotty hitbox for gathering resources which sometimes requires activating multiple times before the game registers the gather, minor graphical issues with turbulent water, the menu Button Layout & Customization for Gamepads does nothing, and no help with how to use new equipment (might be related to the other issue of controller support).If using a controller, practically unusable game.  Until these issues are fixed, I can't recommend the game, especially since it allegedly has full controller support.

The gameplay mechanics are mostly the same (and still great), the open world is huge (too big for my taste), and the story is okay.

Overall it's a good game and I don't regret the time spent playing it but it's also because I have a lot of time. If your time is limited, then only play it if you're super invested in the characters from the first one and are wliling to gamble on the future third game fulfilling the promises made by the first game despite a disappointing middle.The game isn't as good as the first one in many ways. The story is worse (and honestly, it ends up almost exactly where it started so it also feels almost pointless), the main antagonists aren't compelling in any way except maybe one for a very short time.They rehash themes they'd explored in the first one with Ted Faro for example, except they had already done it so much better then. What's the point in rehashing the same themes mostly the same way, except worse?As far as Aloy goes, she was driven by uncovering her heritage and her journey was about her ability to deal with the answers. In this one, Aloy's personal journey is more about the benefit of cooperation and how she need to learn not to push people away. Sadly that's another way in which the villains disappoint as they don't fit particularly well within that theme. It's well explored on Aloy's side of the story, but not with the antagonists.Other than the story and themes, the overall issue with the game is the "bigger is better" mentality. It's really not. It's worse in almost every way here. The game is way longer than the first which worsen the flaws of the story part by making them last forever, it gives you more busywork, the farming is also insane. Upgrading things take forever, it's like they built the game based on the live service model even though it's not.But does the gameplay make up for it? Kind of. Let's start with the new issues related to those systems:Where in the previous game, there was maybe a difference between relatively early game and late game of one order of magnitude, in this one with many more skills and interacting systems it's closer to two orders of magnitude. Meaning your damage is cripplingly low near the start of the game and ends up godly high near the end instead of the progression being relatively realistic like in the first one, where I could take an end game machine on very early on Ultra Hard without spending 10+ minutes on it if I knew how to play.This game seems more about numbers than creativity and skill. Everything can drag on forever in UH at lvl 1, while on the other hand, almost everything can literally be one or two-shotted with minimal preparation with a proper setup on UH at end game. The scaling is completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up because they added too many sources of scaling.So why do I still advise people to play the game if they liked the first one's gameplay? Because not only is the core gameplay still great, but the new weapon types are frankly inspired and make the game even more enjoyable to play.I still boot up HZD to just roam around and take down machines and I know I'll do the same in HFW now. But it took time and effort to get there. Honestly gameplay-wise I've had so much more fun with a fully upgraded and coiled setup in Ultra Hard NG+ than with my original playthrough in Very Hard. That's when the game really opened up, when I could finally use any tactic I wanted to full efficiency (while in HZD, a good tactic would work almost from the start, requiring maybe a couple more arrows to function properly, the larger scaling in HFW works once again to its detriment)So my advice to enjoy this game more: If you want to play in lower difficulties, good. Honestly NG is probably more enjoyable (at least early on) on Hard or normal than it is on Very Hard. If you want to play in Very Hard on your first playthrough, don't try be a completionist from the start. It's really not worth it, machines have too much HP compared to available weapons early game and you will often resort to the same tactics instead of being creative.Instead, mostly focus on the main quest and maybe a couple of side quests that sound more interesting to you. That will open the world up very quickly, get you mandatory quest upgrades that makes traveling across the map more enjoyable, and it will also allows you to access late game weapons and armors much quicker which diminishes the "HP sponge" stage of the game. You can always come back and do everything later, but if you intend to try NG+ (especially Ultra Hard NG+ which I strongly advise you to, it's great), I wouldn't even try to be a completionist at all in that first playthrough, even after accessing the whole map.I would focus instead in getting a setup of epic/legendary weapons you enjoy upgraded and coiled fully (try to have at least one of each type, some weapons that starts off weak will surprise you once you learn how to use them), and then do a completionist playthrough in NG+ (ultra hard if possible so that there's still some amount of challenge).

**SPOILERS AHEAD**Horizon Forbidden West is a fantastic PC port done extremely well by Nixxes, it has zero issues for me when I was playing the game from day one with the patch and I have to say, running this game on the highest graphics with the NVIDIA DLSS is breathtaking, I am of course running this game on a high end PC unit and currently am playing through NG+ UH difficulty for the achievements run. COMBAT HFW takes a step up from HZD and improves upon the melee combat of the game whereby Aloy has different Valor Surges and Weapon Techniques at her disposal, from abilities that can give you extra tear and knockdown damage, to making her invisible to even releasing a shock wave from the spear; all of them does excel in their own way depending on your playstyle, as for me I'm mainly a bow, spike thrower and ropecaster playstyle. While the game introduces us to new weapon types and abilities, weapon techniques that come with them, I found the Shredder Gauntlet to be pretty underwhelming yet situational to use as it only shines when Aloy is able to catch the shredders back and doing it 3 times and launching back at machines will create an explosion. As I expected, the spear melee combat is definitely improved and way more fun to play compared to HFW, it is only great against the Tenakth rebels and Quen Marines. On the contrary, fire damage is not as OP as it was in the first game, it has been massively nerfed but still does do a good job in burning enemies, frost is still KING imo. I also liked the different status effects they've kept and brought over as well as introducing new status effects like Plasma, Purgewater and Adhesive, while corruption was renamed to Acid and Berserk is the new corruption status in HFW. Overall, I found myself liking the Spike Thrower and Ropecaster in this game compared to HZD because as much as they've introduced new ammo types and the damage it does, I'm kinda bummed out that for a legendary bow, I'm only using 2/3 arrow types because the other one feels redundant or not to my liking, my feedback for that is being able to customise what arrow type I can swap out for the third installment.MACHINES & OPEN WORLDMy God, as if HZD wasn't creative enough with the open world and being able to make me explore such a wondrous setting, HFW has outdone itself once more. The new machines such as Slaughterspine, Dreadwing, Clawstrider and Tremortusks are my new favourites and are very intimidating upon first encounter, its also nice of Guerilla to bring back machines from HZD and even from Frozen Wilds. HFW is roughly 1.5x larger than HZD and finishing my first blind playthrough took me 146hours with DLC included, and 100% completion for the base game and Burning Shores. The different Tenakth clans Scalding Spear, Thornmarsh, The Grove, Oseram clan Chainscrape, Hidden Ember, Utaru clan's home Plainsong, and a sudden surprise of Legacy's Landfall from the Quen tribe and the different biomes HFW offers from snowy mountainous tops, to lush greenery and dense jungle, hot burning deserts and finally the shores and San Francisco in Burning Shores. I must give credit to Guerilla for making the desert portion of the game a very exciting experience to explore and Las Vegas is fantastic, it is not easy to make a desert biome fun for players to explore since its mainly sand and dunes, but adding ruins and blending into the story of Horizon is well executed. The colours of the shores, with the bright blue waters as if it was from Maldives inspired was a feast for the eyes as it was so peaceful when traversing. Overall I definitely enjoyed both open worlds, but HFW takes the win for me.STORYAloy ventures out into the forbidden west to find a GAIA backup to restore her with the subordinate functions that she needs and Aloy seeks out to get POSEIDON, DEMETER and AETHER in this game, as after she has finally purged HADES in the HADES Proving Ground. Aloy also encounters Sylens but he only appears towards the end portion of the game compared to HZD where he has more screen time. Aloy has her own battle against Regalla and she goes to the different Tenakth clans, pursuing her goal and helping those in need and while Tenakth are an intimidating bunch, they stick true to their word and will aid Aloy when the time comes. Finally, we now know that NEMESIS was the one that sent the signal to HADES in HZD after the game ended, and we're facing a threat even the Zeniths we defeated are so afraid of. Overall, I really enjoyed the Spectre machine encounter and Specter Prime, as well as the story of this game since we already know what to do at the start and our goal that is set for us, I must admit I do miss the charm of discovering what GAIA, Project Zero Dawn, Operation Enduring Victory when Aloy first discovered everything, it doesnt have the same impact it had on me when Aloy had to solve one problem at a time which was new to her since she doesnt know anything in the first place, compared to now in HFW when she knows her goal, we make our own allies and team and taking down the Zeniths and the technology and equipment required to defeat them. I do hope the third and final installment of Horizon wraps things up and they do not rush the story, it has been fantastic so far.DLC - Burning ShoresWhile I am very excited and happy that we got to fight a HORUS titan, it was one of the best boss and machine encounter I have experienced and ticks off my checklist, I felt that the story portion of the game was rushed as I finished the DLC in 2-3 hours, including the side quests. While it is roughly the same size as Frozen Wilds, I felt that they could have put more time in telling the story better and using more of San Francisco city as a whole. Even when exploring, most of it was Aerial Captures, Pangea Figurines and Brimshine that I can go collect around, machine sites were fine and new machine types were nice but there was only the Stingspawn, which were the eggs from a Bilegut, and then the HORUS machine, even though Frozen Wilds has only Fireclaw, Frostclaw and Scorchers, they prove to be a challenge, whereas in Burning Shores, Stingspawn was very easy to kill as long u shoot a shock arrow in them, and they burst in groups, Bilegut was also very easy for me to kill as the weakpoints were big and evident, sure at points they hit hard but they didnt give me the impact of being strong like in Frozen Wilds where they hit so hard with their attacks. Overall I would say the HORUS fight is the only thing that saved the DLC along with the new DLC weapon I received but it was underwhelming for me. Seyka, on the other hand was really a whiny character the whole way through and I didnt enjoy her character and yes they made it canon for Aloy to have a romance which is Seyka but I chose the option of being just friends. Overall, i felt Guerilla could do more with Burning Shores.TLDRHorizon Forbidden West is a absolute experience by improving most of the systems in the  game and making it so much better, with a compelling story, fantastic PC port (probably the best atm) so we're in good hands for Ghost of Tsushima, and having new diversified weapon types with new abilities, weapon techniques and new tribes Aloy meets in the Forbidden West, with new savage machines and creativity at its finest, I wish Guerilla all the best in making the third and final installment of Horizon, where Aloy and her allies finally put at end to Nemesis. Let me know your comments down below to whoever found this review helpful. This game is a 9/10.

Horizon Zero Dawn was a game that drew me in with its story and world building in a way I did not anticipate when I started playing it. You wanted to know what happened to the world, why and who had a hand in it. Exploring old ruins and old technology was interesting and, if ignoring the fact that they decided to make robot dinosaurs, believable enough. They could have very well wrapped up the story at the end of the game but instead it was clear that they were setting up for a sequel.So when Horizon Forbidden West was finally released I felt torn between excitement of learning more but also a sense that the story had mostly been told. In that department, Forbidden West does deliver and introduces a new threat that has a believable connection to what was set up in the first game. I saw the story through and felt it interesting enough to keep me going. But getting through had me play through a game I somehow felt I had already played before.The game play loop is very similar to the first game and you are almost able to guess the missions and side mission you will get when you start talking to an NPC. The magic and exploration of a mysterious world is not quite there this time and instead you feel that the game is something you get through to advance the story.As with most sequels you have the experience of have become a bad ass fighter in the first one only to have to start the game like if your character got amnesia and forgot most of the cool stuff she learnt. This is ofc to make it easier to provide the player with progression and ramp up the experience over time, but it was one more reminder that you were playing a game instead of being engulfed in the world. Where I in the first game felt excited to learn about the powerful armor and went on multiple quests to try and unlock it I ended up playing the entirety of Forbidden West + the Lost Coast DLC with the starting armor in this game.They do try to introduce some new game play elements and you are for instance able to swim under water and fly. But these new mechanics feel a bit clunky and that might be why they aren't used more than they are. I was expecting to be able to fight under water but at most you hide from enemies. How clunky the under water movement feels compared to on land might be one reason why.On a technical level the game has moments when it looks gorgeous, just the the previous game. But watch out that you don't go over your video ram limit since that really tanks performance. And it is pretty easy to do. On my 3080ti I was seeing random performance tanking bellow 20fps on a 1440p resolution even with DLSS balanced. I thought it was a memory leak since a restart of the game would clear it up for a while but I tried to fiddle with all kinds of settings since it never totally went away. I played through the entire main game like this and was ok with a restart every now and then. But when I started up the DLC after the main game performance was terrible. Then it dawned on me that could this be a vrm issue, on a 12GB card? I changed texture detail from the highest setting  one step down and all the issues went away. So I highly recommend trying this if you are having fps drops, especially since the game visuals are very similar.It might sound like I want people to stay away from the game or I regret spending the time playing it, but that is not the case at all. I was just hoping for a bit more to make the game play and the game loop a bit more engaging and fleshed out instead of feeling like a very big expansion to the first game. What got me hooked on Zero Dawn wasn't primarily the game play, it was good enough to keep me playing but the story was what kept me wanting to play more. If you enjoyed the story of the first game I would highly recommend Forbidden West since it builds on it and expands it. But given that the game once again ends by setting up for a sequel I can't help but hoping for a bit more next time when it comes to the game mechanics and game play loop.

After playing Horizon Forbidden West for 81.2 hours and then putting another 13.3 hours into the DLC, I can confidently say that this game is fantastic. It is an excellent sequel and a great example of a AAA game done well. This is a direct continuation of the first game in story, while having loads of nice QOL changes, and improving areas where the first fell short. The gameplay is a lot of fun, even if it’s not the most original. The graphics are absolutely stunning, and while they may not make a bad game good, they certainly help elevate an already great game. To top it all off, the game runs pretty well considering how good it looks. To start with the story: it’s great. It furthers the world and the lore in ways that I found really interesting and sometimes surprising, but nothing felt out of place. The writing kept me engaged to the point where I did every single side quest I found, including the ones to get all the collectibles and I never felt bored. This is a huge improvement from the first game, where I barely did any side quests and often found the dialog a bit boring, even if I really enjoyed the overall story. The game even reacts to this by having dialog that comments if you already cleared out a quest area or helped someone in a side quest related to the main quest. Similarly, some quests, including side quests, dramatically change parts of the world, which is super cool to see.Another huge improvement is the inventory system. You no longer have a super limited inventory and instead can carry everything. While there are stack caps, anything in excess is automatically transported to a box you can access at settlements. This further encouraged me to explore, fight, and quest because I could keep everything instead of spending minutes in menus deciding what was most important to keep.As for the most important part, the gameplay, I really liked it. Killing robot dinosaurs is a lot of fun. More fun than I remembered it being in the first game, but I am not sure why. I also really enjoyed the exploration. Yes, all important locations are marked on your map, and yes, most of the loot is just boring crafting material, but I still almost always felt rewarded in some way, weather it be an interesting fight, a cool quest with an interesting story, or even just a beautiful land formation that I felt compelled to screenshot.Speaking of that, I was constantly blown away by how good this game looks and I do not think I’ve ever taken so many screenshots in a game. I genuinely think this may be the best looking game I’ve ever played, even if it does not have fancy ray traced lighting, not that ray tracing couldn’t make it look even better. The world is beautiful, lush, and feels alive with the way everything moves. Still, they’ve managed to keep visibility high in ways that mostly feel natural, like having robot drops emit sparks to make them clearly visible, even in the dense foliage.Music is something I don’t often comment on because I usually don’t find it to be anything amazing, but this games soundtrack is fantastic. It’s one of the few games I find myself listening to the music even when I am not playing. The only other games I do this with are Skyrim and Disco Elysium. If you go to the game’s install location, there is even some music files in an OST folder, which is really nice, but unfortunately only has 12 tracks and is missing some of my favourite pieces.However, this game is not without flaws. The biggest annoyance to me is the progression preventing bugs. While I did not have many, and they were always fixed by reloading my most recent auto save, everyone I encountered seems to have been in the game since its PS5 launch over 2 years ago according to some quick searches I did. That’s pretty annoying, and there are other, admittedly small, bugs I found. I also somewhat often found that I had to really fight with the controls in non combat situations because Aloy would just bounce off a hand hold, or use her grapple hook instead of gliding, or refuse to allow me to interact with a quest NPC, or something else that made me have to walk back and forth or re-do a platforming section until the correct behaviour happened.As for Burning Shores, the included DLC, it’s essentially more of the same. I do like it, but I did find it to be a little short and would have liked if there was more too it. While it did take me just over 13 hours to beat, part of that is because it no longer marks all collectibles on your map or shows their exact location. This is an interesting change. It definitely made exploration feel more rewarding, which I liked, but it also probably means on a bigger map I would not bother collecting them all. If I just did the main story and the 3 side quests, it probably would have taken me a good bit under 10 hours to complete, but it’s hard to say for certain. The DLC also ran significantly worse. In the base game, I was getting about 130-150FPS, but the DLC dropped down to about 90-110fps. While more than playable, this felt like a pretty significant decrease for an area that did not look graphically better, and for someone already struggling to run the base game, this could bring the DLC into unplayable frame rate territory. On a more positive note, I did really enjoy its story and its final boss fight was awesome, as was the base game’s.Overall Horizon Forbidden West is a great continuation of the Horizon franchise, and a top-tier game that I would highly recommend to anyone who liked the first game. I liked it so much I did pretty much everything, including getting every single achievement, minus the 3 related to new game plus. I rarely replay games, but I really did enjoy this so maybe I will in the future.

I would clear an area and head back to base and have a ton of dialog to work through out of sync. This feels doubly so because of how they gatekeep tools you need to access areas like the grapple hook/flying/firegleam/deep diving. Parts of the story are really lazy and phoned in.  There are invisible walls. There is a cauldron that you can climb down but when you climb up it loads and you are just at the top. Like just design an ascent. The Ted Faro mission is extremely disappointing.  He has stuffed himself into a reactor to stay alive for the last thousand years which turns him into some grotesque beasty, but you don't even get to see him before an NPC initiates his destruction and reactor meltdown that you have to flee. Like, this man is the sole reason that Aloy is inevitably created! It's almost insulting to the player that you don't get to even visually see the true antagonist of the world.  The Zeniths are phony antagonists. Classic trope egotistical, narcissistic villains. They are boring. Nuance is nonexistent in their characters.  They removed agency from Aloy compared to the first game.  She is supposed to be one of the baddest asses in gaming but she can't whistle anymore to attract machines? Why? She can now only place 3 traps (without upgrading to 4)? Why? That's not realistic. In reality if I had traps in my inventory, I could place them. Why can't Aloy? Also, Aloy is kind of a ♥♥♥♥ in this game. She is like Harry Potter in book 5, a self-important ass. She constantly is running away from friends and not letting them join her because she says its too dangerous, but then I can spend as much time as I want ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ around doing side missions? Doesn't really line up. I started this game really hoping for consistent companions, kind of like how they do in the Fallout games because that felt like a fresh way to spin this game that is really more of the same from the first game. Or they could do it like, say, Mass Effect, where they are in your group and you control their actions. They also added a huge knockdown delay onto Aloy. You will get knocked down and you go into a stand up animation that is so slow that by the time you are upright, the machine is plowing you over again. It's so frustrating. Or they have such range and speed that even running at full tilt away, you can't get away from them until they reach the edge of their coded range. Speaking of companions: Like in the first game, you do have people come with you on a mission specific basis but they are a nuisance more than a help. They will constantly be running up to you and trying to give you ammo, which has two issues. One: they will drag any enemy that sees them right on top of you. Its so annoying for certain machines like thunderjaws. Two: Aloy can build ammo on the fly while running around in battle. I don't need my companion character running up to me trying to give me ammo I already have. Also, they just drop it on the ground. So if you are running around and dodging, chances are you will never even see that ammo anyway until you have finished the fight. And the game has these weird area requirements. So if you step even a foot outside the "fighting area," your companion will stop fighting (sometimes they even leave the area completely) and it wont recognize that you are still doing that part of the mission even if you already activated that step. Like step one is go to area and step two is fight machine. Even though I am still fighting the machine and getting my ass handed to me, if I step outside that area, it will go back to return to area and the NPC will be like "Why are you leaving?!" and I'm like literally being flattened by the thing. No one left you dumb dumb game.There isn't enough greenshine slab.  I have played 153 hrs and I have only found like 8 pieces total.  Considering that a lot of rare or legendary weapons/armor require greenshine slab to fully upgrade this makes it really hard to upgrade in the later game. I keep hoping to find a mine or a way to make it, but nothing so far.  If you are like me and like to upgrade as you go, then this will affect you.  There are certain things I upgraded earlier in the game with slab that I wouldn't have upgraded if I knew that I wasn't going to be finding more of that component.  And even if you sell those upgraded pieces, you only get lower level components like machine muscle, which is very common. So there isn't even a way to recoup the loss. And I've not found a vendor that sells any of it from sliver to slab. Because I can't upgrade very easily due to a lack of slab, the salvage mission that makes you go to four different people in four different cities becomes superfluous.  By the time I finally finished them all, the armor I already had was better than the prize armor for completing the mission. The world is beautiful, and the details in the clothes are really good. I like the makeup addition and I like how you can set a different armors appearance from the one you are actually wearing. I do wish the outfits/body art/head pieces were all separate things you could mix and match. It's lame the only option you have is with or without head piece. I do really love the machines, because they are cool and I like the concept. I will say, the fireclaw is way OP. I like the tideripper because it reminds me of a lapras. I wish you could learn to ride it. That would be baller. Finally, the climbing is pretty wonky. Lots of magic pixels. And there are times where a surface looks so obviously climbable or there are NPCs climbing on it, but Aloy can't. What? Full disclosure: I played this game on easy.

Horizon is as Horizon does, and it did it again.Horizon is a post-apocalyptic open world action series with a variety of bows and arrows and robot dinosaurs and an unavoidable crafting/gathering mechanic. This sequel introduces a number of needless new elemental combat mechanics and weapons for the sake of having something new, but in my experience sharpshooter bows consistently still do the most damage, just like in Zero Dawn, and the elemental stuff is just... fiddly.The new tribe you spend most of your time interacting with, the Tenakth, have some of the laziest 'primitive peoples' design in their dress and environments - frustrating given the superlative design choices in the prior game.And the eternal gripe: don't give the option of stealth skill/equipment investment if effective combat forces you out of concealment and/or boss battles give you nowhere to hide. Stealth combat with humans is entertaining, but the whittling down of huge robots means one or two shots isn't enough, and causing damage reveals your location unless you spend (material expensive) smoke bombs to hide for one shot again. And you will need to have those encounters for resources.So, is it good? Yeah, it's good. Not as good as the first game where you unraveled What Happened to the world and Who Did It. But the fun stuff is still fun, and the story is still satisfying and surprisingly willing to have three dimensional characters. On occasion it can be frustrating - particularly with trying to upgrade high-level items in the late game.I'd argue that Horizon, in general, hamstrings itself with over complicated/too many gamified mechanics. Making the gameplay simpler would help.

I loved the first game and waited, with great annoyance, for Sony to authorize a PC port (in a typically greedy, anti-player move, they claimed it was exclusive to the new PS5 at first). I was thrilled to finally be able to play this game on PC.I haven't much to say about the port itself. It looks fine and the graphics are about what you'rd expect for a next-gen game. I do, however, have a ton to say about the unbelievably annoying gameplay.First, the good:- Whoever designed the character costumes is a genius. They are not only beautiful, they're thoughtful, with each outfit aligning with the character and culture who wears it.- Likewise the sound and music are brilliant. I bought the complete soundtrack and love listening to it when I'm reading or relaxing; it's award-worthy, like the music in the first game.- I love open world games with lots to do and the freedom to do it in the approximate order you wish. This game definitely checks that box. I loved the hinting and help prompts.- The environments are beautiful and creative, as is the lore you can collect.Now, for the deeply hated:- The upgrade and crafting system is just horrible. First, materials are scarce for the really good upgrades. But much worse, upgrades never seemed to provide a noticeable boost. So, why did I waste time chasing down the mats?- Many of the challenges were STUPID hard. I abandoned the hunting grounds early on. Ridiculously frustrating with poor rewards. I couldn't finish the melee challenge because the prompts were not only wrong, but impossibly complex. (The combo system itself is ridiculous. How in the world am I going to get close enough to a machine to achieve such complicated patterns? Worse, when I do, it doesn't really have the oomph that would make remembering the patterns worth it.)- You cannot block (idiotic in a game with so much close quarters combat), so you will get knocked down CONSTANTLY. It's utterly maddening. And when you get flattened, you'll stay dazed for a few seconds. That is NOT FUN. Period. You feel weak, helpless, and annoyed. In fact, it reminds me of life. I play a game to feel empowered and to relax. This was not merely challenging, it was far too frustrating...which is quite a different thing.- I love a good, deep story, but too many of the conversations were WAY TOO LONG, without providing anything of value. Boring, and yet I felt I had to sit through them just in case something turned out to be important (spoiler...it never did).- The bosses, what few there were, were also far more frustrating than fun. They felt like content padding. The Burning Shores boss hit a new low for me.- The character relationships were a mixed bag. Some were fun and rang true; others felt forced and artificial. (The ridiculous interplay between Aloy and her companion in the Burning Shores was a prime example: sociopolitical pandering in the guise of a tale. No, thanks. Not buying it. People bond instantly on Hallmark, but very rarely in real life. I witnessed absolutely no bond forming. One minute they were mildly antagonistic strangers, the next they're best buds. Lame writing.)- Weapons were creative, but I ALWAYS felt under-powered. Fighting machines felt more like a chore than a fun challenge. The stealth component was effective, but try sneaking up on those things with any regularity. They detect you from a hundred yards away. I quickly abandoned that mechanic.- The puzzles, like so many aspects of the game, were too difficult and obscure to be enjoyable. Once again, I felt I had to do them for the achievement, but I didn't enjoy it. (Sensing a theme?)- And now, the biggest disappointment of all: Aloy herself. I admired her in the first game; I liked her. In this game, I found myself becoming annoyed with her attitude an awful lot, to the point where I just didn't care about her story anymore. She's helpful, of course, and she is often selfless. But she's also subtly snippy more often than seems appropriate. And don't even get me started on Beta...wow.I feel like I'm saying this more and more about modern games: they should be fun before they're anything else. Don't try to preach to me or teach me a value lesson; believe it or not, I've been able to form opinions about the important topics of life all by myself without some ham-handed game developer thrusting his or her worldview down my throat. You want to make the world a better place? Be kind. Be generous. Be loving. Be selfless. When it comes time to make a game, just tell a good story and make it fun.Sadly, this one wasn't, so this is where Aloy and I sadly part company. Such a disappointment amidst so much promise and creativity.

Horizon Zero Dawn remains one of my all-time favorite games. So, I was eagerly looking forward to Forbidden West. It is a very good game but I did not enjoy it quite as much as HZD.My first thought is that you owe it to yourself to play HZD before entering the Forbidden West. Although the two are stand-alone games, you will miss far too much of the lore if you have not experienced Aloy's history.I am not a skilled action gamer so I play this type of game on the 'Easy' setting. Despite this, I found Forbidden West to be a more challenging game than HZD. The last couple of boss fights were brutal (for me) and the new machine creatures were tougher. The mechanic of flying was added and the Burning Shores Vista points are achieved by following a flight plan in the sky (rather than locating a certain vantage point). I normally use a keyboard/mouse but a controller was a must for the flight portions of the game. There are some nice changes from the first game. You can dive deep underwater (once you have a breathing device) and explore hidden areas. You have an easily accessible 'stash' that stores resources and extra ammo that won't fit in your inventory. You can change the time of day and it felt like there was much more climbing.  Your spear is enhanced and there are new melee combinations that I could not master! There is also a shieldwing glider that lets you land softly when you fall or jump from a spot too high.Normally, I spend all my initial time doing side errands and exploring to build up my character before getting to the main quest. In Forbidden West, you need to move about halfway through the main quest story-line in order to gather four tools needed for exploration/survival. I left more Steam achievements on the table with Forbidden West because the timing and precision of combat moves to earn some of them (gauntlet, melee pits, hunting grounds) was more than I was willing to work for.Forbidden West is a good story but I did not find it quite as compelling as HZD and I did not care as much about the characters. It is a well crafted and very enjoyable game with beautiful scenery and spectacular moments.  Plus, it gives the player a chance to spend more time with Aloy and Sylens. This has not replace it, but it probably has pushed something else out of my top ten.I play games for their narrative, and boy did these games deliver. Truly love to hate that character.Pros:- Yet another great story well told. Seriously this is how you tell a story in game, but letting the player pick up clues and start to theorize before the big reveal which then ends up with a plot twist.- Top notch acting and cameos, wonderful cast of characters, nice character development in Aloy, it is hard to get me to care about characters but they did leading to some tear-jerker moments- Graphics are stunning (but very demanding)- New gameplay styles are possible, almost overwhelmingly so. I tried them all but some I couldn't master.- So many creative new machines to rapidly and violently dismantle- Lots new toys to do said dismantling with- (Minor spoiler) Flying!Cons:- It doesn't have to be Mass Effect, but some story arc choice would be nice.- I wish we could let Aloy be more reactive in numerous situations, like give more use of the Head, Heart, Fist emotional choices, there are very few of those offered.- Main story is actually kinda short, it is all the necessary exploring to get to the next story point that adds lots of time.- Crazy power curve on Aloy, I went from playing normal (and repeatedly dying), to all the way up to Very Hard and taking on the most potent machines in a straight fight, because Aloy goes from "please don't hurt me" to the Terminator as you progress. Recommended, but with caveats.As of this writing, I have finished the game twice on PS5, have not played the DLC expansion, and am midway through the main story on PC. I had roughly 100 hours played on PS5. For Horizon Zero Dawn, I have nearly 500 hours played on PS4 and PC (not on Steam); and the majority of that time was played within one year of release on either platform, and I've 100% completed twice on PS4, once on PC.The game is really good, and overall a worthy followup to the first. For those paying attention to the background lore in the first game, this one has a major payoff in that respect. The major companion characters from the first one return, and while still not as involved as you might want them to be, they do have more to do in this one. On the surface, the game plays very much like the original, with vastly improved traversal options. The inventory system has a very nice upgrade: you don't have to worry about having too much of anything, excess gets sent off to a stash you can visit any time (there's a fair number of them around the world). The focus mode has some nicely upgraded abilities. Plenty of interesting new characters as well.But after reaching what is roughly the mid-point of the game, I find myself stuttering along with it, feeling no urgency to really plow through it like on my first playthrough, or like I do every time I pick up Zero Dawn. After 30-ish hours into a fresh PC playthrough, I remember why I didn't play the hell out of this game like I did the first one: the game suffers from what I call "the terrible too-s" as in: too much. Too much emphasis on melee; which is still largely useless. Too many different resources. Too many gear upgrades needed. Too many new creatures that are too aggressive. Too many knockdowns/stuns/states, only some of which can be mitigated, that Aloy takes too long to recover from. Too many upgrade resources that can only be obtained from the toughest creatures in the game (if you have to beat the toughest thing out there before you can upgrade, what the hell is the point in upgrading?). Too many side activities. Too many skill trees, filled with too many skills of debatable usefulness, that require too many skill points, that ultimately make side quests non-optional as they are the main source of skill points. The issue this game has is the same as the recent Assassin's Creed games: it gives you content exhaustion. This gigantic open world that is absolutely overstuffed with things to do; but almost none of it feels optional, because the character's upgrade paths require so much in terms of resources (be they skill points, currencies, levels, loot and/or gear upgrades), and the various activities to acquire these resources. All of this only vaguely optional content makes a playthrough feel like a checklist you need to finish rather than something you want to do; and for me it diminishes from the replay value, because there is so much stuff in there that you just never want to do again after completing once. I know I've probably overemphasised the negatives: it really is a very good game, and I do recommend it, but I do warn that  it feels too stuffed, which I feel diminishes from its replayability. If you've never played this game on PS%, you're likely to get a very enjoyable 100-ish hours of enjoyment out of it, but it probably won't leave you with any great desire to go through it again.

The story makes sense with where the previous game left off and has started to expand on interactions with some favorite characters.  The game play is familiar enough to pick up from the original, yet they clearly put a lot of thought into expanding on the basics in positive ways.There are now incremental gear upgrades to be made in addition to attaching coils/weaves.  Aloy's skill points are also enhanced with a wide variety of branching trees you can take to fit your play style.  I like that they enhanced melee combat with maneuvers to be performed for greater impact.There are a lot of quality of life improvements.  Inventory management is much improved with extra items going to a stash found in settlements.  This helpfully includes medicinal plants so you can easily refill your medicine pouch with extras you collected earlier.  The focus is also improved with a pulse mode that shows resources, machines, and points of interest without having to go into full focus mode every time.  Importantly, climbing has been improved with the focus showing interaction points on cliff sides without everything being painted white or yellow like in the original.The only downside I've found so far is some changes to key mapping in the sequel.  Most keys appear to be the same to me, but the weapon wheel has moved to another key as well as the heavy melee attack.  I can see why they made these changes to work with the more intricate combat and I'm working to get used to them, but it has been a minor detraction in these early phases of the game.I'm currently playing normal difficulty while I adjust to these changes and have felt pleasantly challenged but not overly so.  I had previously completed very hard and ultra hard modes in Zero Dawn and may end up increasing difficulty later, but for now it is entertaining as-is!Forbidden West, as expected, is a very beautiful game!  The minimal HUD display gets out of the way while still being available fully with a key press.  The water dynamics are gorgeous and the machines I've seen so far are well designed.  If you enjoyed Zero Dawn, I'd recommend Forbidden West as a worthy addition.  I have no regrets at this point and look forward to exploring this new installment.

Brilliant game that builds on everything Horizon Zero Dawn did and made it better. There are a lot of things taken from other games which makes the whole gameplay experience better such as the glider and many other things, none of it feels out of place and just makes an already fun game better. I found the combat to be more satisfying than the first game (Not sure if that's just me getting better at the game though compared to when I was learning the first one). The world is enormous and full of things to do, and one thing I commend Guerrilla for is evolving the open world activities from the first game. I found in Zero Dawn the side quests and activities were uninspired and boring, it may have added some bits to the overall story of the game and built the world more, but the quests were so unfun for me that I couldn't care for what it does add. It was the stereotypical monotonous side questing experience you expect from average open world games. Forbidden West rights those wrongs by making the side quests more interesting, and diversified what activities happen within those side quests. Exploration is built on in the same way for me and feels a lot more rewarding and fun compared to the first game. In the first game I got to the point where I stopped caring about exploring and just trained the main quest. In Forbidden West I feel much more likely to complete a lot of side and exploration content just on the basis that it's more fun and varied compared to Zero Dawn (and many other open world games).Graphically the game is stunning, it is one of the best looking games I have played to date. Nixxes have done an excellent job of bringing Forbidden West to PC and not falling into the issues many ports do. The controls make sense on keyboard and feel intuitive, and the game doesn't feel like it's clearly made for controller. The performance of this game is what I expect but it exceeds most other ports I've seen (TLOU I'm looking at you). I am running a Ryzen 5600 and a 3070 and I am able to play this game with full very high settings in 1440p (with the exception of textures, which is down to medium, but I cannot see a difference between medium and very high here). I tried playing with very high textures but it seems like the frame rate becomes inconsistent. I'm able to get 60 fps for say 10 minutes and then it feels like the VRAM gets too high and then the game runs poorly until I go to title screen and reload the game again, it feels a bit like what happens if you play Resident Evil remakes and go over the VRAM limit. As mentioned, the difference between medium and very high textures is negligible if everything else is maxed out as is, in my opinion. If you liked Zero Dawn, this game is Zero Dawn but better in every single facet and worth the price tag. I think Ghost of Tsushima is in brilliant hands, Nixxes have proven  to be the best of the best for PC ports, and Ghost of Tsushima should put any conversation about it to rest.

I bought the pre-release deal and this is the first time I've ever made a purchase like this as usually I buy games only if they're on sale.  Zero Dawn and the story line for this series has captivated me from the start and Forbidden West does not disappoint so....  First the positives:Graphics - The game is just beautiful.  From lush jungles, to desert plains, snowy mountains and everything in between, the game is gorgeous.  There were times I would just stop and admire the scenes from the day to evening to night, it's mesmerizing and I don't even have the latest and greatest gaming rig.Gameplay - Aloy and her movements, fighting styles, mounts, and weapon options (once you get them all), are even better (and bigger in scope) than Zero Dawn.  In addition, the quests, machines, characters, and the world at large is twice as big as Zero Dawn and it can be overwhelming once the map is laid out in front of you with so many things to do, place to explore and uncover.  The game is a joy to experience and I was lost in it for well over  200+ hours (which includes multiple playthroughs).Story (no spoilers) - Story is superb and pretty much continues from where it left off with a terrific ending.  Audio - This is the one area I thought Zero Dawn was way better.  For whatever reason, the amount of music tracks are extremely limited in this game and there wasn't much variance as there was in ZD.  The sound itself was fine, no technical glitches, but just limited.  This certainly should not stop you from moving forward with the purchase, just know that ZD had more varied and even better background music.  Cons:Bugs - At original purchase and as of this review, the current version I'm playing is 1.2.48 and the game has been patched 3x and there are still bugs.  Small, minor, and certainly not show stoppers, but still annoying.  Game is extremely stable for like 98% of my playtime, but it has crashed.  There are minor bugs in the game with some environmental effects, movement bugs, loading times (I'm looking at you shader compilations), unable to complete 1 of the collections, etcGear upgrades - I don't know what the thought was behind making drops (to upgrade your gear) rare or heck not even able to find the machines after going to the location the map suggests, but this not a MMO.  I'm pretty sure the studio and dev team don't get more money if players play longer, so I have no idea why the above is even an issue, but it's stupidly grindy, wastes a lot of time, and is not fun. Key Mappings - This was a huge issue especially, with the directional arrow movements (where Aloy would roll if you hit the direction arrow too fast), until I figured out how to remove it.  However, there are others that you can't really customize.  The game has hard coded certain keys and I think it takes some of the fun out of it, but not a big deal, just annoying.      Overall - Game is a blast to play, the story is riveting, the characters and acting was excellent, bugs are minor, and it was well worth my time.  I know it was a risk to pay full price, not knowing how this game was going to be, but I don't regret the purchase.  If you are on the fence at this point, then you may as well wait until it goes on sale as the pre-release purchase price included some starting gear (and one of the reasons I bought it).  Good luck with whatever you decide. Now on wards to NG+ UH :).
