To me, it's a resounding: YES.For every problem I have with this game, there are 10 things I love about it.HFW absolutely blew me away with the sheer quantity and quality of quests and side quests, each and every one with well written, acted and animated dialogues, and I would rate this as my absolute favorite point.What I didn't really like is how little they try and justify Aloy losing all her gear from the first game, dismissing it completely like it never mattered. This, in order to force you to use the new weapons they introduced in the game, most of which suck (except you, drill harpoons, I love you) and I abandoned them all in favour of a flexible loadout of 3 bows (because yeah, you still still need a specific bow to shoot specific projectiles, which is my least favourite thing in both Horizon games).A huge effort went into reworking the melee system, which I'm sure someone will like, meanwhile I tried and avoided it as much as possible, and absolutely hated every time I encountered enemies I couldn't kill with a silent strike. But I like stealth sniping everyone and never be seen. Most people would probably find my play style boring, and that's ok.Another massive L is the way traps work: having them on the same menu wheel as healing items and lures makes using them massively inconvenient and tedious -not to mention their limited number, as Aloy apparently needs to be dressed for the occasion to use more than 3 traps. Which leads me to my third and final complaint: the reworked skill system.Aloy, along with her gear, probably got a pretty heavy head injury, because she forgot how to do most of the things that were in the upgrades of the first game. Things like whistle to attract enemies (which is now replaced by wonky-ly aiming and throwing a rock at your feet to do the same exact thing), or notch more than one arrow on her bow, or override machines indefinitely, and the overrides of all the machines carried over from the first game.What she is now capable of doing instead, is unlocking a vast array of mostly useless skills from 5 different skill trees, which include special techniques for all weapons, often ones that make very little sense from a realism standpoint (like being able to shoot 10 bomb in a single shot, or harpoons that split mid-air for a cluster bombing effect). These skills are the same that are boosted by certain armors and foods. Because yes, there is food in this game, and again, most of it makes zero sense, like some skewers that when eaten lets overridden machines deal more damage.All that said, I still loved this game A LOT. The world is enormous, and took me almost a week to fully explore (and after 10 days, I still hadn't covered every angle of the map), and while being this huge, is still incredibly densely characterized and populated, and absolutely stunning. Almost every collectible is behind a small environmental puzzle, or a beautifully detailed dedicated zone.The new machines are intricately detailed and gorgeously animated, which makes them interesting and fun to fight, if sometimes quite frustrating at high difficulties and with starting gear.The story is captivating and told through incredibly well made dialogues and in-game cutscenes, which would have felt even more incredible if they ever ran above 20 fps, which is a problem they'll hopefully have already fixed by the time you read this review when trying to decide if it's worth it to buy this game.I didn't really like the Burning Shores DLC. It was free, so I'm not complaining too much, but it felt like a decisive downgrade compared to the Frozen Wilds DLC, which eclypsed Zero Dawn in terms of story and storytelling. Most of which, because of the lack of the same level of side quests, which told the story of the land and its people and traditions, along side with some really interesting snippets from the "Ancient World".The Burning Shores while set in an incredibly gorgeously detailed new part of the map that made my 3080 struggle to keep up, makes little effort to give it a history and depth, describing it instead as mostly abandoned.The DLC has a pretty interesting story, comprised of a handful of missions centered around a "you thought you got them all, but there was one more!" pretext that didn't really captivate me. It has a bombastic ending which was a great spectacle, and a lot of fun, but all in all, it didn't manage to not leave me wanting a bit more.I basically detailed everything I didn't like about this game, and yet, I still strongly recommend it, and even though I already have almost 180 hours in it, I will probably play it for almost as much more in NG+.

This game is difficult for me to review, as I was a huge fan of Zero Dawn and I feel that this sequel both fails and succeeds in many ways. Good to the point that it's a detriment to the game experience. All of the textures are so high resolution that it creates a ton of noise on the screen and it's sometimes difficult to concentrate on parts of the screen (especially in busy settlements.) I feel like a ton of development time went on all of these textures that no one will ever fully appreciate. At the same time, this game has perhaps the best motion capture I've ever seen. Generally good, but I have some issues with it. - The new machines are cool, but some of them are too directly based on real dinosaurs for my taste. I think Zero Dawn managed to achieve a better balance with these designs. In that game I think the closest machine to a dinosaur is the thunderjaw, and even that is more distinct than the raptors, pterodactyls and triceratops you can find in this game. The cool thing about the machines for me is that they're strange, unique machines, not exact copies of dinosaurs I already know.- I loved the idea of Aloy making allies. I think the idea of "the base" and GAIA's room are a great addition. - I've seen some people complain about the glider mechanic. Yeah it's not incredibly precise but I think it's generally fine. - Explorable areas are typically linear paths; you can't really veer from it. - Throughout the story you collect more of GAIA's "subfunctions" that are meant to slightly stabilise the biosphere. This is not shown almost at all in the world. In fact, I didn't even notice a single change to anything after GAIA regained her sub functions. I had to read online that there were actually subtle changes to notice. - A shift to melee combat which I'd be fine with if it wasn't so unrealistic. Aloy knocks down massive machines with a single strike from her spear, it's weird. A ton of new combat systems- skill trees, "valour" giving special abilities, weapon stamina and a ton of deployables you'll never really use unless you restrict yourself to traps only. While I do think that the combat system from Zero Dawn can be improved upon, I think the developers way overdid it. - The upgrade system is INSANELY grindy. I think the devs really tried to pad out the run time, and I found myself not upgrading gear at all because I didn't want to spend ages upgrading something which would be redundant after 2 missions. This was an enormous problem for me that made me play almost the entire game with low level armour and weapons, because I didn't want to grind to upgrade slightly better ones. This issue needs to be addressed in the next game. The story was grand in scope and very flashy. It took a bit of an unexpected turn from Zero Dawn, and I don't think that's necessarily a bad thing. There were genuinely a few moments in this game when the scale of the story took my breath away like when  Aloy's allies are very well written and distinct from each other. What isn't distinct are the Tenakth tribes. In Zero Dawn every tribe felt like a new culture, in Forbidden West you have the Utaru and the Tenakth, those are the two categories they can be sorted into. Overall, I think it was well written with some great moments, but it didn't feel as satisfying or as grounded as the story of Zero Dawn. On a final note, about . I don't know what it is about it, but from what we know so far, it doesn't work for me as an antagonistic force. The writers will have to work very hard to make it unique from the normal Zeniths of this game. Otherwise, I think it will end up being tedious. After all, it's basically just Hades + Zeniths in one, nothing new.TLDR: Great game that I would recommend to any fan of the original game, but it is far less grounded than it and held back by a multitude of (in my opinion) bad decisions, espcially in the gameplay department.

Wow, just wow!First of all, this is a game right down my alley. My top favourites were always the great open world games like Skyrim, The Witcher 3, RDR2 and of course Horizon Zero Dawn. At release, I was in awe of Horizon Zero Dawn because of the immersive storytelling and how the developers had made exploration such an exciting and rewarding experience.On to the next adventure, and the continuation of the original story from the first game, Horizon Forbidden West is (so far, as I have played around 20 hours of it), once again an increddible work of fictional game art from the studio developers and writers. I must say this is by far one of the best gaming experiences I have had in a long, long time - probably since I first played Zero Dawn or RDR2 (whichever launched latest).There are so many things done right here, and they work so well. 1. First of all: they stay true to their roots - and as the original game was a huge success, why change it up too much? Really important decission, and a good one at that.With that said, a lot of the game mechanics are more or less the same as the first game. So if you loved, or hated, the combat system, the focus, Campfires for saving, longnecks for unfogging the map, and the XP leveling, be aware that it works pretty much the same here (although there are new skills to learn and evolve).2. The Forbidden West, as an in-game geographical area that you don’t even get to access before several hours into the game, slowly emerges upon the player as you progress further into the story and gain access to new territory to explore. You might need tools you not yet have to get through certain elemental obstacles, hindering your approach. You get constant warnings from other people you come across on your travels, that you would be crazy to even set one foot across the border to the western lands because of the dangers they hold in store, known only by folklore and tales from long ago because no one from the east really venture there. Let alone the gatekeepers even considering allowing you to go through the gates because of the extraordinary dangerous circumstances at the borderline. If you are heading there though, and you will, you must first make a long journey across No Mans Land, until you reach the desert… Now, I could go on about this, but this obviously creates the dramatic picture of The Forbidden West being a big land, far far away, presenting unknown danger for our Saviour princess Aloy. This is a great way of setting the right mood for the game, and what you have in store agead of you. What awaits you further west? This is a mystery and it will take time and exploration to find the answer.3. The game looks absolutely amazing, and the cutscenes are especially fabulous. The facial animations are really well done and evoke emotions from pretty much every single encounter. I become interested in the characters because of this. And let’s not forget Aloys discrete and sometimes «suggestive» reactions to the conversations she is involved in, or overhears. You can tell Aloy is growing into a woman and is thinking about more than just «saving the world» from morning til night. This is fantastic and opens another dimension between player and character - one that was definetely there in the forst game but has been improved in the second game. The lip sync is pretty decent but not perfect, nor does it have to be in my opinion. They have done a good job of making the mouth do realistic movements according to the voice, but it is of course not a 1 to 1 match for every single word. I don’t get hung up on these kinds of things, if it’s really important for you, check a video online for examples and judge for yourself. I feel overall this is a pretty big disappointed after playing Horizon Zero Dawn. This game also fails to fix any of the issues I had with the first game.  It’s not like this is a bad game, it’s certainly good and worth playing if you played Zero Dawn…but it was just such a disappointment to me.  Voice actor wise Aloy and Sylens certainly still crushed it.  I’m not sure how they can make another one of these games with Lance Reddick dead.  I would miss his presence so much…which is why I strongly disliked that he disappears for about 70% of this game.  Most everything else in this game was a disappointment.  The combat in this game I still feel is garbage and I felt worse than the first.  Enemies border on impossible in my opinion.  The game has no respect for the player and expects you to waste massive amount of hours gathering resources that are so remote you have to go out of your way for them and probably should pull up an online guide where to go.  If you don’t upgrade your gear fighting almost anything will be impossible.  Enemy attacks also basically auto target you and dodging multiple enemies is unbearable.  Enemies can fly across the map and hit you wherever you are…which is infuriating in a game that insists on relying on Aloy’s ability to set up traps and repositioning herself…which is not realistic when enemies just can fly from out of no where to attack you.  Also the person that thought having to craft ammo mid fight when enemies are impossible to dodge should be fired immediately.  I’m also confident the climbing ability in this game is far worse than in Zero Dawn.  I died so many times because Aloy would just not make jumps that she had just made previously.  You have like maybe a 50/50 chance Aloy will properly act in the correct way when climbing anything.However, even with all those negatives if the story had been as good as Zero Dawn I could have overlooked soooo much of that…but this story is terrible.  I also am baffled that the player still lacks choices in this game.  No modern RPG should have a linear story…I get that maybe in the first game they couldn’t do it…but come on, not even in the sequel?! There are dozens of quests here, none allow for player interaction. On the plus I enjoyed all these companions, but that annoyed me even more that I couldn’t make choices to affect my interactions with them.  Again though…even with that huge problem if the story had been as strong as Zero Dawn I would have been fine.Since I plan on complaining about the story for the rest of the review I’m just going to mark it as spoilers.  As I said, if you played Zero Dawn, sure this is a must play.  It’s not nearly good enough to spend more than #Worth $30.  Even that seems too high, but it does have the DLC so sure.  Otherwise, go play some better games until it drops like Baldurs Gate 3 or if you really want an amazing scifi RPG…you are probably out of luck…so I guess play this?

If I had to pick one single word to describe this game, it would be: Tedious. Everything - and I mean *everything* - in this game takes longer than it should. By ten hours, I was absolutely exhausted and had zero interest in playing any more. Easily one of the worst experiences I've had with a AAA game in years and I have no idea how it got all the praise it did. The story? Totally convoluted, with even the most basic or seemingly straightforward plot points constantly derailed by endless maguffins, twists, and extra steps that left me totally uninterested in anything that was happening. Why would I care about what my goals are, when I know there's just going to be a random "But wait, first we have to go HERE!" diversion thrown in every ten seconds? Even the conversations with NPCs drag on and on and on through endless bad fantasy dialogue. Just tell me where I need to go so I can get another round of errands done - it's not like I could possibly be invested in these endless fetch quests, so at least get them to me fast!The combat? Hope you enjoy spending 90% of your time in slow motion, trying desperately to whittle down the weak spots on giant, fast-moving enemies that can take half your health in one hit. Nothing ever evolves beyond a dull rock/paper/scissors dynamic, with enemies that are basically invincible unless you happen to have a good bow that matches their weakness. And even then, it just takes *forever* - I constantly died and had to restart, not because the fights were too hard, but because I got bored and started cutting corners (which this game, of course, brutally punishes). There's nothing I find more obnoxious than a game that presents you with boring combat options and then designs enemies specifically to penalize anyone who doesn't want to use them. It's not my fault your game isn't fun!The movement, inventory, and upgrade mechanics? One more time, tedious. Climbing and jumping is hit-or-miss, with constant weird hitches and missed jumps that force you to restart entire sections (either that or insanely "sticky" climbing where you can just push in one direction and jankily hop from point to point). Meanwhile, the resource economy is so reliant on grinding through random encounters that you'll think you're in an MMO from 2008. Inventory management boils down to thumbing through 800 different useless items and checking to see which of your 100 coils will give +5 ice damage or whatever to some bow you'll use twice and then never again. Nothing just... happens. Everything takes two or three more steps than it should.All in all, my time with this game was just *terrible* - a monument to a certain sort of 2020's Open World Action Game Template that will hopefully die out soon. The game looks great and the world is fun to explore, but anything beyond that is going to have you checking your watch before you're even 20% of the way finished. Hard pass for me.

They are inconsistent at best and in most cases traps don't do any damage or inflict any elemental state. It is true that the more high-end your PC is, the less problems you'll have. But even gamers with 4090 have issues and the last patch dropped 7 weeks ago. And unfortunately it looks like a trend for PlayStation Publishing LLC games. Don't get me wrong, these games are playable and Nixxes are working on patches as you can see on SteamDB. The problem is, the more time passes by after launch, the less frequent these patches are. It's good to see that 'something' is happening behind the scenes but it's unacceptable that after the initial 4-5 patches players have to wait months for additional fixes. In case of Nixxes, they are working on Horizon Forbidden West and Ghost of Tsushima but Spider-Man and Ratchet & Clank players are also complaining about crashes very similar these newer games have. So it's an unfortunate trend about Nixxes' games and some of those games are out for more than a year waiting for fixes.What's more and this is a real problem, Sony and PlayStation are starting to became greedier and shadier about their business. The proud 'For the players' slogan changed to 'for the payers' and now it's all 'for the profit'. PlayStation players are eagerly waiting for a showcase because the PlayStation 5 is out for almost 4 years now and not only blockbuster exclusives become a rare thing but the general public has no idea what to expect because there are hardly any announced exclusives (Marvel's Wolverine and Astro Bot are the ones we know about and the former is delayed indefinitely because a very messy leak issue).So PlayStation has only briefings about how they are about to change their business model to rationalize their finances and therefore PC market can have those precious exclusives. But greed and the intention to trick every PC player into buying a console to be able to play these games are starting to become more aggressive: once again PlayStation don't trust their games can convince players, they try to turn everyone into console players. Their games have the option to link them to Steam accounts. Then they made players create PSN accounts and link it to their Steam-accounts for pre-order incentives. Now with God of War Ragnarok they lead a frontal assault: even though it is a single player game, you'll only be able to play it with a PSN account linked to your Steam account. Th problem is, Ghost of Tsushima also requires a PSN account to play the online Legends mode and players report issues with PSN SDK doesn't initialize at launch and you're only able to play offline. I loved the first Horizon, truly loved, and I was thrilled when this was ported to PC. I write that so you know I want to love this game, but unfortunately, it's not easy.At it's core, the game is like the first, with a few gameplay additions, like a glider, and a grappling hook. Both things that increase Aloy's mobility, which is cool, but the grappling hook only hooks on to certain points, and I found myself forgetting I had it, because it's so rarely usable. The glider does let you get down from heights without climbing, but rarely lets you reach an otherwise-unreachable spot - except in pre-designed quest areas, where you instead have no other choice.The rest of the design follows this heavy-handed style, where there is rarely any room for choice or meaningful exploration. There is usually only one right way to go about any task, including navigating the world. There is a sense of being hand-held, which feels totally out of whack with Aloy's independent nature. She constantly tells you verbally that you've reached a dead end, and should go back to the previous area, or whatever the case may be... For me, the game is so well-suited to free exploration, I cannot fathom why the developers chose this route.The combat is still good and varied, much like it's predecessor, but difficulty is not very predictable. A main story boss might be easy, while a sidequest on the way there, near impossible. Even some medium-sized enemies can bring you from full health to death in one hit - presumably unless you have higher level equipment, stats and skills - making these encounters frustrating, and forcing the player to play cheesy and safe, rather than enjoy the full combat system. It doesn't help that reloading takes a while... I've managed to die quicker than the time it took to reload, which is not ideal.After putting enough hours into the main quest, I realized that I disliked just about everything it did to the experience, and just ran around in the wild, hunting robots. That's still fun! But unfortunately, Forbidden West brings mostly shame to the series.

After unexpectedly finding the first game on Steam and falling in love with it in Fall 2023, I was very happy to play the sequel.I do recommend this game, but I highly HIGHLY HIGHLY recommend you stop reading this review right now and go play the first game before you even set foot into this game. The first game introduces you to the the universe and its lore. Something extremely imported to the Horizon story. Forbidden West carries on where Zero Dawn ends. If you have not played Zero Dawn, you will be dropped in a universe where you should already know who Aloy is, the world she lives in, and what her purpose is. I loved this game almost as much as I loved the first. The game has brought a few some great new features and quality of life that past game didn’t + It has a parachute-like ability. This ability is amazing, and it has made playing Zero Dawn harder for me because I can’t just leap off cliffs anymore+ It has a transmog. This means you can equip gear, and then equip a second set to use as an appearance/outfit. This is my favorite feature of any game, and is something that not even Baldur’s Gate has (main reason I don’t recommend the game).+ You are no longer bound by a limited inventory. Excess pickups will go to a storage cache for you to retrieve whenever you want. This something Zero Dawn lacked, and something I complained about in the review for Zero Dawn.My review for Zero Dawn stated that I felt I was cowering in the grass too much just to go anywhere. I did not have this problem for Forbidden West, so if there truly was a problem in ZD, the devs picked up on it and corrected it.Movement in this game is fluid. It feels really good. Even the bow usage is really good. Playing Zero Dawn again, you can really see the difference in how smooth movement and combat is. Forbidden West has excelled exceptionally since ZD.There are moments playing this game where it started to feel like a platformer. I really liked that feeling.As always, there has to be things I didn’t like.- Unless I just don’t remember ZD enough, I feel Aloy’s character has been downgraded. Not in graphics, but as a person. She is a lot colder, a lot more stubborn, and maybe even arrogant. I stated in my ZD review that I loved the protagonist, but I don’t feel the same way this time. She wasn’t the Aloy I liked from the first game.- There is a very limited number of gear/outfits in this game, and of the ones we do have, none of them really look all that amazing.- The story wasn’t as captivating this time around. Zero Dawn’s story was so good, I had to see it through by skipping side content, and leveling as much as possible to see the story unfold. I did not feel the way with this game, and I did not find as much draw to the story in Forbidden West. While not bad, it wasn't as intriguing as Zero Dawn.Thank you, Sony for bringing this to PC to players. I hope you continue to bring us your “exclusives”.

Downvoting solely for the combo system, particularly in light of the pit challenges. It's remarkable how one bad system can kill the fun in an otherwise great game. I think the only comparison I can come up with for how bad the combos and pit challenges are is the rings level in Superman64. It's legitimately that bad of a system. While it's easy to avoid for the rest of the game by playing a ranged or stealth build, it also means that you're cut off entirely from a melee playstyle (unless you play on Easy where everything dies from button mashing without any real danger). Whoever designed the combos in this game needs to be sterilized. Allowing this level of stupidity to breed is bad for society.Alright, I'm harping a lot on the melee combos, and they truly are bad enough to deserve this, but the controls overall are just terrible. Auto-targeting for melee is super-finicky. Aiming is somehow too sensitive and not sensitive enough at the same time. If you push the button to interact with an object, you'll just step on top of it half the time.On top of that, there's nearly no player agency. You get choices at maybe 3 points in the game, which are broken down into a "strong" choice, a "smart" choice, and an "empathetic" choice (represented by a fist, a brain, and a heart respectively). None of these choices seem to matter. You have a skill tree, but you get to fill out pretty much everything anyways, so the choices don't really matter much. Granted, the game doesn't really advertise itself as a full-on RPG, but with ♥♥♥♥ combat and no choice, you're basically just watching a movie. It's a very pretty movie (the graphics and visual design are absolutely stunning and easily the best part of the game), but fails as a game.And for a movie, it has a mediocre story. The world-building is pretty good, but the narrative is "meh" and the characters make some unbelievably stupid decisions, particularly after the final boss fight.Nixxes deserves props for the port, though. It runs fantastically on PC. The port, the visuals, the voice acting, and the music are all fantastic. It's just disappointing that they aren't the backdrop for a better game.

Solid successor to the original game that improves on it in almost every way. 8/10Horizon: Forbidden West has many advantages of its predecessor. The graphics are stunning (in my opinion, the best I've seen in a game), the story is more compelling, and the variety of new machines is extremely welcome. The game takes place on the far-future west coast of America, allowing the developers to include many types of environments that weren't present in the first game. The coast, especially, is beautiful, as are the jungles. The new machines are all rendered wonderfully, and many add a welcome bit of difficulty to the roster.However, there are a few new changes that are less welcome. The first is the "Special tools". Horizon Forbidden West adds in several new tools, including a grappling hook, a glider, and an aqua breather. The glider isn't bad, just under-utilised, and the aqua breather is nice, but the grappling hook is frustratingly slow. Combined with the returning janky parkour mechanics, and it can be a chore. The other is an increased focus on fighting human enemies. The melee combat in the game is more fleshed out, but still feels clunky, especially when compared to other fighting games. Thankfully, fighting the machines still feels great. Overall, I'd certainly recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the first game, and anyone who enjoys exploring a beautiful open world.

THE FORBIDDEN WEST*********************I like the story, I like that you can teleport at least at campfires for free.  I like that you can buy resources.  I like that Aloy is an overall empathetic character rather than the standard "hard ass" main in most games. To be honest, if I didn't like the story as much as I do, I'd probably not play this because I HATE the climbing, which is a big part of this series.  I was hoping it was improved.I do wish the fighting was a bit more streamlined.  WAY too many combos I couldn't remember, and no way to use more than one "surge" without going through menus to swap it out.  With this many options, I wish I had hotbars to use rather than menus.  I couldn't get some of the melee ones to work.  (i.e. -- how long am I supposed to "pause" in between clicks?)I read that the voice acotr of Sylens, Lance Reddick, died.  RIP.  He did such a good job and Sylens is a really good character.  I'm wondering what they will do in the next game, as the story didn't wrap up with this one.  Games like this are often made by VA performances.It would have been fun if Aloy had discovered a stuffed animal on her adventures to show Varl.  If you know, you know.I only experienced one crash during 160 hours.Overall, I would recommend it.  For people that love the grind, it's a great game for them.  For those who don't, there are settings to help.  For me, the story is worth it.*********************FRUSTRATING JANK*********************--The climbing has NOT improved.  Such a tedious part of the game.  Aloy sometimes just stops and won't move, or moves in a different direction than you think she's going to go.  Also, you pretty much SHOULD turn on the climbing surfaces in the settings permanently, because the devs are so inconsistent with what Aloy can climb, if it suits them for her not to be able to, they just tell you "no".  I'll be stuck somewhere and think "Aloy has climbed worse than that, why not now??"Also, many times I latched onto a wall unintentionally in the middle of a fight and then couldn't get Aloy to release.--The controls, at least on PC, suck.  When I was in the middle of a fight, my weapon would NOT fire a good chunk of the time, I would have to release and redraw the bow again (it sometimes happened multiple times in a row), and this made fights waaay harder than they already were.  Same happened when I would try and stealth strike something.  A portion of the time it just would fail and next thing you know, I'm disadvantaged amongst a lot of mobs now aware of me.--Getting knocked down, Aloy takes FOREVER to get up, just for the mob to immediately knock her down again (normal mode).  Also, rolling did not work very well as a defense and didn't move you outside a lot of mobs range of attack.--Having quest companions walk RIGHT IN FRONT OF YOU when you are lining up a shot, or trying to dodge, or trying to jump on something.--I found the flying to be a PITA, so I still tended to use campfires to get around if I could.****************BURNING SHORES (my least favorite section)****************--The "park" was fun to explore--I feel this would have been better off as part of the main story, or a side quest in the main game, it felt like a wart stuck on the main game.--I didn't like the fact they tried to force Aloy into a relationship, specifically one I didn't pick.  I had already had her shipped with someone before BS (lol).  In this modern era, if you are going to have a main character that someone is playing for tons of hours either leave the romance out or allow the player to choose who they want to romance.  Everyone has different tastes, and I was already "attached" to a character.  They didn't even give the option at the end to outright say "Sorry, I'm interested in someone else".  It was like being violated by the developers after spending two games and a couple hundred hours as Aloy.  Baldurs Gate 3 did it right.  This won't bother someone else, but it bothered me because when I play I BECOME the character and I like who I like.  It felt like an unwanted arranged marriage.  That's fine for side characters, but not for my character.  The ending of the dlc was probably my biggest gripe.  Other than the Park, I thought the DLC was rather uninspiring and bland, in general.  With the main game I wanted to keep going, with Burning Shores I had to make myself keep going.

THE GOOD-A stark blue light pierced the tree branches ahead causing you to crouch lower into the grass. The machine terrorizing this sleepy mining village was no ordinary beast. The few who had survived an encounter reported a stark difference in the coloration of its armor, in addition to a strength and ferocity that was not to be taken lightly. Catching sight of the creature as it passes by your hiding spot, a likely weak point shimmers behind its shoulder joints. As the machine comes to a stop to survey the moonlit grove, you seize the opportunity to dash silently from cover and slide under its frame. Losing an explosive payload deftly into each shoulder, you spring back to your feet and glide to a safe distance before turning to observe your handiwork. The creature emits a growl and twitches oddly just before the canisters erupt, engulfing it in a shroud of fire and sparks.The machine, or what was left of it, fell on its side, its gold and black plates shimmering in the moonlight. A quick pair of jabs with your spear’s blade put the terror down for good. Well, it wasn’t as tough as you thought, but then, you remind yourself, these were miners, not soldiers.Forbidden West exceeds the first game in nearly every way. While Zero Dawn will always hold a special place in my heart, there can be no denying that its sequel has even better visuals, musical score, voice acting, character development and deeper combat. Although the overall story is less impactful (Could anything hope to supplant the original story), the storytelling itself tops the original.The combat benefits from a litany of new weapons, buffs and debuffs, consumables and elements. Aside from a minor, yet notable, design flaw, more on that later, you are kept on your toes and no one strategy will handle every encounter. An evolution worthy of a sequel for sure.As almost any review will tell you, this one is a true gem of fidelity. The soundtrack and voice acting is next to divinity and the visuals put practically all other modern games to shame. The characters are leaps and bounds ahead of anything out there at the time of release, with details on their outfits that make clothing in the real world look like plastic rags. The result is an experience that will have you questioning reality. Trees and flowers irl will start to look fake by comparison. I swear there was a moment, just after a rainfall, where I caught the scent of wet grass. It’s actually a bit scary. Hey, maybe the Old Ones really did die out because they couldn’t tell what was real anymore!THE BAD-In terms of sequel-itis, Forbidden West and its current generation rival, Tears of the Kingdom, have almost the exact opposite problem. Forbidden West boasts a brand new map, characters and story. Its character development, combat and aesthetics represent a significant advancement over its already impressive predecessor. However, it failed to introduce many much needed enhancements to its open world exploration mechanics. A glider and a handful of climbable rock faces simply don’t make the cut these days. As a result, it feels more like a behemoth expansion than a true sequel.Conversely, TotK added to an already impressive array of exploration mechanics from its predecessor. They now form a damn near dangerously addictive formula. However, the game effectively has the same world, characters and story as before. As a result, TotK feels more like a rerelease of BotW than a new game.When it comes to climbing, combining a surface based climbing system (ie stone and wood are ok, but metal is a no go) with existing grapple points and auto generated ledges, would be golden. Naturally, this would require a stamina system which could also be used for gliding, swimming, power melee attacks and dodging. Maybe even a progression upgrade that allows brief climbing on overhangs?More ways to interact with the environment are a must. For example, using existing explosive ammo to break openings in rock walls, or blaze ammo to light dry grass and bushes to clear the view on weed infested pathways, or chillwater to freeze a waterfall and make it briefly climbable.The game did increase the combat challenge by adding debuffs like broken bones, but then also put in player staggering. The former is a brilliant addition that makes players respond to more stimulus in real time, but the latter commits the cardinal sin of taking away all forms of player input during combat. That’s a big no no. It’s a black eye on an otherwise greatly improved combat experience.This sequel added a significant amount of tips and hints chatter to Aloy’s previously only occasional commentary on points of interest. While I can certainly appreciate the effort to make the game more accessible to a broader audience, this feature must be placed in the accessibility menu where players can turn it on and off as desired.I strongly believe in this series and I deeply desire to see it succeed at a time when open world games are stagnating. Perhaps cutting back on extraneous activities like errands, hunting grounds, melee pits etc. and focusing on the aforementioned exploration mechanics would help. Leave the creation of additional content to the community, perhaps with an official modding tool? An absurd dream, I know, but I do hope they make the necessary strides and tweaks to make the next entry truly shine and sparkle like a Verdant Jewel!THE VERDICT-If you enjoyed the first game, and are hungry for more, this one’s a sure winner. Nab it when you feel it’s time to chow down on a monster helping of open world RPG. Starting things off, before playing this you should play Horizon Zero Dawn first, if you don't own it already, I'd wait for the Remaster and check if it's any good (but it should be, as there's only updates to graphics and audio for the most part). After I completed Horizon Zero Dawn for the first time knowing there is a sequel, I was very interested in how they will continue that story as it covered quiet a lot of things. Interestingly enough, I'm surprised that they pulled it off as well as they did and even teased for another sequel. I'm welcoming this very much, this is one of the best current Story Games in my opinion (In series obviously). Talking about the elephant in the room: GraphicsYou need a lot of performance to handle this game, so sadly a midrange PC build will struggle with this. If you have seen the Hardware recommendations, the lower recommendations seem to be directed at running the game at 1080p 30 FPS, and to most of us, 60 FPS is the lowest they dare to go, myself included. So if you plan to play this, I'd recommend waiting for an upgrade. To compare, I've started playing this on a Laptop with AMD Ryzen 75800H and AMD Radeon RX 6600M, I've got it to run on 1080p 40-50 FPS with FSR 3 on, but it dips a lot in performance, especially in cutscenes. I did not bother to continue on  said hardware and now I'm very fluently running the game at 1440p 120 on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D and AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX. Story:As said, you should play Horizon Zero Dawn first, this game directly places itself behind that Storyline. It will also clear some things up because of some puns Aloy will drop here and there. I wouldn't say it has the inferior Story compared to Horizon Zero Dawn, but it is certainly very high up. This is because Horizon Zero Dawns Story really has to explain everything from the ground up and it did that very well. Most of the milestones for the story were already laid, so I don't expect much more to come out of it. What they definitely did better compared to Horizon Zero Dawn was the way they immersed us into the story thanks to the way better dialogue sequences. In Horizon Zero Dawn (Original) especially Sidequests and also some Dialogues in the Main quest lacked expression and emotion. To see it improved here makes me really happy and to know there's a Remaster for Horizon Zero Dawn that will (hopefully) fix that issue just adds to that. Getting used to the new melee system was a bit difficult to me since I'm used to the one in Horizon Zero Dawn. It isn't much different, but the new Melee combos weren't a playstyle for me. Same goes for some of the new Weapons. I didn't really get used to them, and avoided them in the best way possible since I either like to stealth or use a Bow or Precision Bow. They are just not fitting for my playstyle. The new elemental effects are pretty great though, though I'd like to have Tutorials for using them correctly. I've been confused a lot of times when using Plasma arrows or using the Shredder Gauntlet. Aside from all that, as always, you decide your playstyle, how you go in, what weapon you choose, if you sneak by or attack. Aside from the hunting grounds and the melee fights it will always be in your control how you fight. Difficulty wise, it's similar to Horizon Zero Dawn, Easy to Learn, Hard to Master. So even as a beginner with knowledge of the basics of a controller and knowing where which button is by muscle memory will be enough for you to enjoy this game. I very much recommend to play this (obviously after having played Horizon Zero Dawn)

The Horizon game series first came to my attention when my father purchased the original HZD game in 2017, and played it when I was thirteen years old. Throughout the years, it is the only game series my father and I have both paid attention to and played. Video games are one of the few ways we connect, and this specific game series is one of our favorites. Having said that, having finally finished the main story on my PC, (I'd previously managed to sneak on his PS5 and play a few hours in) I can't wait to talk to him about it next time I have the opportunity to. This second game does not fall short of the first, and it brought back a lot of joy the original brought me. Here is what I feel are the pro's and cons:Pros- A relatively engaging story line, or at least I found it to be, and this is coming from someone who gets bored super easily. I feel that this second installments story continues the first quite well. The start is a little slow but once you make it past the two hours or so it improves. I found it to be so engaging that I had to force myself to complete side quests to try and spread out the main quests, and I am now regretting speeding through the story line because it's complete now. If you purchase this game and don't like speeding through the main story line, I'd recommend that you do multiple side quests in between main story quests so it feels like it lasts a bit longer!- Machines. Lots and lots of cool machines. some original ones, some new ones. They're challenging in their own way and I always get this sort of happy feeling every time I spot one I've never seen before.- Combat system and skill tree. I'm someone who barely plays games with any combat and this one is simple enough for me to understand but also seems expansive with its weapon rosters and has options for people who want to play differently. The skill tree is large and takes some time to complete but it's worth it and really makes things easier. I genuinely enjoy fighting in this game and it's challenging in a good way. Sometimes it takes a couple tries to figure out what works best and I think that's good.- The world is really beautiful. Marveling at graphics and environment isn't really something I do with games anymore but something about the environment and the different biomes is really nice. Travelling is kind of fun because of all the different environments you get to experience. The world feels full of life--the NPC's in the settlements, the NPC's sometimes roaming the lands outside of settlements, and there's different animal species for each biome too. It just makes the world feel more alive and the attention to detail in that regard is better than HZD even in my opinion.Cons:- Aloy randomly talking anytime she picks up anything. Later in the game I think she talks less, but in the beginning I swear every time I picked up anything she would say something that didn't add anything to the experience. Things like, 'Stocking up', 'this will go in my stash', etc. Just kinda feels off I think because in reality she would not probably say that out loud to herself every time she picks an herb. It just breaks the immersion a bit for me.- Aloy's movement seems to be a bit messy. Multiple times I would get too close to a wall or step on a just barely uneven surface while walking up a tower staircase or something and Aloy would immediately proceed to roll off the staircase (dodge type roll) and fall to her death. I never pressed the button to roll, she would just do it. And unfortunately, I died a couple times to this and had to redo a minute or two's worth of climbing. I'm not sure if this is intentional or unintentional, but it is definitely a bit frustrating.- My PC is about five years old and doesn't have problems graphically with other games, but it kind of struggled with this one. I made sure everything was updated, so I know that's not the issue. The game only ran at 60FPS when I was on low graphics for most settings. The game is still enjoyable on low graphics, but the cut scenes would have dropped frames or fail to load everything properly at times. If you have an older PC it might be something to keep in mind if you want to purchase this game.To summarize, I think this game is worth its price. My personal rule of thumb is for every dollar spent I should get an hour of game play, and I know without a doubt I will be putting at least another twenty five hours into this game, and feel my money was well spent. I will finish this review by saying that although I may be a bit biased due to my longtime positive associations and memories with the series, I wouldn't be able to enjoy this game and continue to do so if I didn't truly like it, which I do. Thank you for reading!

TLDR; Good game. Awful sequel. Manage your expectations and put on your "Leroy Jenkins" nametag.PROS:Just like HZD, HFW is beautiful & compelling. The new landscape and machines are interesting, and I couldn't wait to continue to explore this map and learn more about the mysteries of this new Earth. Not to mention the addition of many cool new features and skills for the focus! I think the story and tech developments make sense, and as a stand-alone game it would have been incredible!CONS:HZD left some big shoes to fill, and HFW falls a bit short in comparison (but only in comparison). Overall I think that HFW has tried to emulate more 'conventional' adventure game tropes and markets, which would be fine if not for the aforementioned large shoes. But as it is, the characters are more one-dimensional/leaning more heavily into tropes (Erend a sad drunk, Varl a naive puppy, Aloy a suffering loner, etc.), and the new menus/mechanics really break the immersion in a way that HZD didn't (not to mention they make the game feel much much older, circa 2010). All of this would have been easy to move past however, if not for my final gripe...If you were a stealth player in HZD... this game is going to be a struggle. In HZD where you could find a vantage point and stealth/snipe your way through all but a very few circumstances (Sun Ring, Cauldron bosses, etc.), HFW may as well have come with a nametag that reads, "Leroy Jenkins" for all the subtlety HFW affords you in battle approach. Every plot battle I played for tossed me into battle Sun Ring style with very little opportunity for trickier sniper-style solutions. Maybe there's ways to do this but the mechanics, as far as I saw, were not even close to the what I was able to do in HZD so... do with that what you will.TAKEAWAYS:As a stand-alone game it's good, REALLY good. However, it just doesn't stand up against the experience that was HZD. After 22 hours of trying to live with it, I'll be giving up and watching a playthrough of it instead.

I’ve beaten Forbidden West on the hard difficulty after passing Zero Dawn again to refresh it in my memory. So here are the results of the comparison.Forbidden West is a great game, in some aspects surpassing Zero Dawn. If you like Zero Down, buying Forbidden West is highly recommended. A long story, a huge open world, a great world design, new types of puzzles, new monsters, new tribes – it took me about 170 hours to finish every main and side quest (without the addon) and explore every corner. Although quests have remained basically the same (go somewhere, kill monsters and find an artefact or a survivor), they all are written individually, so they don’t bore.However, developers of Forbidden West have seriously disrupted the game balance, and also added some senseless distracting stuff. First of all, is you prefer stealth and sudden ambushes, your life will become much harder. Enemies now almost always detect and attack you after the first shot, there are little chances to wait till they calm down and hit them again. It’s still possible, but it’s no fun anymore and involves much running around trying to hind behind an obstacle. The supposed gameplay style is now arcade-like head-on attacking (so new spear attack combinations and the valor concept were introduced specially for that).Traps have become incredibly expensive and do much less damage, there is a very small hard limit of traps on the battlefield, and they can’t be recovered after placing. So they are completely useless now. I didn’t use them at all after initial tries in spite of being their fan in Zero Dawn.The skill tree is now huge, but most skills are useless. Even those potentially attractive are doubtful. For example, double and triple shots lower the precision drastically, shields can take very little damage, scattered shots deal too little damage, and so on. You can’t whistle-lure enemies to your position, but should throw stones instead (which complicates the situation without adding anything to the gameplay). Strike from above and Strike from below abilities are enabled by default, but there is practically no chance to use them (enemies immediately notice you if you’re hanging below them and they are looking at your direction).The same is with weapons and armors. There are several tens of different weapon kinds, each with the possibility to upgrade 3 to 5 times. However, but they mostly don’t differ from each other and don’t possess any special effectiveness even in spite of the game’s urging to hit specific monsters with specific arrow types. Precise long-range bows now are denied the insta-kill headshot ability (in fact, headshots deal very little damage now because enemies are wearing helmets), so forget about silently sniping human enemies from a distance. And even silent strike doesn’t kill most human enemies requiring several spear hits to finish them off, which usually results in the general alarm and enemies’ mass-chasing you.Also, upgrades are extremely expensive. They require both common resources in huge quantities as well as rare resources in significant numbers. This is seriously aggravated by the fact that you need to shoot off external machine parts to get them, and this is practically impossible when a machine (especially a big or flying one) attacks, is aroused or is patrolling. You’ll also go crazy collecting hundreds od medium machine cores needed for upgrading practically everything but having a very low probability of appearing on machine corpses. And as previously, not every bird has a feather, not every fish and animal have a bone. I upgraded all bags and about ten of weapons until it bored me to death, and forgot about the rest. Anyway, I finished the game using one hunting bow (90% of time) and one sniper bow.And lastly, the developers failed again to add even tiniest elements of RPG to the game that is begging of it. Choices don’t matter, and you’re simply not given any. You can only take a quest (no possibility to resign after you’ve initiated the dialog), resolve it in a single possible way and take the reward.Again, it all doesn’t mean that Forbidden West is a poor game that shouldn’t be bought. It’s a masterpiece, and I still highly recommend it. Just be prepared that the gameplay style might be significantly different from the one you’re used to in Zero Dawn.

Players must progress through the main story to unlock special gear that allows them to explore previously inaccessible areas.This game evokes a similar captivating allure that was present in Witcher 3.Even ascending tall neck to reveal the map does not become repetitive as in Assassin's Creed games. In one instance, you will be scaling a tall neck from a large structure, while in another, you will be hunting down a tall neck from a sphere.**Advantages of the PC Port:**- Extensive customization options for graphics, HUD, controls, and quality-of-life settings, such as an autoloot feature.- Enhanced graphical fidelity compared to the console version, assuming the PC meets the recommended specifications.- Minimal bugs encountered thus far, with only one minor issue affecting a side quest that was circumvented. This demonstrates Nixxes' capability in successfully porting PlayStation games to PC, boding well for the upcoming Ghost of Tsushima port.**Advantages:**- The gameplay remains excellent, largely consistent with Horizon: Zero Dawn's gameplay, with some enhancements to the combat system.- Graphically, the game achieves an exceptional level of visual fidelity. The human character models and facial animations, in particular, are arguably the most impressive I have encountered in a video game.- The narrative continues to be a strong aspect of this series.CONs:-24 hours in, I don't think I have any complaints, besides the one bug I've encountered.In terms of my gaming performance, I am running the game at 2560×1440p with HDR enabled. All settings are set to High, and DLSS is set to Quality at 75%. Initially, I locked the game at 75 frames per second (fps), but experienced occasional drops to 60 fps in urban areas. Subsequently, I adjusted the lock to 60 fps to ensure a consistent frame rate.One additional reason for locking my frames per second is the temperature of the graphics card, which hovers around 80 degrees Celsius while the game is running. This is due to the ambient room temperature of approximately 36 degrees Celsius, a result of the current summer season.This locking mechanism also assisted in maintaining a cooler temperature for the 3080ti, approximately between 65 to 68 degrees Celsius.My system specifications are as follows:- Intel Core i7-12700K processor- 32GB of DDR4-3600 memory- NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Ti graphics card with the latest NVIDIA drivers- Windows 11 operating system with the latest buildTwo significant video games were released this week, one of which was Dragon Dogma 2, which received negative reviews due to its performance issues. If you enjoy open-world adventure games, Horizon Forbidden West is highly recommended. I initially intended to wait for a sale before purchasing the game, but due to the positive reviews, I acquired it five days later and have no regrets.

I was hoping that this would be better then the first game, but it has the same exact issue: Great product, not so great game.Before I air my grievances: The port is well done. At least on my 7950x, 4090 rig, it runs as well as you'd expect. Weirdly it's the cutscenes where it drops below a 100FPS but with frame-gen and DLSS set to quality it can hold 130-144 during gameplay.My issues:- Traversal: It's slow. The game's word isn't even that gigantic (which is not a negative) but getting around is boring and takes too long. On foot it's slow. You have the ability to climb but it's usually not straight forward what is and isn't climbable. You need to scan every surface just to figure it out and even then you might run into a wall that's only climbable to the halfway point. You have a glider, but it is more for breaking falls as for some reason it doesn't glide as  far as you'd expect.The alternative is riding one of the tamed robots. That however is like riding in any other game: Finicky. It's unsatisfying and really only works well on open terrain. They also opted for a toggle to speed up/down system which makes it really un-intuitive to use.You'd think, you can use fast travel to avoid the tedium, but you can fast travel for free only from bonfires, and you can only fast travel to other bonfires. So if you've just finished a mission and don't feel like riding back to a town, you will have to spend a fast travel pack. Exploration isn't really a factor either. For the most part, you can see points of interest on the map already, and when you're in a new area, your first thing to do will likely be to climb a tall-neck and lift the "fog-of-war".- Story/Characters: This is where it's slightly better then the previous one. Zero dawn treated "twists" that anybody with a functioning brain could see coming as the biggest revelations. This one is slightly more restrained. Don't get me wrong it's still incredibly formulaic and basic but at least it's slightly less self-indulgent. The side-quests however... Those are still terrible. There is an entire story line about desert people struggling for water, but there is a literal lake less then a mile (I think) from their capital. They are usually generic fetch- or kill-quests. There is a bit of exposition dumped on you before then after and that's how the game tries to motivate you. They don't tie back into the main quest, or to people, places you may know. They are the equivalent of filler episodes in a show. No consequence and no prior knowledge needed, just mindless busywork.The characters are essentially non-existent. They talk to you but say virtually nothing of substance. There are no dialects, no weird way of incorporating new made-up words into english, or having new languages with english being incorporated into them (both would make sense a 1000 years after the fall of civilization). The text is flavorless, the way people speak is dull. The characters have no personality. They get 1 trait if they are lucky, but the names already melt together, because there is nothing unique or memorable about any of them.Aloy as a protagonist is also very weak. She has no aspirations, needs, wants, desires. She wants to save the world, because she is the protagonist. I can at least sympathize with that cause she happen to live in said world, but why does she feel the need to help any and everyone she comes across while simultaneously pushing everyone who tries to help her away?- Combat: This is probably the best aspect of the game, however I still have issues with it. Stealth is an option. But unless you're after machine parts there isn't much of a point in using it. When you fire at an enemy, it will go into search mode and will stand around for ~30 sec while you cannot hurt them or they detect you. This is frustrating, especially if you are against a higher-level enemy, that you cannot fight head-on. (certain quests will force you into engagements like this). I like playing stealth, but it felt like a wast of time in this game.The melee combos sound neat, but executing the mid combat is more or less up to luck. I'd have appreciated if available combos were displayed somewhere, so I knew what I could try executing at a given moment, and it'd have been nice if they didn't incorporate stuff as pause for a specific but untold amount of time or hold a key in the middle of a combo.There also don't really seem to be i-frames, as long as the enemy is in the attack animation, if it hits your hitbox, you will get hurt.Conclusion: This is not a bad game. But it's mediocre in a segment that's a bit over-saturated to begin with. If you've played a TPS action-adventure game in the last decade, you've played this game. It has nothing unique to offer but the setting that's let down by a sub-par story. It adopts from other games without innovating or really even understanding of what made something work there. I guess it is at least pretty to look at.

TL;DR: absolutely great game that improves on the systems from the first game.  While the story took a direction that kind of felt a little out of place with the sci-fi, Aloy had so much to say that it was sometimes a little unnecessary, bit of stuttering (especially in Burning Shores,) and some controller issues are very minor and do not ruin a great experience filled with a wonderful environments, stunning visuals, strategic battles, fantastic game great character development and one of the best protagonists in video games. Loved the first one years ago when it came out and was excited to get this one now that I got rid of my consoles.  This is just as fantastic as far as gameplay goes.  It takes what made the first one so good and improves on it greatly, adding more options and strategies as well as new machines to fight and more quests to do.  I do have some criticisms, but they are somewhat nit-picky and do not detract from what is a phenomenal game.I must say, playing games for 30+ years, Aloy seems to stand out as one of the best protagonists in my opinion.  They really did more with Aloy, developing her into a wonderful character you get invested in.  She no longer goes it alone and develops friendships with characters you remember and enjoyed from the first game.  With that being said, the story took a turn that I was not expecting which kind of changed the tone of the game a little.  The bigger threat you find out early on takes a little bit of a strange turn into more sci-fi that seems to distract from the world that was built previously.Controls can get frustrating at times, like climbing, flying, and sometimes not being able to execute an action.  While this may be in part due to my experience this time going through entirely on the keyboard, it did suffer a few times.  I played Zero Dawn on console with controller where climbing, dodging, attacking, and movement in general felt very fine-tuned and well done.  This one gave me some troubles throughout the game which led to some mildly frustrating parts.  I definitely recommend turning off double-tap for dodge.Visuals are absolutely fantastic, which should not surprise anyone who has played Guerilla Games, save for some stuttering.  In Burning Shores, going to the main village was pretty nasty in frame drops and stuttering, but otherwise everything else worked pretty fine.  The track record for console ports to PC have been pretty bad lately, but this one, minus the few issues, was hardly problematic to devalue the immersion and experience.  The environments are all very well done, changing from arid deserts, snowy mountains, and lush forests.  They are also often populated with animals, machines, and people so no area felt desolate.  The commentary given by Aloy much of the time was welcomed and interesting.  She would comment on the area, a mission, story, or a number of other things.  However, there were times where she liked to comment on aspects of missions that were too quick and took some of the fun out of exploration and discovery.  It felt sometimes like she almost immediately gave hints about things to progress that gave me little time to figure out puzzles.  That could be toned down a bit.Overall, highly recommend this game and the franchise it has become.

The game is wonderful. Often here, you'll see standard reviews with check marks, and this is truly a game that will make you forget what reality is!Visuals, gameplay, main story—everything is generally well done, with no major issues. Yes, we’ve lost that sense of being a pioneer from the first game, but I can't think of a way they could have preserved it.Now, on to the drawbacks, though these aren't exactly negatives but rather points where I felt disappointed:The Tenakth—I really hoped they would be somewhat like the Thenns from Game of Thrones. The embassy opening was promising, but no, they ended up as slightly over-muscled, feminine, cowardly men, with more strong women and the rest being children desperately in need of help. This is not how I imagined the most formidable, bloodthirsty, and dangerous clan in the game. Overall, everything I didn’t like is tied to this. The strange mission with the mountain shot, the chief who was once the most dangerous warrior in the region, then spared an enemy and is now a trembling bodybuilder endlessly begging Aloy for help. I would have preferred to see a bloodthirsty killer who realizes the futility of fratricidal war and tries to set things right—but I understand that’s difficult to write.Positives:The mission in Las Vegas and the spark of chemistry between Aloy and one of the trio. YouTube is flooded with videos of this cinematic; it's fantastic, and thank you to everyone who worked on this quest. Smiles all around during the entire quest, and how beautiful Vegas is, both on land and underwater. Thank you!Talana's quest was great. I want to take a few minutes to dwell on this before even commenting on the game itself. First impressions are important. They can be lasting and we can form quick opinions based on them. In a nutshell, my introduction to Forbidden West was fantastic. In terms of performance, it is undoubtedly demanding. Nevertheless, it runs very well and it feels as if it was optimized appropriately. On my end, everything is buttery smooth (unlike the 1.0 release of Zero Dawn as some of you may still remember). I have read of exceptions and I am very sorry for those who have run into issues; I can only give an account of my own experience which has been stellar. The game launches fast for being such a performance intensive and large-scope title. From start until finish it’s around 20 seconds to get in-game; 10 seconds to get into the main menu and around 10 more seconds to load your most recent save file to continue. I do realize that on paper this does not sound fast, but trust me when I say that it feels exceptionally fast compared to all the recent AAA slop that has come out in recent years. The two splash screens that play during bootup are short, elegant, and most importantly skippable. The main menu/title screen loads instantly and is very responsive. As soon as you hit continue, it immediately loads you in.Then there is the main menu and UI elements in general. Finally, a game with fast and reactive menus, without overdone animations and without any of those painfully low-FPS transitions or mouse-over effects. Seriously, how many games still insist on reinventing the wheel when a simple text list is already as close to perfection as it gets? You are bound to fail and you are guaranteed to make things worse than they were! I would never trade performance for aesthetics. And it appears that the people behind the PC port of Forbidden West are of a similar opinion. Utilizing lists does not mean that it has to be ugly. You can still stylize and color everything according to your game’s theme, as long as it’s pleasing and not over the top. Consequently, the settings pages are neatly arranged and display a wide range of options that can easily be discerned at a quick glance. Why do I keep yapping about this seemingly irrelevant stuff?! It’s simple. I’ve been around for a while. I’ve seen and experienced what boundless incompetence and ignorance can do. I’ve interacted with large panels, terrible menus, laggy transitions for far longer than any sane person should tolerate. My review aims to illustrate how a first impression is forged, if you are willing to open your eyes to these sorts of things. Everything, every little detail matters from the moment you hit Launch within your Steam Library. Every minute detail can speak volumes if you focus your perception accordingly. Forbidden West sets a good tone from the very beginning. As an end-user I am happy, I feel safe. Because I can clearly see that the people who stand behind this project are intelligent. They clearly have put thought into the small things. They clearly take notice of the person sitting in front of their video game and they do not treat their customer with disdain. I am not a fan of holding down my mouse button to aim. I am not a fan of holding a key or button to crouch. I don’t want to hold shift to run. I don’t want to repeatedly hold <interact button> to watch a micro cinematic play. And yet, so many games still do not implement toggle settings for these actions. Sometimes, you have to leave your game and write a macro or script. If it gets particularly bad, then you have to hope and pray that someone will take time out of their day to not only develop a game modification but to also publish it in due time. Imagine my elation when I saw that this game allows you not only to set all of these actions to toggled events, but there is also a setting that can automate resource gathering. If you are someone who prefers to remain in their immersion, the default option will have you go through an animation as you kneel down to pick up sticks, flowers, and other salvageable resources. That’s great for the first few hours of the game. If you are like me however, you will love to see that Guerrilla/Nixxes allows you to skip the animation entirely and auto-loot by walking over gatherable materials. Another big positive in my book. Usually, this is one such instance where you have to hope for external mods to alleviate some of the tedium that accumulates as you play these sorts of games for many hours. Very commendable. Thank you for thinking of this. Similar to its predecessor, the game boasts with beautiful environments and a wide variety of mechanical beasts to hunt. It starts off a little slow to ease you into the story but eventually you’ll be hunting down lots of machines for their crafting components. The combat is as fluid and as challenging as ever. If you liked Zero Dawn at all, then I think you will appreciate this one just as much. Admittedly, I have to progress some more through the story to form a stronger opinion on Forbidden West’s strengths and weaknesses. Consider this section under construction and <to be continued>One noticeable flaw from the intro is already apparent however. This game, similar to other AAA titles with anything remotely resembling a puzzle, insults your intelligence and has the protagonist spoil any sense of experimentation or exploration. I’ve already frequently run into the following scenario: way forward is obstructed or you need to climb up or around an obstacle and the monologue/voice lines will immediately point out the solution. Although saying frequently is inaccurate. It ALWAYS happens, without exceptions. As a matter of fact, the game does not even give you a single second before pointing out the solution. I wish this trend finally ended. At the very least, it should be a toggleable option similar to all the great features outlined in the beginning.

(though, it was strange to compare a man choosing to wear women's armor to a man attempting to climb to the summit of a mountain alone in a snowstorm to prove his worth when he had been looked down on his whole life - especially since nothing in the game world had shown us that transgenderism or homosexuality was frowned upon in the Horizon cultures... so it's presumable that it would have been perfectly normal for a man to wear a woman's armor and not be ostracized for it).Original review:Robots, Dinosaurs, Armaments, Planes, Vehicles. These are a few things most boys, and particularly boys, grow up naturally gravitating towards and enjoying in their childhood and carry into their adulthood. Which is why, ever since Zero Dawn, I couldn't totally understand why they would choose to use a female lead in a game that's essentially about using an array of Armaments against Robot Dinos - a game clearly designed to lure male players by pulling at their most base instincts. But you know... I think for the narrative that's being told, and the way it's being told, I've come to realize that this a female protagonist that works - I certainly couldn't see a male character making some of the decisions or emotional inflections that she makes. And, to be fair, in a market with lots of very preachy, anti-male rhetoric spewing, woke culture worshiping female characters in media, Aloy is definitely not among them. She's more complex, more nuanced, and more balanced. She has emotions that make sense and opinions that have context in her wider environment, and the characters around her are also complex and nuanced, who blend into their contextual environment.Anyway, on to the technicalities and game specifics. This game is wonderfully ported. Aside from some issues with the mouse interface on the map and letter boxing on some menus, everything feels fluid. On my 4090 and 5600x, I'm hitting 90 - 120fps, with dips to 80, on a 1600p 38" ultrawide, without* DLSS (averaging 200 FPS with DLSS, with dips to 140FPS). I wish the LOD was further, as there are some pop-ins in places that I would not expect (e.g. when going down the lift-carriage thing and meeting the sunpriest).Speaking of fluidity, my goodness, animations in this game are an amazing step up from most titles I've played. Not just in combat and open world elements, but even the facial animations and motion acting during dialogs are just excellent. Combined with fantastic voice acting and great writing, I found myself watching the dialog in most interactions play out in full.At this time, I can't see anything particularly negative. If you enjoy open world RPGs, just buy this and play it already!

'Beautiful' is the only word that describes the gameplay, story and visuals of this game. Let's break those three things down. - GameplayI am constantly amazed by how many ways you can play the game compared to Horizon Zero Dawn. There is this new skill tree, in which you can go various ways. From Hunter to Override, from Stealth to Warrior and some more. Choosing your skills will drastically alter the way you play the game and plan your plan of attack (e.g. on a base or herd of machines). It's smooth and the game constantly provides you with tutorials on the newly unlocked abilities. You can travel way easier, since fast travel is free now (only if you travel from one campfire to another). If you prefer travelling by mount, you can ride a lot of new ones as well. The amazing new machines added to the game, make it a totally different experience.There is though a bit of a grind you have to do sometimes to level up for a mission, hence the side missions. Some people like to spend some time leveling up, some don't. That's for you to decide. - The storyI am at the moment some 33 hours into the game, and I am beginning to see the end of the main campaign. After that, there's still the DLC left to complete. Of course, there are numerous side quests and jobs you can do if you wish. I find myself playing much longer than anticipated, purely by the excitement of what comes next. This beautiful campaign sets itself in the West of the post-apocalyptic USA. Exploring this world and encountering various famous landmarks like Las Vegas, makes it all the more fun to explore without actually having to. I won't summarize the story, because you should really just experience it yourself. - The visuals:The amazing landscapes make you sometimes stop during a quest to appreciate the environment you found yourself in. The machines are beautifully designed as well. With a RTX 2070 Super, AMD Ryzen 5 3600 and 32 GB of 3200 MHz of RAM, I can run this game at ultra settings at some 80 - 90 fps. The visuals you get are simply stunning. Overall, it's a 10/10. Having played it for 33 hours I still haven't found anything to complain about. I sincerely encourage you all to buy and enjoy it.This was my first elaborated game review, so I apologize if i have forgotten to speak about some things or the wording seems off.

It's hard to hate on a game that is this well made, but please give me a shot. Both this and HZD have been overshadowed by other games and the general consensus is that they'd be more popular had just the release timing been better. I don't think that's it at all, but rather the core design elements of both games making them unappealing to many players.Fundamentally these are games where you go from point A to point B in order to progress the main story along its predetermined path and every aspect of the game has been specifically designed to help you get there. You get a simple quest log, detailed map, GPS, yellow paint, and a protagonist that won't stop backseating you to help you along. The game is designed so that no actions taken by you--the individual player--will have any major impact, nothing you do will make it significantly easier (or harder!) to finish the game. It's not neutered just when it comes to the story, but also when it comes to how the game plays. You won't be able to make anything unexpected happen through loot discoveries or upgrade choices. The skills and weapons won't synergize, so just pick and use whatever you feel like. There will be absolutely no emergent gameplay of any kind.The Horizon games are the young adult fiction of video games and that's fine, but it shouldn't come as a surprise when experienced gamers completely ignore their existence. They're getting overshadowed by games that are actually interesting to play, despite (or more likely because of) not being polished to the mirror finish Guerilla has managed.
