Absolutely love this game and its predecessor. Favorites for sure. The story, the characters, the graphics, the exploration, the mechanics (especially all the new fun ones added on top of Zero Dawn), the combat styles, the customization for a variety of builds and play styles ... *chef's kiss*. So much fun for me and I don't regret a single hour I played (well... probably should have spread the hours out to do more IRL things over these past few weeks but... meh).Sure, it's pretty clear that they basically wanted to have a remake of The Witcher 3, even down to activities like racing and such, but I don't mind that so much.My one major gripe... NG+ ... it was like a cheap, last-second "oh yeah, we should do that" idea, and they made the lowest level intern throw it all together over a sleepless weekend just before release. Enemies don't seem to have any degree of upscaling, so even bosses that were difficult in the first run become utterly trivial. They add in 8 new legendary weapons which aren't even better than the legendary weapons you already have (plus the ease of obtaining them is a joke).If you were even mostly a completionist in the first run doing all the missions, errands, activities, and required farming for upgrade materials then you easily complete the entire skill tree by the end of the DLC, and they didn't add a single thing for NG+. The "Ghost" levels past level 60 (which is easily obtained before even doing the DLC in the first run) do absolutely nothing whatsoever. I suppose since the enemies aren't upscaled, then it would be even more of a joke to make Aloy continue to gain strength in the DLC, but not having the ability to gain more strength and power for an entire NG+ playthough just makes it boring. I can't say that I don't like feeling like a god, easily stomping every pathetic like Thunderjaw, Rollerback, Dreadwing, and Tenakth rebel boss under my feet as I go through NG+ but... that just gets boring after a while. Upscale the enemies and give the player the chance and need to continue to level up. Without that, you have stagnation. And what's the point in having 100+ unusable skill points just chilling in the upper right corner??If you're going to copy a game like The Witcher 3, and not do anything fun mechanically for NG+, you have to at least do something else like have the player's decisions and conversations have an impact on the story so there can be alternate story lines and endings (e.g. PLEASE give me the chance to kill that d***bag Sylens and allow for some other way for Aloy to find the information he provides in the DLC or for game 3). Give real consequences for story and conversation decisions!In summary: No enemy upscaling + no skill/strength/power advancement + mediocre-at-best new weapons (and only a handful of them) + no impact on the story with decisions = completely worthless NG+.Am I still playing it through to the very end and probably multiple times including fresh games and NG+? 100%. Still one of my favorite games of all time.

Horizon Forbidden West brings players back to the captivating, post-apocalyptic world of Aloy, where technology and nature clash in a stunning open-world landscape. Building on the strong foundation of Horizon Zero Dawn, this sequel enhances the story and gameplay, delivering a richly layered narrative with more nuanced character development and a deeper look into the mysteries of the ancient world.The gameplay is a refined mix of exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving. Forbidden West introduces new weapons, tools, and abilities, such as the Pullcaster for quick traversal and the Shieldwing for gliding, which add depth and variety to movement and combat. Combat against the robotic creatures feels more fluid and tactical, with expanded customization and skill trees that let you truly personalize your playstyle.Quests and side missions feel engaging and well-integrated into the main storyline, with choices that impact relationships with key characters and the outcome of certain events. The game maintains a strong balance between exploration and action, making the open world feel dynamic and rewarding to explore.Visually,  is breathtaking, with intricate detail in environments, character models, and animations. The lush landscapes—from deserts to dense jungles and underwater caverns—are some of the most visually stunning in modern gaming. Lighting, particle effects, and weather dynamics add realism, making the world feel alive and immersive.Horizon Forbidden West excels in nearly every aspect, blending high-stakes storytelling with deeply satisfying gameplay and awe-inspiring visuals. The enhanced combat and exploration mechanics add more layers to the experience without losing the core appeal of the original. Though some side content may feel overwhelming at times, the main story’s pace and richness keep the player invested.For fans of open-world RPGs, Forbidden West is a must-play, delivering one of the best-crafted worlds and narratives in the genre.

Forbidden West is an excellent example of how to make a sequel. It took all of the great things from Zero Dawn and elevated them further, while also adding new gameplay elements of equal quality. The world is beautiful, the story is engaging, and the gameplay is great.

The story was never going to match Zero Dawn, but they did a phenomenal job with the combat system, fleshing out the spear combat while also deepening the machine combat by adding gear upgrades that require specific machine parts, and the story has many, many great moments. Some people criticise the game for making Aloy's character arc take a step back, since her arc in this game is so centered around allowing others to help, despite there being so many allies in Zero Dawn that she had no trouble allowing in. However, she's never really had trouble letting people help in a fight, and she doesn't refuse others' help in combat - what she struggles with is allowing people into her understanding of the old ones. Which is understandable, given the Nora's hostility towards the old world, Eclipse's cooperation with Hades, Sylens',.,.,., Sylensing, and so on. Aloy is no teacher, she doesn't sit hunched over texts from the old ones, getting deep into their cultures and such. She's a tinkerer and a warrior, in desperate need of allies, and this game does a phenomenal job showing her progress through this issue. So while obviously there's no grand series of reveals about Zero Dawn or Enduring Victory or the Faro Plague, there's a really genuine story about Aloy despite the Nora, learning what community, cooperation, and allyship means when faced with [REDACTED].

It's as if the devs read all my criticisms of  and addressed most of them in this ambitious sequel. The result is a big fat satisfying package. It is burdened by having too many systems, which will inevitably result in some of them disappointing some of you. Still, as a whole,  proves that in the right hands big budget AAA games can deliver astounding experiences. It's one the best games I've played in a while.It looks and feels incredible to traverse this world. The design and technology work cohesively to achieve a world-building vision that is tactile, visceral, and very immersive. I often avoided mounts and fast traveling because taking the long way was just so pleasurable. And maybe I would discover a new secret along the way? Unfortunately, Ubisoft-style map markers for most of it rob you of much of the delight of discovery. Also expect red herrings and some empty areas. I'm OK with that: I'll always prefer less but better content. (*cough*  *cough*) And even when there's no "stuff" to find, there is plenty of memorable atmosphere.Tech side note: I did not have any crashes in over 130 hours of play. It took minimal tweaking to get over 60 FPS at 4K, and it felt fluid and satisfying throughout. HDR is non-gimmicky and really adds to the look and feel.I'm not a fan of the  backstory. It's at once too convoluted and too reductive: The downfall of humanity ends up being all about the eye-rolling drama between a handful of immature people on the one hand, and an all-powerful and yet stupid Greek pantheon of AI on the other. It's all quite Marvel-esque and trite. The living characters are also severely one-dimensional over-the-top caricatures. Happily, again, the design and technology come to the rescue. The facial and gesture animations breathe so much life into the blandness that the first game, , could never overcome. Aloy is an uninteresting protagonist, but at least you're able to experience and sympathize with her single-mindedness, lack of patience, and passive-agressive Midwest nice. I don't especially like her. But I can't help but respect her.The best stuff is in the littler stories: the inter-tribal politics and intrigue, individuals and their passions and losses. The themes do get a bit repetitive in a game so big, but I still experienced many surprising and delightful moments.As I said, there are too many systems, though you can safely ignore anything you don't like. There's a lot that's not my cup of tea: I avoided most weapon types, potions, and the cooking system. Also,  copies from  by introducing an in-game board game, but it's so ill-conceived despite being so elaborate. It's not worth complaining about specifics here, but the bottom line is: it sucks. Another annoying piece of side content is the various combat challenges. Look, combat is generally fun and emergent in , but when push comes to shove it falls apart. Uncooperative cameras, getting stuck in terrain, enemies that can throw you into stun loops, all lead to chaos and frustration. You can brute force your way through this crap in the main quests, but the challenges won't let you avoid the worst of it. I only cleared the rest because I had 10-point piece which is basically unbeatable.- input explanations for mechanics is just awful. there are certain moves that have to connect from the first otherwise the chain does not execute. But once obtained, it was super helpful to grab certain things or cheese certain areas.- the orb puzzles are difficult, maybe too difficult sometimes due to lighting.- there should've been some level of underwater combat IMO.- should've had fishing instead of just swimming around and grabbing fish.- wildlife should always drop the necessary resources because catching 50 of the same 1 fish for a single fish bone is insane.- if you move too quickly through story areas, the dialogue cuts off and you miss it- item usage was god-awful. While Zero Dawn was slightly better on the gameplay and had a captivating story with great scifi ideas, this part is still great fun.The different tribes and cultures are super cool. Luckily the relations are more complex and not too black-white as in ZD.The world is, once again very nicely based on the reality, and especially Las Vegas is a great piece, in the middle of the desert but not what you expect. The cauldrons are much better this time, with a lot of changes between them: working cauldrons, broken cauldrons, even flooded cauldrons! Also the tallnecks are more interesting this time. I love those silly tallneck buddies. And the way the world reacts to your achievements adds a fun aspect. Suddenly a whole tribe knows about your deeds and mentions it!Near the end of the game they add the special mount which is a fantastic addition to the gameplay and adds fun options. I also really like Aloy giving hints on a puzzle when you're stuck. It is helpful and a quite clever. The loading times are amazingly fast for such a beautiful game, great optimisation! And the dynamic downscaling when there's too much happening on screen is pretty neat. And having a direct exit options from the game is the way to go.Complaints on the story:The addition of space bad guys was completely unnecessary. They could've kept a cool AI fighting story with scifi ideas just as is. On top of that, they add a "good" baddy that turns out to actually be bad, who could've predicted this?!Really, what are you saying about 'the old ones' with this? That they are all terrible and irredeemable? You set up this person to be different, use it to highlight some Dutch culture (great!), but in the end they are just the same. Boring.And why do bad guys always show up when you're winning? Maybe I've played too many games, I just want to see some tropes be broken every now and then.Here are some minor complaints on the mechanics, as it feels Zero Dawn was much better at this:- The double tap dodge is stupid: the number of times Aloy dives off a massive cliff because I was trying to move a small distance is entirely too many.- Fast travel should be smart enough to not cost a travel pack when standing next to a bonfire.- The damage output when using regular moves is really way too low. This makes the combat very tedious.- There are way too many damage types, you have to constantly change loadout to get the right type for the machine.- There are way too many weapon types combined with damage types, see above.- The items slider on your belt is very tedious to use: finding the correct potion takes ages, which will kill you in battle. To add on that, you're basically constantly eating healing berries in combat. This indicates something is wrong with the combat system.- Mounts cant jump (horse physics is hard, I get it) and get stuck on rocks. So don't try to run away from battle unless the field is clear.- The detection of flying mounts by enemies makes dropping in not really viable, you will be tracked most of the time.- Setting R for both items and reload on weapons makes you accidentally use potions when you want to reload.- The melee pit challenges make no sense and are too strictly defined. Only after finding a trick on the internet are they doable. I mean its interesting fight mechanics, but I just wannablast em!

This game (and its predecessor) are, in my opinion, the best combination of action and puzzle solving I've ever had the pleasure of playing. Like some other RPGs there is the option of running in, "guns blazing" as it were, or sneaking through and taking out your enemies silently. The puzzles provide a good sense of accomplishment when solved, as well.These games also, finally, bring the characters far up the slope out of the uncanny valley, making the graphics of the entire world, humans included, breathtaking.Five stars! Two thumbs up! Will (probably) play again.There's still room to improve, but every negative thing I have to say about this game is nitpicking. Nevertheless, I'll do so:Hair "physics" is  wonky, and anyone with long hair (especially Aloy) has to contend with it often clipping through armor. Pretty sure some (or most) of the facepaint used by the tribes in the game is to cover up their overuse of Botox. Most of the characters have fairly emotive faces, but for a few bits that are a bit too stationary. And some are mostly frozen in place.There are too many. Three different types of bows which work at different ranges, boltcasters, tripcasters, spear-throwers, slings, a boomerang-thing that only seems to "return" in the animation rather than the ammo count, plus the spear. And I'm not counting the heavy weapons you can grab from certain machines or the fixed ballistas, or one further weapon which I'm fairly certain exists but I haven't gotten yet. Each one of these may have multiple types of ammo for different elements which the enemies might be weak to. Plus targeting ammo. And there are so many different elemental types now! So you've finally managed to work your weapon inventory to have one or two of each elemental ammo. You come across a machine that's weak to one of them, but your character, who's built for ranged combat, only has a close-range weapon with that elemental type. Or you run into one of the myriad machines who aren't weak to anything in particular, and, as a matter of fact, are strong to nearly everything. There are ways around this, and weapons which don't have this problem, but learning it took me dozens of hours. Oh, and why does each weapon have to have its own targeting reticle?While I understand wanting to do most of them within the game engine to make everything as seamless as possible, a bit more of a hands-on approach to directing them could have improved a couple of them greatly. Clipping is again a problem, and showing a character pull where a handle should be and having the handle bounce off it with the physics engine was a bit jarring.This is the nitpickiest of them all, probably, and I've certainly not finished the game, but there are so, so many sidequests! This has its upsides and downsides. For upsides, I'm never short of things to do. For downsides, there's no way aside from guides to know which sidequest might yield which gizmo. I know all the necessary ones are on the main quest, but the sidequests have yielded some interesting ones! Fortunately so far the content has seemed to mostly level with the player, so I don't feel  over-leveled even if the quest indicates it's for level 15 and I'm level 31. That could also be because I suck, though.

I have played Horizon Zero Dawn on both PS4 and PC, and Forbidden West on PS5 for a few hundred hours combined across all systems. HFW fixes and improves upon every single flaw, problem, nitpick and issue I had the original HZD and delivers an absolutely solid sequel in almost every possible way minus a few personal caveats and gripes.I have an AMD 5800X3D w/ a 7900XT (AMD Adrenaline 23.40.19.01 drivers at the time of this review) and 32GB of DDR4-3200 G-Skill RAM. This game plays at absolute max settings with zero issues at all at both 1440p, and also at full native 4K without so much as missing a beat. Average FPS from the intro mission is 80-100FPS with effectively no stutter, lag, hitching, or massive frame-time drops/spikes. Nixxes Software did an absolutely solid port of HFW to PC and it shows.For a launch day release this performance blows the PS5 away and is damn near perfect. If you can push the quality, the visuals exceed the PS5.Without going into any spoilers or specifics, Forbidden West does a lot of things well and my gripes are by no means a slight against the game as a whole. This is going to be subjective to everyone and is mainly my own two cents. For the things HFW does excellent; it extends and continues the story of HFW, grows the lore of the world, has fantastic character interactions and growth. Lots of awesome cinematic moments and action sequences that really do well, and ofc really leaves you anxious to know more about the world and what is to come.However, I feel like it falls off towards the third act of the game with the introduction of certain characters. Both in regards to the how/what/why of the certain secrets/motivations that are revealed for the overall plot and the characters(s) of the game. Certain characters feel underutilized or shoved off to the side, other characters feel extremely shallow or trope-y to the point of being very cheesy or don't feel as fleshed out enough.Also certain plot elements feel like they were resolved too quickly or were hand-waved away for the sake of other aspects of the story. I don't know if this is good, bad or questionable.With the way the game ended, in retrospect I am not sure if I like what is coming. It feels like it could go massively epic for Horizon 3, or if this potentially has the 'game trilogy problem' and we're walking into a into a Mass Effect 3 landmine.If HZD was Mass Effect 1, this feels like Mass Effect 2 with all the good and bad. I am just hoping that Guerrilla has the ability to pull off the magic with Horizon 3.

While it has many strong sides, it makes too many classic faults of any sequel. Short version: The story endures, but gameplay mechanics fail miserably. Worth buying off a sale, but not regular price.First the upsides. The game is gorgeous to look at. It's not just scenery either, but the characters and robots have wondrous amounts of detail. The absolutely pristine graphics are supported by a simple yet well functional soundtrack. This game is massive, you have gameplay for a long, long time. The characters are mostly well planned and balanced, with a nice package of old and new. The plot offers sufficient quirks and charms to keep the mind active, as well as sufficient story events to make you truly enjoy your victories. The plot will nicely twist you along the way and more shoes drop here and there, for joy and sorrow. There is a humongous amount of dialogue, which can be tiring, but skipping it is usually possible. Personally, I appreciate the depth of the lore. Moral dilemmas without a clear right choice are also a beautiful part of the pack.This can be up or down depending to your taste, but Forbidden West is far less action, far more puzzle, in just about every mission, main and side. Personally, I found most of the platforming puzzles infuriating to no end. While the puzzles aren't that difficult to figure out, the platformer part means repeating things over, over, over and over. When you finally finish it, there's no sense of achievement. That's bad. Another up-or-down thing is the complexity of weapons, skills, attacks and such. Gameplay can become excessively complex trying to figure this all out - but you can ignore most of it. It's such a pity that game designers seem to forget that simple is beautiful. Unless you're an arcade fighting game veteran, there's little chance to remember every key combo for every special attack in every unique situation. But if you are such a veteran, you might find fun new styles of gameplay. The biggest downside is horrendously bad game controls. An excessive amount of platform puzzles combined with a constantly failing control system is a deadly mix. You will fall down from simple staircases now and then, and from complex jump-glide-hook combos even more often. Early in the game you will drown, because the diving controls are even worse. And if you're in a fight instead of a puzzle, you will find yourself stuck in a corner, unable to move, far too often. Whether it's adventuring or fighting, you'll find yourself unable to see anywhere or figure where to go with trees and more masking your way on all sides. It's really no single one thing, but the combination of this all makes gameplay immensely frustrating. The problem builds on itself at times. For example, trying to get all fighting achievements is supposed to be tough, but should not be miserable due to gameplay bugs and other issues. Twice the complexity needs ten times the quality, not half of it.If you want all the goodies and upgrades, you will grind trying to get all the parts. It's not supposed to be too easy, but trying a good fifty times just to get the right subtype of enemy to show may cause keyboards to fly. The balance needs tweaks. A slow and inconsistent map makes this worse. As for the DLC, it builds upon gameplay mechanics discovered at the end of the main game. Again, very strong storyline and great characters, including some events I absolutely could not have guessed. The amount of puzzles is more reasonable than in the main game, and the option of using more stealth is available, but not forced, in several missions. Like the main game, the greatest fault is gameplay mechanics which fail even more in the DLC's scenery. But that scenery is really something.I can appreciate the difficulty of creating a sequel far too well. One needs to add more content, yet avoid excessive complexity. It needs to work for the veterans and newcomers. They certainly added more, but failed to make it all work. Unfortunately, I could not recommend this, not at normal price anyways. Nice try though. Maybe third time's the charm?This review was updated throughout after finishing the main game, DLC and all quests.

SPOILERS BELOWBefore I start, absolutely turn on the setting which highlights climbable points and skips the picking-up animation. This will greatly improve your overall experience. Now then...I'd rate this an 8/10. The story I thought actually started really well and was engaging, a seamless transition from the excellent story of the first game. The world is beautiful, Aloy has tons of new skills and options, and the new machines are really cool. However around the midway point, the cracks started to really appear and dampened the overall experience for me.  The story started to go off the rails after Gaia recovers her three subordinate functions. Up until that point, I thought it was great- the biosphere is failing and this buys needed time while a more permanent solution is sought. I think this world should have done without the Far Zeniths, I loved the speculation that humans were still out in the universe somewhere from the research facility, but when they actually returned... It was really lackluster. We spend 99% of our time with them thinking they want to reseed the earth, then at the last second we get a twist that no one saw coming from Tilda saying they actually just wanted to use Earth as a waypoint to keep running from Nemesis. To me, this flew in the face of everything we learned about them and was just dumb. Then Tilda turns evil at the last second, says she loved Elisabet and that Aloy is her more advanced self and she wants her to flee to the stars with her... then immediately turns into a giant robot and tries to kill her. WTF lol. The map is gigantic and has lots of different environments, all of it beautiful and fun to explore/interact with, however a pattern does emerge relatively fast in the quests. Just go and collect things for little reward. Scaling a mountain for an item is only fun so many times- there needs to be more incentive for doing this and finishing all of the metal flowers, for example. My biggest gripe about this game which IMO brings it down from an 8.5-9 rating alone is the melee combat. It's so bad. The game gives you all of these cool melee combos to unlock, but any time you try to pull them off, an enemy just interrupts you. On the flip side, it's very hard to impossible to interrupt enemy combos. The animation appears to be off, and I came to accept I would just get hit and couldn't do anything about it except heal right after. Aloy also does almost no damage with her spear (which unlike all her other equipment can't be upgraded), even on what are touted as high damage moves like grapple strike. For ranged combat, the machines will often "fake you out" with either bad animations or programming and dodge your arrows on what should be surefire hits. Just play the game for a few hours and you'll see what I mean. Two other things I wished were improved were the mini game Strike (in theory this is awesome but needs more tool tips during your opponents phase to explain what is going on during their turn), and an explanation of Apex machines and the specific loot they drop. There is something about the day/night cycle (also just thrown in the game and never explained why you would want to skip time) which affects this, but quests will point you to a specific area to kill a machine and it's not actually the Apex variant you need where it told you to go. Last thought, I don't like that the Burning Shores expansion can't be started until after the main game. I know this was due to it being only available on the PS5, but I'm honestly burnt out on Horizon and am not sure if I'll play it. Would rather do that mid-way during my play through. TLDR: If you liked the first game, you will probably like this one. The story is good until the halfway point before it loses itself. Melee combat needs to be buffed, and some enemy animations need polishing.

Reviewing a 100+ hour game is always a difficult endeavor. There's always a plethora of activities to partake in. There's metagames to play and games within games within games. There are things to collect and catalogue and I wouldn't be surprised if there were taxes and forms to file in game as well. Having played 91 hours of those hundred and only having obtained 61% of its achievements feels like I am still missing out even after spending so much time in game. I still have so many greyed-out illustrations in the overworld. I still have side missions to complete and vistas to admire. I am still missing out.~ Estimated reading time 4-6 mins ~Most of the time that's how games like these make me feel. The all consuming behemoth of the open world collectathon formula. There is always more to do, more to see, but unfortunately you are always left feeling a kind of emptiness. A kind of emptiness that makes playing the game a numbing experience. It feels like it wants me stuck in a mandatory loop of hyperfocus - crossing out items on a checklist. Every box checked triggers my brain into releasing tiny little drops of pure liquid dopamine.I realize that I'm very much describing what burnout is in a way. I realize that maybe it's my fault for interfacing with the game in the way I have. The story is actually well paced (albeit with way too much exposition for my taste). It wasn't really necessary to binge the game like I did - but in my mind the experience feels paradoxical in a way as well. How could I not binge it when it's very clearly designed to be played like that? Burnout feels inevitable in games like these my friends, so please heed my words of warning.In any case, this game is absolutely stunning! It's a marvel to look at in every moment. It's definitely the most beautiful and inspiring (graphically) game I've ever played. Out of my 91 hours playing the game probably at least 30 were spent in the photo editor (joke). The amount of detail is overwhelming and it's hard to grasp the amount of work that went into the game. Everything, from the way the grass sways as the wind softly nudges it, to the FLAWLESS facial animations, to how machines discombobulate when you hit their weak points with an arrow, exudes polish. I mean, it's a game where water actually looks incredible! they found a way to program waves and everything. Words mean nothing when trying to describe the visual integrity of the game and how well it connects with everything. I adore that it's very exploration focused and that it delights the player with many different vibes and biomes. As I played it I remember mentioning to my wife how cool it must be to be in charge of designing the looks of the different tribes that appear in game. The structures and their fashion choices change depending on the biome. Whether it's a marsh, a snowy mountain or a tropical beach you can rest assured that the people that habit the area will be dressed accordingly. This does wonders for immersion.Another high point of the game is its combat (for the most part). The game has an incredible amount of monster variety (around 43 different types). It helps that monsters are machines modelled after real life animals most of the time - so you have monkeys, hippos, deer, panthers, rhinos, a mix of some and elemental variations of some as well. You never stop seeing new mobs that have different dangerous looking hooks and claws that can kill you in 10 different ways. Aloy (our protagonist), thankfully, has a huge ass arsenal of light and heavy weapons to defend herself and tbh this is one of the main reasons the game is so addictive. You only start with a bow & arrow, but as you start offing machines you can find and upgrade new weapons with their machine carcasses. Weapon progression is very nicely paced (with exception of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ piece of ♥♥♥♥ iron flowers which aren't really weapons, but a ridiculously thick-skulled way of stopping player progression altogether) and depending on how much you grind you can become very overpowered. There is melee battling in this game but there is not a lot to say about it. It feels flimsy and underpowered throughout the whole game (even taking into account the new combo system introduced in this game) and it was way more annoying than helpful.The story is pretty cool. I can always vibe with a post apocalyptic interpretation of the world any day. It has all the really good sci-fi stuff: clones, machines, aliens from outer space, sentient AI and a tiring humongous quest to save all humanity from itself. Despite the voice acting being one of the best in the game (heh), the game suffers from very bland character writing and it is SUCH a shame to see. At many points in the game I felt happy to see so much potential for a character but it was crushing to be immediately disappointed when they were revealed to be the stereotypical ultra villainized 1980s James Bond character. Bad guys that can't be empathized with aren't really good bad guys, they're just lazily written bad bad guys if you know what I mean.I really don't like giving a mixed review for a game with so much effort and polish behind it. I had so many good times with it, but they feel like they were always tarnished by something - and most of the times it was the crashing. I have no clue how a 69x triple A game passes QA when it crashes like this game does. A story that is unfortunately becoming more common in modern gaming. I rarely complain about this, but I feel like it shouldn't be acceptable for a game nowadays to crash so much that it deters me from wanting to play it (and yeah, I spent days troubleshooting everything). I almost gave up on it, but I am glad I didn't.All in all, Horizon Forbidden west is an extremely aesthetic experience with very finely tunes controls and combat. It's a joyous experience until the bloat gets too overwhelming or the game crashes on you 420 times per second.I give it a 3 Aloe out of 5 🌿🌿🌿

I really loved HZD. The story gripped me and I appreciated how experimental the game was when it came to fighting all the different machines that were a sight to behold. This was one of my most anticipated games of the year, but something felt off while I have been playing it over the past few months. I think it finally clicked for me that I just hate how overcomplicated gameplay wise this game is. The first game definitely had the Ubisoft formula design when it came to the open world; however, that game felt really tight. The game never forced you to fight hundreds of the high level beasts to upgrade your gear. There was a linear progression to upgrading your weapons. Even something like the outposts only had like 5 locations for you to do. In this game, there is like 20 outposts and 5ish camps that are more akin to what is found in the original.I hate how many weapons there are. I hate how much of a hassle it is to upgrade your weapons. I hate how material intensive some tools are with traps basically being nonexistent for me because of their cost. I hate how aggressive the enemies are now and how they can knock you around like crazy. I hate how long it takes for Aloy to get up. I hate how the melee works. Sure, they “improved” it by adding actual mechanics instead of just pressing two buttons but hits still don’t have impact and they just drag down the pace of fights. Why is there no parry button either?I hate how much the enemies move around, not only do the move around way too much while you're trying to target a weakspot but there are pieces of armor that obscure said weakspot and even if you get a shot in you are asked to do that again another 3-5 times before disabling / removing the component all while running out of focus and having other enemies wail on you. I'm at the point now where I just avoid combat altogether, it's simply not fun. Every time I have to enter combat now I just groan because it’s always a war of attrition. "Horizon Forbidden West" is a triumph in gaming, building upon everything that made Horizon Zero Dawn a masterpiece. Guerrilla Games has truly pushed the boundaries of open-world gaming, delivering an experience that's as visually stunning as it is captivating in gameplay and storytelling. Set in a lush post-apocalyptic landscape teeming with advanced robotic wildlife and complex tribal societies, the game combines high-tech wonders with ancient mysteries in an engaging, well-balanced way.The protagonist, Aloy, is central to the appeal of Forbidden West. In this sequel, Aloy’s character development shines even brighter. She’s determined, empathetic, and an absolute force to be reckoned with, but it’s her vulnerability and humanity that make her truly unforgettable. Through her interactions, we see her struggle with the burden of being humanity's savior, while still caring deeply for the people around her. This depth adds layers to her character that resonate with players on a personal level.Visually, Forbidden West is a marvel, with the game world rendered in exquisite detail. From shimmering coastal waters to lush jungles and towering mountains, every landscape feels alive. The combat system is more refined than ever, blending fluidity with tactical depth. Aloy’s arsenal of tools and weapons has expanded, allowing for varied approaches in taking down the diverse range of mechanical beasts. Each encounter is a puzzle, a dance of strategy and precision that’s immensely rewarding.The narrative is also superb, with themes of environmentalism, technology, and human resilience woven seamlessly into the game. Guerrilla Games managed to craft a story that keeps you invested not only in the fate of the world but also in Aloy’s personal journey.Overall, Horizon Forbidden West is a stellar sequel that improves on its predecessor in every way. With its compelling protagonist, stunning visuals, and immersive gameplay, it’s a must-play for fans of open-world RPGs and anyone looking for a story-driven adventure that’s both meaningful and exhilarating.

Forbidden West is similar to Zero Dawn in many ways. The game mechanics remained largely the same. There are new machines, weapons, armor, skills, and even things like food from various cooks scattered throughout the map and a board game mini game.The problem that Forbidden West has is the writing. While most of it is okay, there is too much crybaby stuff going on. Beta is the worst. The amount of religious zealotry is almost sickening, not to mention it's been done a million and one times. The Burning Shores DLC is also very bad in this regard, and is, of course, yet another story that has been ruined by some flimsy romance introduced at the last second, despite it having one of the best villains for how short your exposure is to him. For real, Walter is a great and truly horrible POS. I don't know what it is about Sam Witwer, but he should have gotten way more into voice acting.Like Zero Dawn, Forbidden West doesn't really start until NG+. You keep almost everything, but there are a few things you might not want to bother with before NG+. Override progress gets reset. You're given the only two you really need, so don't bother with the others until you reach a permanent game state. Also, only prepare as much as you need to for whichever difficulty you plan on playing. The gear you pick up before NG+ will be out shined by NG+ versions. Hit level cap if you plan on playing ultra hard. Coils and Weaves are mostly obtained from vendors, and they never replenish their stock, which means you'll want to make sure you obtain what you need on each play through, including the first. I do not recommend playing all content, though, as you'll want fresh stuff in the new game.Feel free to reset your skills at will. You'll eventually get enough points to pick up everything. Don't be afraid to spend materials on upgrades. The only time it might not be smart is if you're playing on hard or ultra hard, since things are more difficult to farm.My last bit of advice is to play Zero Dawn first if you haven't already.

I'd like to preface this with, Horizon Zero Dawn, this games predecesor, is one of my absolute most favorite games I've ever played. It is one of the most diverse, touching and immersive games I've ever had the honor to play. The characters, and cultures in that game are derived from deep thoughts on how humans would grow and gain culture in different situations. The lore was so detailed, and the cultures so impressive, it all felt as though they could really happen.I spent 145 hours in HFW with the above in mind, and I have a few things to say.But first, let me give you my scores:Graphics: 10/10Gameplay: 8/10Base Game Story: 5/10DLC Story: 2/10Graphics: By all that there is I've never seen anything quite so beautiful, the artists did such a fine job of making the end of the world a place one would love to see the sights of. I found very few graphics issues, and I couldn't be happier with how the visuals of everything turned out. Splendid!Gameplay: An absolute improvement on the original, this game shines in combat in ways the previous game couldn't hold a candle to. The machines, new and old are splendidly crafted works of brutal art that I couldn't hope to achieve in my dreams. Although, those who played can easily attest to the invention of some damage sponging mechanics, the inventory management, the grinding for item upgrades, and the aggressively buggy parkour and various minor issues in the game that make you want to take up residence as the next thunderjaw to spawn by meridian. But all in all, it's easily overlooked and bypassed.Base Story: Here's where things get a little less lovely. The overall straight through story for the base game isn't the worst thing, not by far. However, they did abandon some very interesting plot points, and pivot midway into something... odd, and then the set up for the 3rd game is essentially the same thing as this game, just more annoying.The resulting plot seemed somewhat, off, but workable for the most part.You might wonder why then, the game has such a low score for me if thus far the praises are flowing? Well, they did the worst possible thing they could, they abandoned their own beautifully crafted world, cultures, story telling and wonder and instead substituted in IRL political leanings. Quests are just methods of showing you how dumb men are, or which 'isms' they're pointing to, or just as a way to point out that the characters are in an LGBTQ+ relationship.You will not find beautifully crafted cultures with the new tribes, no, they're just a few themes slapped together, sometimes just to point out how xy or z is bad IRL. The game is what you'd call WOKE, now don't get that confused with it being diverse. The original game was a fantastic example of diversity, some of the best I've seen.As for characters, it's even worse. Strong, respectable Alloy starts the game as a very unsavory mean spirited individual a real backend, to her friends and her comrades from the first game, or to random people on the street. They characterize it as burdens of the savior, but in reality as soon as she finds another woman she changes personality completely. She spends the majority of the game as a spiteful, mean spirited person, with exceptions for, well only women or LGBTQ+ individuals. And the DLC doesn't help the strange personality flipping, which feels extremely forced.80% of the NPC's you speak too are the same flavor of angry facebook female, and some of their dialogue seems ripped from posts you'd find there. More often than not, every single one of them is long suffering the effects of some ignorant male that you then need to deal with in some way shape or form.All but maybe 4-6 straight male characters are, stupid, simps, pathetic, emasculated, LGBTQ+, jerks or evil ranging from puppy kickers to I kid you not, literal Disney villain. And of course all of them are single dimensional, all the male villains are straight evil with zero extra qualities, the female villains are almost completely vindicated via sad backstories and feelings.The DLC is all that much worse, it's just an shallow anti capitalism, anti establishment, anti law enforcement hate festival with what has to be the coolest boss fight in all the series.My final thoughts:When I finished the base game, I actually didn't want to continue onward to the DLC. I felt exhausted, whittled down and utterly unsatisfied by the world that was laid out before me. It was empty of all the depth I'd hope to see, and filled with reflections of the day today in American politics.I'm glad I stuck to it and played the DLC, its a beautiful map, with some really nice places to visit, and it has the coolest boss battle ever. But even still it was also, just a sad reflection of our reality. Not the cool, amazing world that we first got a look at years ago.Though the majority of the interactions in this game are bunk, I do feel I should point out that there are some truly fantastic moments in this game, untainted, or only slightly tainted by the woke agenda. I hope you enjoy those moments as much as I did, and I hope to see more of them in future games.Recommended Buyers:- If you don't care about story, dialogue, depth of world building or anything of that nature- If you are an avid fan of HZD and really wanna know whats happening, hopefully theres a 3rd game and it is much much betterRecommended Skippers:- If you are a person who cannot stand woke content- If you are a person driven by story or character depthI will be returning for the 3rd game, if one is made. For those of you who want to see this beautiful world and great cast of characters flourish, make sure you speak your mind on these things.Rest In Peace: Lance Reddick, I hope you found your Apollo

This barely qualifies as a video game. I'd call it a "semi-interactive story told through computer graphics".HFW has top notch production all around. Even outside of cutscenes Aloy and her pals don't stop blabbering. Compare to Elden Ring. ER has the vaguest sense of story lines. You're expected to use your imagination to fill in the blanks. And it works.To be frank, this is a game built for women. Constantly hearing about everyone's feelings, relationships, motivations, and inner struggles isn't something that works for most men. That's fine, obviously women play games too, but just know what this is. I'm sure I'll finish this game at some point.  For what it is, this is still a great game. It could have been so much better if they'd toned down the storytelling and focused on combat. Here's a story: an alien AI seeded earth with artificial life and we have to wipe it out. Give us missions that are built around increasingly more challenging combat scenarios... like all souls-like games. Simple and satisfying.A word on the world, and controls. It's yellow paint run amok. I'm old enough to remember the earliest video arcades. There was this new game called "Dragon's Lair" that entered the fray. It essentially a collection of video clips. You were  expected you to press some control at the right time to advance the game to the next video clip. HFW has a lot of similarities. For example, the climbing is just press up, press right, press A, and so on. There's no danger of falling. As long as you press the direction, Aloy does her fancy move. It looks great, but there's no skill involved and no danger or chance of failing. Again, this just makes you feel like you're just advancing a story, not conquering a challenge.

Ok so, i've spent 20 hours on this, so i think i can draw a more accurate review than my old one (which was mainly a technical review on how the port runs).I confirm everything i said in my initial review with some minor tweakings: i did come across a couple of graphical glitches, mainly concearning the LOD (basically distant objects like mountains) and the sky. Under certain conditions (i cannot verify which ones, but it's mostly happening when you are in ruined buildings) the sky at points turn black with the LOD glitching out during certain camera angles. It's not the end of the world, but it's noticeable and distracting, especially considering how stunning this game looks maxed out.Performances fps wise are 98% the same as my initial reviews, what i noticed tho that once you unlock the "west" (you'll understand what i mean, i don't want to spoil) i noticed that for the most part the cpu usage increases. For me it's not an issue as i have a moderately new gen 8 core (5800x) but be sure to have adequate cooling for your cpu, as mine with a 420mm liquid cooler and being undervolted can reach up to 65 degrees, and i would imagine the same cpu under stock conditions and most importantly cooler, it might get loud and toasty. Nothing that will break your cpu, im just making you aware if you all of a sudden notice your pc being louder. I only in one instance (was a mob fight) had a single stutter.Now for the stuff i actually didn't like that much: The default keyboard layout (not an issue if you decide to play with a controller). Having the weapon wheel on F was a bad stock choice (i don't understand why they didn't keep it as the tab key like its predecessor) and the focus being on the V key might require some time to get used to. Nothing too drastic, but still worth a mention. I don't understand why they didn't keep the same layout as HZD which was very good. Another issue i have (still it's mostly with Keyboard+Mouse set up) is how badly small movements are to control. You don't know how many times i fell from stuff because aloy decided on herself to take 20 steps when i only pressed the W key for a millisecond lol. That can get quite annoying especially in the esploration/puzzles part of the game.I've read a lot of reviews complaining on the combat system, and i have to somewhat agree. You have no on screen indication you're at low health (sure, there's the auto heal function when low hp in the accessibility tab options in the game, but what if i don't want to make the game do stuff for me... i want to actually play this game, not having some sort of automated macro that does things for me). Weapons DEFINITELY feel extremely under powered even when fighting mobs 5+ levels lower than you (and yes, all upgraded and slotted with coils), especially compared to HZD. I started the game on hard, but had to quickly revert to normal, and stuff can get pretty rough still (not just in the first few hours when you are objectively under powered). I could be more ok with this if this wasn't made to be a more action based game compared to its predecessor (as i said, stealth is still an option, but it's clearly not the way devs intended this game to be played). Overall "thanks" to the poor keyboard mapping and the clunkiness some fights can bring it can get pretty frustrating (and not in a good way as a souls game or monster hunter can be), especially in the first few hours of the game.So yes, aside these few issues, i can confirm everything i've said in my first review: fantastic port (from a technical standpoint) and game if you like open world story driven rpgs and can overlook the clunky (at times, not always) combat. I'd say compared to the first one, it leans more on the action side of things. Stealth is still a thing, but it's definitely not as "OP" as it was in HZD. You can still clear mobs using stealth but it requires A LOT more patience to do so. So yeah, if you liked HZD for its "stealthiness" you might get disappointed here, so beware of that. Cheers, and i hope you can enjoy the game as much as i am! Welp, nixxes did it again.Superb port. Granted, i have a high specced pc (5800x, 32gb of ddr4 3600mhz cl 16 and a 6900xt as gpu) but this port runs flawlessly 1440p native at around 85/90 fps (no fsr used also, and be mindful that you need to go in the options of the launcher and disable it, because it is on by default). The game looks amazing. I haven't played the ps5 version but there's already a digital foundry video explaining the various difference, and while they might not seem a lot, it looks visually stunning.Im still pretty much in the intro, and no bugs have been found (granted, it's still early, but usually when a game is a mess it is from the get go), no crashes, no visual glitches.The gameplay and game mechanics will be plenty familiar if you played the original (horizon zero dawn). They added a few nuances expanding the exploration even more (you got some sort of grappling hook that can tear down stuff, granted, it has to be possible it's not like you can tear down every single object lol, this is not minecraft).The soundtrack, much like the gameplay, is pretty much a rehash of HZD with some recurring theme from the original game, so if you like it (i did, very thematic) you'll like the one in this game too.What else to say, if you are a fan of the first game, this is a must purchase. Incredible port and thank you nixxes for that again (naughty dog, you should learn something from these guys). If you never played it, see it as if the witcher 3 and assassin's creed (the modern open world ones) had a wonderful baby called Horizon Zero Dawn. So if you like open world (without being too vast and empty), sidequests, robotic monsters, a deep story without being too contrived, this is an absolute must buy for you.

Horizon Forbidden West (HFW) is a fantastic experience, especially with the Burning Shores expansion, which feels more like an extension of the series rather than a standalone game. The controls will be familiar to players of the previous installment, with some new battle mechanics and weapon styles added. If you prefer sticking to the classic bow and arrow gameplay, that’s perfectly viable too.The game does have its downsides, particularly the grind required in certain areas, seemingly just to extend playtime. The progression could have been streamlined for a tighter experience. On Ultra Hard difficulty, success often relies more on grinding for legendary gear to win through attrition rather than pure skill. The melee system feels unnatural, locked behind a skill tree, and even when fully upgraded, melee combat in the open world is riskier than ranged combat.Machine Strike is an interesting addition, but once you figure out how to exploit it with a long-range, wide-attack piece, the challenge diminishes. Playing it in real life would be tedious without a way to record damage, health, and terrain effects, leading to constant checks and potential disputes.Certain design choices, like invisible walls around Demeter, can be immersion-breaking. Some puzzles feel unnecessary when it seems you could easily reach your goal without them. The inconsistency of climbable surfaces is also frustrating, with some obvious routes being blocked off while others that look impassable can be climbed.Despite these issues, HFW is an exceptionally polished game. It does tend to hold your hand a bit too much, with Aloy frequently vocalizing hints just as you’re figuring things out, which can undermine the satisfaction of solving puzzles on your own.Overall, it’s a very solid game with a lot of polish, though some elements could have been better executed to enhance the immersion and player experience.

I want to split this review up into two parts, Horizon Forbidden West and Horizon Burning Shores. It took About 82 hours to get through both at about 90% completion at what I consider an average pace. First, let's get the basics out of the way that are echoed in other reviews:Yes, it is a good port. (Sad we have to count this as a positive but, hey that's the game industry now)Yes, the foundations of the first game exist in their entirety and are genuinely built upon with things such as flying mounts, new robots, new weapons, etc.Yes, it check boxes every open world trope in the book save for a few items.Yes, this is a single player narrative game where the developer/publisher wants to collect your data. It does not require you to be online. (If you care about these things)Yes, It is a good game. I mean really it is a good game. Not the best game ever. Not the most amazing thing out there. But it is a good 6/10. Why? See below.Still here? Great! Spoilers discussed further.Horizon Forbidden West: Is it worth it? I think so.A complex continuity issue... not from Zero Dawn, the developers do a great job of explaining away Aloy's shield armor being broken and her weapons being gone. Because, now only the Zeniths get that fancy shield tech and you need a reason to re-acquire all these new fancy weapons which are neat! But, require a significant grind to level up (seriously they needed to tone that down with Apex spawn rates being what they are). It really is all of the other things that don't quite add up.The beginning of the game establishes that Aloy spent her time post Zero Dawn relentlessly pursuing Gaia. In that pursuit she forsakes her closest allies and unintentionally burned some bridges. I admit it was hard for me to look past it when I first saw how badly she treated Varl, her closest ally and only Nora companion. Not only Varl but the others as well. She gets the welcoming she deserves when reuniting with certain figures from Zero Dawn. Let's all remember now that Horizon Forbidden West is a product of its time. However, progressive and problematic that may seem to anyone. I don't blame the character as much as the writing and direction of the game. Aloy displays toxic traits towards her closest allies and towards key characters in the story along the way for no real apparent reason. This could be rooted in her past as a Nora outcast but she always seemed to push past it and focus on the task at hand like an intelligent mature human being. So what changed? The mission to restore Gaia and save the world being a singular focus, maybe. But that's not really it. Some things don't add up, and it shows. This is where we dive past the volumetric clouds, the dynamic day/night cycles and over all amazingly beautiful art direction this game has compared to Zero Dawn. The cracks begin to form and show just how shallow the game's writers portray Aloy, her companions, key NPC's and the world's events can be trivialized.In Forbidden West all that really matters are the game's main events. The rest are unfortunately fluff. Notches on the belt. Token checkmarks to no real ends. And believe me, if Guerrilla Games is going to insult the player by allowing Aloy to 'squeeze through' small spaces, but then require players to get past a locked door when the only thing between them and the other side is a human sized gap in a rusty metal frame? They are going to insult you with trivialized fetch quests.Forbidden west doesn't even give the Tenakth the respect and understand they deserve as a major power in the region. The Carja, the Nora, the Oseram are all very distinct and uniquely cultured. Zero Dawn defined these people through main/story and side quests. It's clear that not much care was given to define the Tenakth, unlike the Utaru who are distinct in their own way. The Tenakth are separated by blue tribe, red tribe, and magenta tribe. It's kind of laughable in most of the side quests how trivialized they are as a major threat to anyone. Heck, even Aloy's first meeting with the Tenakth Chief Hekarro goes about as well as a Karen asking for the Manager. To Hekarro's credit he handles it like a boss. I don't know if that was the writers intention but they made Aloy look like like a complete idiot. Just like you as a player because the game's more concerned about wasting your time by trying to get one crate on top of another to get over a rusted chain link fence than it is with portraying any depth to the world building.Oh yeah, the Quen exist. They represent the 1%'s fan base on Twitter. They are about as goofy as the Fallout Vault Dwellers. That's really about it.Speaking of the 1%, The Zeniths... Space Jeff Bezos is the key big bad. Or is he?!  Seriously, I really don't think this was given a lot of thought, and it shows in its execution.Now for what it is worth I won't mention some of the bigger events in Forbidden West which actually does make all of this worth it. There are some amazing side characters who do have compelling and wonderful stories to share with you as a player. You'll experience their emotion, good and bad. It's not all just fetch quests and check boxes. Two Oseram sisters and their big adventures with explosions lighten an otherwise heavy mood. Meeting an old friend in Burning Shores. How Aloy and Beta are so starkly contrast but eventually find common ground. Even Sylens's (RIP Lance Reddick) part shows that the narrative can at times be mature! That every character has their flaws and are redeemable. A story about humanity should have a very human element and this story does.So that's Forbidden west, in a nutshell a somewhat contrived continuation of one of the most compelling and original Sci-Fi IP's in the recent decade.Burning Shores: Is it worth it? Not really, no.What's to say? Aloy goes to LA. Unlike modern LA this one looks nice as it only took the end of the human race to wipe it clean. HAH. Anyway, she is trying to track down the escaped Zenith Howard Hughes... or is it Elon Musk? I don't know at this point. But, before she gets past the cut scene she gets shot down by the plot McGuffin. She then meets Seyka a Quen Marine. It's really hard to write anything positive or negative about this particular DLC. Whomever pitched Burning Shores clearly had something in mind but wasn't given the time nor the budget to give it the proper place in the Horizon IP that it deserved. Which begs the question, why even try?Really though, I won't waste my time on the story or anything else because Guerrilla didn't either. This story had all potential to be as equal if not more amazing as Frozen Wilds. It really could have taken its time to really do more world building. It could of focused on flushing out the Quen's story. It could of helped solidify Aloy and Seyka's relationship into something real and compelling. It could of been the proper launching point into Horizon 3 that it deserved to be. Instead, Burning Shores just exists...So yeah, that's Burning Shores...

The difficulty. I'm playing on "hard" for a little extra challenge. When the game is easy its very easy. I tear through enemies with zero problems and it isn't even close. But when it's hard? It's frustrating. There is no in between. You're either falling asleep mindlessly killing enemies or dodging a trillion attacks and watching Aloy try to draw a bow between. This goes for the minigames and training pits too. You either steamroll or get steamrolled. Play anything less then "hard" and you might as well be on "super easy", play on "hard" or above and be ready for the quests that force you to fight three massive machines at the same time in an open area with zero cover. I'm aware this is a skill issue but I'm writing this for people who don't beat fromsoft games blindfolded with a dance pad. 2. The melee combat. They've added a bunch of new combos that change depending on whether you throw a light, a heavy or hold one for a second. This is fine except the combos hardly ever work and in a real fight they are mostly useless. Enemies will sometimes let you spam the same hit 15 times, sometime they'll counter you after the second consecutive hit.  The melee pits that train you how to use these combos are terrible and even when you do the combo EXACTLY as you're told you'll still fail it. Finally, even with lots of upgrades the spear is mostly useless against anything but the weakest enemies.3. The parkour. Aloy will sometimes just not grab ledges or ladders despite falling against them. Happens rarely but when you have to climb back up its pretty annoying.4. The upgrades. This is the biggest complaint I've seen thus far. Upgrading the best gear requires you to kill the toughest machines in the game over and over and over. Horizon: Forbidden West takes the strengths of the formula established in Horizon: Zero Dawn, but with significant improvements over the areas that needed it.- Quests and NPCs are pretty much universally better written, more engaging and emotional. No filler content, every quest you do is a story in itself.- Map exploration is engaging. Wide variety in environments, and a number of objective to pursue. I gotta admit, my attempts to just run from one point to the next mostly thanks to being blissfully sidetracked.- Gameplay-wise, enemies are varied and different not just in shape, but also in movement and pacing, making each of them a very different combat dynamic. There is also a large variety of weapons offering different gameplay style and letting you choose which style fits you best.- Higher difficulties represent and significant challenges, forcing you to make the best use of your equipment to deal with them (except traps, traps bad). While some content is a bit overtuned at higher difficulties (hello, Enduring), most of it is simply challenging as the player requests, with certain harder fight the you might expect to have to retry once or twice. Or you can go for lower difficulties for a still interesting, but less punishing gameplay.I loved playing the game. The main story and interactions with the characters around it was engaging, with a satisfying ending and great cast interactions. I'm looking forward to the next game to continue the story.

"I'm not a hired killer!" Protested Murder Waif while trying to hide the mountain of corpses she accepted payment for.Horizon: Forbidden West is fantastic, especially if you love the Murder Waif genre. However, there are some things that are just off about it. If the overall game wasn’t as excellent as it was, many of these would blend into a background of mediocrity. Instead, they blare, like burrowers trying deafen you with their soundshells.Let's start with settings and controls. Key mapping does not carry over to any menus or even their board game. ESDF works as intended for main gameplay, so all good... until you discover that ballista aim is not inverted on the Y Axis, like everything else. That's not terrible, I mean who wants to use ballistae? Plus, it’s not like there's multiple different buttons for interacting with objects, which could be a matter of tapping or holding the button making for four common ways of "interacting" when all you need is one. And it’s not like there's also three or four different context dependent ways to cancel out of an action or menu. Nor is it like when you're doing keyboard and mouse jiujitsu to craft arrows in battles you can get locked into spear attack animations upon finishing. And surely there aren't attack combos that you must perform in a controlled environment that are essentially impossible to pull off in actual battle. Right? Look, controls should follow KISS when possible. H:FW fails hard here, delivering poor key mapping and overengineered controls.That said, I mentioned animations, and let me tell you they are gorgeous. The artists here did a fine job of crafting emotive characters, to say nothing of Murder Waif's hair. The lip syncing is normally off by a mile, but that's only noticeable because the rest is so good. Though, strangely, in this post apocalypse, all the 18-24 year olds (half the population) are sporting that trendy dolphin skin look, which is a bit weird.I also mentioned crafting, so let's go ahead and address the worst aspect of this game: Inventory. It is garbage.First, there are too many weapons. What is different weapons should be a more limited selection of weapons that can handle a broader array of ammo, as you basically wind up with a version of each weapon for each ammo type for each tier of weapons, plus some that combo different ammo types. I get that for gamification purposes they wanted a fire bow and a plasma bow. Plus, there's the inferred need to introduce new weapons on top of those in the first game, because you aren't confident enough in the strength of your story (which is overall great btw) to keep people interested. You also gotta fill up that six weapon wheel menu with something. Never mind that toting six bulky active weapons (plus spear) at a time makes no sense, to say nothing of what's in your inventory menu screen.Usable items are out of control. Where you can choose one of six weapons on the fly, to find the right trap or potion, you're scrolling left or right through everything you might have picked up at some time, even stuff you aren't carrying. By the end game this is 20+ items, but by the early game you really just set it on your best healing potion and leave it there, essentially closing down avenues of gameplay. Oh, and I hope you didn't accidentally hold the use item button in combat, because that will open up the craft item menu while foes are still active.The crafting system is crap. The interface is... let's move on. The requirements are horrible. First, its grindy as all get out. For instance, 5 Dreadwing Fangs is a common ingredient for legendary gear. Only one Dreadwing spawns at a given location at a time, and, at most, it will only drop two fangs. That means you will spend a lot of time rubberbanding to that location to farm those guys instead of enjoying the game just to get your gear up. Second, its ridiculously gamified. Line, castors, and the like would make sense for a bow upgrade, but how do tail fins from a mechanical plesiosaur fit in? All upgrades are like that - they're just parts you can get from a foe of a certain difficulty arranged so you have to go farm them. That is lazy design with no thought given to what you are crafting.Fortunately, H:FW recognizes that the true endgame is fashion. Unfortunately, it has little actual fashion sense. Thank you for bringing back the Carja armor at least. Though spikey bits will kill you if you bend too much. However, this does expose a weakness in world design.Leaves and skins won't stop giant metal jaws nearly as well as Carja lamellar, but its rated better. I've played enough fantasy games to not be too worked up over that, but then you look at how those aesthetic choices carry over to the greater world design. You wind up with farmers who can't forge metal wearing palm leaves and shirtless himbos in the high mountains. Where I'm sure Murder Waif appreciates the sights (or she would if these guys actually understood grooming), I'm also sure that most of the NPC population will die from exposure, not whatever plague or famine is threatening them.Speaking of exposure, the climate is out of control. Terraforming is cool and all, but climate still follows basic rules established by axial tilt, planetary rotation, and the placement of land and water formations. Rich jerks screwing over the planet and its people are 100% believable, but a California/Nevada jungle is perhaps the most fictitious thing in the game.You'll quickly discover that Murder Waif is angry and driven; makes total sense given that she's a red-headed savior child soldier whose been through some stuff. Definite psychological issues there, only not. It turns out she's really only angry and driven in the context of the main quest and never even tells the Admiral about his fleet. Side quest Murder Waif is sweet, caring, and helpful in a way that belies her exiled and isolated upbringing, not to mention the timetable to save the world. It’s not like the baddies are just going to wait on me to advance the story. *sigh* So much for having a three-dimensional character whose personality is shaped by their experiences. Wait! What's this? A dialog option for how to respond to an NPC with my choice of emotional, rational, or screw you?! Yes! Um... why does this only appear eight times in the game? Guys, have faith in your writing team. They do a good job, except in the DLC. They just grabbed some high schooler's English project for that. You totally could have run with that mechanic. At least give me the illusion of agency!Enjoyment is set, in part, by meeting expectations. Discussed above, consistent controls is an expectation, when not met, you get frustrated and don't enjoy yourself. You expect things like mounts to move at certain speeds, but your opponents in races are just plain faster than you (ostensibly to 'keep it interesting'). You expect that listening to an NPC when he talks about a red light to mean that checking out the red light would lead to something instead of having to swim to the center of a dome to trigger a specific waypoint first. You expect default sound balance to allow you to hear what Murder Waif is saying over sound effects and forgettable music. You expect all explorable parts of the world to have something, even Hoover Dam. You expect that the game won't throw up an opaque level up notice on screen in the middle of combat, preventing you from aiming properly. You expect vistas to... you know what? Screw them; they're just frustrating. I expect refined hit detection when tearing components off baddies. I expect picture vistas to not require finer tuning.Look, H:FW has great overall gameplay and an good story about Murder Waif fighting not just the legacy of rich jerks, but rich jerks themselves. It’s a great game with a lush, beautiful world. I heartily recommend it, but it also most certainly has its flaws.

I really wanted to like this game. The premise is fantastic - it's a sequel to Zero Dawn (which I very much enjoyed!) and as such, you'd expect to keep the progression you made, right?Wrong. Without spoiling anything, the early-mid game strips you of everything you're used to, and adds new elements, which are very unintuitive. Some aren't even marked as important - it doesn't break the game, but it kind of hints that if you play a different build to what the game wants you to (without telling you), then you're locked out of some early stuff until you invest in those skills.Unfortunately this theme's prevalent within the game - you have to progress, to unlock, to backtrack. The beauty of Zero Dawn was that once you'd completed about 1/3rd of the story, you could pretty much see and do whatever you wanted at your pace. Forbidden West locks a lot of stuff behind progression-driven plot armour, and I genuinely don't see a need for it. Why can't I open this room or tick off sections before moving on? Why can't I move on in my game as if I wanted to see it as a chaptered storyline? What sense does it make for my character to run back and forth across the map, when the storyline is about urgency, just to unlock something later on in the game, just to run back to a location at the start of the game and find it's stuff I could have picked up elsewhere?I should say that some of the additions are decent - there's a minigame in particular that is infuriating at first, but is brilliant later on. Some of the other improvements - like not losing tagged enemies - are also very good.That said I do think that Forbidden West is a little too focused on change for the sake of change, rather than just evolving the story. It's not a -bad- game per sé, and I'm sure if you played this before Zero Dawn then you would dismiss my review as tripe. However, it's in the key details. It's different enough from the previous game to irritate players, especially early-game when you want to try and character build.To summarise - it's not a bad game, but the Horizon you're used to isn't what this game is. Some of the stuff you're used to is missing, some handy stuff has been added. Personally, I prefer Zero Dawn, but I have no complaints against those who prefer Forbidden West. Maybe watch some non-spoiler gameplay before you decide whether or not to purchase this game.
