I consider HZD to be the best single-player game I've played in my life. HFW is NOT this!Of course, 10 to 1, people positively review this game, so I'm an outlier, but reviews like mine exist to warn like-minded people that FW is NOT ZD in the fundamental ways that you loved about ZD!Of course, many people say variations of, "It's not Zero Dawn and not trying to be." But I consider that a bad argument. People like me bought FW because of what a great game ZD was, and FW is supposed to be a "sequel" of ZD, with the same characters, weapons, etc. That's how it's marketed, and the marketing intentionally leveraged the popularity that ZD had generated.So, when I say that FW is NOT even close to the great game that ZD was, I mean that it feels like a bait-and-switch.1) The combat is clunky and feels entirely contrived. This stands in stark contrast with ZD, which had the most intuitive "feel" of any comparable game.2) The weapons are overly complicated to no actual improvement to the gameplay. With ZD there was no steep learning curve to the weapons, so you could assemble an arsenal that fit your play style and have a very predictable set of outcomes. In FW, after 35 hours in-game, I still don't feel like I understand why a particular weapon does what it does and what I might do to "upgrade" or replace it. I don't want to need a manual to make the "right" choices!3) Aloy can't MOVE! Her directional controls feel like driving a car through deep mud. I HATE how she moves and feels in-game! This is one of the worst parts of FW. Climbing has become an absurdity. Jumping (which you will do a LOT) is ridiculously counterintuitive and OFTEN has you doing things you did not intend, frequently to your demise. And there are janky glitches! For example, Aloy is five feet above the ground. Hitting C to drop to the ground doesn't work. She WILL NOT drop to the ground. You can go up, left, and right. But somehow the dumb game thinks that she needs to drop down to a "ledge," and there is no "ledge" below. So the stoooopid game won't let you drop to THE GROUND! Worse, you can't predict when such stooopidity will emerge, so the whole world feels a bit odd.4) The endless, story-telling cut-scenes are tedious and ponderous. ZD had you PLAY the story out. FW makes you sit through what amount to movies that force-feed the story to you. It feels like HALF the "game" is you sitting through ponderous, slow, heavy-handed dialog cut-scenes.5) The gameplay itself is not even CLOSE to as enjoyable as it was in ZD. To say that FW is a "different game" from ZD is an understatement. This hot mess should never have been called "Horizon" AT ALL! This thing really bears NO resemblance to ZD, but it tries so hard to market itself as just a "continuation" of ZD. It is NOT! The things you most loved about ZD are either backgrounded or broken in FW. For example:    A) Both claim to be open-world, and ZD felt vast, open, and sensible. You had a sense of your place in the world. But by stark contrast, FW "looks" on the map like it's "open," but really the gameplay feels almost on rails. This is hard to describe, but FW does NOT feel like one vast, open map.    B) Not only is the combat tedious in FW, it is relentless! EVERYWHERE you go are endless hordes of machines. You literally cannot run between towns without encountering swarms of hostiles. You can't explore even a small region without dealing with swarms of hostiles. It's like the developers thought, "People liked the combat in ZD, so let's give them a LOT of it in FW." But that was a vast mistake!    C) Unlike ZD, in FW it's very, very difficult to become OP. But when I play a game like this, I WANT to EARN my way to OP and then enjoy BEING OP! But the machines are all ridiculously hard compared to ZD. Only the lowest-end machines are "trivial," even once you're up past level 18 (which is where I am now). Even with fully upgraded armor and good weaves, a couple of chargers can give you a very bad day. And that feels ridiculous compared to how things seemed to scale in ZD.    D) The boss fights are just ridiculous. I HATE these arena-fights with a purple-passion! ALL these fights amount to is: "Did you get your weapon perks just right? Did you take off the Grimhorn's weapons and armor just right? Did you switch weapons in just the right order? Did you dodge at the correct split-second to avoid his rush/stomp attack?" I HATE it, and this is NOT what I expected after having enjoyed everything about ZD.    E) The "gameplay" amounts to, "Pick up a quest, travel toward the quest, fight monsters tediously, get to the quest target, fight some higher-end monsters tediously, complete quest, return, cash-in, and rinse and repeat." It's just raw tedium. Oh, punctuated by arena boss-fights. NOT FUN!    F) Jumping puzzles! And more jumping puzzles. Like with the machine combat, the devs clearly thought, "People spoke positively of our climbing/jumping puzzles in ZD, so let's give them a LOT of them in FW." So, as with the combat, it's just tedious. And glitchy. I personally dislike jumping puzzles, but in ZD they at least felt balanced and not tedious. But it can honestly be said that FW is a JUMPING PUZZLE game! You will do a LOT of it. And you will do it with MUCH WORSE Aloy controls than you enjoyed in ZD!Believe it or not, I could still go on and on and on with this rant. After (eventually) completing the Tau Cauldron, I realized: "There was not ONE time in the entire playthrough of ZD that I felt angry like this." FW is a different game that emphasizes a different sort of mindset and skillset than did ZD.And it's been widely and correctly reported that the subtle changes to the character designs are NOT welcome. Aloy went from pretty to masculine and angular. Her facial expressions mostly amount to raised-eyebrows with deep wrinkles in her forehead. She's developed a sniveling, narcissistic, entitled, ♥♥♥♥♥♥, snarky attitude that amounts to: "Oh, woe is me, having the weight of the whole world on my shoulders, being literally the savior of humanity and everywhere actually called 'savior,' so I'm oh so very, very special and don't have any time nor tolerance for people including my best friends." It's RIDICULOUS, tedious, unnecessary, and PAINFUL to play! The Devs turned Aloy ugly inside and out. WHY?My recommendation for FW a hard pass. But if you get it for something like $15, you'll probably get your money's worth before you get sick of it. For my part, I don't know as I write this if I'm going to bother with it anymore. I may return to it now and then, but I have come to really dislike it.

﻿I've waited years for this game to come out. Spoiled myself a little for it: I'd watched a bunch of YouTube clips and more or less knew the entire plot. The animation & motion capture looked awesome, and at a glance I quite liked the direction they took the story. Fast forward to the present, and things are... not quite as smooth as they seemed. Don't get me wrong, the core concept of fighting giant robot dinosaurs is still awesome, and the new additions are VERY cool - Plesiosaurus and Spinosaurus are my favourite dinosaurs, so of course I'm going to be biased towards the Tideripper and Slaughterspine. But there are many issues, technical and narratively, that only compound as the game progresses. By the time I got around to the DLC, I was pretty burned out. For the first half of the game, I would have said this title was a knockout, by the end I wasn't so sure. There's a lot to cover, so I'll try being as succinct as possible. Total spoilers below:Story:Positives:-I liked the overall direction of rebooting Gaia, collecting the scattered AIs, and fighting off the Zeniths. It established a good sense of scale & threat that jumped off the previous game's storyline quite well, and establishes a solid direction for the next game.Negatives:-The first 2/3 of the game had generally good pacing, the last 1/3 tries to cram in too much-The Aether storyline feels like it was awkwardly split in two to artificially create "threat" for the last 1/4 of the game. Regalla's initial attack is built up well, but the final boss fight just kind of fizzles out, gets awkwardly pasted back in near the end of the game, and is unceremoniously resolved in the span of about 15 minutes-Frequent xenophobia began to wear on me in the end, the Quen are especially guilty here-Revealing that the Zeniths could be killed early on was a mistake. The "use EMPs to disguise the merging of Hephestus" plan was stupid - Beta figured it out as soon as she arrived, and there's only one possible location you can use for the merge, it's ridiculous to assume the Zeniths wouldn't have figured this out too. You've already established that Sylens has a weapon to use against the Zeniths, that the Zeniths are invincible without it & have mechanical scouts, and that Aloy's team are willing to spend the time laying out the groundwork for their plans to succeed. Why is THIS the one critical detail that gets completely overlooked? Combat, Upgrading & Accessibility:Positives:-Fighting robot dinosaurs is still awesome. I had a bad habit of not properly using elemental attacks in ZD, but I had a pleasantly diversified arsenal here. The exploding javelins became my favourite secondary weapon-The midgame opens the entire map up, exploration is generally fun and I did feel a rush scouting out areas I was severely under-levelled on-The new swimming system is largely a success and I loved the new areas to explore-Questing for upgrade components felt like a main quest all on it's own, for better and worse-The new skill trees make levelling up and completing missions more appealing/worthwhile. Hunter is the best overall, Infiltrator is good vs humansNegatives:-There aren't always good ways to prevent dinosaur's mobility. Goo doesn't really seem to do anything when it matters, and electrical stuns wear off very quickly-I rarely died to what I'd consider "fair fights", the vast majority were one shots from electrical damage, falling off cliffs/pits, or getting stuck against geometry. It probably makes sense that the giant mechs could just smush you into the ground with their weight, but this is not particularly fun to fight against-Aloy can sometimes climb sheer cliff faces, but not artificial structures like wooden houses. There are also frequent issues actually getting over the final edge of cliffs in general-The advertised mounts are disappointing. The pterodactyl comes right at the tail end of the game, and the raptor is slow as sin. IMO, they should have given the flying mount as a reward for Aether's quest, water breathing as a reward for Poseidon's, and a fast combat mount version of the raptor as a reward for Demeter's-Aloy REALLY likes to complain about being low on air. Not necessarily arguing against this, just weird how she can't hold her breath for more than 15 seconds-There is a LOT of grind regarding legendary equipment. Many require completion of multiple high-level quests, or grinding out fights in the arena to unlock. Upgrade requirements are generally not consistent, many steps are heavily front-loaded in difficulty. Stormwings and Dreadwings are particularly guilty of this, having a singular, hard to reach location for most of the game, require multiple kills for parts that are easily destructible, and often force you to fight both at once. In general, purple-rarity items feel like the working man's tools, while orange-rarity items felt almost burdening with their harsh upgrade requirements-Some of the skill trees are memes or have extremely limited utility. Trapper and Machine Master are specific examplesCharacters:Positives:-Aloy learning to trust her team a bit more was a refreshing change of pace. Having the final battle fully incorporate your whole party was a satisfying conclusion to the plotline-Sylens went from one of my most disliked characters in ZD, to one of my favourites in this titleNegatives:-Aloy occasionally has inconsistent motives and tolerances, with a bad habit of threatening friendly characters and being almost timid towards certain hostile ones-Very few characters have even the simplest grasp of psychology, which becomes increasingly frustrating. The biggest sore spot is how they handled Beta, who's portrayed as a timid, almost cowardly character. Nobody has the intelligence to recognize that someone who was held captive their entire life, grew up in isolation, and is frequently compared to a historical figure might be having trouble suppressing feelings of inadequacy. Nobody ever points out that having a techie might be a useful addition to a team of generally tech-illiterate warriors, and Aloy herself treats her shockingly poorly after just 3 conversations. Point of interest: a news story came out recently about a woman cloning her dead dog back to life. She actually got two copies back - they both looked similar, but shared no behavioural similarities to the original. The writers wouldn't have had this information when writing this game's script, but having this knowledge now makes Aloy's argument about Beta "not living up to Elizabet's legacy" SO much more painful to listen toDLC:-Generally speaking, it's merely alright. Being burned out didn't help, however-Being able to explore an entirely new location with your flying mount was nice, and I very much liked the new machine types (with the Bilegut being my favourite).-The new legendary weapons are rather nice, not having to grind for hours to obtain them is much appreciated, and having generally reasonable upgrade requirements was very helpful. Minor complaint: the only Sawtooth nest on the island never spawned for me, even after multiple visits-Frankly I don't like how the Quen are handled, both in this DLC and the main story, so I never really resonated with their plight. Aloy having a romance is... nice? This was something many people harped on (myself included), and it's good that she's no longer a robot when it comes to relationships, but I felt there was more chemistry with characters from Zero Dawn and Frozen Wilds than there was here. There's also a lot of needless drama from both characters not being honest with each other, which traditionally is not a sign of a healthy relationship, and further exacerbates the point that the romance subplot was perhaps just tacked inOverall this title's okay, but... I was frankly hoping for a slam dunk, and this wasn't quite that. Hunting robot dinosaurs is still fun, but everything surrounding it is inconsistent at best.

Amazing graphics and amazing story continued from Zero Dawn. Suffers a lot from pretty irrelevant side quests, which, while often have interesting stories themselves, have zero impact on the main story (even less than in ZD where ). The side quests really boil down to how much you're willing to grind for XP, skill points and vague lore, which is not really a good design. I loved the music but couldn't really remember any of it once I finished, though I gotta admit it its much more seamless in terms of transition from exploration to combat. That said you can still expect many surprising twists and turns in the story, and I really encourage you to resist the urge and not spoil it for yourself by reading the wiki or walkthroughs. Storage system has been vastly improved from Zero Dawn, but still has some shortcomings. I get the potion pouch mechanic, but the fact that it is impossible to change your potion loadout without accessing the stash is just a huge pain, and it's not really documented anywhere.Contextual tips, even when set to "important only", are often way too intrusive and will remind you to make use of mechanics you learned at the very beginning even in the late game, while you're actually doing them.The melee fighting system, while also much more evolved from ZD, is a pain in itself. Executing combos with pause in them is pretty weird and clunky. Your spear is still pretty useless vs machines with the exception of grapple strike. Loved the racing activity, much more entertaining than in, say, The Witcher 3, but still suffers from the same thing - once you get in the lead, everyone else just speeds up like crazy and is back on your ass in mere seconds. There's no way to win those races by any significant margin, you're always milliseconds ahead.I'd say the overall balance in the game is a bit off. Some Apex machines you can encounter fairly early on are absolute menaces compared to some final bossfights, and conversely some early bossfights are such a pain in the ass with the equipment you have available at the time (). The grind for parts to get significant upgrades for your items is also much more than I'd expect from a Horizon game, and the reward isn't even that satisfying considering that the final bossfight is a walk in the park compared to everything else you've encountered before. Machines have way too much health on higher difficulties, it just makes beating them unreasonably time-consuming. If I detach every possible detachable component, the machine should basically be already dead or at least very close, but that's not the case when you're playing the harder difficulties - instead of the fights actually being harder (like making invulnerability windows shorter and more precise, attacks faster and more frequent), they are just longer. Halfway through the game I was so tired of it I just manually changed machine health to normal levels while keeping everything else at hard.Mount autopilot on roads just sucks, it often takes the wrong turn at intersections and will sometimes even get you offroad on straight stretches of road, leading your mount to go through a river instead of a bridge. Also I don't get why the  mount is so unbearably slow. The  mount steering on PC is really unclear, learning how to fly this thing fast except when close to the ground took me an unreasonable amount of time.As far as exploration goes, I had explorer mode on - Aloy either yaps way too much, or she just doesn't give any tips when the player is obviously lost. Getting into a ruin and having her point out the not-so-obvious route you could take before you even got a chance to take a good look at your surroundings sucks. Similarly, on the other end of the spectrum, she sometimes doesn't say anything when you're lost for a couple of minutes, except maybe "my Focus could help". Yeah, no ♥♥♥♥ the Focus would help, I'm pinging it for the last two minutes and can't figure out where to go, so thank you for the useful insight, I'm just going to look up the walkthrough.The Focus changes themselves are very good, I love the new ping vs hold mechanic, and I absolutely love the sonar. Being able to tag specific machine parts is also a huge game-changer.Climbing can be pretty buggy, especially in non-critical areas.As far as writing goes, I find  to be a pretty shallow character. MAJOR SPOILER: , That said, I still like most of the other characters. They're believable and coherent, and Sylens is IMO exceptionally well written.Overall it's a very pleasant RPG with a believable and entertaining story. It has some shortcomings, but they shouldn't deter you from playing the game. If anything, just lower the difficulty level and enjoy the lore.

After almost 60 hours of Forbidden West, I can say that there is much to love about this game. Environments in this game are more or less pushing the boundary of how beautiful video game environments can be. The side characters are much improved in this game, and the characters that are recurring from Zero Dawn are substantially more developed. In terms of plot, Forbidden West is excellent, delivering shocking and exciting twists that still feel authentic and plausible within the context of the original game. The enemy design is also on point, delivering enemies that are as fun to fight as they are to look at.  If there is any criticisms I can give, I would probably say that this game has an excess of grinding for better weapons. It seems silly to me here that every single weapon requires substantial upgrades and coils to reach even close to its maximum potential. I came close to 100% Zero Dawn (only thing I didn't do was NG+), but I couldn't even imagine bringing myself to 100% Forbidden West. But YMMV, as plenty of people love endgame gear grinds - I'm just not one of those people. Original Review at launch (3 hours played):Runs like a dream, phenomenal graphics, especially environments (probably some of the best on PC now, impressive for a 2 year old game), no MTX (unlike a certain overhyped Capcom game that came out the same day!), and great combat. After playing Zero Dawn, I can already tell you after the first 3 hours that I recommend this game too.

I must admit I was jealous of PS5 players getting Horizon Forbidden West, I'd recently sold my PS5 not long before it came out and got some serious fomo, thankfully Elden Ring kept me busy.Fast forward 2 years and finally we get HFW on pc, only for it to be overshadowed once again by another game releasing on the same day, that being dragons dogma 2.However I did pick this game up and was quite excited to play, even though I thought zero dawn was a bit of an average game overall I still enjoyed the setting and characters enough to want to revisit this world, however my first impressions weren't great, the intro was a bit slow and the environment was just so bland. It felt like DLC to the first game.That was until I ventured into a certain area of the game that I'll avoid naming for spoiler reasons, this was a beautiful biome that was so different to anything that came before and the way the old world was captured, with it's destroyed buildings and bleak environment really managed to pull me in, I was hooked from that point and I've had a really great time with this game.Negatives Climbing is better in this game as there is more things to climb on but it's really restricted and I found aloy's jump to be floaty and inconsistent. Maybe I'm misremembering but I felt her jumps were more accurate in HZD, I would rather they do away with the climbing spots and have a system similar to BOTW/AC but then many of the games puzzles just wouldn't work. Melee combat is still really bad, like it's better I guess but it's still just a case of spamming RB. They did try and expand upon it with more indepth combos but most are just too tricky to pull off in the heat of battle and they aren't as effective as just spamming RB, RB, RT. I again don't really know what they could do to expand on this system as the game is mostly a third person shooter but it needs some serious tweaking to make it less floaty. The last point is a big one, this is still just a filler open world game with many side activities being copy pasted from other games, they have tried to put a new spin on them such as the tallnecks (thing ubisoft towers.) being more puzzle based than a climbing challenge but ultimately this won't sway you to open world games, it doesn’t redfine them or make them more interesting. it's the same stuff again just better than before. Oh and they removed the pause menu Positives This game is beautiful and is an incredible port. I was constantly getting 165fps and was able to play this game in full 4k on my 65inch TV, it was stunning. The environments start off really same-y with plenty of forests but once you hit the desert/snow areas then it really opens up and just simply looks amazing. Combat is fun if not too complicated, it retains the same open ended approach as the first game by giving you many trap weapons and the enemy ai still seems competent enough that it feels fun to lead them into the traps you can lay. Human enemies are still mostly boring but they have really ramped up the robots. The story is much better this time around and I actually enjoyed it a lot more, it's still silly but it feels much more fleshed out and the characters are much more complex, speaking of which...Aloy is so much better in this game, she's much more withdrawn and skeptical of people whilst also brushing off the beliefs of the tribes. She's uncomfortable with the hero worship but is still fiercely loyal to her friends. She's also no longer naive to the old world. All in all a much better character this time around and a bit more edgy which is what I wanted from the first game. conclusion I started this game not feeling it, getting sick of it's generic open world content but the more I stuck with it the more I really grew to love the world and characters much like the first game, the world building and unique enemies keeps this game fresh despite the cookie cutter open world fluff.

Big fan of Horizon Zero Dawn, and almost five hours in, here are my thoughts thus far:1) GraphicsIt's obviously visually stunning, but I feel like it's so detailed that it almost ends up hindering the gaming experience a little. I imagine that's why the item icons aren't always enabled like in HZD, but I'm constantly having to Focus when I'm trying to find a small animal I killed while I'm also having to fight off lots of machines. It's possible this is a setting in the game I haven't found yet.GRAPHICS UPDATE: Post-hotfix, I've been getting some weird purple and green boxes on the bottom part of the screen. What's up with that?2) Controls (I play mouse and keyboard)It feels less sharp than HZD, and there are too many different things to keybind, in my opinion. HZD had multiple things going to one button and felt streamlined. When doing the dialogue wheel, you actually have to click on the text instead of it using the general area of where your mouse is pointing. That one might be a nitpick, but it was pretty nice to have when I would close my eyes and pick a choice at random. The constant need to hold down a button to complete the action is a little annoying, especially for fast traveling. Holding down also feels slower (in a bad way) than in HZD. Not to mention, the mouse isn't accurate and I have to point off to the left of the map's symbol in order to select said symbol. The constant fumbling with controls does take some of the fun out of the game.CONTROLS EDIT: I was annoyed enough at the fact that I could only have 4 Frost Bombs, but now I can only have 2 Trip wires set? I assume I have to spec into something, but that's gonna be a big BRUH from me. Also, I have to have a separate bow for Fire Arrows now? :/3) StoryI haven't really done enough of it to really have an opinion on it yet, although thank you for bringing back Travis Tate.All in all, I would certainly recommend the game, but I feel like there are a few screws that could be tightened up to make this a truly wonderful game, especially when it's predecessor had these conveniences.SUMMARY EDIT: (7 additional hours in) I want to like this game. I really, really do. However I find myself getting so hung up on the sometimes inexplicable game play changes from HZD to HFW that I don't see myself playing much more of this. If you never played HZD, you'll probably have a better time than I did. I don't mind changes when they improve the game play, but almost everything has felt like a downgrade. Changed my recommendation from "YES" to "NO."

100/100The best game series I have ever played in my life.To my surprise, this game was even better than Horizon1 in many aspects. One of the major factors that I enjoyed is the larger map size. It's definitely much larger, with many more missions and sub-missions, and tons of places to explore. They added several different features that didn't exist in Horizon1.(1) Item stash: Now we can collect as many items as we want, and if the bag is full, the extras go to the stash, which we can access at certain locations.(2) Melee pits: We learn melee attack combos using skill points, then there are pits where we can practice those combos. However, the timing of the attack buttons is very subtle and not shown. It was a frustrating experience to repeat the same combo practice over and over. This needs to be changed into some sort of rhythm game where we know when to push the button to achieve a certain melee combo.(3) Tomb Raider-inspired puzzle game at ruins: I'm not a big fan of puzzle games, so I don't even try to solve them; I just check YouTube videos for solutions.(4) Mario Kart-like racing game: I'm not a fan of this either.(5) Battle arena: This one is interesting, but at some point, I could not beat it at the Hard level, so I lowered the difficulty.I'm a slow player, but for comparison, it took about 70 hours to finish Horizon1 at Normal level. Then I played New Game+ for Hard and Ultra Hard levels, mostly focusing on the main quest. I played about 130 hours for Horizon1. Compared to Horizon1, I spent much more time in Horizon2:2 hours: The first couple of hours of tutorial were very slow, and it almost made me regret buying this game. But after this, when the real open-world game started, I began to love the game as much as Horizon1.50 hours: I usually like to explore and hunt animals, upgrade weapons, and do as many sub-quests as possible, but after 50 hours of play, I was appalled to find that I had only uncovered 50% of the map and still had many quests to do. It was about 30% completion. I felt overwhelmed at this point.100 hours: I haven't finished the main quest yet. It's about 60% complete, and about 80% of the map is uncovered.150 hours: From 130 hours to 150 hours, I spent most of my time killing big apex enemies to upgrade weapons and playing in the arena, hunter grounds, and melee pits before finishing the game. At this time, I finally started using elemental damages (fire, ice, thunder, etc.) to weaken enemies. Melee pits are so frustrating; this part needs to be improved for Horizon3.153 hours: Finished the game for the first time at the Hard level. Since I upgraded weapons and practice to fight against lots of enemies beforehand, the last boss seemed easy for me. Finally, "Burning Shores" is unlocked. I keep playing and will probably play Ultra Hard after I finish Burning Shores, but I played enough to post my review for this game.Bugs:(1) Lost Supplies Salvage quest: This bug was also reported on Reddit, but I was not able to override a bristleback. I needed to override a bristleback somewhere in the north and call it to the site.(2) Grimhorns' cores: I wasn't able to give 2 Grimhorns' cores to Zo in the field. I had to go to the base to give them to her.(3) Vista point images at the Memorial Grove & Coast and another location: These were gone before I found the right spots. I had to find the right spots without the images.(4) Air balloon crash site: When I revisited the site where the air balloon had crashed, the fallen tree that served as a bridge was gone. It was impossible to get out from the site, so I ended up using a travel pack.(5) Aloy's comments: Aloy's comments were triggered automatically at some places over and over even though there was no more gimmick or event there.There are many tiny bugs here and there. Sometimes an item is there, but I cannot take it. An item flag is there, but the item isn't there. Explosive barrels are found buried underground instead of being above ground. I set up a large text size, but after the new update (v. 1.3), the text size changes depending on the people I talk to (it's fixed after v. 1.4). These bugs are minor by nature, and the production team is regularly addressing and fixing them.

Many have written some troubling stuff about the game, and I was afraid to buy the sequel to Zero Dawn which I liked very much. In all honesty, after 10 hours, I feel like this:- The combat is alright, and all the chaos it sometimes brings is in inverse proportion to the amount of my own focus. I don't mean Alloy's. I mean, as a player. I had a skill issue with it right away; I just had to get better. I haven't noticed anything along the lines of the impact dmg reputably being sub-par, nor have I felt any over-the-board need for switching elemental attacks. Maybe it's true later on, maybe not.- Relatable stories of characters I met. Believably original, well-portrayed characters so far. I haven't met any of the more toxically woke ones yet. So I don't know how much I'm going to suffer from those, hh.- Upgrades, gathering, and items in general are alright—I felt the first upgrades quite significantly, having thanked myself for taking the time to acquire the special parts beforehand.- Exploration is great, actually. I can abstain from using Alloy's focus, and that way, the game is heavily based on my own perception. Chests, scrolls, collectables, and other lootables are not that easy to spot, each find is palpable. Kudos to the devs for this! - Alloy: I'd address this in two parts. The part where she just comments on her feelings and decisions is okay. I personally even like it. I don't mind if she's overly chatty. However, the part where she comments on every puzzle, every mission goal, every moving forward, and where literally two seconds after she confronts such element—that is really bad. That's nagging. Devs went overboard; I don't know whose bright idea was this, much less not including the option to shut this nonsense down for those, who want immersion and not stupidly-forced passiveness.Fortunately, there's already a curated mod that remedies this abberation of an overstep.- Puzzles: I've just spent nearly 30 minutes figuring out how to get into the closed room in the first derelict building beyond Chainscrape—translate it as an environmental puzzle. I knew all the stuff I should have done, but I had to figure out how and where. That is, with the Alloy Shut Up mod mentioned above. The said mod allowed me to come up with the solution myself as opposed to the vanilla game, in which the manual would've been forced upon me in two seconds of looking at the bulding.I mean, I am amazed. This is awesome. I am playing a modern, open-world, action RPG that also lets me use my brain! Is this even possible in today's world, am I dreaming :D ?- I won't comment on graphics, you can see that for yourself, however, I would like to add that I run the game in 1080p on an acient I3 and nVidia 1660 6GB, on HIGH with antialising on, and game runs around nicely playable 40fps. Also, I haven't had a single crash and encountered only one slight bug, such as some item's descriptions flickering. That's a testament to optimalization levels unheard of in today's world of troubled bugfests of nearly every modern release.- Last but not least, the soundtrack is solid, great even. I was pleasantly surprised. I don't know if the game turns into a sour or boring grindfest later or not, but seeing 10 hours out of it, I know I'm going to like it for at least several tens more.-------------------------Edit after 50 hours-------------------------1. I said that the stories of people were relatable as in the first installment. However, that was true only in towns and the surroundings. The open-world random meetings can fall flat or outright immersion-breaking. Example: I just met 3 groups of trapped Tenakh people, who are supposed to be like these true savages, you know. Man... they talked to me using proper English, were all thankful, and joyful, eyes merrily shining, and all. Eh, that struck bad. Fortunately, these are only episodes.2. Having played Zero Dawn extensively not a long time ago, I'm beginning to get somewhat weary of all the "same style, different content" kind of things. If I hadn't played the first installment, I'd be playing this with the same enthusiasm for at least 50 more. Still, I am not regretting buying this.

If you’re looking for a game that’ll have you glued to your couch for roughly 200 hours—and still leave you only halfway done—then look no further than Horizon Forbidden West. It’s got everything you need: robots the size of mountains, endless collectibles, and a storyline so gripping you’ll forget what day it is. Who needs the real world when you’ve got this?First off, the graphics are mind-blowing. I’m talking about the kind of attention to detail where you could practically count the blades of grass Aloy runs through. Everything in this game is so meticulously designed, you’ll feel like you’re playing in an animated nature documentary—except there are machines, and they want to kill you. Small detail.You think you’re in for a short romp? Think again. This game is like an endless buffet of action-packed quests, side missions, and things to collect. Sure, you might aim to 100% it, but at 200 hours in, you’ll realize you’re still picking up stray machine parts and wondering why Aloy’s not the one wearing an exosuit by now. Good luck with that!The soundtrack is as epic as the battles themselves. It’s got that "save the world while looking incredibly cool" vibe. Perfect for those moments when you're trying to sneak around a ThunderJaw or SlaughterSpine ...or, let’s be real, when you get caught and just start running for your life.Ah, the story. It’s fantastic. Full of intrigue, twists, and even a hint of romance for our beloved Aloy. Yes, amidst fighting machines and saving humanity, she manages to find time for a little bit of flirting. But, if you're hoping for a full-blown love story, don’t hold your breath. She’s got bigger (literally) things to worry about.Honestly, battling machines the size of small countries? Sign me up. The thrill never gets old, and every fight feels like you’re David facing off against Goliath...if Goliath was a mechanical war machine with missile launchers. Fun stuff., basically for me, Horizon Forbidden West is an epic ride. The game gives you breathtaking visuals, an extensive world to explore, robots that’ll terrify and amaze you, and a story that'll pull you in for the long haul. It’s worth every hour... all 200 of them. Just don’t forget to eat. New Game + here I come!

Horizon Forbidden West is an excellent game if you never engage in any quests or combats. What does this mean? The game's studios put all their resources into 3D graphics, making it a perfect walking simulator with a marvellous 3D environment. But they lost their sense of proportion in almost all other aspects. TL;DR, the game HFW, has an extraordinary 3D world that immerses players in beautiful landscapes and lighting;  Unfortunately, this is a game rather than a showcase of PC graphics. Considering it could do much better in narratives, gameplay, and controls, it is recommended that you take it in with a considerable discount. Hear me out; it will help :The superficial story1, the absence of narratives: I heard that Horizon Forbidden West (HFW) has a much better story than Horizon Zero Dawn(HZD), but this is just a marketing slogan. Where is the conscience for marketing trolls to mislead players like this? In this game, you only get to lay your eyes on the ultimate antagonists a few times and for 1-2 minutes each time. They are absent almost the whole game until the last hour(1%-2% of the gaming); you don't know the antagonists' motivation, plans, and characters. They are just senseless evil; you just get a premise and an armageddon; developers simply ignore everything in between and leave players a "premium story" that can be concluded in one sentence: they must die and don't ask why. 2, Flimsy characterizing: Many NPCs give side quests in HFW, but none are impressive due to their perfunctory role design. Developers didn't spend enough time on individual NPCs except for the collective character for each tribe, so most NPCs look soulless and lifeless despite the dramatic body language and ostentatious lines. Players don't get to know even their closest companions; there is simply nothing to discover about them. They just don't exist before players meet them. 3, Witless Lines: people don't talk like that! Many dialogues are intolerably horrible; they feel like two or more people keep beating the bush around with senseless replies. Everyone knows which sentence should be picked up, but they just can't catch it; this includes the MC: Aloy! For many times I just yelled in my mind: stop it, just cut the crap and get to the point! Later, I stopped reading the dialogue of most side quests; The over-complicated combat and scavenge.Not every game needs a good story as long as they can provide other enjoyment in different aspects, like combat and scavenging. But the combat and scavenging in the game are not enjoyable at all. 1, overwhelmingly complicated combat: compared with the over-simplified story, the combat is overwhelmingly complex. With five elements countering each other, ten types of weapons, forty-three types of machines, over eighty kinds of ammo, and more than one hundred active and passive skills, you can imagine what a messy, bustling hodgepodge the combat is. The most difficult thing in combat is avoiding making mistakes, which is primarily impossible; you must swatch and select the correct bows and arrows, choose the right skills, aim at a tiny spot and manage the cooling down period while you dodge the attack from all directions. It requires you to do too many things at the same time. Eventually, the combat makes you a fool, and you would feel stupid even if you won the fight. Where is the enjoyment when you make a fool of yourself? Besides, the game tries to exploit players' mistakes, which is inevitable(as mentioned above). The combat system is so complex that players must follow specific patterns like you must carry out reconnaissance with your "focus"--- a smart AR device that is extremely important in this game. However, you can't fight enemies when it is turned on(you just can't). You usually need to sneak and get close to your enemies to use the focus before you engage in the fight and expose yourself. However, in many main quests, the game just throws the enemies at your face and exposes you regardless after the cutscenes, so you won't be able to use the focus before making many mistakes during the blind fight. 2. Weird challenges: Unlike the classic PRGs, you won't get a better MC or weapon or stronger enemies in this game. Instead, you get weird challenges. For example, you need rarer material to upgrade your better weapon(you must, or it wouldn't be "better"). To get that material, you are required to dismember machines alive, meaning you can't kill the machine until you drop certain parts with a particular arrow. You will get this funny scene:  the machine tries to kill you with all it has while you are trying to keep both the machine and yourself alive long enough so that you can get that material --- another contradiction makes you a fool. 3. It sabotages players, meaning it often debuffs you and many weapons. Have you learnt a new powerful skill, or have you just got a new legendary weapon? You'd better check how they get debuffed before the celebration. For example, you could learn a powerful hunting skill, but you must tolerate the poor accuracy and limited shooting angle(you can't shoot any enemy above you on a hill or in the sky); Some legendary weapons seriously suffer a sluggish shooting rate. Anyway, if you are an action-game fan who craves a clean and quick kill, or you love to see a stronger MC along with the gaming, you would surely be seriously frustrated. Of course, one can practice on a solo colossus (the easiest combat in the game) and get a perfect kill, but what is the fun of that kind of drudgery? Conclusively, HFW has an extraordinary 3D world that immerses players in beautiful landscapes and lighting; the developers invest a lot in graphics(and marketing as well). Unfortunately, this is a game rather than a showcase of PC graphics. Considering it could do much better in narratives, gameplay, and controls, it is recommended that you take it in with a considerable discount.

Horizon Forbidden West is the sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn and is in many ways a worthwhile continuation of the series. It expands upon the first game's beautiful world and mechanics, bringing innovative new improvements while remaining recognisable and retaining a feeling of continuity. The game does however fall short in certain areas when compared to its predecessor, namely in its writing and sense of progression. I would certainly recommend playing Zero Dawn first, and would say that I do personally prefer it out of the two. Still, Forbidden West has many strong points and I greatly enjoyed my time with it. This review presumes a degree of experience with the first game and will use it as a frequent point of reference. It is also spoiler free apart from mentions of central mechanics and structure.Where Forbidden West shines most is through the improvements it brings to Zero Dawn's established mechanics.What stood out most to me was the expanded movement and maneuverability, which greatly adds to all elements of the game. With the addition of a grappling hook/pull tool, the ability to swim underwater, and a glider, you are granted a far greater level of interaction with the environment. These additions also make climbing/parkour feel much more interactive rather than just holding to move forward (which Zero Dawn suffers from). Everything is beautifully and smoothly animated as always.I also liked the significant additions to combat through a greater variety of ranged weapons and an expanded combo-based melee system. Alongside this, there is also mounted combat that lets you use mounts in battle, and other things like a variety of buffs you can trigger. These new combat mechanics are all around brilliant and give you lots of freedom to play however you want and try out different strategies.Unfortunately there are fewer new machine/enemy types than I was hoping for but the new mechanics keep things exciting even for the ones you've encountered in Zero Dawn, and they particularly improve human fights.As a final point, I also really appreciated the better degree of customisation through face paint and armour dye options, as well as the ability to set a different visual outfit to the one you have equipped.Unfortunately, Forbidden West's writing is where I was quite disappointed, particularly in comparison to Zero Dawn. So, there is a lot of complaining in this section.To begin with, the tutorial lasts too long, and after it you are immediately thrown into essentially an epilogue for Zero Dawn's ending where you tie up loose ends. While I understand the need for this, it drags on the game's beginning and was quite frustrating when I just wanted to start the new content.When it comes to the main story, the whole game suffers from the central plot being too urgent/apocalyptic for it to make sense to do any side quests or explore properly. Its pacing is also very inconsistent. Like in Zero Dawn's Nora lands you are initially locked in a relatively small zone of the map and this point of the game also drags itself out too much. There is a big buildup to how exciting the Forbidden West region will be, and when you think you will enter it, you are hit with another interim area. Both of these early regions are very good but they throw off the pacing and feel like they go against your expectations. The story at a point takes a... truly unexpected turn... which I personally didn't like but isn't inherently bad (I guess). Regardless, it doesn't ruin the game. It does however make the structure of the plot feel even messier and is yet another example of poor implementation of what could have been an alright concept.You are eventually given a base to which you can return at any point. For some reason this only occurs maybe a third to halfway into the story. It has limited functionality and feels a bit clunky and unfinished from a game design perspective but it's a nice enough addition, though you have little motivation to return to it of your own initiative. Each region after this is more in the style of Zero Dawn where they are accessible at the same time but also build on each other. It's just a shame that such a significant part of the game is spent essentially building up to this point.Other aspects feel clumsily done, like certain quests and locations being locked behind mechanics that you obtain through story progression. In theory this lets you return to areas for new content but realistically feels like a more hidden form of a level cap that makes you waste time backtracking. I spent a lot of time looking forward to unlocking these elements only for them to be either very few in number () or massively underwhelming in terms of rewards (eg. ).All that being said, Forbidden West does still engross you in the world and is full of varied and loveable characters. You are shown new areas of the post-apocalypse USA and there is a great variety in environments, all of which are beautiful. The new tribes are interesting and different, and the design of various locations is excellent (eg. ). I really liked how story and quest events would at times radically change an area's landscape, and the writers were clearly more confident with including larger and more-influential story turns. However, there are locations that seem designed for quests or fights that never happen, which makes me wonder if there was a significant amount of cut content.Both returning characters and new companions are well written and there are some really great additions to the cast. Aloy's own development is a bit forced and cliché, but is still nice to see if you enjoy that kind of thing. Less significant characters throughout the world are also mostly likeable and there are certain very memorable figures.The DLC unlocks after you finish the base game. It suffers from the same bad writing as the main storyline, and to me it felt like it was compensating for the somewhat empty final region of the base game, recycling ideas that could have been used there. The main benefit of the DLC is that it lets you take advantage of mechanics that are only unlocked quite late and would otherwise be underused. Some memorable moments but overall a bit rushed and with less content than I expected, far less compared to the Frozen Wilds.Forbidden West was disappointing in many ways.  – the game is exceptionally fun in its gameplay, and is even more detailed and beautiful in its world than Zero Dawn. I wouldn't recommend it as an entryway into the Horizon series, but I would recommend it to returning players and fans of the series, just with a few caveats ---Forbidden West is an odd mixture of excellent visual design and excellent gameplay combined with strangely poor writing and fundamentally flawed progression. The game has a lot of content to offer and was clearly lovingly made, there are just a few baffling decisions from the developers that are unfortunately very central. If you keep these things in mind and appreciate the game for the good elements it has, it's very fun and certainly worthwhile. I only wish the writing would not have been quite as much of a downgrade as it was, and that there was less repetition of the various open-world activities.My sentiment is bittersweet: I had a lot of moments of disappointment, but overall I loved the new characters and expansions to the world of Horizon, and really had a lot of fun with the combat and puzzles throughout the game. Just because I'd change some things if I could doesn't mean that I didn't love everything else.

I loved the first game so had to try this. While I do enjoy it and would recommend it, Id like to share some of my thoughts that keeps me from actually liking the game.  Here's what I mean:This is literally 10 times the game Zero Dawn was, in every way. You now have a skill tree that looks like Path of Exile's with Valor Surges which operate like Action Skills if you're familiar with Borderlands or any game with some advanced power that requires a cool-down after use.  TLDRGood- Openworld is the most beautiful I have ever seen, without question. Its literally the only thing keeping me playing now. 11/10- Openworld is "alive"; there are tribes and machines fighting in the background all the time even if you're not close. You can stumble upon a tribe hunting a machine and just watch it unfold.- NPC idle animations are S-Tier. I saw a guy trip over a rock while carrying a box, turn around, yell at it, then continue on with his day. I have never seen it again.- Weapon variety is nice- Skill tree is good once you figure out how it works- Underwater swimming and environment is literally perfect. You will be creeped out by how accurate the water is and you can even turn on "thalassaphobia" mode to turn it down a notch if it really bothers you.- Lots of settings to customize your experience; you WILL want to change a lot of things, trust me.- Machines are interesting, varied, and well animated. BAD- This game is not for casuals; even Normal difficulty was frustrating for me and i beat ZD on Ultra Hard- UI is needlessly terrible and uninformative with wasted space- Navigation marker is horrific; I still get lost and check my map regularly- Using tools in combat is so clunky I can't even use them and you definitely need them- Every machine has some unavoidable absolutely cheap and frustrating attack that will knock you down no matter where you are. Be prepared to literally have machines spawn camp you so the instant you stand up you get knocked down IMMEDIATELY.  And that is done multiple times in a single battle.- Way, WAY too many NPCs and story beats going on. They wanted to make this a Christopher Nolan and James Cameron themed interactive movie. Trying to be way too smart for it's own good and ends up convoluted and bloated. Half this story could've been saved for Horizon 3. I skipped nearly every cutscene after the first couple hours, I just couldn't follow anything and didnt care.- Melee combat was heavily emphasized and absolutely sucks and is not why we like Aloy- Aloy is also just a puppet in this game; she doesn't feel like a Connor, Ripley, or Leia. She is more of a sidekick and does the bidding of the myriad NPCs you run into. REVIEWThere are at least 30 machines not including variants of many of them. Lots of new weapon types and outfits with stats.  So yeah, get ready to make "builds" in a casual 3rd person PvE open world game. And lets not forget there are also HOURS of cutscenes that after about 30 minutes I couldn't even follow and just started skipping everything. The first 3 hours of this game is an absolute snoozefest, I barely survived. I LOVED the story of Zero Dawn but his is pretty much trash. I won't spoil it but I was very lost and disappointed early on. It wasn't all bad, but nowhere NEAR the quality of Zero Dawn. More isn't always better! Also the music was terrible; within the first 30 seconds I was trying to turn it down, I have no idea what they were thinking with that intro song.It seems like literally every idea Guerrilla Games (GG) ever had was stuffed into this game. It seriously has an identity crisis. And now they have a heavy emphasis on melee combat. Melee combat in this game is so clunky and frustrating I still, after 400 hours, havent even completed the melee tutorials. They are horrific and the idea of melee in this game is not appealing. No one ever thought "ya know, these explosive arrows kinda suck, let me hit them with my spear".  Again, no idea was rejected during the making of this game.Why melee combat emphasis? Well because GG also decided to focus HEAVILY on the human side of the story. In a game about robot dinosaurs from the future they want us to fight many, MANY, different tribes of humans which were so similar I still can't tell who is who or why they are important. In battle it's nearly impossible to determine whos on my side. I was unable to focus on the story due to so many tribes and characters being introduced.  Seriously, if there are less than 100 named NPCs in this I would be shocked. Its ridiculous how overstuffed this game is.Also, I think GG forgot that this was a 3rd person PvE openworld game because the grind involved in this makes me think it should have loot boxes and a shop to help speed up the process.  Holy balls, you've seen nothing like it in a non-live service game. The grind to get anything upgraded in this game borders on tedium and totally sucks the fun out of killing dinosaurs and turns it into work.And speaking of the dinosaurs; they are awesome as you would expect. The variety is great; flying and swimming machines were added and work well. But, they are also mostly bastards. Every single machine has at least one absolutely cheap and frustrating attack that can't be avoided and always seems to knock me down. And knockdowns in this game are insane; you will want to throw your controller against a wall it takes Aloy like 9 minutes to get up from even a small knockdown its so frustrating. All the machines swarm you, are never alone, and always have at least one cheat move. Plus, everything has like 10 times more parts to remove, some are microscopic and the machines all have very jerky animations so you are guaranteed to miss some shots due to erratic and unrealistic movements. Everything is against you in this game; nothing is easy and seems like its difficult just to be difficult. Theres almost no casual fun to be had here; even the race events are absolutely brutal. On easy you still get rekt and I almost always lost on the last possible frame. Again; just frustrating and not fun.  And dont get me started on the Arena. That is the most unfair, unfun "challenge" I have ever had to sweat through in a PvE game. Its a completely miserable experience and I turned it down to story mode and STILL got frustrated at some of the fights. Also they nerfed the hell out of traps; one of my favorite aspects of Zero Dawn. I would love setting up tripwires and steering herds into them to watch them explode. Well, youll get none of that in FW.  See, GG didn't want us having fun in this game. They purposely limited the number of traps to 2 by default, down from 15. Also they disappear after a certain time and you can now be damaged by them. WHY?! In this game you could really use these but you have to give up so many other sources of damage to get them viable it's just not worth it and won't work above Normal difficulty.And also, the UI is terrible and STILL makes no sense. Why can't I see what item I have created a job for? Why do they have random arrow types on the same bow? Why can't I tell how many items I am selling easily? Why are weaves and coils so similar in shape and most are useless? Why can't I see my loadout when changing weapons when there is more than enough screen real estate to show it?To sum it up; this is a frustrating sequel to a near masterpiece. It had big shoes to fill and GG decided to stuff them full of as much crap as they could, but failed to include what made ZD so memorable. The story is as bloated as the skill trees and the entire game feels directionless. GG couldn't decide if they wanted to make the next Lara Croft or Sarah Connor and ended up with a cardboard cutout of Rey Skywalker. Yikes.

This isn't just a review, it's a thank you note to Guerilla Games. Horizon Forbidden West isn't a game, it's an experience. It's the kind of title that redefines what open-world adventures can be.Aloy's journey through the Forbidden West is nothing short of phenomenal. The story is captivating, weaving intricate threads of humanity, technology, and the lingering threat from the past. Every narrative beat lands perfectly, leaving me desperate to see what unfolded next. But Forbidden West goes beyond just a good plot. The characters, both new and familiar, are richly developed, each with their own motivations and struggles that feel genuine. Aloy herself continues to be a fantastic protagonist – strong, resourceful, and with a heart of gold. I found myself genuinely invested in her well-being and the fate of the world she fights to save.Visually, Forbidden West is a knockout. The environments are breathtaking, from the lush jungles to the desolate wastelands. Every corner of the world feels meticulously crafted, teeming with life and detail. The machines are even more impressive, each one a marvel of design and animation. But the true beauty lies in how seamlessly the story and world intertwine. Exploring these landscapes feels like unraveling a forgotten history, a testament to the incredible world-building by the developers.The combat is another highlight. It's fluid, strategic, and immensely satisfying. Aloy's new arsenal of weapons and skills offers a ton of variety, allowing you to approach encounters in creative ways. Whether you're setting traps, exploiting machine weaknesses, or going in guns blazing, there's a playstyle for everyone.Honestly, this is the first time I've felt like a developer truly deserves the money I spent on a game. Horizon Forbidden West isn't just worth the price tag, it surpasses it in every way imaginable. It's a landmark achievement in storytelling, world design, and gameplay. If you're looking for an unforgettable adventure, look no further. This is a must-play for any gamer, and a shining example of what video games can achieve at their finest.

Overall I quite like the game, it's a step down from the first game, but still well worth the time and money.I'll get the negatives out of the way first.- The story is a bit bland, I can't really put my finger on exactly what it is, probably a combination of a lot of things. The companion characters are decent, but doesn't really play much of a role. The main antagonists shifts the atmosphere  which I feel takes away from the otherwise very solid tribal/sci-fi.- Combat is solid as ever, but I feel the new machines doesn't really capitalize on what makes the combat so utterly satisfying in Horizon. Much like Dark Souls, Horizon combat lends itself thoroughly to deliberate one-on-one battles, but many of the new machines are quick, aggressive, comes in groups and have to few weak spots/components compared to their health. Especially the new  are a pain and a half to fight.- Politics. I will readily admit that I feel like a ♥♥♥♥ bringing it up, but I cannot review the game and not do so, because it is pervasive and obnoxiously obvious. It is quite clear that the writers had, if not an agenda, then at least very strict writing guidelines. Women are morally good, capable and cannot fail. If the story calls for an antagonistic character or for somebody to have failed, it will be a man and specifically a white man in the case of an antagonist. It doesn't usually bother me, it was also the case in Zero Dawn (albeit to a lesser extent), but it was so in my face playing this that it was difficult to overlook. Asked to check on a lost group of warriors? You can bet money that it'll be led by a capable woman who's valiantly protecting the wounded men. Somebody speaks ill of their leader, it'll be a white man. A woman is acting like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? Oh, she's being forced to do so by a man and will overthrow him.Just to reiterate, I do not mind capable women in my games. It even make sense in the world of Horizon, you're not beating the machines with brute strength, so men do not have an advantage. But it is distracting when the writing is this bound to some meta writing guidelines, on some level it feel like the game was written by activists rather than actual writers.- Critical hit. A critical hit is me hitting a weakspot, weapon, exposed component or triggering an elemental state. I don't need or want a percentage chance to deal extra damage or to instantly inflict an elemental state. The first game didn't have any luck involved when it came to taking down machines, if the machine died it meant that you beat it, your strategy worked, you exploited the weaknesses and won. It felt great formulating a strategy for specific machines, it gave you a feeling of "this is MY way of killing a Thunderjaw". That's still present of cause, but I think the introduction of variables like crit and instant-status cheapens the feeling of conquering a machine through strategy.That's the negative out of the way.The good stuff is 100% the world and combat and I personally feel that it makes up for any and all shortcomings of the game. The world is beautiful and interesting, the machines, environments and cultures all make up a great world to explore and immerse yourself in. I adore the marriage between the tribal and futuristic in the clothing, equipment, adornments and weapons.The combat is incredible like the first game, even if the new machines are not quite as good as the old. There's a palpable satisfaction in nailing a weakspot and seeing components flying. Formulating a strategy based on weaknesses, exposed components, which attacks and abilities to disable. I cannot stress just how great it feels to fight machines in this game and its predecessor (specifically machines, human enemies are pretty uninteresting).They've introduced a melee upgrade tree and I do not understand why. You're not going to engage the machines in melee for obvious reasons and human enemies are better engaged at range as well. It really seems the tree is just there for the melee pits (like the hunting grounds, but for melee against humans).Overall I'd give the game a solid 7/10.The combat (majority of the game) is bloody great, but the story and especially the distracting politics is dragging the score down. Still, it's an easy recommend.

I loved Horizon Zero Dawn and enjoyed Forbidden West. Not having played the games on Playstation, I basically experienced them on PC as they got released. Horizon Zero Dawn became one of my favorite games of all time so I had pretty high expectations of Forbidden West.In a nutshell, I had a more pleasant experience with Zero Dawn, than Forbidden West. I think it has to do with two things: (1) I found that the way the outstandingly brilliant story unravels in the first game (and the quality of the story itself) was better (than in Forbidden West)(2) at times I felt overwhelmed by the many types of combos, techniques, ranged + melee combos; the developers wanted to make Forbidden West bigger and better, I get that but sometimes less is more and while I do appreciate some of the new elements, it simply felt like a bit too much to remember; some of the new mechanics are amazing though, others not so much. Combat in general feels better in Forbidden West but they could have simplified a couple of things. For someone who doesn't really play games like Tekken, Street fighter, it felt like I had to play a different game in order to finish the fighting pit challenges. As I said, I'm sure a lot of people see this as a positive. My personal opinion is that it is a bit too much. And needless to say, you don't have to become a melee combat master to beat the game; this is only related to optional challenges like the fighting pit.One other aspect I didn't love in Forbidden West is that the challenges (like the racing competition on a mount, fighting bots in an arena, fighting people in a pit) will give you most of the legendary items; would have preferred that there were less legendary items and that you'd get them by exploring some unique areas (like the Shield-Weaver in Zero Dawn). Instead there is a simple (somewhat lazy) formula that seems more prevalent in Forbidden West: complete all challenges, get most legendary items. That's it. This was present in the first game too, just not to this extent. You do get legendary items by completing side-quests too but from what I can tell, most legendary items are won by completing these challenges so you're basically being somewhat forced to play the mini-games in the game to get better gear, rather than the game itself. And yes, I do consider these challenges mini-games - even though they use the same mechanics as the core game - simply because of their complexity.All that being said, Forbidden West is still an amazing game and I enjoyed most of it. Some of the new mechanics were amazing. I would love it if the next game in the series would be the best of both worlds: story and pacing from Zero Dawn and some of the new mechanics from the second (a bit simplified for us simple folk).The DLC - Burning Shores - still needs some technical optimization; had a few crashes, several cut-scenes where a character was completely missing from the cut-scene (you could only hear them) and long loading screens while exploring that would just pop up out of nowhere.

I beat the original Horizon on PS4 and PC, but hadn't yet tried Forbidden West. A couple hours in and my first impression is: this is the most polished PS4/PS5 port I've ever played on launch week. With DLSS and frame generation, HFW hits an astoundingly consistent 120 fps in the open world, with drops to ~90 fps in busy settlements. This is at Ultra settings at 1440p. Basically, HFW is rendering next gen graphics with even better performance than I've ever been able to get on HZD's PC port at Ultra settings & 1440p (80-90fps, with drops). I can't even imagine what Nixxes' dev team did to produce such optimized performance, but it feels like voodooIn terms of the game itself: I was never that enamored with HZD's story or world-building, but the game does a decent job of picking up soon after the events in the first game with an interesting premise for Aloy's next main quest. Unfortunately the player-character is reduced back to level 1 in terms of skills. But in the tutorial mission you learn enough moves and mechanics and new weapons that Aloy's skill amnesia is easy enough to look past. The action feels much faster and tighter, though that may partly be from how HFW makes heavy use of the rumble features of the PS5 DualSense controller.One big improvement: the designers seem to have eliminated HZD's annoying feature of making you spend 20% of your exploration time in the inventory menu cleaning out junk. It's never really explained in the tutorial but you just pick stuff up and if you have too much ridge wood, it goes into your "stash". Not sure how the stash interacts with the inventory but I haven't yet had to deal with a "Inventory is full" message.Speaking of the inventory system: bless the designer who added the auto-pickup option in the Accessibility settings. It's surprising how removing the endless tedious button-pressing to harvest ridge wood ends up making the gameplay feel so much tighter and more fun.

There's no doubt this game is worth playing, especially if you're like me, having finished the last battle in HZD and couldn't stop wondering what's next. The quality of the port is top-notch, as always - you can't expect less from Nixxes. That's why I bought HFW on day 1, and that's why I'm waiting for Ghost of Tsushima later in May 2024. , I'm somehow getting a much better picture with the built-in on-device FSR 1 rather than the provided in-game FSR 2.2. On a mix of low-medium settings, I'm getting a solid 30 fps and am slowly progressing through the story.

I'll be frank, in my opinion the Horizon series is the best ARPG since the Legend Zelda series dropped. I know that is a bold claim but it is not one I make lightly. That is why I got this on PS5 and now PC. I really can't speak highly enough about this game. The story is amazing and the graphics while not flawless are seriously impressive. Everything rendered in great detail, rich in color, with good lighting, hair physics etc...you can even see a light peach fuzz on Aloy's (and others) face, love it or hate it. I know some roast Aloy's looks as ugly but personally I think she is cute, be it in a bit goofy and nerdish way. She isn't a super model that much is for certain. Aloy is more like the smart girl from next door. Though it helps I always like an attractive red head who is tough and smart even if she has some light peach fuzz....AND it is nice to see everyday people as the heroes. Not every character in a game needs to be a perfect ten as I in fact prefer things be more in line with real life as I find that more immersive and realistic. Now the graphics do have some abnormalities but most aren't that big of an issue. Honestly the most annoying issue for me usually shows up in cut scenes with faces/hair back-lit by lighter out of focus backgrounds where the filter's blur effect breaks down. Things go from hazy to clear near hair, faces and sometimes even character models in these lighter areas. It basically creates a distracting halo effect I could do without. Unfortunately you can even see it in game-play at times. Sadly this was also present in Horizon Zero Dawn (HZD) as well so I suspect it's an issue with the Decima engine used for both games. Beyond that one glaring issue everything else feels/looks very next gen and leaves me without any big complaints. Yes they should have added ray-tracing (path tracing would have been even better, want more of that in all games)...the water physics could have been better but these are all small critiques that are common in many modern games which is exactly why I would file them away as extremely minor and barely worth mentioning category.The controls are good and I'd argue a bit more polished compared to the first game. I'd also say going with a fully open world feels better for the most part but I would have been more than fine with the semi-open world like HZD employed. Both titles like most modern ARPG/RPG/MMO titles, did suffer from some fetch quest fatigue though it wasn't nearly as bad as some of the more recent titles to drop. Long story short if you enjoy a good ARPG, this is the game for you. If you do not, move along there is nothing to see here for you.

I loved the first game and was looking for more of the same, and that is exactly what we got. HFW has made at least minor improvements to almost every feature of HZD plus added in a bunch of new ones. Some things have been vastly improved (like climbing, fast travel, melee combat, item storage, and character building), while some have just been tweaked (scanned enemy HUD, dialog navigation, and map locations, among others). Same high level of storytelling with lots of twists and escalations in the stakes, and the battles feel so epic, just like the first game. Only things I can think of that aren't obviously improved are the weapon system, which is (at first) confusing and offers too many options, but this gets easier with experience and pays off in the late game (and, I assume, in NG+), and also the item pouch system, which is tragically broken. Good thing the only items I ever really use are rocks and health potions, because selecting and maintaining the right amount of traps/potions/food/etc in your pouch is nearly impossible. Otherwise, as someone who enthusiastically 100%ed HZD, this game is pretty much perfect. It feels like an extension of the original game with noticeably less friction in the UX and a handful of unexpected improvements. What more could you possibly want from a sequel to one of the best games in recent history?I should say that my play style is "clear all side quests asap while looting everything." The Horizon series rewards this exact play style, and its worst possible scenarios arise when you are outmatched and under-provisioned. I never really worry that I'm going to miss something essential to the story or not have strong enough weapons to fight whom/whatever I encounter, but it takes a lot of time to play this way (140 hours at time of writing, ~90% completion, still with some major main story ahead of me). I imagine this game is less fun if you expect to be able to rush through it, but there are some late game perks that would make lots of the side quests easier. I think on my NG+ playthrough I will focus on the main storyline before branching out too much. Again, I have the impression that this is how the Horizon series is deliberately structured, so please note that I give it a glowing review from the perspective of the type of player Horizon is geared towards.

Just finished Horizon Forbidden West on PC after around 150 hours and thoroughly enjoyed it.  I took my time completing most side quests and following the story line before finishing the game.  I also really enjoyed the first one Zero Dawn.I found with Forbidden West the character immersion during quests was better, delving more into each one and actually feeling like you knew and connected with the people you came across.  Some quests touched on some important issues like dimentia, peer presure, bullying and also self worth, companionship and teamwork.  I experienced a wide variety of emotions from hate to love and also sadness when a main character died almost shedding a tear.On another note was also some bad points.  The game crashed alot and sometimes took half a dozen times to load before it would run.  I run a Intel i9 13900k with 64gb ram Asus Z790 Prime MB and 3 Samsung SSD M.2 and Asus GForce 4070TI card.   I think alot of the crashes were due to the instability of the 13th and 14th gen CPU's and MB manufacturers exceeding recommended thresholds creating shader loading issues and multiple crashes, especially during certain cut scenes.I recently did a bios upgrade that seems to have solved alot of the problems not only with this game but others as well.I did find upgrading weapons and armour to be very grindy and time consuming. The melee skills also felt hard to use and master with multiple different mouse and button clicks to remember.  Personally I completed the game using mostly ranged combat and it was good to see the improved variety of weapons and elements that they offered.Overall I thoroughly enjoyed it and it was worth every cent.

A perfect sequel to an already amazing first game. Added pretty much all of the "Quality of Life" features I wished Zero Dawn had. (e.g infinite stash) It's a direct continuation, so it builds upon the story told in Zero Dawn (and Frozen Wilds), but it's set in an entirely new massive region with different biomes. The graphics are some of the best I have ever seen in an open world game! The landscapes are stunning & incredibly varied, from deserts, forests, seas & all the way to snowy peaks. The character rendering is also fantastic & the facial animation during dialogues has been much improved from Zero Dawn. I love game photography & took hundreds of pics during my time with Forbidden West. So many breathtaking views! There are new tribes, tons of new lore to uncover & I truly love the whole cast. The open world is gigantic with plenty of side quests & other activities (mini-games, racing, underwater exploration, dungeons and others). It tooks me about 130 hours to do basically around 90% of the available content + the Burning Shores expansion. The story was very intriguing thanks to a new mysterious threat and it was really fun discovering all new lore about the world of Horizon. I really enjoy the universe of this series, it's so well put together. Overall, this is one of my favorite games, easily jumped into my all-time top 20 & I can't wait to play Horizon 3 whenever it happens (my guess is 2026/2027). Definitely buying the Lego Horizon game to get my fix for the time being :)
