Having played extensively on my Playstation, it should tell you how I feel about the game having bought it a second time. It's a great game, but not perfect. On the good side, the graphics, environments, and look of the thing is incredible. Exploring the Forbidden West is constant eye-candy. Surprisingly the game runs very smooth on high settings. I'm playing on a 3050 graphics card, the recommended is 3060. So far I've had no frame-rate issues at all and everything works great. gameplay-wise its fantastic and loads of fun shooting big metal dinos with an arsenal of wacky weapons. Towards the end you can fly around, and believe me I wanted to explore every nook and cranny of the map. The story in my opinion is a great idea ruined by terrible dialog.The villains (slight spoiler) are basically generic bad guys in Star Trek outfits, but there were moments where they did feel like a proper threat. Now for the bad. Aloy is so freaking pretentious in this one. She constantly treats everyone aaround her like they are stupid, yet she does some some pretty dumb stuff herself. In the first game she wasn't so insufferable, but in this one she acts like she walks on water. The constant talking to herself is maddening. "Please shut up for ten seconds!" I found myself thinking the entire campaign. The dialog here is eye-rolling bad. It often feels like a Netflix show for teens, and I skipped half the cutscenes in the game because it. There's defiantly some heavy political correctness in this game as well. Every male in the game is either crushing on Aloy, an absolute incompetent idiot, a crazy meat-head, a wimp, or a gullible irritant who's just in the way. The women in the game act like dudes half the time, just girlbossin all over the place and accomplishing physical feats a seasoned bodybuilder would struggle with. The bad guys, in a game chalked so full of diversity it could be a community college ad, are amazingly all white rich people. Yeah they were real subtle with it. To summarize, the game looks and plays fantastic while the writing and dialog are ultra cringe.

I enjoyed Zero Dawn a lot. I played it both on console and PC. This port is solid. I've had some small crashes and a bug or two, but that is acceptable considering how frequently the game is saved.However, some aspects feel pretty dated and might steer you away from a purchase.- Climbing "puzzles" do what Assassin's Creed games did 10+ years ago.- Moving a box/cart/charging a power cell puzzles are tedious as heck, and the fact that they are a mainstay is surprising.- Some areas of the game are arbitrarily gated (via unlocks as you progress the main story). This really doesn't add anything but a bit of frustration as you explore.- There's some really good writing and interesting characters (mostly the quirky and goofy ones), but some parts are pretty poor and feel low effort. E.g., baddie committing suicide with a bomb that only takes him out and doesn't even harm Aloy because of plot armor, or characters acting way more stupid than anyone staying alive in a world as harsh as this should be able too.- Weapons of higher rarity tend to outclass any lower rarity weapon, making it too advantageous to adjust playstyle according to your weapons rather than picking one that you enjoy. This is a smaller problem thanks to upgrades though.- Combat against humanoids is still pretty boring and janky. It feels largely the same as Zero Dawn.- Cauldrons are identical to what they were in Zero Dawn, except for some new climbing mechanics and visuals.- You can only respec all talent points at once, not one at a time, and relearning them takes a lot of time (hold to learn). Making a mistake in the process is infuriating.- NPCs are pretty lifeless. Multiple times you'll run into traders just chilling next to a campfire 20 meters from an absolute warzone as if nothing is going on.It is a shame that quite a few issues from zero dawn remained, and that some new ones were introduced. Some introduced features feel pretty janky, e.g. the grappling hook (Rocksteady nailed this 15 years ago).However, If you like the world/setting and a visually appealing experience, there is enjoyment to be had here. The combat is engaging if you spend time crafting a strategy. But if you are sensitive to tedium or poor writing, or want a gameplay loop with instant gratification this game might disappoint. That said, I have changed my initially negative review from negative to positive after spending more time with it. What you get in the first 10 hours is very barebones, and then it starts to open up a lot.

An extremely good port that I was worried would not run on my 2019 laptop, and yet... it does so *wonderfully*!!! I am incredibly astounded by how well it plays from start to finish, and even working well with mouse and keyboard controls after some adjustment. Much like the first game, a lot of time in the game is spent exploring, parkouring, and a small slice of it puzzle solving (with a lot of the puzzles being tied to optional content), but there is still tons of combat to be had as well. Learning how to best tackle machines, especially when terrain is unique or there are other smaller machines around, feels so darn satisfying still. Playing on Very Hard, the game starts *very* hard, and I would probably recommend it more for people who have played Horizon Zero Dawn on a higher difficulty, and even though the player gets a fairly significant spike in power later into the game, it will still be an uphill battle. If you are the sort to upgrade every weapon to the max, expect a *lot* of grinding, which typically involves fast travelling to the machine(s) you need parts from, killing, then fast travelling elsewhere for more machine parts, and kind of going back and forth. Never in my playthrough did I feel it necessary to upgrade all my weapons to the max, and just playing through the story casually I often had more than enough parts for most of the weapons I wanted to use. However. Very Hard difficulty aside, so long as you do not play on *Ultra* Hard, you can change the game's difficult at any time, if you ever feel you are stuck, aren't having fun with the difficulty, or just want to grind certain machines without needing to sweat over killing them a dozen times each. I enjoy the story, and in particular the side quests that have you learn about the cultures and going ons around Aloy. I think the new machines are very fun and makes the roster even more diverse feeling, even with a lot of returning machines. I enjoy the collect-a-thon feel of trying to get 100% completion, and though I'm a sliver from completion, it has been fun the whole time for me. However. There are two bugs that kind of hurt the game for me but don't kill it. With auto-aim off (forced to be off at higher difficulties), some shots don't connect, even though you can see the arrow pass straight through machines, and I'm not certain what a workaround could be. It has never been consistent enough to happy a lot, but it *is* there. The second bug is that explosive traps you set down do not damage enemies unless they walk into them. Virtually *none* of the explosive traps you can place down or are in the environment you can blow up affect enemies, but they certainly still affect the player. Trapping isn't something I'm super big on, but the game has a ton of support for people who do like to trap, so it's a shame that it's just non functional.With all that being said though. Honestly, absolutely A+ pick for an action adventure game. The pros far outweigh the cons for me, and the fact it plays so well on my laptop is a blessing. Even if I can't play on high settings, I can still pause the game, turn settings up to max, and use the new (and way better) photo mode for taking screenshots too!

Fantastic game with interesting combat, a lovable protagonist, beautiful world and unique setting. Absolutely recommended, especially if you liked the first installment. 10/10Gameplay and combat feels like a solid improvement on what made Zero Dawn so appealing. New weapons, skills and abilities, weapon techniques, and an improved melee combat add even more layers to the--already engaging--combat puzzles. New transversal options and better climbing are welcome additions. The story is great, but franky does not match Zero Dawn's. It does nothing groundbreaking new and therefore feels a bit predictable. However, the writers still made a fantastic job with Aloy's character development. Living through her early life and overcoming the struggles in ZD lets the player connect with the protagonist; in Forbidden West Aloy grows as a person and finds her true self. It seamlessly continues the quest for her identity from the first game. The exact same thing can be said about the Burning Shores DLC.There is even more side content, and the recurring activities (e.g. tallnecks or cauldrons) are more interesting as they they are all unique. Loot system is more complex now, as you need specific machine parts for upgrading your gear. This gives you a reason to hunt machines outside the quests.I also want to praise how the devs handled continuity: most skills from ZD are unlocked from the start, which forces the skilltree to offer something new. It is a great balancing act which suits both new players and veterans alike. Graphics, Music, Sound, Animations etc are all as you would expect from a AAA title.Overall it is the perfect sequel in every aspect. Well done, Guerrilla.

Steam really needs a better rating system because this game deserves a solid "meh."  The combat with machines can be at times incredible and it should make for a great game but so much else drags it down.  The devs seemed to really take to heart that more is better.One of the worst parts of the first game was all the climbing.  It was boring, took way too long, and the only challenge was running around until you found the colorful spots where you could climb.  Forbidden West removes the colorful climbing spots so it does not look as goofy and instead you have to constantly push down RS to highlight climbing spots, that's not an improvement.  What's worse is they added SOOOO many climbing spots where they serve no purpose at all.  No purpose except that if you run and hit a climbable wall Aloy has a long animation of grabbing it and stabilizing before you can do anything.  This is annoying when just exploring but potentially fatal in a fight.There are SOOOO many weapons and armor now that nothing feels special.  Essentially every status effect can be found on some variant of each weapon but the major problem is that if you find a weapon you really like odds are you will not find that same combination of ammo types and buffs on higher tier weapons.  Higher tier are not necessarily better versions of the weapon but rather a different mix of buffs and ammo types with higher tier having more.  Because more is better right?Melee combat was a weak spot in the first game but it was doable.  All machines other then flyers and the very largest could be reliably fought with melee.  Despite having an entire talent tree dedicated to melee Forbidden West decided to drastically nerf it.  The spear seems to be the only weapon that was ignored as there is only one variant (that I have found in my 50+ hours so far) and there is no upgrading or customization for it at all.  They added a combo system to compensate for this a bit but it is mostly worthless.  Machines are immune to any kind of stun lock so you can't hit them enough times to complete a combo before they hit you.  Humans are more susceptible, until they aren't.  Higher tier humans seem to be immune to combo effects like knockdown or they just break stun and hit you with a rapid attack breaking your combo.The story in the first game was great.  You had the mystery of who Aloy was, what was the deal with all the machines, and general world building.  All of this was handled very well and Aloy herself had some incredible character development as she grew from an unsure child into a force of her own.  Forbidden West was at a major disadvantage here that the mysteries were already solved and Aloy is a hero now but they started off well by having her go to an area that may not care that she saved Meridian and introducing a new mysterious faction.  However, everyone in the west seems to still know who she is either as the Savior of Meridian or some deed she did in the west and her character development is basically just further planting her feet in the ground that she knows everything, everyone else is dumb, and she and she ALONE can save the world.  It gets tiresome before you even leave the first area.  Aloy just seems to know everything without having learned anything.  I haven't gotten far enough to learn much about the new faction but I don't really care.  They are so advanced that they are seemingly invincible but I am sure Aloy will find a way to hurt them through some miraculous inner monologue discovery.Finally the puzzles.  In the first game I found these to be a minor annoyance as they were not super challenging and really just time sinks.  Well, more is better so there are WAY more puzzles and lots more time consuming elements to solve.  But of course any interesting challenge they may have is narrated away as Aloy dictates exactly what you should do so your only challenge is pushing the buttons and waiting for the animations to play out.Horizon has a great system with machine fights and it needs to stick to that.  All the rest is just fluff that brings the entire game down.

Overall, this is an amazing game with many great improvements over Zero Dawn. I highly recommend this game to anyone. But there are some drawbacks too. Here are my thoughts:   Like the first game, it has astonishing visuals. The landscape and environments are breathtaking, encouraging you to explore more of the land.  The game offers a lot of content. Aside from the main missions, you will have side missions, errands, rebel camps, cauldrons, collectibles, races, vistas, minigames, pit fights, hunter challenges, an arena, and so on.  This is a great quality of life improvement. You don't have to deal with inventory space problems. Any excess material goes to your stash, and you can access them through shelters.  Most of the side quests in Zero Dawn were plainly boring. This time, however, there are some interesting ones. But of course, you still have to deal with some old game type tedious quests.  You have a variety of choices about how to deal with your enemies. The only small drawback is that your weapon wheel can have 6 weapons at max, and unlike Zero Dawn, you probably can't prepare yourself for every combat situation.  There is a huge variety of robots and upgraded versions of some of the older ones. It's always fun to tear them piece by piece.  Some of Zero Dawn's mechanics are improved. For example, riding a Tallneck or finding a vista point requires a bit more effort and challenge. Although this may be unimportant for most people, it is important for me. I don't like wasting time on unskippable game launch logos or pressing the continue button multiple times to start your game (like in Cyberpunk 2077). Just press Esc and continue, that's good enough.   Aloy talks too much to herself. I can't remember how many times I yelled at her to shut up. On some occasions, I even tried to dive underwater to stop her talking.  This is probably the worst aspect of the game; it is so frustrating. Once you get knocked down, you lose like 3-4 seconds and can't do anything (except quick crafting for some unknown reason) until you stand up again, only to be knocked down again, because your enemy was already preparing the second knockdown ability while you were lying down. Some enemies overuse their knockdown abilities to abuse this stun lock. For example, there is a Loch Ness type robot which can jump like 100 meters as if gravity was nonexistent, and since the machine is huge, it is nearly impossible to dodge the knockdown. By the time you get up, it uses the flip swap ability and you get knocked down again. When you think that 2 knockdowns were enough already, this time it uses the water jet ability, and voila, you are kissing the ground again. It gets worse in enclosed spaces with multiple enemies, especially the arena. I wish there was some kind of trait for knockdown resistance or reducing its duration. There's one valor skill that gives you a trait named "crushing resistance". I don't know if it works, but it requires valor points which can be used for better valor skills.  At first, I thought it would be great to enter an arena to fight with a variety of robots. I thought it could be fun, like in Hogwarts Legacy. But no, as you play more, it gets more frustrating because of getting knocked down over and over again. Your maneuverability is further reduced by scaffoldings placed in the arena, and machines are not affected by that because they can easily crush them. The only way to even the odds for you is spamming spike throwers. Fortunately, spike throwers are overpowered against machines. But I guess devs have found another method to take your joy because every 4 levels you are forced to use pre-selected equipment.  The game introduces new melee combo types, and I found them very unappealing. I only used them during the fight pits because they were required. Some of them are very confusing, like "click 2 times left button, wait for a second, then while clicking W button click again left button, then hold G button, when unholding G button click middle button, while in the air fire an arrow". Why add such combos to a game that doesn't even have proper block or parry options? You can easily finish the game without these combos.  This is probably the worst and most unrealistic way to catch fish in a game. You have to swim over the fish and catch them by hand. I mean, you have a bow and a spear, why not use them? In AC Valhalla, you could use your bow.  This is also quite annoying. The focus mode tries to auto-lock to a target while it's in proximity. You can't target another enemy if they are close to your target. It's also very difficult to target weak points of constantly moving enemies, such as Slitherfangs. Unfortunately, you have to fight with your focus before engaging the enemy. Upgrading very rare and legendary items requires a lot of grinding and patience. They require hunting very hard to find robots and materials not guaranteed to drop, like 3 apex slaughterspine circuits and 2 apex stormbird hearts.  If you like exploring like me, you would probably encounter them a lot.   I think that having a dialogue wheel in this game is unnecessary. This is not an RPG game like Mass Effect. You have very limited options to affect the story.  I recommend everyone uncheck this option. I don't remember how many times I have fallen from a cliff or had to restart a platforming area because of this. Fortunately, you can uncheck it since you already have a specific dodge button.

After completing the main story I decided to post my review. So while I have marked this as positive I have a lot of feedback or issues with the game but for me not enough to say the game is horrible. I loved the start I enjoyed interacting with the people and tribes in Forbidden West the story flowed nice at the start and I was hooked until one particular point the story took a weird jump and then just started feeling like HZD rewritten almost to a T and it became choppy and uneven and the ending while it has me curious for a 3rd game I am not going to be a day one buyer for the next one. I will list some of my concerns below for others as well. ProsBeautiful WorldRuns wellWell written dialog with NPC's Lots to explore and do (however there will be a con to this as well)Can see how feedback from HZD was listened toSome side quest story lines are very interesting and fun to playThe world does feel unique to be in ConsMain Story is based of 2 or 3 notes from HZD and takes weird jumps that seem to feel off as well as multiple quests that start without warning that you wont be able to save and get out before you go out the door of where you are to get to the closest save point and the quest is min an hour long and your stuckWay to many new weapons/battle modes/skill tree options compared to HZD making it very hard to follow and know what to unlock what to do and where to find whatTo many weapons only do one thing or you end up with 5 weapons that do the same thing with small differences and no real clarity on ways to go example hunter bow you knew as you upgraded what you would get in HZD in HFW its like you get stuff you need and stuff you don't need or is duplicated on 4 other bowsWhile there is more to do it becomes overwhelming and feels so much like busy work and fetch quests and it doesn't half the time figure out you already have something someone needs and makes you get it againKeyboard controls are horrible...there is no other way to word it and trying to keybind to others is sketchy at best add that to the weird combinations needed to trigger all these new weird modes it just doesn't make the game easy to playClimbing ALOT I had to keep focus lines on in order to do it somewhat smoothThe focus use feels clunky holding down a button to lock while trying to scan just makes it more frustratingLOTS of dialog and cut scenes and not easy really to hear or interact with notes as easily it feels to listen or read them and lots of information dumpingAt the end I do still recommend this game and my pros and cons are only the tip of the icebergs. I did overall enjoy it once I basically ignored most of the added weapons focused on ones that gave me a similar style to what i had in HZD I did try all the new stuff a few times but felt most of it was meh. So I would say watch some videos from ps5 players or experienced players if you have doubts I have not finished Burning Shores as of this review (just started it) but I hope that the devs fix the keyboard controls or allow for better remapping soon the tab key is a BIG one and that if there is a 3rd game that maybe dial it back just a bit on how much new gets dumped in and that they can somehow pull this story back in to bring us back to what was so special about HZD.

Horizon Forbidden West is the second part in the Horizon series following Horizon Zero Dawn. It continues the story of the first game, introducing new places with new tribes to discover, characters to interact with and machines to fight. Alongside these, the game comes with new gameplay mechanics, a revamp to the skill and gear upgrade systems, a greater overall graphical fidelity and various quality of life improvements.Like the previous game, the story and gameplay are fantastic. The worldbuilding is stellar, revealing more about past and present events both directly through story missions and dialogue, as well as indirectly through side missions and various different encounters and collectables throughout the world. I often found myself simply wandering around while taking in the scenery and even more mundane tasks like gathering specific resources to upgrade gear were enjoyable due to the excellent combat system and diverse catalogue of machines.For anyone who has played and enjoyed the previous game, continuing the journey with Horizon Forbidden West is a no-brainer in my mind. For those who have not yet played the predecessor, I can only recommend doing so before continuing with this one, as you will otherwise be missing out on a lot of key aspects regarding the story and the world surrounding it.

I have claimed to be Horizon's biggest fan and biggest hater since I first played and beat Zero Dawn on PS4 at launch. I claimed that game is the definition of a 7/10 and after replaying it on steam I only came to hate it more. I still preordered Forbidden west on PS5 though, and after getting to the actual open world I stopped.Being the biggest Horizon fan that I am though, I made sure to get it on steam as well. This time though I was genuinely taken aback. This game eclipses the first game in just about every single way for me, I enjoyed just about every single thing in this game MUCH more than I did in the first game or in just about ANY sony game. The combat felt so much better, the presentation and story was more engaging, the side quests I actually cared about. It even has one of my favorite missions in ANY game. Of course it is absolutely beautiful too! If ZD was a 7/10 this  is much closer to a 9/10 than anything. It definitely didnt run the best at times, which is fair considering how beautiful it is, but it ran good enough to the point it didnt impede on how I played.My biggest issue with the game, especially on PC, is the DLC. Burning Shores, which is only able to be done after the base game, feels like such a step back in just about every single way to me. I absolutely LOVE water in games and this area is so beautiful, but it is also so boring. It feels much shallower than the base game, the side quests just made me bored, and I couldnt wait to finish the main quest. The new enemies were also just not fun to fight, especially with how poorly the entire DLC ran! The biggest positive I can give is that the final boss is genuinely a really cool setpiece and one of the best things in the series yet.Forbidden West is absolutely a great game and is MUCH better than Zero Dawn in just about every way to me. The biggest difference between this and Zero dawn to me though is that the DLC of Zero Dawn was leagues better than the main game, here the DLC is MUCH worse than the base game. Either way I think it is a great pick up even without the experience of Zero Dawn, with a quick run through of the first game in the first hour you can kinda just tell what is going on.

System specs:  Tuf 3080 10GB variant  Ryzen 5800x3d  32GB of ddr4 ram at 3600 MT/S  Samsung nvme drive  Resolution: 3440x1440p  TL:DR  -Good story - great side quests-the game is harder-Too many items to manage-absolutely insane characters animation-game looks great  -Burning shore is kind of a must to play, easily a 100+ hour game especially if you do new game+.   Read on to a more detailed review with all my thoughts slightly out of order. Okay  here we go:   Good intro that sets up Alloy's main quest with breadcrumb trails revealing more. I like it because it’s linear before exposing you to the entire map giving you time to get settled into the gameplay  Barren light is almost too much of a tutorial area, but it has some interesting quest to make up for it like solving a mystery plus machine strike if you like chess-like minigames  Introduced to too many unavailable collectible at once if you're the exploring type forcing a lot of backtracking if you want to collect everything. I wrote this while in Barren Light. It does not get much better until you unlock what you need via story quests.  skill tree is kind of confusing and honestly a little too much. Too many passive abilities that makes me feel like I'm not really unlocking much and many of the weapons techniques don't feel that useful. It's also not really explained that well because I didn't figure out valor surges until I looked it up and even then, the ultimates feel too short lived to be useful.  Additional notes: 80 hours in and I played most of the game with part breaker valor surge and just now figured out that some of the other ones are beastly if you use it right. Especially powershot with a properly upgraded spike thrower paired with the spike trap technique. My feelings on the skill trees are largely the same. It just breaks the flow of combat if I pause just to swap out a Valor Surge. Weapon techniques are where it's at mostly.  Environments are beautiful and varied just like zero dawn. The art direction is on point. Every area/biomes just feels distinct letting you know what machine might live there. Many of the characters are more memorable for me, especially with the animation work adding to their personalities. The dialogue is way more natural and feels less like I'm listening to an audiobook. The characters themselves give me an uncanny valley feel with how well they managed to animate the smallest details on a character's face. They took the criticism of Zero dawn and just took it as far as they could possibly get.  Enemies are trickier to fight and harder too. Not bs hard like frozen wild but definitely requires learning their weakness. No longer can I just spam tearblast/corruption on many of the enemies to literally rip them to shred. Melee is so much better this time around, but I still feel like using arrows is just better against machines due to how deadly their attacks are. There is a learning curve to fighting each machine type and even their apex variant. I played 100 hours of this game and still get my butt handed to me on a silver platter if I don’t pay attention to the attack pattern and weakness of what I'm fighting. Your outfits matters a lot here too in surviving the elemental attacks.  Honestly this game has too much weapon and outfit variants and too many rarity types for them. I spent a lot of time upgrading them. I don't like the greenshine requirements for upgrading them because it feels arbitrary? May mod that out in future playthrough or use cheat engine to make it irrelevant. There’s already a ton to upgrade. I just got tired of collecting stuff even using the method I learned in zero dawn’s playthroughs (aka collect everything in sight right from the beginning).  The lore for the old world still exists but it's not as personal as zero dawn. I feel like I'm learning more about the actual old world rather than just only about the final stand. It still sucks me in and I still want to seek them out. Many of the ruins tells a story too by environmental cues. It's still cool to see places I visited in real life be represented in the game. All the datapoints and relics ties into the overall tone of the game. World building is still this franchise's strong points so far   This game is demanding. I started with a 3070 and upgraded to a 3080 when I had the ability to obtain one for cheap. The extra cores and vram helps a lot at 3440x1440p. It still hammers my cpu and gpu pretty hard. Related to this.. I'm not going to lie. This is probably one of the best looking game I've ever played especially with the character details. HDR is a must here if you got it (make sure it’s not that fake HDR 400).  Ultrawide support is so much better on this compared to zero dawn. 80 hours in and still have zero issues. The hud makes sense. The cinematics all work. Fov feels right.   The map is much more detailed and actually has names under the marker now, so you don't have to remember what machine is what based on the symbols. I also like that when you discover something you can't access yet, the game will mark it on the map for you.   I'm running into the same problem I did in zero dawn. I keep getting distracted by the side quests before moving on to the main quests. Many of the side quests are practically the same quality as the main quest lines. Some of the random encounters even lead into a small quest if you help that group. I’m not even sure if this is a negative for me but it could be a negative for you. It does ruin the pacing, but I'm used to that with games in the rpg genre.  People react to alloy's exploits in the game as I move on through the story which is the side benefit of getting distracted by the side quests. This makes the respect given to Aloy feel earned because I did do those things and makes the game world feel more alive in this sense.   Slight warning to those of you starting this game out. The story slows down a good bit but then do a huge info dump on you but start picking back up after that.  Too many items in the hotbar on the bottom left that I completely forget I even have them. ex: I forgot that smoke bombs even existed after all the items I collected on the quick bar. Yes, I can fix that, but the problem shouldn't exist in the first place.  Potions are cool but I would just prefer a set amount per potion rather than a limited selection. too easy to pick up a bunch I don't want   Swimming kind of sucks without being able to use my spear. I understand fighting underwater isn't easy but why isn't stealth attack at least an option? I suppose the underwater section are pretty but meh.  This is a great way to get better at fighting machines and get some great gears. I just need the timer in the matches to be just a bit longer because most of them are too short. Also why do I need to pay shards to fight?  It should have been the true ending of the game. The main ending of Forbidden West feels incomplete without it. This is quite different compared to its predecessor Frozen Wilds which simply added more context to the story while adding more enemies. Burning shore also feels more linear pacing wise. I didn’t feel the need to go explore everything or do the many of the side quests (not that there were much... I don’t think). The main villain of Burning shore was better than the ones for the main game. This led to kind of an amazing final boss fight. You do get a better feel for one of the new factions introduced in this game through this villain.

TLDR: If you really enjoyed Horizon: ZD then you'll love Horizon: FW. It vastly improves and expands upon both gameplay and story. Just be ready to listen to a LOT of dialogue!Overall Thoughts:I would highly recommend this game to anyone. As of this review I haven't yet finished the story but felt I've reached a point where I can give an honest review. I really enjoy(ed) this game. If you played HZD back when it first came out I highly recommend continuing the series with this game. HFW expands greatly on the features and experience of the first game. New weapons, more characters, more enemies, better skills, you name it. HFW feels like they wanted to fully flesh out every aspect of HZD for the player to enjoy. The Good:- Heavily expanded upon combat with weapons now feeling more purposeful and diverse.- More enemies to fight, each with their own needed strategies to overcome.- Improved skill usefulness and uniqueness. Introducing "valor surges" and "weapon techniques" that push a player's playstyle even farther in the direction they want.- Amazing characters, facial animations, quests, and encounters.- Several fun collectible grinds that help fill in the massive world.- Beautiful landscapes and visuals for what the modern market offers. (I have a 3060 with a i-7 and can run this game on high graphics with relative ease).- An interesting story that mimics the pace/structure of the first game's.- Several QoL additions including features like easier access to your stash and more fast travel points.The Bad:- The game is VERY (and I mean VERY) dialogue heavy. NPCs have a LOT more dialogue compared to the first game and there are a LOT more NPCs you can interact with. If you're a person that can't stand conversing with NPC's a lot, be prepared to spam the skip button often.- Another point with the dialogue is that it's way too hand-holdy at times. I can understand including dialogue to tip the player on what to do next but man does this game do that a lot. A prime example occurs later in the game when Aloy needs to figure out a lock for a door with another character. You scan and read a data log that 3 feet to the left of the door which says the password for the door is the month + the year of the companies founding. Aloy mentions this to her friend, who mentions that the company was founded on October 2030. Aloy then says we need to combine those two together to get the code. Pros- excellent graphics and environments- runs great (well optimized) as long as you don't have 7 year old hardware you expect to run everything released- can see effects of changing visual settings in real time- some interesting new weapons- combat is fun for the most part- easy transmog available- far better facial and character animations than the first game- lots of gameplay customization options- better Ultrawide support than most games have- actually launched with a current version of FSR (2.2, which is basically FSR 3.0), most games launch with old versionsCons- Aloy still talks like she's struggling to force words out at times (it's a choice by the VA, but I find it grating). Aloy also talks to herself A LOT. I wish there was a way to tone it down so she only talked to herself during the important stuff.- while the game has good Ultrawide support, the UI is still spaced for Widescreen- So far, the story and writing is nothing special, and at times the conversations feel like exposition dumps. There is a lot of blunt writing too, not much nuance in many character personalities.- Aloy is kind of a ♥♥♥♥ to her friends. I understand she needs to do stuff alone, but the writers could have done a better job of her handling her companions than just trying to abandon them constantly. For instance, maybe the story was they were also assisting, but they needed to all split up and handle other areas, instead of Aloy just being the sole person who isn't useless.- At least on PC, the full scan of robots is a bit clunky. It tries to stick too hard to it's target (I assume a holdover from controller use) so it's hard to move to the next robot to tag at times, and the interface to cycle through options to do things like tag parts when scanning a robot is a bit cumbersome.- I hate how notifications are directly in the middle of the screen, obstructing vision. I had just cleared the quest to get to go into the Forbidden West, and I basically had to wait about 30 seconds for all the notification popups of all my stat points and levels accrued to stop popping up on the screen before I could do anything. It's also something I wish I could change in Helldivers 2, move that stuff to the top of the screen where it doesn't get in the way.- the game does suffer from noticeable pop-in of assets at times, as well as some instances of NPC's appearing out of nowhere. Not the end of the world but kind of jarring- just a weird thing, but at least early in the game it seems odd to me that so many people are so damn thick. I'd normally think in a post apocalyptic world where people still need to struggle to survive, there would be more people actually in better shape, either from needing to really work for their food or not having excess food to eat. Not that everyone needs to be a supermodel, it just looks odd when most everyone I run into (so far) looks like they frequent McDonald's. Maybe it's just the people of a certain region?- The side quests feel so bland so far, basically just you going to kill or gather things for people, I'm just having a hard time getting interested in the narrative.It may seem like there is more negative than positive, but that's just because they require a bit more explanation. I am sort of enjoying the game when I pop in to play it (a little bit at a time, since it hasn't yet really gripped me into playing it consistently).All that said, since I wrote this review I haven't really been interested in playing again, being more interested in my 7th or 8th play through in Cyberpunk. I should probably play some more just to see if the story manages to hook me in, but right now the combat (which at times seems like a hassle) and exploration isn't enough to keep me playing, I also need an interesting story and characters I like, which so far is not a thing from what I've seen in my 11 or so hours playing.EDIT: After trying to play some more and just being bored by the narrative and quests, and THEN getting Ghost of Tsushima and seeing how much more I enjoy that game, I am giving this one a 'do not recommend'. I really loved Horizon Zero Dawn when I played it on Playstation some years ago, and I was really pumped to play its sequel maxed out on PC this year. From a technical point of view this is one of the most gorgeous and well optimized games I ever played. Also the gameplay has been refined and expanded in every way possible, with many new weapons and ways to hunt your preys. I appreciated that cities and villages are more believable now, everything is well crafted and the attention to detail is incredible. I ultimately found the story a good step ahead from the first chapter and can't wait to see where it goes with the third game of this series.But....I think Forbidden West is a bit too much bloated with a lot of secondary stuff, which is the weakest part of the game, and due to this the game looses a lot of its focus. I understand the developers wanted to offer a lot of optional activities to the player, in order to enrich this amazing virtual world with content, but unfortunately there's nothing memorable, apart from some incredible Cauldrons, which are a pleasure to explore while trying to reach their cores. What remains are a lot of missions where you need to help boring characters to find something or someone. There are also a lot of collectables scattered around but I was not compelled by finding all of them, even if I'm interested in the lore of the game. There's a lot of Ubisoft open world DNA in this game, you need to decide if this a positive or negative for you.I have to be honest, due to what I wrote in the previous paragraph, by the half of my playthrough I was a bit bored and not compelled to continue playing the game. I was continuously sidetracked and my intial excitement lost steam as I played. I also found the upgrading system for your weapons and gear a bit cumbersome, and I was not compelled in going around to hunt the necessary machine parts. The new skills are instead really awesome and add a lot of variety to the game loop. In the end I was able to force myself in completing the main campaign, and also the Burning Shores DLC, and I'm happy I did it because some battle encounters and setpieces are really incredible. The final Burning Shores boss is probably the best encounter of both the main games and relative DLCs combined.Even with all its flaws I still recommend Forbidden West. Because all the secondary fluff is optional, and this is still a very enjoyable game with an interesting plot and a very good gameplay loop. It is a MASSIVE game and in order to see everything you'll go well beyond the 100 hours. So what Guerilla is offering here is a very good deal, even at full price, without a doubt. If Horizon Zero Dawn was an 8/8.5 experience for me, I would put its sequel just a little bit below that, between a 7.5 and an 8, only because I was not continuously excited to explore and discover as I was the first time. But that's me, and even if I've not loved everything about this game, I still put 107 hours in it, and I don't think there's a better proof of the quality in display here!

The climbing is limited to only yellow handholds. Surfaces might look identical, but only one is climbable. You also have a poor excuse for a grappling hooks that more basic than even Far Cry's hook. You wish it played like Halo Infinite or Just Cause, but it's extremely limited. The combat feels good at times, but clunky at others. If it wasn't for the damage indicators and health bars, I feel like sometimes I wouldn't have even realized my arrow hit the target. For all the beauty and polish, a lot of how the game plays feels dated and often uninspired. A gorgeous nature-infused post-apocalyptic world with deviously deep lore set in a game where the "triple-A" component can't help but bleed through. There's plenty to enjoy about Horizon Forbidden West: the continued story and lore, the fast-paced monster-hunting gameplay, and the phenomenal environmental design. What matters is whether you have the stomach to handle another open-world stealth action game with crafting and collectibles.HFW is a screenshot factory. I still can't get enough of the series' meshing of sci-fi, mechanical, tribal, and organic visual elements. Everything from each culture's unique buildings and clothes to the complexity of each type of machine speaks to the game's worrying high-effort art direction.The core gameplay is strong but questionable at carrying such a lengthy game. As a sequel, HFW gets a good number of additions to gameplay. Melee runs with the usual light/heavy affair with the sequel adding in a few combos. Ranged combat features an improved variety of weapons that can sadly be overlooked in favor of a selection of similar-feeling bows.Even though HFW doesn't do the best job at encouraging you to engage with a majority of its arsenal, the act of dodging around, causing elemental reactions, making dramatic slow-motion shots, and going out of your way to use more explosive ammo types on a diverse selection of robot dinosaurs is a loop that takes a while to get old. The music, sound design, and visual polish also do everything in their power to make hunting machines as tactile as possible. The PS5 controller's haptics also deserve an honorable mention here. Every button combo on the controller is mapped to something so, by the end of the game, you'll be playing your controller like a musical instrument.The stealth gameplay, as anyone would expect, is still generic, slow, shallow, and wildly uninteresting. Thankfully, it's essentially optional and can be skipped without consequence. Using it to get a jump on priority targets. Puzzles, optional or not, leave a lot to be desired since they mostly revolve around moving a box, charging a battery, or finding a key. Since push boxes and lifting batteries aren't exactly fast processes, the puzzles are also annoyingly slow to work through.HFW stretches itself thin by throwing around collectibles, crafting, upgrades, trivial sidequests, and uninspired puzzles like the more excuses you have to not address the immediate narrative threat the better. You know things are bad when the quest menu is divided up into main, side, errand, and collectibles. What's heartbreaking as well is the visible effort that's gone into rendering so many landscapes and towns that serve little to no purpose outside of split-second eye candy or a vapid sidequest interaction.If you've played and enjoyed Zero Dawn plus haven’t burnt out on open-world games yet, I'd easily recommend HFW in order to see more of the clever writing and all the helpful adjustments/additions the sequel makes to gameplay. A lot of things feel fresh and it's better all around. If you haven't played Zero Dawn, HFW would still be fun, but the story won't hit nearly as hard and you'll probably be more confused than invested.

As of writing this review, I have yet to finish the game.I've made quite a bit of progress all the way into the far "Forbidden West", working on clearing all the question marks and side missions (climbing and combat/roll abilities) and an entire world underwater to explore.The skill tree has been split into several different trees/branches, a lot easier made for early specific builds too.I was caught off guard with the vast improvements from Zero Dawn, especially the stepped up graphical fidelity.I reached player level 50 today, thought it was about time to start working on a review.Been playing on "Hard" just like I did in Zero Dawn, felt the difficulty scaling was still very much the same (well balanced).As for the main positives I can point out so far:1.Forbidden West feels quite a lot larger than Zero Dawn, the biome transitions and environment works out very well.2.Game looks amazing, from textures to foliage it all just works (wish I had a OLED panel with HDR to play it at its best).3.It runs great for how good the game looks and haven't experienced any game breaking bugs or soft-locks as this far, probably one of the best PC ports I have seen in a while.4.If you played Zero Dawn you'll be in for a treat, as there's quite a bit of interactions with both old and new companions.Obviously like all games they're not perfect, as an example a few Negative points I experienced so far that messed with me:1.This is more or less exclusively to KBM, but for whatever reason the equipment wheel has been changed to the "F" key and "TAB" & "M" keys are doubled mapped to the Map(You would think remapping the assigned F key for the equipment wheel to "TAB" would solve this but no, it is still taken priority by the "other TAB-keybind" for map that can't be unassigned nor shows up in the keybindings).Reason why this is a problem is mainly for returning players or those that just finished up Zero Dawn, since this change could take quite some time to rewire your brain to (at least it took me quite a few hours to stop accidentally opening the map mid combat since ZD used "Tab" for the equipment wheel - Mouse 2 is used now for crafting in the wheel while it is Mouse 1 in ZD)2.There are climbable cooling vents and crevices throughout the game that may be frustrating, at least it was for me.Example:As for the cooling vents, they are very "jittery" to climb and depending on the area they are, I found in certain Cauldrons I was straight up unable to climb or jump from them (would just drop off rather than lunge from the panel), so I had to find an map. Over 24 hours playtime and it's been a fun game so far.  This sequel is definitely challenging compared to Zero Dawn, but it's a fun one.  Game play has been smooth on my end (for the most part).My major complaint so far is the FPS drops during cut scenes and certain areas of the map.  I did some tweaking to my settings and it somewhat fixed it, but still hate watching them when it's barely pushing 20 FPS.  I did find a work-around to temporarily fix it (until the next FPS drop), but it's annoying to do so every time it happens.  Tough to enjoy a story when it's nothing more than a glorified power point presentation.  Mind you I have a RTX 3070 ti (8 VRAM), intel i9-12900KF processor and 64GB of RAM, so I should've been fine...  Fingers crossed this will get fixed in the future.A full review will be added once I finish my first play through, DLC included.  For now I'd rate it a 6/10 - Still a better launch than Zero Dawn, for damn sure!EDIT: (4/7/2024)Finished the main story.  I think Forbidden West is a solid sequel.  I had a lot of fun with it, despite the FPS issues I had to endure.  Did find a "fix" until more patches come along, but it was very playable and I enjoyed it. I wasn't a fan of the main story, despite all that happened.  I thought Zero Dawn's was more put together.  Also wasn't a fan of the villains.  Seemed.... cliche and laughable.  Combat was fun, but there was way too much to keep up with in terms of weapons, elements, armor and your gear in general.  The tribes were more memorable in Zero Dawn than here and while I love the addition of new machine (especially dinosaur ones), it seemed a bit too much.  And you thought Zero Dawn had a lot of Side Quests?  Well buckle up because this one's got even more! (if that strikes your fancy)If I had to rate it as its own game (not as a sequel), I'd say a solid 8.5/10Don't care for story and you just want to be that archer character that just shoots machines down with a bow and arrow and smack people down, unga bunga style?  This game is for you!As a sequel, i'll give it a 7/10There were a lot of improvements, but I felt like they took a few steps back on certain things that made it inferior to Zero Dawn.  It was good, but not too great.  Overall, I'd say a worthy 2-year wait for this PC port.EDIT: (4/16/2024)Completed the DLC.  It was average at best.  Frozen Wilds was a great DLC and Burning Shores had big shoes to fill and it couldn't accomplish it (for the most part) - I will admit.  The finale was pretty epic.  A LOT better than Frozen Wilds.  Other than that, the world felt empty and the Quen were still uninteresting.  It was beautiful; devs did a damn good job on the environment.  But it suffered the "Breath of the Wild" treatment: So much to see and so little to do.  And yes... I will agree the romance felt forced.  I'm all for Aloy going gay or bi for that matter, but that felt rushed and unnatural.  It was neat to see Aloy have a vulnerable/sensitive side to her (considering her attitude during most of the main story), but I'd pick a different choice for her romance.  If anything I saw it as character development for Aloy and her FINALLY understanding what it means to work together rather than alone.Overall, it was an average DLC.  I'd give it a 6/10

To end my gender and sexuality feedback on this game, why is almost virtually everyone apparently a version of LGBTQ+? It's like they didn't even try because just about everyone in that game you interact with is the first two letters of that category. With the exception of like a  heterosexuals. .  Off rip, Aloy talks way too much in Forbidden West, (Dial back the amount of monologue) ". It just feels so invasive, like damn girl let me try and figure this out and stop telling me what to do or how I should play the game with your loud ahh thoughts.   The overall quests in this game seemed excessive and not very rewarding. Not like you need to have some kind of benefit to doing every single errand or side quest but at least in Zero Dawn everything you did played into the final scene of the game. Forbidden west feels like you're just running chores for everyone and all for either irrelevant lore or just for the altruistic benefit. I want to throw hands with whoever made me go chase ridiculous survey drones and play every damn Chessmaster in the world. For what? So I can stare at some pretty holo in the dome I'm barely in or earn literally nothing of value other than some strike pieces? Oh can't forget the little ornaments so I can light up Las Vegas woooooooo siiiiickkkkk! . They must really want you to use the photo mode feature or something.  . Weapons and Skill Tree, boy does this hurt me so... I essentially stuck to using Hunter Bows, Sharpshot Bows, Spike Throwers, and a liiiiiiiiiiiiilllllllll bit of the Blastslings (but not much). I can't use my Ropecaster anymore to bind some real monsters because now the lines are made of air practically. Machines shrug it off like it's a joke. Now you might say what about upgrading those items? WELL! I hope you're ready to spend some serious time grinding the resources hunting down the best monsters in their apex forms just to 1-Up your new shiny gold weapon. Machine looting during this process is crazy because if a machine dies and you didn't "tear off" a component, all it's other parts break (explain that one to me)...  They also nerfed stealth into the earth so it isn't much of an incentive to be quiet late game because you can't take people down with a strike without some crazy ELITE coils or outfits that has been upgraded to benefit that one category. So you end up playing dance dance revolution with your weapon wheel during each fight or pausing the game to open up your inventory to swap something out mid combat just so it works in your favor. All those skills for all of them, if not most, to be very ineffective. I use MAYBE 3 of them at best. Great concept behind weapon techniques and some valor surges but again, it didn't really deliver. They just missed several marks they did really well in Zero Dawn compared to this one. Last one on weapons and or major gripes I had in gameplay is heavy weapons. No more are the days of tearing off a disc launcher from a Thunderjaw and feeling like a complete UNIT. You might as well be firing cotton balls at them now. It's not worth it even when you get the passive buff from the skill tree. I really miss long roll from Zero Dawn too...  All in all the game is great and all those things are not horrible and at best tolerable. I recommend this game just as much as I recommend the last one. Boy oh boy where to begin. Graphics: The graphics are absolutely breathtaking. This is one of the prettiest games I have ever played. Don’t believe me? Check the pictures I have posted on my profile. When exploring the various biomes you often find yourself just standing around and taking in the beautiful views. And the sunsets, my god they always make me just stop and watch it go down. Story:This is a great sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn, continuing on Aloy’s journey, she has now become a legend all around. Furthermore its refreshing to see that Aloy now shares the burden of her journey with others, unlike in Zero Dawn where she mostly faced her challenges alone. The writers have done an excellent job with the characters you meet, like Varl, an old friend from the Nora tribe who provides great companionship throughout. You'll find yourself caring a lot about their fates throughout the game.A few other remarks, The side quests are fulfilling, each with their own stories that align with the main narrative. Data points add to the sense of exploration, offering insights from the previous world. And even though mounts are available, I usually just ran around because the exploration is so rewarding.Combat:The combat is very satisfying thanks to the new varied designs and behaviours of the new machines and humans. Melee combat is completely different and now much more enjoyable compared to Zero Dawn. And with thanks to new ammo and weapons, you now have several options or playstyles to choose from. Personally, my favourite was the explosive spike thrower which was a must when fighting bigger beasts. All in all, the new upgraded combat/talent systems is much more engaging and fun. Verdict:Zero Dawn still stands strong with its own amazing story. Forbidden West somewhat still continues from the same level (After getting past the starting area) The story is touching, the graphics are stunning, the lore is rich, and characters delivers a great performance.Overall if you like open world games, this is a 10/10. But please play Zero Dawn first or you will be missing out. 😊 PS: Plz add underwater combat in the next game.

First of all, this game is a technical marvel in most respects. It's incredible what Guerilla and Nixxes has been able to make run and make it run so smoothly (for the most part). The facial animation is great and overall it's just a really beautiful game. The story is also fairly interesting and original and keeps you going. My problem with the story is that I would say that it has 3 first acts, which is kind of annoying. The other problem is that while the story is interesting it isn't delivered that well. I am not talking about voice perfomances but rather the way they have chosen to convey the story.For me the gold standard when it comes to story presentation is God of War 2018. In that game the pacing is just perfect where the game allows you to have time for side-quests that are cleverly portioned out to you so you don't overdo it (which I tend to do). Admittedly God of War 2018 and this game are completely different games in the sense that the former is more of a hub-world open-world game that is more confined and designed where this is a true open world-game where you can roam free. While both has it charms I do realize, after playing this, that I prefer the hub-world type of game. Not that this game/franchise should be changed but I do wish they could introduce a better pacing somehow. I have no idea how to accomplish that though.Because as it stands I spent about 20 - 30 hours more or less do the story stuff (thato's me OCDing and doing every little thing before progressing the story) until the game world really opened up and then I got sidetracked for about 30 hours doing everything but the main story essentially and overleveling like crazy. After having done all the side-quests, errands and anything that really has a story I went back to the main story and just cake-walked it (understandeably).Now I would like to focus on the story but games like these have taught me that if you don't do all the side-quests then you might miss out on main story parts as well. Not really saying that there is that component here but doing side-quests definitely adds to the flavor of the world. The world by the way is really well realized and everything as much sense as it can more or less.When it comes to playing the game I think it's not as good as the first game. I think the weapon system is worse and more convoluted and I ended up just using Hunter Bows where in the previous game it was fun to mix things up. The skill-trees aren't that interesting either. There were many instances where I had 20 - 30 skillpoints (which is kind of a lot) and not finding that much interesting to spend it on. I just ended up unlocking random stuff but don't think it really provided that much to my gameplay-experience unfortunately. I definitely preferred the "simpler" system in the previous game. I couldn't really find the energy or interest to invest in the systems in this game besides the ones I already knew of from the previous game.I want to remember that the previous game had a better size and pacing than this game for me. I don't remember being fed up with collecting things and trinkets in the previous game but I certainly became that with this game. Also, a lot of the best gear is locked behind really annoying challenge stuff (detailing more would be spoilery) as far as I could tell and I didn't find those challenges that interesting and compelling to do. Now I did fine gear-wise with what I got but that still bugged me.Overall, I would say that this is a really good game though but I think the previous game is superior when it comes to the joy of playing it. At least when comparing the first experience of playing this one and the previous one.

Great improvement upon the first game. Everything about Zero Dawn has been tuned and refined to be a much more enjoyable experience than before, with the caveat that there's too many weapons and too much to grind for.Forbidden West tunes the machine tracking from Zero Dawn to be far less aggressive. Machines definitely still track to your location during attacks, but much less egregiously. Most of the time when you get hit now, it is your fault and you can actually sprint out of the way of attacks now. There are still a couple of bad cases, but much less than in Zero Dawn.Glinthawks are much less annoying because the Sunwing showed up to the party. Then in the DLC, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Waterwing. The Waterwing is entirely the reason I uninstalled this game. They're a midweight machine with the healthbar of a heavyweight. They're unbelievably obnoxious, constantly give you tinnitus and only are engaged in groups of 3 or 4. I have more fun fighting Bileguts, Slaughterspines, Thunderjaws, Stormbirds, Tremortusks, Fireclaws, Tiderippers, Rockbreakers, Shellsnappers and even Dreadwings than I do Waterwings.That said, you at least get a weapon wheel with 6 instead of 4 slots this time. So you get a lot more options to toy around with mid-battle. Shredder Gauntlets are weird and I hate trying to catch them, so I don't use them. Boltblasters are slow and unwieldy, but powerful. Warrior Bows are a close-range damage dealer, but I also didn't really use these.For the Shredder Gauntlet in particular it really didn't help that the "tutorial" mission I happened upon with the boom sisters pit me up against the Shellsnapper whom I had only fought once before. Trying to one-two-three that thing while it's playing a game of Diablos Dig and spamming ice rocks at you doesn't make for a fun tutorial.They did improve the character-to-character interactions from Zero Dawn, though. Their faces are much more expressive and detailed, there is a lot more animation involved as well. The improvement was enough for me to want to sit through dialogue rather than think it's a drag like Zero Dawn.Overall, it's pretty solid and worth experiencing.

The original game was a promising yet flawed open world exploration-heavy game with a great setup and great worldbuilding. It was a very "PG-13" corny theme park experience sometimes and the best moments were rooted in the lore, not the actual story of Aloy. But especially the first half was a great hero journey surrounded in mystery with some rather harrowing plot twists. The villains weren’t that important, the main focus was the unravelling of the mystery of Aloy's origin and getting to know the history of the world. Horizon Forbidden West was in a difficult position – Aloy couldn’t continue on her discovery-filled journey. She was all-knowing now. Unfortunatelly Guerilla opted for a classical Marvel-like structure with a cookie-cutter world saving story and it fell apart quickly. There was also an attempt of something like "Mass Effect-ish" plot development with the  but it fell incredibly short (it just doesn't work well with the premise of a solitary hero like Aloy I guess).Once again – the world itself is beautiful and well realised. But now the side content just repeats itself with little to no innovation. Side missions are slightly better then in HZD but - boy oh boy! - the main story pisses itself so hard so quickly. The premise of the dying world could be good, but right after the  mission you realise the main portion of the game consists of three to four big fetch quests – these are supposed to bring you to the different areas of the map which they achieve but it feels very unorganic. The writing is like a watered down Avengers story with unnatural and cringey dialogue, unlikable NPCs and cliché after cliché after cliché…I actually liked parts of the exploration. The traversal while not being flawless was definitely better and snappier than in HZD. Guerilla "borrowed" once again from better games (Zelda and others) and introduced a glider, a grappling hook, rebreather and a free climbing mechanic - but for some reason you can't use them while solving puzzles. All those are completely on rails and strip you of your abbilities, which is utterly and completely frustrating.Side activities were completely unoriginal and there were some mindboggling design decisions, but for a limited time I really enjoyed walking through all those beautiful forests and I loved all the different vistas – but that was it. I basically facepalmed the back third of the game, constantly on the brink of putting the game down. One of the most criminal parts of the story setup were the villains. What on earth were those  supposed to be? They’re introduction and basically every second of their screentime (except for  ) were one big comedy nonsense.And of course – there is the  Please Guerilla – you’ve managed to create a good lore and a beautiful world, now you should really work on that writing.If you consider buying/playing the game maybe just put the main story aside and enjoy the world itself and the things Guerilla is quite good at - the combat and the machine variety. Because the story might kill the game for you as it did for me.(While not being the main problem, the technical state of the game wasn't the best - despite what was said about this Nixxes's port since release. It still needs a few patches - the frame generation was a welcome addition, but it is not very well implemented, there are also some shadow flicker issues, particle artifacts, frame dips and some inexplicable performance degradation over time. Some of it could be on my side but some of it are definitely an engine related issues and should be adressed.)

Honestly this series needs to pivot away from the open world formula, almost everything that is actually wrong with this game is a direct consequence if it being another one of today's "everything needs to be a 100 hour open world RPG".While it has an absolutely infuriating dependence on the slow down mechanic to do anything at all, the core gameplay is still solid and where the game shines most. Unfortunately the enemy and encounter variety is not nearly enough to fill out a map of this size and by the time you destroy your 20th patrol of ridiculously spongy enemies, you're just over it. The baffling decision that every enemy in the game outright one or two-shots you on anything but the easiest difficulties is absolutely incompatible with the same dumb hitboxes and enemy animations from the first game (not to mention every overworld fight is a gank with 5+ enemies). Taking forever to clear a single patrol because you analyse its movement patterns, lay traps and use stealth to thin them out before engaging is incredibly fun the first 5 times, not so much after you've done it a hundred times.And while I can't say too much about the story without spoiling anything, the game largely follows in the footsteps of the first one, but without the compelling mystery of what happened in the past this time:- Most of story stuff involving the old world is very interesting- All of the current world stuff is boring and cringe inducing- Aloy is once again some sort of perfect magical girl who's every action is objectively correct, while being as unlikeable as humanly possible. You could accurately predict who is evil/antagonist and who isn't by how Aloy reacts to a person in the first game and it's exactly the same thing here.This series desperately needs to strip away all the repetitive open world stuff and focus on their strengths, namely tightly curated encounters and world building. This game would be infinitely better if it was half as long as it actually is and thus is never goes beyond a resounding "meh".Get it if you REALLY enjoyed the first one, but don't touch it otherwise.

Definitely an overall positive experience, a lot of fun new beasts, a major combat overhaul, beautiful landscapes (even with a 1660 graphics card and no ram), and more of the horizon story, which I personally think is one of the most interesting environments and stories in media. If you liked the first game, this game is an amazing continuation that both rewards players who were already skilled at zero dawn while still being its own learning experience. However, I have one major criticism of this game. Before I dive into it however, it is prudent to first examine the nature of sequels of this style. Frequently when an amazing game gets a sequel, there is a lot more that the player knows to expect from the setting, especially for open world games. For example, when going from breath of the wild to tears of the kingdom, God of War 2016 to Ragnarök, Hades to Hades II, or  Subnautica to Below Zero, there is a lot that the player already knows to anticipate.  The combat in Zelda, the number of bosses in a run of hades, the threat of leviathans in Subnautica. These things that were iconic discoveries in their debuts are weakened when we revisit these settings in a sequel. A lot of the weight of these games comes from that first experience of something, and after a playthrough we understand more about how the game is structured. The best example is the reaper leviathan in subnautica. In your first encounter, you are scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by the biggest beast you have ever seen in game, and they continue to be a source of terror as you try to get the courage to brave the depths. The fear of what else could be lurking, given the baseline of the reaper, is a big part of the atmosphere. However, once you beat subnautica, you kind of know how the developer codes leviathans into the game. Big monsters that roar at you, have a fast but non-agile charge ability, and a grab attack that one shots the player and can damage vehicles. Going into Below Zero, the first time you see a chelcerate, you immediately understand that it is this games main leviathan. Even though it looks nothing like a reaper, your prior experience with reapers in the first game prepares you for the reaper reskin in the sequel. Because of this, the chelcerate can never hope to reach the levels of horror that the reaper instilled, because the player knows what to expect from a subnautica style game.This creates a very distinct problem with how sequels can retain the intensity of the originals where the audience knows what scale to expect. There are a lot of problems in horizon forbidden west that I am sure are also in the first game, but due to the novelty of everything happening for the first time, I never noticed them. In forbidden west, the fatal flaw that brings it down is distribution. The sum total of content in the game is vast, diverse and engaging, but the way in which it is presented to the player is extremely underwhelming. This attribute rears its ugly head in a few places which I will go through in the following bullets. 1.)	The biggest change in HFW is the introduction of new machines. There are a ton of new machines, with distinct behaviors and features, and very few feel samey. Where this is most obvious is in the large machine category. Large machines are the peak of this series, where you face impossible odds against titanic robot dinosaurs covered in weapons and missiles. Learning to fight large machines is a super cool puzzle and experience, and definitely the highlight of the game. HFW blows HZD out of the park with it’s large machines. HZD has the Thunderjaw, Stormbird, and Rockbreaker (technically the Fireclaw is also in that game, but it is the final boss of the DLC so it is never encountered). The stormbird was coded poorly, and only showed up once, and the rockbreaker never showed up in the campaign since its burrowing mechanic confined it to one random area. Forbidden west, in addition to the old large machines, also has the Slaughterspine (Plasma Spinosaurus), Slitherfang (tunneling king cobra), Tideripper (ichthyosaurus), Tremortusk (Mammoth X aircraft carrier), Dreadwing (giant invisible bat jet), and Shellsnapper (Snapping turtle tank). There are now 10 Large machine fights, with incredibly diverse ecology, mechanics and fights. They are extremely well designed, but for some reason, the game decides to hide them and stop the player from encountering them at all costs. THEY NEVER ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SHOW UP. Each large machine shows up *ONCE* in the story, then has one or two machine sites on the map of hundreds of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ machine sites. These fights are the peak of the series, and the developers don’t have faith in their work for some reason, so to make sure they have an impact they minimize the number of encounters as much as possible. The Slitherfang shows up in the intro of the game in a weakened state, then is never seen again for another 20 hours of gameplay. The dreadwing is a boss fight in a dungeon, then has one machine site in the middle of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nowhere that shows up long after you’ve left that part of the map. These machines are super awesome, but instead of fighting them 7 – 10 times intermittently throughout a playthrough as you scale and become more powerful, you are told they exist, then you don’t see them for half of your playthrough, then you need 15 slitherfang earthgrinders to upgrade a bow so you fight them 8 times in a row to farm them. This decision is so baffling. By making sure we never encounter these machines unless we are searching for them, you ensure players only encounter the best fights in the game when they are extensively or overprepared. You never get the feeling of progression where you avoid them like the plague in the early game when you are weak, then slowly crawl your way up in the food chain as your strength increases. It is the worst part of forbidden west. Large machines get this the worst, but it is a definite problem. There are tons of unique machines, but around 60% of your encounters are going to be with either bristlebacks or elemental clawstriders. JUST LET ME FIGHT THE 45 AMAZING ENEMIES INSTEAD OF THE SAME ONES OVER AND OVER. They literally have all the assets they need, there was no need to copy paste2.)	The next problem is the distribution of gear in forbidden west. Obviously the biggest factor in how well you can fight is the quality of Aloy’s equipment, but a glaring issue is how the equipment in this game is distributed. You have no idea where to go to get certain weapons and armors. You would think that going to the cold region would let you get the best armor against ice damage, but nope. At one point in the game, there are 3 branching paths for the order in which you complete dungeons. I wanted to give myself a fun challenge, so I went to the one with the highest level requirement first, thinking I would have a tough time, but maybe get a good boost in power as a reward. Actually, no, you don’t get any weapons or non-situational gear for completing the hardest 2 of the 3 dungeons, but the easiest one unlocks an arena where you get currency that can unlock the best hunter bow, best sharpshot bow, and best boltblaster in the game. (these are by far the most used of the 8 weapons). The vast majority of towns offer no unique gear,  for one town which offers the best ropecaster by an enormous margin, and there is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nothing telling you that this town has good ropecasters. The quality of weapons has nothing to do with the environment or setting, it is just arbitrary. Some side quests give you nothing worthwhile, while one random basic quest I did because I accidentally marked it on my map gave me the vindicator spikethrower, which has the best drill and explosive spikes in the game. There is no rhyme or reason to getting better gear. A lot of your ability to progress in combat will depend on random chance or looking up the location online. Once I discovered the Arena existed, I grinded until I bought all of it

This is a huge contrast from the first game where there was a natural progression through the story with each level having a set of meta weapons that could help you deal with most enemies.This brings me to the level system. Whoever designed this system I hope they never get another job again.... because this is by far the worst i've ever seen. Talking from the perspective of a very hard playthrough... in the later stages of the game with larger enemies.... unless you are almost 5-10 levels higher than the game recommendation.... you are not going to enjoy the quest. Virtually every larger enemy has some form of a one shot attack and even later game human enemies can easily one shot you after 30 mins of trying to clear them all out. The game in short... doesn't make any combat moments enjoyable. Whenver you do feel you finally got the hang of things... the game throws in a fight where you just have to accept you'll get one shot any time.The stamina system aswell is extremely badly designed. Outside of the explanations for the world's state, there's nothing remarkable in the sequel nor in this game. The writing here is juvenile and afraid of challenging the player. For example, the main character's allied faction did some war crimes in the past and we're tasked with finding some relatives that were involved, but the player is laughably assured that "they were one of the good ones that tried to stop all the war crimes". Made to be digestible to a large audience, presumably mostly of teenagers.It's a well-functioning entertainment product that you'll enjoy and then move on.
