The Horizon series is a stand out example of incredible writing, wonderful artistic direction, amazing game design, and clearly passion and love from the creative teams involved.Set in a far future somehow inhabited by machines, and small pockets of humans living mostly tribal lifestyles. The follow up to Horizon Zero Dawn, Forbidden West is an incredible entry in the series. Our main character Alloy, after discovering the secrets of old humanity, and the secret's that made her who she is in the first game, must now explore farther than she ever has. Leaving Mid-West of the USA, she must make her wake west to the coast to learn more about how to stop the encroaching doom that is settling over earth. You get to explore new cultures, find ancient cities, swim below flooded ruins, and learn more secrets of how to restore the incredible Zero Dawn project and save humanity. New characters and old help along the way and we get to see the flaws and the development of an incredibly lovable main character.One of the most seamless open worlds i have ever had the luck to play, Forbidden west is both an incredible tour de force, and an artistic triumph.I recommend highly playing the first game of course, but I can say loudly and proudly that this series is by in large my favorite set of games, and I am already chomping at the bit for the story to continue.Do yourself a favor and play these games, you will laugh, you will cry over the challenge, beauty, and triumph. You will come away with hope for humanity, and in awe of what we can do when we work together.

I cannot tell you how disappointed I am with this game.  I have over 280 hours on ZD and could still play it again.  I could not put that game down.  FW seems like they simply ran out of ideas and threw the whole mess in the mix.  The new weapons system is a complete drag, tedious and a total grind.  Take weapon upgrades for instance.  It is now a major part of your time playing to just find the items you need to make your weapon better only to find out that you wasted all that time when a better weapon comes along.  Or find out that three of your bows in your weapon wheel use the same exact arrow, and if you used the arrows in one, the other bows are depleted.   Or the fact that the items you need are on machines that don't populate, or need to be harvested at a certain time of the day.  Why on earth do I need so many bows that use the same exact arrows???  In ZD the wheel and weapons were manageable and could be changed in a fight.  Now it's so clogged with stuff you can never remember where the weapon you need is.  They did the same thing with the bottom potion and food area too.  And why on earth can you hold endless amounts of rocks but can only hold 200 ridge wood for arrows???  The stash box is a mess and cumbersome.  The amount of stuff it takes to create a arrows now is so huge that you lose as much as you gain in a fight.  And really good weapons don't come along until the DLC and by that time your already almost done with the game.  So now to enjoy those weapons and coils, you have to play the game again.  And that is just weapons.Lets talk about graphics, absolutely beautiful right?  But now the whole world is covered in this haze and fog and it's everywhere, no matter what kind of weather.  ZD had amazing views and vista's and you could see for miles.  But in FW they mask those views with this constant haze or fog.  The only reason I can imagine they would do this is due to the amount of graphics rendering required, and needed to make it work with older hardware.  And this would be fine if you gave us the choice to turn it on or off.  But it's mandatory for everyone, and it ruins the world.  Now the world feels small and cramped, you get to see that there is something in the distance, but you cannot see it till your right on it.  This is a cheap way of making your game work with older hardware without making the game look like garbage because drawing distances don't matter anymore since it's just a bunch of haze and fog pixels.The story line takes waaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaay too long to tell.   I felt like I spent the first 20 hours walking through the story before the game even really started to get interesting.  This game is like reading a book, or better yet having someone read a book to you with some tedious weapon building in between.  Taking away the ability to jump out of the way of machines and making the time it takes to get back up much longer is truly baffling.  Now if you want to avoid getting hit, you need to do this weird combo of run, slide, jump mechanic all the while trying to find your weapon on the wheel.  And since it doesn't always work, you get hammered.  The buy sell program is so confusing as to be impossible to know what to keep and what to sell.  You never know what your going to need to keep since everything takes two or three of some obscure animal or machine to make.  So you hold on to everything for fear you might need it soon.  But then your stash gets cluttered with so much stuff that you don't know what to do with it all.The open world seems very small compared to ZD.  ZD had machines and animals everywhere.  In FW, you can walk through a large portion of map and not run into any machine or animal at all.  Go off the beaten trail and it's desolate.  In fact, when I first opened the map during the first hours of play, I could not believe how few machines where on the map.  I was like, where is everything?  There are clusters of machines but you have to hike to get to them.  All in all, this game is not very fun to play.  The game it's self plays very well, it is beautiful to look at when your in smaller areas like indoors or at night.  I have fairly decent hardware running a 5800X3D with 32 gigs of ram and a 6800XT and I get around 70 to 90fps  1440p on high settings and no frame gen.  But having a really nice world to run through, and then hindering it with fog and haze and tedious tasks like weapon building and nerfing your abilities  just ruins it.I will try to finish the game, but I'm not sure I will play it again.  I'll go back and play ZD before I play this again.

Okay, if you enjoyed Horizon Zero Dawn and liked the combat, story, etc, then I believe Forbidden West is a great buy and you will have a positive experience with this sequel. FW has pretty much the same exact gameplay experience as ZD but adds some much needed quality of life improvements and some fun new mechanics like flying mounts, underwater diving, and new weapons. However, if you haven't played ZD yet and are curious about the Horizon series, I recommend getting ZD when it's on sale to see if you enjoy the gameplay and story first, then pick this one up if you liked it.However, there are some things I would like to criticize about FW. As you can probably see from some of the other reviews here, a lot of the side quests in this game feel very repetitive. A lot of them start out with Aloy meeting some random NPC(s) who ask her to save their friend, family, squad, etc. Aloy agrees, then when you go to save these people, you usually have to fight a group of machines, save the person, fight another group of machines or miniboss, then you go back to the original quest-giver to finish the quest. It gets very repetitive after awhile and a lot of the side quests just feel like they don't have a lot of weight to them. I would rather have less side quests in the game if that means each quest is more unique and is given a higher standard of quality. I also have a similar complaint to the multitude of copy-paste weapons and outfits in this game. Don't get me wrong, there are plenty of weapons and outfits to collect in this game, however you will find that if you compare your earned weapon or outfit models with each other, a lot of them will share the same exact 3D model. All outfits in the game have different stats, but the only visual difference between the ones that share the same 3D model is the color (which is lame because you can dye outfits different colors anyways). This is the same deal with weapons, but there are some that look exactly the same, no difference in color or anything. This ends up meaning that your earned epic/legendary gear can look exactly the same as the rare/common gear you've already acquired. This is lazy game design and is especially frustrating to see when you put in time to get better gear only to have it look exactly the same as the gear you've already earned. To reiterate my last point regarding quests, I want to see quality > quantity in the future.

I do like this game, but as I was playing, I had some glaring issues that really ruined the experience until I found a "fix". I preface this by saying this might be a me issue.I loved Horizon Zero Dawn. Such an amazing great game. Had no issues with the controls, everything worked great, loved the bow fights and everything. Here comes Forbidden West. I turned off all Aim Assist things in the settings (as I did in Horizon too). From the start, I felt the game "fighting" me when I tried to aim, it all felt clunky and horrible and I just thought, "I am bad at this game or smth is wrong with how you shoot the bow". I also had issues with dodging, the camera moved weirdly and sometimes would get stuck in a weird angle which made fights horrible. I spent almost 30 hours like this. Then I found the solution in a mod from Nexusmods called Gameplay Tweaks. There are 2 options you can turn on in the file there, that are NOWHERE in the game settings: FocusMagnetism and CameraMagnetism. I put them on TRUE and suddenly, I had no more issues with the combat, with aiming, with camera, it all felt smooth. This is unacceptable to me. Clearly to me, even with all aiming stuff on off, the game was STILL trying to aim for me and it felt horrible. This makes it a bad PC port to me. Then, the mounts. The land mount gets stuck in almost anything ALL the time. The flying mount (which you get super late in the game imo due to MSQ) also just feels like a land mount with wings, which doesn't get stuck in stuff on the ground, but also can't actually properly fly over things as you'd think it should do (you have to ascend in a straight line to get up and when you try to fly at that speed, it dives back down. Cool, cool cool cool cool. The story is nice, that is an aspect I like in the game. That gets a thumbsup from me. There are some moments where I am frustrated with Aloy, but I understand why. The writing is top-notch and the side quests are great too.I am not done with the game, I will finish it, but with the sales going, I thought I had to put the issue I encountered in a review. Maybe they are others that encounter that or is a dealbreaker for them (maybe they don't want mods, which shouldn't even NEED to be a need to have).

HFW improves every single one of the elements of HZD, which was an enjoyable game by itself.The combat is more evolved, with more weapon and elemental types, traversal is vastly improved due to the grapple and glider being introduced, and another type of traversal that comes later in the game, and the exploration has more meat on its bones, with better resources to find and puzzles to interact with.While it can be argued that the story is not as good as HDZ's (mostly due to the revelation of what actually happened to the world, and the same doesn't happen in the sequel, since it's already known), I would still argue that that every element of the story is better in HFW - main quest is still highly enjoyable, especially in the later parts, and there are many side quests that are written very well, as well as a wide array of side characters that either accompany you on your main quest or you meet on side quests. The world itself has lots more to give and offers more insight into the world and characters that came before. Not to mention meeting all of the new tribes which expand this setting even more and makes it a more believable and "lived-in" world. I especially love how each tribe (both in the previous game and this one) have unique views and perspectives on religion, machines, the "ancestors", and the world that was before that influences their actions.The map is huge and offers classic open-world shenanigans that might annoy you, but I found the activities highly enjoyable, as the developers made an effort to put in more varied activities. For example, in the previous game, you'd climb these Tallnecks (robot dinosaurs that act as your towers to reveal the map) and you'd usually just find a high spot nearby and climb onto the Tallneck. In the sequel, these activities are highly varied, offering combat encounters, puzzles, traversal elements, as well as story beats, all in an effort to gain access to the Tallneck. Every other activity is like this, offering you something more, something different, than just copy-pasting the same activity 10 times.As for the graphics, I think I can easily say this is THE best looking PC game on the market right now. The graphics of the environments are absolutely stunning, and the details on Aloy's model as well as other character's models are amazing!If you are at all interested in this game, or were a fan of the previous one, I highly recommend it!

Runs perfectly fine on Steam Deck. I’ve enjoyed HFW a lot! As there are already many reviews praising story, quests and gameplay I’m not going into that. I just want to explain why I think the ‘Unsupported’ rating for Steam Deck is incorrect. I bought the game directly when it came out on PC and indeed Steam Deck was barely up to the task. Some crashes, disappearing audio, disappointing visuals. But then XeSS 1.3 was introduced, which made rather smooth gameplay possible at XeSS Quality mode and with mostly Medium graphics settings. Not only on the Deck’s 1280x800, but also on an external monitor at 1600x900. Sure, it does not come close to a 4K 100FPS experience, but everything looks beautiful, as long as you are okay with mostly 30 FPS, sometimes lower. Improving FPS will cost you sharpness and depth and introduction of graininess. Also, using Dynamic Resolution Scaling (at 30 FPS) significantly impacts image quality when moving around. But, overall a smooth and very enjoyable ride. When entering Burning Shores you need to further tone down on the image quality to be able to play at all, but Steam Deck gets the job done at XeSS Balanced mode. With the introduction of FRS 3.1 everything improved even further. Smooth gameplay, beautiful scenery, nicely detailed machines.Don’t get me wrong, the game looks much better on more appropriate hardware, but I’ve had a great time playing HFW on the modest specs of the Deck so I don’t see a reason for Steam to state it is unsupported. Guerrilla Games and Nixxes have done an amazing job!

Just like it's predecessor, I give Horizon: Forbidden West a solid 9/10. I find so few problems with this game, and it gives a massive amount of content full of exciting and rewardingly complex combat.\The very few negatives in the game can be boiled down to occasional bugs, the melee pit challenges being insanely precise, and the sheer level of extra questions you can ask in dialogue. I find myself often skipping these extra questions which I would normally always engage in for the added story, but having to stop the gameplay for 10 or more minutes to ask each and every one or it vanishes for is quite infuriating.Aside from its few faults, the game does a wonderful job expanding on the previous story in exciting ways that shocked me with its twists more than once. While I'm not normally a fan of the "this society only respects strength, so if you show them you are strong in combat they will respect you" trope, it works well when you discover where this tribe set down roots. Worldbuilding has always been Horizon's strongsuit, and I find myself routinely impressed by how everything knits together in the end.The combat improves as well in the sequel, and I find myself constantly enjoying the new mechanics and weaponry. While I wish ammo types wasn't tied to the weapon and I could choose which ammo varieties I was using at the Stash and unlock the ability to use new types and more at once as I progressed, I understand that the decided direction was likely the best in terms of game balance. It can just be a little annoying scouring the world for weapons with my preferred ammo varieties attached to them. The i-frames from dodges can be a bit inconsistent dependent on the attack an enemy is performing, which has led to a few frustrating deaths, but I chock that up to more of a skill issue on my part.Exploration gets a whole new level of depth (and height) with the expanded vertical movement with full underwater exploration, gliding, and a wide array of available climbing space. Seeing climbing expanded to more than just preplaced handholds is a wonderful addition that I can't stop loving. While I wish there was some added use for the glider and its forward momentum was a bit increased, it is still a pleasure to use in-game.All-in-all, while I give it the same score as its predecessor, there is just so much to experience that is new and it has improved on what made Zero Dawn so great. I seriously suggest you give it a try if you haven't, and I eagerly await the third installment in the trilogy.With love and honor, RIP Lance Reddick

Horizon Forbidden West is an exceptional sequel that brilliantly builds upon the foundation laid by its predecessor, Horizon Zero Dawn. Developed by Guerrilla Games, this action RPG takes players on an unforgettable journey through a stunningly crafted post-apocalyptic world.Story and SettingThe narrative continues Aloy's epic quest to save humanity from a looming ecological disaster. Set in a breathtakingly beautiful and diverse world, Forbidden West introduces new territories teeming with mysterious ruins, lush forests, and arid deserts. The game masterfully intertwines its rich lore with compelling character development, ensuring players are deeply invested in the story from start to finish.Graphics and Art DesignVisually, Horizon Forbidden West is nothing short of spectacular. The attention to detail in the environments, character models, and animations is remarkable. The game leverages the power of next-gen consoles, delivering stunning graphics that make the world feel incredibly immersive and lifelike. The day-night cycle and dynamic weather systems add layers of realism and beauty to the already impressive landscapes.Gameplay and MechanicsGameplay in Horizon Forbidden West is both familiar and refreshing. The combat system retains its satisfying mix of melee and ranged attacks, but with added depth and complexity. New weapons, gadgets, and abilities provide a diverse array of options for tackling challenges. The introduction of underwater exploration and enhanced climbing mechanics expands the sense of adventure and discovery. Additionally, the skill tree has been revamped, offering more customization to suit different playstyles.Audio and SoundtrackThe audio experience in Horizon Forbidden West is outstanding. The voice acting is top-notch, with Ashly Burch delivering a powerful performance as Aloy. The sound effects enhance the immersion, from the rustling of leaves to the roar of mechanical beasts. The soundtrack, composed by Joris de Man, Niels van der Leest, and The Flight, is a masterful blend of orchestral and electronic elements, perfectly complementing the game's atmosphere.ConclusionHorizon Forbidden West is a triumph in game design, storytelling, and visual artistry. It successfully expands on the strengths of its predecessor while introducing new elements that enhance the overall experience. Whether you are a returning fan or a newcomer, this game offers an unforgettable adventure that is well worth exploring. With its captivating story, stunning visuals, and engaging gameplay, Horizon Forbidden West deserves every bit of its 5-star rating.

There are many things to like about this game, and I certainly feel I'm getting my money's worth.Let's get this out of the way: play Horizon Zero Dawn first!After that, continue the story with this one.So, now let's review this game.First of all, let's make sure that it is clear that the game is completely build around a few systems: movement, stealth, combat, skills and crafting.1) The movement is your basic walking/running/jumping and climbing, extended with gliding and riding mounts.2) The stealth is your typical sneak and hide in tall grass sort of thing, with near-instant takedown mechanics - some enemies are not instantly taken down, they just take a large chunk of damage. There is noise and vision involved in the sneaking around. 3) The combat, whether it is against humans or machines, involves using your strengths against their weaknesses. There are a bunch of different weapon types, that actually feel unique, and as you progress the higher level ones will allow multiple types of ammunition to be used. Creating a pretty diverse set of tools at your disposal during combat. NPCs also fight each other, machines and humans alike.4) Skills are bought for skillpoints and, especially in the beginning, enhance your playstyle. You decide which way to go here. There are a lot of passive skills and a few active skills per weapon type.5) Crafting allows you to enhance your gear, create traps and ammo (on the go). So even when you run out of arrows during combat, you can easily create more in the heat of the fight. Obviously, gathering and hunting, wildlife and machines, is also part of this gameplay system.Now, the awesome thing here, is that all of these systems combine really well. You can ride your mount into combat, jump off, fire arrows from the air, while your mount joins the fight. Or sneak around, place traps, start the engagement and call your mount when things get tough for some extra aid.Even when overleveled by 10 levels, fights can still end up challenging when just running in and engaging a large camp by your lonesome. Although, so far, the human enemies don't bother me as much as when they bring big ass machines or a bunch of faster ones.Even in the wild, it is easy to get overwhelmed by a few groups of machines that are triggered by the noise.Then there is the narrative, which so far has surprised me a few times. It starts off pretty straight forward, but it has some interesting twists and turns that I did not see coming.And let's not pass over the fact that so far all side-quests feel unique - although they obviously utilise the same systems - in their stories and characters. There are only a few 'fetch' or 'kill X' quests, and these are generally not marked as side-quests, but put in a different category. And even these are completely voiced with still rather unique encounters.The only negative about this game is that even 2 weeks after release, it is still plagued by random crashes to desktop. Walk out onto some platform to look out over a valley and poof, desktop with a crash reporter. And others are reporting even worse types of crashes, that I have luckily not experienced myself.My specs:Ryzen 5800X3DAMD RX 6750 XT 12GB32GB RAM @ 3200MHzPlaying off an SSDUsing High pre-set, with shadows turned down to Medium, @ 1440p, 60FPS stable.

Horizon Forbidden West is a visually stunning sequel that builds on the foundations of its predecessor, Horizon Zero Dawn. The game takes place in a post-apocalyptic world where robotic creatures roam the land, and players once again follow the journey of Aloy as she navigates through this beautifully crafted open world.Graphics and Environment: The game's graphics are a significant improvement over the original, with lush environments, detailed character models, and breathtaking landscapes. The attention to detail is evident in every corner of the map, from the towering mountains to the sprawling forests. The dynamic weather system adds an extra layer of immersion, making the world feel alive and ever-changing.Gameplay: The core gameplay mechanics remain largely unchanged, with a focus on combat, exploration, and crafting. The combat system is satisfying, with a variety of weapons and strategies to take down the mechanical beasts. The addition of new machines and the ability to customize weapons adds depth to the combat experience. The side quests and activities are plentiful, providing hours of additional content and rewarding exploration.Story and Characters: The story is engaging, with twists and turns that keep players invested in Aloy's journey. The characters are well-developed, and the relationships between them add emotional depth to the narrative. However, some characters feel a bit underutilized, and the pacing of the story can be uneven at times.In the end I have to say that this game is a fantastic sequel that delivers on its promises with stunning visuals, engaging gameplay, and a captivating story. I'll give it 8.5/10 and I think it's a journey that you should experience.

After two years of studiously avoiding spoilers and eagerly awaiting this game, I am very pleased I held out to enjoy this game on PC. Does it capture the sense of wonder that the original's narrative had? Of course not, it was never going to. If anything, the first game revealed a bit too much of their central mystery. The narrative here is predictable if you paid close attention in HZD, but it's still satisfying enough. The "chosen-one" trope does grate at times, but that was true of the first game too. Aloy is essentially Lassie in human form. It is what it is.Game-play improvements are mostly for the better, and combat now feels even more dynamic and exciting with less opportunity for some of the cheesing from the first game. It took some getting used to, but I came to love it. Just note - if you are playing with K+M I strongly recommend a gaming mouse - I wouldn't want to play this without at least a few programmable mouse keys. Also, they've allowed remapping Tab now which should make the adjustment easier. The combat and damage systems have changed a good deal since HZD, so be prepared to relearn some stuff (and if you haven't played the first game you absolutely should before playing this). Normally I am not super invested in graphics - there is more at stake in modern games. But sometimes a game and environment comes along, like with RDR2, where the visuals truly supercharge the experience. This is one of those games. The environments with high end settings and DLSS are absolutely stunning. I will probably get out my old ultrawide because this is one game where the aspect ratio absolutely enhances things - though you can set it to ultrawide aspect ratio on a regular screen too. I have no idea what people complaining about stuttering are referring too (outside some light judder in select cutscenes). I suspect they are running out of VRAM. Also, the game is quite long - it took me 45 hours to complete with the DLC, and I did very little of the side content. I am getting increasingly weary of long games, but this one actually respects your time for the most part. You absolutely can main line the story and finish sooner if you don't mind the challenge. Really the only way it is tedious and unneccesarily grindy is in the high-end upgrade requirements (which decrease with DLC gear). This issue is fixable with PC mods or trainers, and I think there's no shame in doing so to skip the grind as long as you gate yourself reasonably.You may see people giving this game a thumbs down because it's woke - it isn't. Yes, most of the "admirable" characters are women, and most of the buffoonish villains are men. It is a bit overblown, but it's hardly misandry. And Aloy's primary, loyal and upstanding companion is a dude. Also, having some gay characters doesn't make a game woke - it makes it realistic. Almost all relationships portrayed are straight. One person here said "almost every character is gay" which is completely untrue. I count two. And it completely fits the characterization of both of them (i.e. it isn't forced or retconned). Seriously, if this game counts as "woke" then what these players are expecting is a total absence of gay or non-straight characters. That isn't anti-woke, it's just bigoted nonsense. Get real. Fortunately I have seen less of this kind of response since the early launch period.Overall, this is both a superb game and a superb port. Is it perfect? Absolutely not. Groundbreaking? Outside visuals, no. That said, I don't get the "it's a fun game but not as good as first, so thumbs down." PC gamer did the same thing. Games don't always have to excel in everything to be worth your time or money. Personally, I was prepared to be disappoint with this game, but it exceeded my expectations. Just don't go in expecting that same compelling mystery from the first game, and I highly doubt you'll leave disappointed.

Great franchise.  Loved the first game and the port to PC is pretty well done.  I personally didn't have any issues with either games and was able to fully play and enjoy both from start to finish.As for the 2nd game in the franchise and how I feel about it after having finished the story (including DLC)...The good:- Same familiar gameplay with almost identical weapon and enemy mechanics.  If you enjoyed the first game, this one is more of that.- A few new toys such as glider, flying mounts, and grapple hook to mix things up a bit.- Fully voiced story and side-missions.  Some side missions are quick standard experiences and others are long detailed story missions.- Lots of seemingly new damage types and tools to work with.  You can take multiple approaches to fighting and likely find one that you enjoy and works well against most enemies.The not-so-good:- There don't appear to be any cool hidden or super special weapons/armor to work your way towards.  Most of the best gear is locked behind doing arena matches or gathering glowing rocks around the world.  Pretty lazy approach.  I really liked the first game where you had to find your way into a lab and gain access to advanced shield armor.- Items you loot, such as parts that are blown off enemies you fight, seem to have a 50/50 chance to be either Press "e" to loot or HOLD "e" to open a loot window.  This is very annoying as you're never sure if you have to hold or press especially while running around in crazy fights.- The focus mode to scan machines can be very annoying to "lock-on" to enemies and stay locked on to highlight or check parts.  This is especially bad during boss encounters where you can't be stealthed and take time.   For example, some enemies are so large, if you try to cycle through and highlight their tail... it simply loses the lock-on entirely and the focus UI goes away.  I've had encounters where I simply could not get the system to let me lock on to one or more of the monster parts.

I have played many games in my days. I have had my share of parasocial attachments, post game depressions or whatever you want to call it. I have watched Alyx Vance lose Eli Vance, only to see Alyx reawaken him. I have watched Arthur Morgan die. I have made many factions triumphant over the Mojave and the other Wastelands. I killed Alduin the world Eater. I have reignited the first flame many times. I became the Elden Lord. I built factories and Dyson Spheres. I have played hours and hours of GTA. I battled in most of the Battlefields. I beat the Soviets in Red Alert. I have stood victorious in countless of Total Warhammer battles. I recently became Starborn. I watched Amicia end her story in a horrific way. I have killed thousands of Automatons and Terminids for the sake of democracy. I became a Pirate Legend. I even became an Assassin more times then I can count. I followed Geralt of Rivia's story multiple times. Finally, me and Johny Silverhand owned Night City.However I cannot put into words how this game made me feel. It's the story, OST, the visuals of the open world and the acting that make this game so disgustingly good. I engaged with every character, I was curious how Aloy's friends would react to GAIA. I wasn't even sure how I would react to GAIA and damn did I exhaust every conversation when I was inside the base. I thought about Horizon when I was at work, doing things with friends or when I was working out. Hell I was even thinking about Horizon while I was playing a different game with my friends. I put every free hour I had into the game and even when I wanted a break from the story I could grind my way to better gear or play sidequests that were equally as engaging for me as the main story. I finished the whole DLC in one sitting and one day. I couldn't get over the fact it had ended and a week later I am still drowning myself in Horizon's OST, I finished almost every single side quest or job there was in this game. If you like open worlds with a great story, buy this game and it's predecessor . You will not regret it. Well, you might regret it when you are finished and feel as empty as I do. Sequels are hard. The first game in this series got a very high rating from me because, among other things, both the story and the gameplay were innovative, and the characters were interesting. Unfortunately, the first two are much harder to achieve in a sequel, and this one didn't. This world is much larger, and there are MANY more options and things to try, especially in the way of equipment and gameplay. If you are a huge fan of action and combat, this may be a good thing, but for me it felt like filler. In contrast to the first game, some of the climbing scenes in this sequel were a close thing for me in terms of difficulty, and at least one of these was in a main line quest.The companions were a missed opportunity. They each have an interesting back story and an important character quest, but apart from that, they do not adventure with you.The Burning Shores DLC (included now) is worthwhile, and I really liked Seyka, but she has no life outside of this modest addition.In contrast to Zero Dawn, which was amazingly clean, Forbidden West had a fair number of technical glitches. Fortunately, all of the ones that blocked progress could be worked around by reloading from a recent save. The two most notable problems were:  - Stuttering in graphics, even at lower settings. This was somewhat mysterious, as neither GPU, nor CPU, nor disk were maxed out these times.  - One character quest deleted ALL of the quick saves at the start. It was fortunate that I was able to complete it without having to revert to a previous save, but it was scary in the meantime. This problem has been documented for years, but for some reason has never been fixed.On the good side, Aloy is still very much her extremely likeable self. Apart from the stuttering mentioned above, the graphics are again excellent. The gameplay again offers low difficulty settings that make it possible for incompetents like me to play an action-heavy combat game with minimal frustration.Overall, I give it 7 out of 10. The story sets up a clear path to another sequel, so let's hope it actually comes out in the not too distant future, and addresses at least some of the shortcomings of this one.

A sequel done wrong. Might be confusing considering my recommended rating but hear me out. It's a good game, but it fails on some key points. Let's start with the world. It's a slight downgrade from it's predecessor, as it's more arid and less colourful. It's still a beautiful and amazing world with more pre-apocalypse landmarks than in the previous game, but it's a really nice environment. However traversal is not as fun as in the first game. In the first game I barely ever used the fast travel mechanic because it was a joy to traverse the world and it was so beautiful but in this I used it frequently.The combat is basically the same as in the previous game, it's great. No complaints. There are new skills of course, but the core is the same.The problem with these points is mostly that the game doesn't bring anything new to the table. It's basically the same game as Horizon: Zero Dawn in a new environment and just a few new skills and a new story. It doesn't distinguish itself really and that is a negative point for a sequel.Now the story is where it fails. While Horizon: Zero Dawn had a great air of mystery and discovery with a story that just worked. This game lost a lot of the mystery and discovery by the nature that the main character Aloy knows all about the past now, she knows what needed to be discovered in the first game, and that's just the nature of a sequel. But in such cases the story needs to lift it and in this game it doesn't. The base story that needed to be there for the sequel to exist is there and it's pretty nice, it explains itself, but it creates a new threat. This threat, honestly, was not needed. The story without the new threat would be enough since there is an inherent threat if they fail their goal. This new threat is also just not interesting or fitting in the world, which takes away what could be a great story. I also have to point out that closer to the end of the video game the story devolves into typical tropes and clichés that were definitely not needed and were just frustrating.7/10 for the game, with the combat getting a solid 8/10, the world an 8/10 and the story a 5/10 (with the ending getting a soft 4/10)

We already know this game is pretty good, but should you buy this game on PC? In my opinion, wait a month or two for the bugs and performance issues to be ironed out. On my build (RTX 3070, Ryzen 5 5600X), on high settings: - Performance is pretty good and the settings offer some flexibility. - Many cutscenes tend to tank the fps (down to the 20s), and it seems to decrease sometimes as time goes on (memory leak)? Reloading the game restores the framerate. - NPCs on screen tank the fps too. - One instance of the game image freezing, while from the sound it was still running. - textures visibly loading during transitions in cutscenes. Edit after finishing the game: This game is a step up from Zero Dawn in nearly every aspect. Here is what stood out to me. Minor spoilers ahead. - Technically, it's very impressive: this is an open world with beautiful graphics where you can navigate the land, the waters and the sky and it does it very smoothly most of the time. The technical issues mentioned above are still there however. There is a DIY fix for the lagging cutscenes that you can find on the internet, but I wish the developers would address it. - The game is harder than Zero Dawn overall. In the first opus, I played in hard mode without too much trouble. Not so in Forbidden West, where big enemies can kill you in two hits in this difficulty setting. Finally I settled for normal. The many added game systems are a bit much sometimes. - The traversal moveset is... surprisingly janky for a game with this amount of polish. I guess this is a result of the climbing becoming more organic. Climbing can be a bit finicky and the sliding down ropes animation can be difficult to trigger, leading to annoying falls. - The narration is better than in Zero Dawn, with the companion missions being the stars of the show. I just wish there was more of them, because going adventuring with Aloy's friends was the best part of the game. The characters are engaging, though again I wish they were a bit more fleshed out. Their interactions with Aloy and other members of the group were well done, all in all. Actually, it would have been great if there was an assist system where Aloy could call on her friends to help her. Despite being a sci fi world, there is a distinct fantasy vibe to the game, with each tribe being reminiscent of elves, dwarves and other fantasy races, so the game was begging for some robust adventuring fellowship action. Anyway, this is a great game. It is an open world, meaning it has repetitiveness, despite the efforts of the developers to make well-written side quests. If you don't mind that, then this is amongst the best open worlds you can play.

The gameplay in Horizon Forbidden West is absolutely fantastic, I would even say its flawless. Aloy is given a fresh set of movement abilities with this second entry into the Horizon franchise. These include gliding, diving underwater, flying, swimming underwater with a mount and much more. Improved features, like the new ways to heal, trap placement, and a diverse selection of weapons add depth to the gameplay. The addition of new damage elements like purgewate, plasma, adhesive and acid as well as the new weapon types heightens the intensity, offering thrilling and engaging battles. The combat stands out as some of the most thrilling and action-packed fun you can have (especially in the Ultra Hard difficulty preset). Mastering the machines weaknesses and dealing some crisp huge damage combos is extremely satisfying. The game is a challenge on this difficulty, but it’s the way I highly recommend playing it, its absolutely fantastic. The graphics in Horizon Forbidden West are breathtaking, with a lush and highly detailed world that dwarfs most current open world games found on the market. The expansive map features diverse and distinctive locations to explore. Included are huge and vast mountainous areas, lush and highly details tropical locations, wide and turbulent deserts to the volcanic areas of burning shores, this game has it all. Guerrilla games did an absolutely good job of creating a world that you want to explore and spend a lot of time in.The PC port was done by Nixxes and often runs very smooth on high end systems. However, it is not perfect by any means. I played this game on a RTX 4080 and 10900K system. For the most part the game averaged 90 – 110 FPS at 4K Max DLSS quality FG OFF. The base game often runs well, however the DLC area of burning shores is poorly optimized especially in the main city of fleets end. The CPU is absolutely hammered, and framerate and frame times drop hard, with terrible 30+MS frame times which you can feel even on a VRR display. Something I would like to see improved in the future. Furthermore, as seen with previous Nixxes ports with lower – mid tier hardware especially 8GB or less VRAM cards the game is almost unplayable. As they program their ports in a way to not respect the VRAM budget of your card causing huge frame time fluctuations requiring a game reboot. I personally played this on a RTX 4080 with no issues, however I did see the game consuming upwards of 14GB of video memory. The one thing forbidden west does worse versus the first entry, Horizon Zero Dawn is the story telling and character development. A core element for many players is a well written story with interesting characters. Horizon Forbidden West does a satisfactory job at telling a decent story, however it falls short often feeling very generic and safe. On top of that the character development is seriously lacking, you don’t really develop a sense of attachment to any of the characters in the game. Most side content characters are very forgettable. They also made most men in this game sound feminine and most females sounding masculine, however a proper and realistic blend is always favorable versus pushing the agenda towards the latter. Ultimately the characters and story in this game fall very short from what most players would consider good or even satisfactory and is a huge negative point for such a well put together game.Overall, Horizon Forbidden West has been a fantastic and very satisfying experience. The game took me a little over 100 hours to fully 100% complete on New Game + Ultra Hard difficulty, with all the achievements unlocked (something Rytox can NEVER pull off). The gameplay is so dang good, and I recommend anyone playing this to set the game to very hard on their first playthrough then blast it to ultra hard on the second run. Although the story and characters do fall flat, the fantastic game world, graphics and fantastic gameplay / combat well makes up for its shortfalls. If I would rate horizon forbidden west it would easily get a 9 / 10. I really hope Guerilla games can perfect their craft with their next entry and give us a story to remember.

I expected good things, and wasn't disappointed.Much like the first, this game was a delight. Mechanically it was a good time, everything ran well (usually), the controls were more responsive than fluid, which in a game where you're not triggering insta-kill combos all the time, is my preference.Combat-wise, my only beef is the complete lack of block/parry, etc.  Shields exist.  They're a thing, but all I can do is steal a busted one at the beginning and use it as a glider, while fighting like 700 randos sporting more of them which I'm just leaving laying around because . . . reasons?!  And even without it, I have a spear, most of which is a long stick.  I should be able to block at least some things if you're gonna try to get me to engage in melee with the new combos and all.The plot itself is good, it's mostly well written. There were a couple annoying bits, but neither of them factored into things terribly long, so not a big issue. I don't think there were a TON of new machines brought to the table, but that's whatever - it's not pokemon, that wasn't the point anyway.  It's just directly adjacent to the last game, it'd be kinda weird if there were, actually.Which does bring me to one thing that always bothers me looking at a map, when I can run across it in 30 minutes but it's intended to represent like 2,000 real-world miles.  I mean, I get it.  If the actual area covered represented the amount of distance traveled at that speed in that time, basically no games would have more than one or two biomes.  Which would be boring if every game did it, so again:  I get it.  It's just weird, right?  Also why are there jungles in the American southwest when the environment is basically restored?WHATEVER, though - ANYWAY, it's a good time, and I wanted more Aloy and I got it.  I think the only thing that annoyed me story-wise throughout the game is the general lack of growth from the whole first game?  It's like "save the known world!  Go from outcast to leader (not in the sense of having followers but of being the one in the lead on this whole thing) and learn the value of your "tribe" of chosen allies!"  And then we start off with her immediately like, "NO, AFTER NEEDING ALL THIS HELP WITH THE LAST THING, THIS *NEW* THING I MUST DO ALONE."  It didn't really seem to make sense to me, but like I said before about my story issues being minor, this was one of them.  Just venting.The main takeaways are:  Fun game, runs well, good writing, and you don't actually NEED to melee 99% of the time anyway.  Enjoy!

Not that far into the story yet but whilst it started very well, it's already becoming annoying.To get the good points out of the way, the PC port performs very well. It looks stunning and keyboard and mouse is fine after playing through HZD on PS4. The VA is excellent, character animations are slick, and the attention to detail is magnificent. The art team has done such a fantastic job of creating locations and clothing.The problem is that you have to interact with this world, and it kind of comes unstuck.You are fighting enemies and whilst they are facing one way, they tend to path towards your dodge destination for no reason other than to make the game harder. It clearly isn't a natural movement or what was intended when the animators created it.All the platforming puzzles are linear and Aloy snaps to each yellow beam on simple command, until they aren't and, because this is so infrequent, it's so jarring as to think the game has actually bugged.The story is pretty hampered by the success of the first game. In HZD, Aloy is trying to make sense of her world and herself, but in HFW Aloy is trying to save the world, and it is everyone else who is trying to make sense of it. This means that Aloy (and the player) is several steps ahead of almost everyone else in the game, and talking to them is like placating a child. Aloy does her best to leave all these other characters behind, to the point where it is annoying when they show up again.The set-piece battles tend to spoil the combat elements which make the game great. You tend to lose all the stealth options of hunting, and spend your time rolling around trying to get a quick shot off and healing the inevitable damage. The game is truly at it's best when you can simply hunt a pack of beasts with your tools, have it go wrong, and deal with the consequences.The tools are another issue. I haven't gotten that far but the amount of weapons seems insane so far. Why are there so many different types, and the elemental arrows are attached to different versions. Switching through 4 weapons during a fight is not creating engaging game play, it is tedious.This is not a bad game, it just has a few too many bad parts in it.

After one of the greatest storytelling games of all time, I really looked forward to this entry.  I am not disappointed by it. But I am not overwhelmed or excited by it.  Story elements are good not great this time around, with a multitude of new characters and a few returning ones.  Lots of new environments, machines, and gear.  Gameplay is virtually copied over, with a couple of new surprises.  There is one massive, major flaw in this game's design.  An excessive amount of quests are built around what I'll call precision jumping. That is, you have to specifically jump exacting, prescripted ways that make no real sense in universe most of the time, and there's not alternatives available.      This is annoying and makes for unnecessary repetition of elements if you don't immediately get things right each and every step of the process.  Had level designers picked more options to accomplish quests instead of scripted precision jumping, this could have resulted in a richer experience and far more varied and interesting replayability.  For side quests and an occasional (ie, one of every 100) main quest elements, this might have been fine.  More level designers need to play Super Mario Brothers to understand how to make things both accessible, variable, and still entertaining.  I really hope the third entry finds a way to avoid this issue, and keep or even improve the story elements.

Pros and Cons after 50ish hours:+ Story, writing, characters - LOVE what they've done with Aloy. It's such a natural development to have her - someone who is absolutely not used to trusting people - think she needs to do everything alone. Love the supporting cast and how they deal with Aloy's messiah complex. Love all the little historical tidbits that show us how the Tenakth built their culture from relics from "our" time. + Music is top notch, just like last time. The mix of electronica and "tribal" music is done so skillfully and really gives the correct vibe for this setting.+ Graphics and optimization are amazing. This has got to be one of the prettiest games I've ever played. You could take a screenshot every 10 seconds and not get one bad picture. I haven't seen any screen tearing, stuttering, fps drops, crashes, bugs, etc. - but since this is PC, your mileage may vary. + Variety of landscapes/areas - once again, they managed to build a world with diverse geographical locations that feel really distinct from one another, including the sound design, weather effects, etc. This makes it actually feel like you're travelling large distances. From the beautiful waters of the coast, to the stormy desert around Las Vegas, every location was just beautiful and stunning, and well designed (environmental design wise).+ Combat is really open-ended and every strategy of tackling human or machine enemies is fair game...- ... until it's time for boss fights. And while the game allows you to snipe enemies from up on the next mountaintop in the open world, for boss fights, the game forces you into a very small arena with incredibly fast and aggressive bosses, who sometimes also have ads. This is an issue that plagues many/all action RPGs but it's still frustrating as hell. - Too much bloat. I didn't need challenge runs AND the Strike mini-game AND melee pits AND hunting challenges AND an arena. But then again, maybe that's fun for people who are more about the gameplay.- The relic ruins are a neat addition but have a tendency to get frustrating real fast, especially when Aloy keeps telling me "I should look around" every 20 seconds. - Backtracking. So much backtracking. There are various locked areas across the entire map and you won't be able to access them until much later. Sunken caves, Firegleam, the weird Metal Flowers, a locked(??) Tallneck? Did we really need that many justifications to go back to old map areas not just once but multiple times? (Of course you can just keep it for the endgame, but by then, most of the gear etc. behind these locks may be obsolete.)- Gear and Pouch upgrades can get pretty grindy later on. To the point that you can't just play normally and pick everything up along the way - you actually need to do specialized grinding hunts for machine parts and (my least favorite) animal parts. _________________Overall, HFW is a less tight experience than HZD. It's still fun and engaging, and the various difficulty and accessibility options ensure that the level of potential frustration is kept to a minimum. The world and story is still absolutely genius. And Aloy as a character feels even more like an actual person now, which I appreciate tremendously. I just wish there wasn't SO much extra stuff that it actually distracts from the main narrative sometimes.

It's almost always the core gameplay of a game that acts as the adhesive for my attention. HFW, just like its predecessor, has the most essential aspect - fighting interesting and visually stunning enemies - down with aplomb. Fighting a Thunderjaw or a Tremortusk on Very Hard is a frantic, heart-pounding experience and that is what I keep coming back to because I can't get enough of that thrill. While the action alone would have garnered a recommendation from me, there's also the game's story. HZD was lauded for having an outstanding sci-fi story and HFW continues that without breaking a sweat. The story of how humanity fell and how it continues to thrive a thousand years post-apocalypse is extremely interesting, to say the least. Its cast of tribal characters don't disappoint either. Each tribe brings something new to the table in how they view the world and how they survive and I think the writers did a great job of grounding them in the world that they've crafted. I really couldn't recommend the game enough, especially for fans of the original.

If you enjoyed the first and want more of the setting, you will probably enjoy this one. It's absolutely gorgeous and the sight-seeing is pretty cool. The story is good and the companions are interesting and fleshed out.but, gameplay is a mess, and frustrating from start to finish:- Mechanics in general just feel janky and untested- There's plenty to do, but camps and side quests get pretty repetitive- You are locked into long animations; some conversations can be quick-stepped and some can't and there's no specific reason why (the voice acting is great, but I personally read the subtitles and hit next)- Too many weapons, too many ammo types, too many upgrade and crafting materials- Upgrades cost a ridiculous amount of materials, especially late-game. For example, to get 6 legendary weapons to full upgrade, you will need 12 slaughterspine circulators (iirc)- Because of the previous, if you want to upgrade legendaries, you will have to grind them. If you don't turn on easy loot and play as intended, you will have to grind even more. Some upgrades use removable parts (fun), but top upgrades use RNG drop hearts (not fun)- Combat should be fun, but it isn't- Aloy will self-talk you the solutions to puzzles sometimes before you have a chance to figure out what exact configuration of boxes you needAll of the previous would be fine if the combat were not such a chore. It seems like it could be fun, and it had fun moments, but in practice it's just not. Enemies move entirely too fast for their size, turn instantly, and have animations that when combined with the terrain cause their model to move suddenly in unexpected ways, so it's often extremely hard to hit what you're aiming at even in concentration. Draw speed and overdraw on weapons is very slow also compared to enemy speed. You have to hit weak points in order to do any appreciable damage at all and enemies tend to be health sponges. If you get hit you get knocked down most of the time and it takes Aloy a full business day to stand back up and can't roll out of it. Speaking of rolling, there is some invulnerability when you roll, but because a lot of enemy attacks are wide AOE, you will be caught by it regardless. A lot of enemies can fly across distance extremely quickly and hit you before you can get out of the way. Enemies are often grouped in packs with one big one and a bunch of annoying turds around them, so you can either spend an hour stealthing them down before going in for the big guy or just go for it and deal with flying attacks from every direction. Medium-large enemies have a ton of special attacks and will spam them. You can use something like the berzerk aoe ability which works pretty good, but most of the time they will continue attacking you if they already were. Melee does almost no damage to machines and very little to humans (at least they stagger a little) unless you are at the end of a 10 point combo, and you will likely be broken out of it before that. The charged heavy attack is good early game against small machines to get a knock down, but that's about it. So combat is a loop of get one good solid hit from cover, get knocked down, get up, try to aim, have to dodge before draw is finished so fire early, get hit anyway and knocked down, run away to get some distance, try to aim, machine activates ability that either instantly rockets directly into your face or causes fire to just appear under your feet. Rinse-repeat until you no longer have a will to play video games.Occasionally, things will just not work. Potions will just not activate, aiming will get locked out when you get out of the water until you switch weapons, jumping and climbing is static-animation based so sometimes you just miss a jump or jump the wrong way or just do a little hop instead of a jump, puzzle locations were designed in a way to make it as tedious as possible.The utility belt is not useful. You have a limit of 8 carried potions of any type, but the resource box will auto-refill them at random and you can't throw things away. So you can't use auto-refill for materials because it will fill up your health potions with milkshakes or something. Thankfully just shoving berries into your face works fine, so that's all you need.The bones are good, as they say, but it's just too janky. It's like it was designed and shipped without anyone at the studio ever having actually played it. All that said, flying down a canyon in the sunset and doing a barrel roll is top kino.

The game - magnificent. This is a careful sequel, where there are no revolutionary changes, but there are quality improvements to the gameplay. Perhaps the most significant improvement - side quests became more interesting story-wise and more diverse in terms of gameplay.The PC port came out well, but unfortunately, there are some issues at the start. I hope they will be fixed with patches. 1. The game's link to PS account doesn't work intuitively: when Sony servers are busy, the menu item simply isn't there. To get bonus costume and spear, players start doing pointless actions: changing Steam settings, restarting their computers, etc. The correct solution: wait and restart the game a few times until the item appears. It's strange that developers didn't make an informative message about why the item is missing in certain cases.2. The Forbidden West saves and settings are stored in the "Horizon Forbidden West Complete Edition" folder in the Documents of the user. This is not a very good solution because it clutters this folder, especially since Windows has another folder designed for such data. The developers overlooked a detail regarding Windows' Controlled Folder Access feature, which can prevent data saving if enabled. This requires the user to grant access for the game in Windows Defender to the disk, and this is not an obvious step. Another issue that's equally non-obvious is that the game cannot save data if the path to your Windows profile contains non-latin characters. This is peculiar, considering the studio has experience with porting games.3. The controls are inconvenient and cannot be adjusted to work like in the first game. Moreover, some bindings aren't visible in settings. Switching weapons to the F key - inconvenient solution.4. Input lag. The game reacts with noticeable delay to button presses on gamepad and keyboard. Considering that some Aloy actions require timing, such control peculiarities hinder the experience.The gameplay is enjoyable. I liked the addition of physically correct interactions with the world of the game, like dragging boxes and water behavior. Machines have become a bit smarter and behave more diversely.The gaming world has become more diverse. It is now larger compared to Zero Dawn. Verticality was introduced in the game: on the Forbidden West, there are underwater caves and towering cliffs that are fascinating to explore. Climbing has also been improved - now Aloy sees places for grabbing in AR mode, which looks convenient and logical.Also, I liked the role-playing system. It was interesting to see what the developers would come up with in terms of character progression since by the end of the first part, Aloy becomes almost as capable as Mary Sue. Not significantly reducing abilities but adding new interesting possibilities - this approach to character progression seems sensible to me.The game has become more similar to games like Witcher 3 and Assassin's Creed series, but its uniqueness remains. I am delighted with such a high-quality sequel. The first part is enjoyable to me, and Horizon Forbidden West is even better.

The game is very good, but feels like it lost something, or rather shifted its focus a bit. Hunting and scavenging is what I liked most about the first game but that aspect seems to be somewhat suppressed here. That said, with the improvments in the story im genuently engaged even in minor run-ins on the map or side quests.I'm still playing, this is just my most recent impression.The story feels better than the first game, being driven by charecters to a large degree, the way the new map is structured and the quests play very well together, and it all feels connected with sidequests and random encounters being mentioned in story dialog. BUT the story really picks only after a few tutorial-ish missions and its not without noticable weakpoints later, but is a clear improvment in feel and overal quality. Some new wepons are really interesting in use and mechanics, great additions to the arsenal.I like Aloy's casual remarks about scanned machines' weakness, resistances or picked up loot. The new models are also good, especially noticaple on Aloy.You can actually just sit back on a mountaintop and look at all the beautiful and WALKABLE terrain to the horizon, its very impressive.Npc conversations also feel WAY WAY better, with heaps of new animations and well connected dialog options.now some things that annoy me a bit:New equipment is just handed to you, not intentionally crafted to face a certain threat. While I can undertand the game starting out from almost nothing again, there is literlly not a word about the loss of all the gear from the first game.The tutorial of the first game was LEDENDARY in how well it introduced the world, it's missing here, I feel like Aloy could have used the first area with Varl a bit better but alas.Aloy is painted as uncaring and almost hostile to any attempt to assist her for the first few hours, this feels wrong, especially when she suddenly stops.The disappearance of resource canisters upon machine destruction breaks immersion.Machine communication lack the finesse and polish from the first game, some returning machines lost parts of their signaure sound designThe lack of an ammo indicator for the triple arrow shot is a minor yet frustrating omission.Ammo managment seems to take a very weird approach where the capacity of the quivers is small (and, unlike the first game, they don't grow nearly as much) but the materials are completely trivial to get and you can near-instantly craft anything you need while getting stomped, tossed around, falling of cliffs or even drowning. I wish there was a limit or time requirement but no, you run out, get out the magic slow-motion wheel, and craft everything you need on the spot, I dislike that.Everyone is suddenly gay, by that i mean that 3/4 couples prominantly mentioned and seen in quests are gay, and while im not bothered by that, the ratio and the way its presented is very hard to ignore.Its basically "they are gay" and that's it, little to no build up, literally no follow up. It feels forced and out of place.now a VERY annoying part:The game scales incredibly poorly with difficulty, opting for cheap and simple "you get one shot and everything takes hours to kill" instead of making combot more chalenging and complex.This is especially terrible for trials and challanges. For example, the stealth trial is nearly impossible on very hard because you can't silently takedown machines that have inflated HP, even with the best appropriate gear available far above that level.The wording and actual conditions of the challenges are a complete mess that's contradicted by the actual game logic, I actually hate that you have to lower the difficulty just because the design of the challenges doesn't account for that sort of thing.The first game had this kinda BS too, it did NOT get any less infuriating.

Main story is really interesting so far (I have gotten quite far).So what do I not like?I dislike the difficulty and the amount of fighting - even in story mode the enemies can take way too many hits and melee combat is mostly sh*t, because all enemies attacks either stuns you or knocks you out (for way too long time too) and many attacks can't be avoided and no attacks can be parried. Also, when you are knocked around by the monsters, there is a high risk you fall down a ledge or in a hole (I even fell down in a crevice that I couldn't get out of and I had to teleport out of there. One of the most annoying things about melee combat is that your attacks NEVER interrupts the enemies attacks, but the enemies attacks ALWAYS interrupts your attacks. Horrible. BUT, the archery/missile combat is excellent and a lot of fun. So to sum up  too much combat and too prolonged combat, but shooting bow is fun.Some missions have you travel across a large portion of the map, just to have a npc tell you to go back or to another far away location. To put it simply, Horizon: Forbidden West is an extremely phenomenal game. I personally found it better than the first entry in the series. The graphic, artistic, writing, character, and audio design are all beyond stellar. Truly something that can't really be described in writing and need to be experienced. I left my time with Horizon: Forbidden West and it's accompanying DLC feeling both accomplished and much more invested in continuing Aloy's story. I'll be anxiously awaiting the next title in the series.Now, that being said, HFW is by no means perfect. I can definitely corroborate the reviews that note the intense grind, and minor performance issues. Despite being able to run the game very smoothly, I felt that my hardware was pushed to its limits. This is a good wintertime game so your PC can heat up your entire space. There were a few sudden crashes but they happened so occasionally and sporadically for me that they were really negligible. My biggest criticism of HFW is that it is maybe a little too long and at times too fleshed out. There are moments where there is A LOT of dialogue even for those who are interested in the story and lore. The combat, while amazing, also does become repetitive and cumbersome towards the end. Be ready to invest at least 100 hours if you plan on completing the main story, collections, side quests, and the DLC. Overall a very satisfying and worthwhile experience.

Story is supposed to be a selling point of the Horizon series, but Horizon: Forbidden West remains plagued by same-y dialogue and forgettable characters. Good luck remembering all the minor characters from the first game that somehow make an appearance in the so-called "Forbidden" West.Aloy's personal journey remains undercooked relative to the amount of impact it's hyped up to have on the plot. Her three conflicting personality traits - emphasized to varying degrees through dialogue choices - are being stubborn, understanding, and clever, but none of these dialogue choices have an impact on the plot.Indeed, Aloy's established character traits don't seem to have an impact on the plot in any way. For example, Aloy literally stepping over boundaries during peace negotiations at the border between two territories has no substantial impact on said peace negotiations.I'd also like to see more of the ingenuity Aloy supposedly possesses as a . Skill points are so incredibly easy to come by, and so easy to respec, that it left me wondering what the point was of allowing us to choose Aloy's ability upgrades at all. It feels like Horizon wants to market itself as an "RPG", but doesn't allow us to make any decisions that could get in the way of our railroaded experience with the gameplay and plot. It's a problem common to many open world ARPGs, unfortunately.Traversal of the open world is meant to feel like Uncharted/Tomb Raider/Assassin's Creed, but movement just feels unnatural compared to the platforming elements in those games.Worst of all, the developers do not appear to have taken the criticisms HZD received from Native American games journalists to heart.The nicest thing I can say about Horizon: Forbidden West is that I had more fun playing the Machine Strike strategy mini-game than the game itself. It's engaging without being too difficult. I'd buy a standalone Machine Strike game before I'd buy a third Horizon game.

Horizon Forbidden West is a breathtaking sequel that surpasses expectations, offering an expansive open world filled with stunning visuals and rich detail. The game seamlessly blends an intriguing story with deep, engaging gameplay, as you explore a diverse range of environments from lush forests to arid deserts, each teeming with life and mystery. The combat is thrilling, with a wide variety of weapons and strategies to tackle the intricate, dynamic machines that roam the world. Aloy’s journey is both personal and epic, driving the narrative forward with emotional depth and powerful moments. Horizon Forbidden West is a must-play, delivering an unforgettable experience that sets a new standard for open-world adventures

The main story lasts around 30 hours, excluding everything else. Once we account for the side activities and time spent traversing the game world, we're looking at up to 100 hours of playtime, possibly more to fully complete the game and get all the achievements.Gameplay-wise, Horizon Forbidden West does everything its predecessor did but improves in a few key areas. As the game genre suggests, the gameplay revolves around the main story, the side activities, and exploration. Even though the gameplay has drastically improved, it's structured around the same concept as the first game, with a few fresh throw-ins. The only three additions worth mentioning are the gliding, diving, and flying gameplay mechanics. The glider thingie is super neat tactical equipment, while the diving is enjoyable and brings relaxation far away from the tension. The flying mounts stuff gets unlocked so late that the game could do without it.As someone who doesn't like long games but jumps into a few lengthy titles here and there, I feel like this one offers too many activities for my taste. I'm unsure if a game can have too much content, but this is it. The only side hustles I found enjoyable were the cauldrons and the relic sites. As for everything else, I somehow managed to cope with them, but I wish I could skip most of them. The developers tried to make each of them unique, but there's only so much to differentiate one from another before they become repetitive. The combat is a bit more challenging and refined when compared to the first game, the new weapons and tactics add variety, and the boss battles require more planning. Also, I feel like there's too much hand-holding in this one compared to its predecessor, where even Aloy starts repeating the same clues over again.However, where the game takes a step back is the movement in general. Mounts constantly trip and jump over the smallest of obstacles, making them stop in place. Aloy's jumps and movement are both very inconsistent and precise, all at the same time, and you never know what you'll get. The objective marker was already a problem in the first game. But somehow, it's even worse in this one to the point where you never know where the next objective is unless you look at the map to see which path leads there. The marker sometimes shows an objective you know is right around the corner and leads you via the furthest path possible, or it updates its waypoint position every second.Since this is the second installment in the franchise, I'll first say that there isn't a single thing left unimproved over the original game, and the second installment is leaps and bounds above it in all respects. The game now offers proper motion capture animations with some of the best animations and character attention to detail I've ever seen in a video game. Only a few games out there can match the density. Underwater sequences are mesmerizing and add so much to the experience. The vastness and openness of the play area can only be fully fathomed by flying a mount high into the sky or climbing on top of the tallest mountains or structures in the game. However, a video game this good can only go so far as it's not without the drawbacks.Some foliage in certain areas flickers, appears and disappears, and grows from the ground as you come closer, and tons of pop-in is visible on various objects. Certain characters and NPCs, especially enemies, are so repetitive that differentiating them by their looks is often impossible. I even found a few side-quest characters appearing as doppelganger enemies in certain places, but it might be just me being good at remembering faces and noticing them. The variety is not there to match everything else the game does. None of this takes much from the overall presentation, but it is worth mentioning. The soundtrack is excellent, and the frequency of play is on point each time. Voice acting is satisfying to listen to, and the overall sound design and quality of the effects are satisfactory.The story of Horizon Forbidden West picks up at the end of Horizon Zero Dawn. While the main quests kept me interested, everything besides the main story, I just wanted it to be over as soon as possible. Don't get me wrong, it excels in many areas over the first game, but everything besides the story is all over the place. The feeling of mystery I felt playing the original game was replaced with excitement that never stopped delivering, while all the side stuff was overwhelming besides a few activities. I couldn't care less about some NPC losing a family member and Aloy's constant blabbering of: "Maybe my focus can spot it. My focus might find something. Maybe my focus can help me find it." while doing the same side stuff over again gets annoying very fast.Since it's a game where you must tackle all these things and can't enjoy just the story for what it is, I'd say the side activities take away more than they add for my taste. The ending of the main story felt satisfying. As for the Burning Shores DLC, it's not on par with The Frozen Wilds. There are a few interesting missions, but it's mostly there only to demonstrate how good Guerrilla Games' clouds and water rendering tech is, and oh, to show that another PlayStation female protagonist likes scissoring another female character. It's just a PlayStation's obsession with lesbians. What can I say? Most of their female leads seem to be into some girl-on-girl action. I have nothing against anyone, but it's getting out of hand.The perception of the technical side of things varies when we're talking about the PC platform. Obviously, this is Guerrilla Games' finest technological endeavor to date, but it might leave a lot to be desired for some PC gamers using older hardware. The amount of PC hardware required to handle this game, even at a stable 60 FPS, is higher than usual but reasonable if we consider what the game aims to achieve. The game scales well on various hardware. However, technical issues arise with configurations with insufficient amounts of hardware resources. The amount of CPU power required varies drastically from one in-game location to another, and it can be CPU-heavy. The Burning Shores DLC is significantly more demanding on average compared to the main game. Hence why it it was dropped from the PS4 version. The sheer amount of detail speaks for itself, and it's unrealistic to expect a game this dense to run "fine" on older generations of hardware.It's possible to run the game even on older hardware, but keep the expectations in check and be prepared to optimize the gameplay experience accordingly by utilizing FPS caps to avoid frame drops and performance inconsistencies. An SSD is a must for this game. A 6C/12T CPU of any kind with a GPU with at least 6GB VRAM and 16GB RAM is the bare minimum I would recommend for a stable gameplay experience based on my testing on various hardware, and this is for a stable 60 FPS with console-like settings. I haven't experienced any issues except the inconsistent loading times, where it loads the same location, with a variety of 2 to 15 seconds. Other than this, I experienced a single instance where the game pegged my CPU to 100% and started skipping frames and audio cues in that underwater cauldron due to the rising and lowering water levels. Other than this, I experienced no performance issues, even on an older configuration.Horizon Forbidden West is a generational leap and an ambitious continuation of Aloy's adventure that excels in all areas over its predecessor. However, despite everything going in its favor, it somehow gets trapped in the looming shadow of Horizon Zero Dawn.
