HFW is an incredible adventure, probably one of the most beautiful open worlds you can play today. Every mission, character, side quest, main quest is fantastically realised. It’s definitely on my list for Game of the Year, can’t wait to play the next one. 9.5/10StoryAloy starts where she left off- on a mission to find Giai and recover her strength. The game does a great job drawing you in the various twists and turns, as the adventure unfolds the gravity of the reality facing Aloy becomes more grave. You can stick to the main story if you want, but you’re going to see so many beautiful places, so many well acted characters you’ll want to talk to them and explore. One of the brilliant aspects of this game is its ability to draw you into another conversation - another personality , another life to learn about. All the characters are well developed, some have extensive storylines, others are just part of the main adventure. You can learn so much about the game lore from optional interactions with comrades Aloy acquires along the way. Graphics Holy cow. I thought after Cyberpunk I couldn’t be impressed - but boy, does HFW deliver. You experience incredibly detailed vistas, intricately detailed character modelling, lighting that is indistinguishable from a Hollywood movie - a plethora of technologies; HDR, RTX, DLSS to name a few - this game is utterly gorgeous. It’s one of those games where sometimes you stop and just have to take it in. What’s even more incredible is you can run from one end of the map to the other .. without a load screen. From deep forests, barron deserts, icy mountains and rural escapes - you’ll just keep running, or ride a machine to make it even more epic. GameplayI do like the combat in HFW a lot, in principle it’s quite basic (shoot the machines) but there’s a lot of variety in the weapon types as well as how you approach larger machines. The game rewards versatility and upgrading your gear so you can approach a problem in a new way is equally as satisfying. There is a minor grind element to the higher end armour and weapons, which I did not appreciate , but nevertheless I did manage to upgrade a variety of gear and after 60+ hours polished off the end boss in no time at all (very satisfying) Music The music in HFW is refreshingly brilliant - so many games of late are so flat, and I loved all the different orchestral pieces arranged and delivered during the adventure FX is brilliant too, the world feels alive with birds, trees , winding streams, I helps to add to such a visually immersive game Performance With DLSS and VSYNC I stuck at 144 FPS for the majority of the game, even in intense battles the frame rate never let me down.Some minor artifacting with lighting did occur, but it’s expected in such a rich environment. I also experienced 1 crash which occurred during a cut scene , but I wasn’t able to replicate and I went on my way I did experience a few random black (1 second) screens - I couldn’t tell if the game was loading something or what, but it was annoying. I would say I saw maybe 1-2 every 8 hours of game play so it was in hindsight very minimal Overall : BUY! It’s a fantastic addition to your collection

See my playtime? Yeah, it's worth it...I was a fan of H:ZD and instantly bought H:FW after finishing the first game. There are game mechanics here that fans of the first game will hate, and I'm still on the fence on some things. But H:FW has tons of content and way more to offer to players that care about skill and more complicated enemies. I personally hate the loot system (machines now destroy all their detachable parts upon death) and how weak spears are to machines. I also hate the extreme requirements to improve high level weapons; grinding midlevel machines is one thing, but they want you to kill many of the toughest enemies just to add one upgrade rank to a weapon or armor. They basically force us to lower the difficulty and save - restart scum to get all the high level kills we need for upgrades. And I biggest problem with the game is the abundance of non-hackable machines. As in, you might not encounter a hackable machine in 10 encounters in a row, even at the 50% point in the campaign. They give you a whole skill tree for using hacked machines, and then make it harder to impossible to use those skills. That's ridiculous. Outside of these issues, I found the game to have a compelling story and very rewarding exploration and combat mechanics. The graphical quality and super optimized engine is very impressive; every moment is cutscene quality and my FPS never dropped from start to finish. Have a look at my screenshots! In my experience, the Horizon series may be my favorite set of games I've ever played. It's definitely top 5. The pros greatly outweigh the cons here. I can't justify most AAA fully priced games, but H:FW is worth it even if not on sale.

Wow, what a journey! After almost 170 hours while completing most quests and activities, I can say a few words about this game.Zero Dawn was an amazing game, so Forbidden West had to continue at least from the same level. Did it succeed? I think yes, except for some aspects that I will cover at the end of the review.This game is before anything else, quite pretty. Everything looks great, and can look amazing if you have the right hardware. This is a very good port, I could play it okay-ish on a 2 years old gaming laptop. The game rewards you for exploring everything, if there isn't some loot cache or special crystal to discover, there is a beautiful view. There is always something to do.It would be a shame not to play the first game before this, because of how well the story is unfolded in Zero Dawn, and how it ties with this sequel. Aloy is now a veteran, her deeds from the first game precedes her, but the start of the game is a bit slow because of the starting zone where she is blocked until the story picks up. This is fine, the first area has a lot to offer, and it also serves as a sandbox to learn the ropes.The combat is great, you still need to use the weak spots of the machines you fight, learn their vulnerabilities or even use the terrain against them. You get new cool weapons which can be upgraded with rare resources. I like how developers thought of different play styles, and included terrain to help you, like you can snipe from high ground, or you can use stealth. The skill trees offer many new attack types and combos for weapons, but also useful defence special abilities.What I love about FW is how the map has places you can't access in the beginning, and as the story advances, more areas become available, as you'll have means to return and dive underwater, fly, or clear certain obstacles. These are tied with interesting puzzles and new cool ways to fight.Many times, the things you do have an impact on the places you visit. The game offered me several pleasant surprises after I completed certain quests.The story in this game is not as good as in Zero Dawn. In my opinion, the antagonists had so much to offer, yet the writers decided to waste all that potential on some disappointing villains, probably the most pathetic villains of all that I have defeated in games.I enjoyed most of the characters, however, I couldn't help notice a pattern. Try to do a count, and see how many women in this game are strong characters and good leaders, saving their tribe, spouse, friend etc, while men are mostly useless, immature, ingrate, weak, evil or unhinged. That being said, I really liked Aloy and some of the female characters. But towards the end of the DLC, I started to get annoyed with this pattern.Anyway, I really recommend this game, I think it's a must of you like open world games like this.

Horizon: Zero Dawn (HZD) is still a top 5 game for me in the story based RPG / open world genre. Horizon: Forbidden West is a strong contender as a continuation of the story arc. Keeping much of what was good and only introducing a few poor choices as it builds on the story of the lead character Aloy. If you have not played HZD - you NEED to play it before this, else the story will NOT make sense. HZD is still today a hallmark game of excellent graphics and plays well. Some mods can enhance this further. "Forbidden West" is everything a player could look for in a modern Open World, Story based adventure with a variety of combat mechanics and a solid progression tree for your character to level, grow skills and abilities.The graphics are top tier, with foliage and character hair or other details that are crisp and behave well when you move. The world is colourful and has a variety of regions you explore. The Burning Shores DLC adds to this with a sizeable extension to the main storyline (I'll discuss it below). Music score is excellent and worth having on. Story - It's worth playing to explore the world and seek out the stories of the past not just the current time.The story continues from Zero Dawn and it is not as compelling I thought; Having a key element that  seemed forced to me whereas the narrative of Zero Dawn made sense in the world. Burning Shores suffers the same issue of forcing a storyline that seems like the hardest way the enemy could have got what they want. In saying that, it has a well put together cast of people and places with broad sweeping side quests that feed into the main story progression. There are fragments of "the woke agenda" where characters make overt statements or act in a manner that speaks to OUR social discord around Progressive ideology and pandering to those who trash reputations / DEI... and it isn't value adding. In fact it stands out as being what it is because it couldn't possibly be an issue in their world of surviving on the edge. Burning Shores amps it up, and goes "boss-girl" in a way the game has largely avoided. A key character seems wholly built as a "foil" a means of forcing Alloy along a path instead of being a full authentic character - and it shows. If you can ignore the political and cultural lecturing of the Left it's still good fun. Just don't let it influence and rot your brain.Gameplay - the ranged combat with bows, spears, discs and traps is well put together, offering a range of styles and a need to use different approaches on different beasts. Once you get the better gear the settings you choose for difficulty and loot MASSIVELY influence combat challenge - it's essential you know this else you can have too easy/boring lategame or NG+ replay.Sustaining challenge needs a REAL understanding of settings. If you turn on "easy loot" which means killing a beast offers all components rather than needing to shoot them off, you can just use ice to double your impact damage and smash weak spots to kill while still getting the parts to craft ammo and upgrades. Melee combat is interesting with a console style approach of button combos to unleash different attacks. Frustrations: - Climbing now requires special locations that you can view as yellow lines on a surface with your focus. This removes the free feel of the first game and is a hindrance in many fights or moments where you latch onto a small boulder.- double tap move to dodge. Alloy will dodge right off a cliff to her death because you are trying to move carefully. This is a massive bugbear of players and thankfully the option now exists to disable that and use a button to dodge. Turn off the default setting. - Aloy will still melee her way off cliffs or when throwing spears which cause her to take a forward step she will throw herself off as well. So much for Master Warrior! :P  ... Just be aware of it and work with it. - some of the puzzles are frustrating as heck - especially door codes or needing to use ledges to stack multiple "climbing boxes". If you don't like puzzles or have a short fuse this part is easily solved by short walk through's or code lists that don't spoil the game at large.   If you play NG+ with a solid loadout you need to be on the highest levels else the combat becomes empty feeling as you just smash mobs with ice to freeze then impact damage to utterly destroy them.Tips for the best experience: 1. Update your DLSS or FSR version in the game as it makes a big difference to DLSS image quality and removes a lot of blurring when grass moves. Search online - tweaktown has the generic DLSS versions to do this for any game with it. 2.  Colour tone is off badly. HDR especially is bad. I recommend using a reshade from Vortex Mods. Look for one you like and beware which are good for HDR or not. I use the "Auto Colour Correction" reshade. 3. Remove intro videos mod is helpful too. 4. HFW doubles down on the HZD formula and iterates on it in a very fun, satisfying and engrossing way. It's more of the rich open world filled with stunning environments, more of the machine combat with all its aspects, more of Aloy's largely linear but enjoyable story... and so on and so on. Combat in particular feels a notch harder than in HZD at the same difficulty levels, requiring even more attention to elemental weaknesses and modules/weak spots. New machines are very nicely designed and the boss fights make for very engaging encounters, even on lower difficulties. In general combat remains quite tactical and the game rewards taking your time to deal with the machines - and humans - rather than trying to rush them. Burning Shores DLC ramps the difficulty up again, though less noticeably. Visuals are stunning as you would expect, with the extra 5 years of general game tech development on top of it. Music and sound design keep the bar of the first game as well. While the story doesn't quite deliver the mystery and reveal combo that HZD did, there is still a nice slow burn of trying to figure out what the hell the bad guys are actually up to, and the revelation at the end sets up the almost certain third game very well. HFW's plot feels more character driven than in the first game, which was in comparison a bit more centered around the sci-fi concepts and the secrets of the past that Aloy was trying to uncover. The DLC story is short and sweet in comparison to the main game, but expands on it neatly. Its smaller scope and stakes allow it to get more close and personal with Aloy and let it be more of a personal chapter in her story. The PC port has some performance issues still but they are not glaring. Most notable as of early April 2024 are the significant frame drops in cutscenes/conversations with multiple character models in view. Some areas, especially in the more linear missions throughout the game, also suffer from framerate problems. Internet discussions seem to point to VRAM as the primary problem, but fingers crossed it can be addressed at least to an extent.Guerilla and Nixxes have so far seemed to be paying attention to bug reports, but time will tell whether updates will be substantial and regular - or will they dry up after a handful of tiny patches. I loved HZD and so it's no surprised that I loved HFW - it's more of the same, with improvements, but no revolutions. I am  therefore very much looking forward to Horizon 3. And hopefully the PC release will be much closer in time to the PlayStation one than we are used to...

There are only a few games that made me feel completely immersed in the world.The first one was Crysis where not only the graphics and gameplay were compelling but the story and in game rendered cutscenes created an insane atmosphere.Other honorable mentions are Alien: Isolation, Half Life 2, Dead Space.This game achieved the same thanks to the best of the best in many of the important areas:The game render engine is awesome with an insane amount of vegetation, water, physics, detailed and huge amount of entities without closed levels, long loading times or a small view distance (and without the classic Unreal Engine trick to switch between low poly models which can look awful).I got on medium graphics good enough fps (70-100@1080p) most of the time (was on high at the beginning but that was too much for my RTX 3060TI and AMD RX7800X3D on Linux with GE Proton 9.10).The acting, models, motion capture, voice acting, music and animations are breathtaking.On top of that all content/cut-scenes are rendered in game with customizable character clothes, face paint, etc.This game has at least 70h of content with an amazingly written story building on top of the first game where even side missions that don't directly tie into the global story feel fun.Besides the final part of the game it didn't feel too easy on the Hard difficulty.If you upgrade your armor a little it's probably even easier but I had no patience.The points this game can still improve upon but are MINOR compared to what it delivers:The controls are cinematic with a lot of software support but especially on MnK tapping twice left to evade made me mad at some points.On Linux with Proton the audio engine crashed like 25 times, and sometimes you are unable to manually save or see the map but I'm not sure if the port or wine is to blame - since this game has a lot of savepoints it's not a big deal and the unsupported Linux support could be WAY WORSE than it is.The AI for humans and machines was good enough for a compelling atmosphere but it's not on the same level as in DOOM: Eternal.I got stuck twice in the world and once something that should have spawned only spawned after I left the location and came back (Electronic Arts dreams of this quality).The waves and waterdroplets (could also be a wine thing) look a bit bad but I never played a game that made it much better lol.I really enjoyed the writing but it felt at times that Aloy and some others weren't really showing any emotions (grief, happiness) which sometimes made her feel less like a real person and more like a generic video game protagonist.Get it if you played the first one (Horizon: Zero Dawn) and want to watch a 70h movie with an even better story while being the main protagonist.I especially loved the detail that you could customize your face paint and clothing and will then see it in every rendered cutscene.

Horizon: Forbidden West improves on every aspect of its predecessor with better graphics, sound, voice acting, puzzles, quests, and deeper combat. The graphical details and design are brilliant, especially the machines, architecture, and characters are great. I find it fascinating to just see how different each tribe look (clothes, hair. tattoos) and how the folklore of a tribe is influenced by the "Old Ones".I also like the way the story and quests are told as well as the general atmosphere of the game. The quests are very well designed because they are varied and offer a motivating background story. Forbidden West focuses on world-building and characters which is great, because for me, the NPC characters were a major shortcoming of the predecessor. Aloy acts now more self-confident in conversations, but sometimes also distant towards her companions. I like her general positive and pragmatic attitude.Another nice change are lots of items to collect which are spread across the world, so you can't just upgrade all your equipment straight away. This makes upgrades rather expensive and leads but there is still a nice feel of constant progress.There are only a few things to criticize: Objects pop up in the distance, some textures sometimes flicker (especially in conversations with NPCs), higher hardware requirements in the Burning Shores location, and the enemy AI acts quite simplistic and sometimes cannot handle it when you shoot from far away or hidden spots. In addition, some NPCs and companions are a bit annoying (yes, Alva, I mean you and Erend's inferiority complexes). The companions could generally have more character.I also didn't like the quest with Boomer, which contained a strange message that it's okay to endanger other people as long as you're special. Personally, I would have liked more puzzles and especially more different types of puzzles - most of the puzzles follow a similar theme, which is still fine because the developers have made an effort to bring in as much variation as possible.

Great game. One of my favorites to come out of Sony's publishing so far.The story, characters, and gameplay are great in my opinion, making for a wealth of experiences I enjoy on every playthrough. I also enjoy being able to play this with KB+M. This is an easy recommendation for me. I love this game!However, as with all things in life, it has its issues. The climbing is highly restrictive. Encountering so many invisible walls along with arbitrarily placed climbing paths (thankfully more than there were in the first game) sorta breaks my immersion when playing. I genuinely hope they just rip-off the climbing mechanics from BotW/TotK for the next game.On the topic of KB+M support, I agree with others who note that too many controls are tied to the same keybind, leading to moments where I attack instead of overriding certain network access points. Sometimes, this causes Aloy to attack forward and fall down, losing a certain amount of progress. It's only about 15 seconds of frustration and backtracking, but it certainly doesn't enhance the gameplay. They have been detaching certain commands as more updates roll out, and all I'm getting at with this is that there can never be too many. Certain commands came naturally to me, though, having played through the PS5 version before-hand (like aiming and hitting another button to switch to the grapple hook).It's also strange that I still have to pull things out of storage manually in order to unlock my overrides; even stranger that I have to do this in NG+, too, given that one conveniently needs not do that for the workbench. Why make it different here? Please update that QoL, and speaking of, if I recall correctly, there might have been a setting on PS5 that allowed me to skip having to hit space when finishing loading. If I’m not just missing that option as a result of being dense, please implement it, too. Thank you.Lastly, the implementation of language selections through Steam works poorly if at all. When I switched it to Japanese on NG+ for practice (ゲームとかアニメで日本語を練習することが好き), the audio was still English, even when leaving the UI alone. Since I already criticized this inconvenient and roundabout implementation in Miles Morales, I likely wouldn't have complained about it this time if it at least worked. Nixxes otherwise did a great job on the port.Now, the reason I still recommend it, despite these issues, is that they are circumstantial enough to not get in the way of the gameplay through most of my playthrough. They only annoy in select few moments, so as a whole, I still love this game. I'd love it if they could address these, but I still certainly have fun with the game, regardless. I hope you enjoy it, too. Cheers!

There should not be any big spoilers, but it will hint about new machines, mechanics, differencies etc. and it assumes you have played Horizon Zero Dawn before this! So spoilers related to stuff in/from that game.  Let's start with the good stuff.This is a great continuation of Horizon Zero Dawn, if you have not played it, play it first! The story is immersive, and there are lots of small stories to discover. There are lots of places to discover on the mapYou have plenty of ranged weapons to collect and upgradeThey have fixed the perfomance issues that still plauged the HZD for quite some time.Cauldrons is not having perfomance issues anymore. It is great lookingDifficulty, you can change it freely throughout the game, unless you select the hardest. I recommend to play on story or normal difficulty to enjoy the story and prepare for any new game+ runs you might want todo. New game+ is a replay option where you bascially have all your gear and skills from your current game, some limitiatons apply.So save your highest difficulty playthrough for the New game+.So overall, it is good game, that offers many hours of gameplay, and for the most part, play on normal or even story mode. But as you can see, there are plenty of text below, and these are things I find problematic. So lets get into the bad stuff. Much these revolve around combat and machines. So lets start with, the combat is worse than in Horizon Zero Dawn, and most of the new machines are very annoying and time consuming. Difficulty. Something is very strange here. I expected to be extremely squishy on my new game+ on hardest difficulty, I was wrong. Raiding NPC camps I can be as reckless as I was on my normal playthrough, the difference is that I now have all skills unlocked and much better gear and I have learned to aim etc. It is very obvious that machines have alot more health. Machines are alot more aggressive and their attacks are more relentless and they take faster turns when there are several machines present. But they do not feel to do much more damage than before, you only have shorter time to recover. So all this does is to drag out the fight.So you end up repeating either * Move, dodge, maybe attack* Move, hide in smoke, sneak, attackFor casual game play the default auto aim good. it makes hunting animals a breeze, but you will many time miss weak spots, as the arrow will instead target an armour plate instead. Easily solved, turn off auto aim. Enter new game+ on hardest difficulty, auto aim is disabled, and now you discover a new thing. auto miss is now enabled instead, you can watch the arrow steer away from the perfect sneak attack on the non moving NPC headshot. You can repeat this experience over and over, you will randomly automatically miss your target. Reload save move to same spot, line up the target and see how many times you but doing the same aim every time. The climbing stuff is quite annoying, it is worse than in Horizon Zero Dawn. You can still get stuck to on rocks during fights, but now can get stuck climbing on rocks and on climbing puzzles, where Aloy refuses to acknowledge that highlighted spot is not valid spot to move to, this is totallyh random and for climb puzzle, reloding the last save point will most of the time fix the issue, even in the Cauldron with a otherwise nice jumping puzzle. The only improvement is that you are now very unlikely to accidentally jump off the cliff you are climbing, it takes alot more effort to this now, but that was not really a big problem before... Bigger elemntal attack that will push you if they hit, will always push you away, unless you are moving, then it will push you in the oppositie direction. Example, machine shoots a stream of high preasure water at you, if you stand still it pushes you away, if you move away, it pushes you towards the machine! very stupid. So you will often encounter, moving away from a machine doing these kind of attacks will pull you in, unles you stop moving before getting hit, but you are more likely trying to go into a dodge or just comming out of a dodge when it hits you. Melee combat, the nicest thing I can say about this is that it is complete joke and the person who designed totally missed the mark with this one. So let tell you about your melee options, you have ONE weapong, and you have 3 moves for melee: * Light attack * Heavy attack* Dodge There is no block, and you basically do pathetic damage with either Light or Heavy attack. To do real damage, you have to use combos. There is not enough room to go over how over complicated the combo system is, and all it has to deal with are light attack, heavy attack and <pause>... yeah they managed to overcomplicate a concept of two keypresses and a time element.  Ignore anything you see NPCs do in regards to melee attacks, they defy most things you are allowed todo in regards to melee combat. Block, elemental attacks, use different melee weapons, use cool shields, etc, etc. you only have your spear and dodge at your disposal. The new machines. So this forces player to keep moving. Does not make for more engaging fights... just more booring. Example of old boss machine, that many players had problem with, including me. So move on rocks instead. Next thing to learn, de-claw Rockbreaker, and it can no longer go underground! once learned/discovered, Rockbreaker became one of my favorite machine to fight, it was far from a pushover, but it was rewarding. it pains me to say since Horizon Zero Dawn is possibly my favorite game of all time, but I can not in good conscience recommend this game - to anyone interested in this series, play the first game, and anyone who already did, just play it again...There's multiple things bothering me about this game:- The controls are awful and unintuitive, it's obvious that this was ported from console with no thought put into the M&KB button layout, some menus have "confirmative" actions in menus as LMB/Space (mostly hold, not press, but you get a popup asking to confirm anyway, turning everything into a slog), some only LMB, some for some reason RMB, and then there's the map where you dont fast travel with LMB on campfires, not with RMB, not even with Space, no you do so with "X" of all things... or the fact that you open map with M, but can't close it again with M, only Tab and Escape... absolutely horrendous, no consistency, and unintuitive and needlessly convoluted as hell - The "RPG-ification", from weird "ultimate" abilities that you charge with combat actions that magically give you weapon buffs, chain damage, and other stuff by "bolstering your resolve"; to artificially fluffing the grind by giving every weapon/armor several upgrade levels depending on their rarity; to the completely inflated skill tree where 90% only gives you stat increases rather than actual skills (aside from aforementioned ultimate abilities); to buff foods that arbitrarily increase stats or resistances or stuff like "stealth damage"; to the inventory having infinite space but only being able to have a single stack of each item, and telepathically teleporting any excess to a "personal chest" acting like an ender chest that you can access from any settlement, breaking immersion and completely removing the survival/inventory management aspect that I liked about the first game, and just cluttering the chest with things you never use (no, you can't sell stuff from the chest, only your inventory, so you run back and forth between the chest and merchants to sell any excess you don't need); to the obligatory board game that apparently every game needs nowadays (I'm surprised they didn't add fishing to the game), and so much more I probably can't think of right now- they added an "elaborate" melee system with combos and stuff, and most human enemies now have helmets so stealth-sniping isn't an option anymore, forcing you into melee stealth if you want to avoid combat which I actually like, but most of the time you end up discovered and thus are forced into melee fights, but the melee system feels really clunky to use, the combos aren't really intuitive and different moves don't seem to serve a purpose other than making combat look flashy in clips; enemies can just randomly break out of their stun and instantly turn around to kick you without any warning so you're unable to react, especially if you're mid-animation unable to dodge; you also can't parry, only dodge, and often enemies will just execute hour-long combos that you have to wait until it ends, on top of that you get staggered if you roll more than 3 times... Sony buying Nixxes is the best decision they have made. The reason being is Nixxes is far more articulate with porting games to PC that it will put other AAA studios to shame. The bad news? I don't think Nixxes can help other game development studios, who wanted their PC ports to be polished for their releases.Technically speaking, Horizon Forbidden West had the most stable launch that a PC game could have in the recent years. While there were technical issues with this game, the game is playable and does not suffer from severe game breaking bugs that are so common in PC game releases. Horizon Forbidden West still suffers from a couple of issues here and there, but they are not such a huge deal (at least for me as I have not suffered from a lot of the issues that were reported). Horizon Forbidden West seems to be using a hybrid shader compilation, where it'll compile some shaders during the loading screens, and compile the rest asynchronous in-game. You cannot tell if the shader compilation is happening during in-game, unless you monitor the CPU usage, as the game seems to be very optimised with the async shader compilation process.Graphically, there's no doubt that this game is beautiful. Beautiful, but admittedly demanding. This game punishes your CPU and more importantly, your GPU. Despite this, I can get between 80-120 FPS 4K @ Max Settings with an RTX 4090. There are plenty of FPS drop during the cutscenes, as I am assuming that is because more graphic features are present and/or intensified (e.g., Depth of Field). I do think there is a room of optimisation in this field. Worth to mention that all cutscenes are not Pre-Rendered.Now, the gameplay. This is the one area that I believe that Guerrilla has ruined with the sequel. In Horizon Zero Dawn, the combat and gameplay was pretty good and responsive. In fact, I would frequently engage in combat with difficult machines, and I would not mind if I would die because of the difficulty and Aloy wasn't difficult to control. She was much more controllable and lightweight to control.With Horizon Forbidden West, it's like Aloy had a recent brain damage. She is quite unresponsive, sluggish, and is prone to being ragdolled around. There were many situations where large machines have pummelled Aloy onto the wall or ground, while the camera was facing in an awkward position. And who even thought, adding an RNG to make Aloy trip while dodging was a nice idea?When Aloy get knocked down, she could either do a maneuver to get back up quickly, or will take about 10 full seconds to get back up, resulting in getting damaged again due to the enemy's aggression being ramped up in this game. She can be painfully annoying at times. For the enemies, they have been much more aggressive in HFW. They are much more punishing, which makes playing the game more annoying, when pairing up a brain-dead protagonist, with hyperactive ADHD powered enemies that loves to get physical with Aloy. Enemies are difficult to knockdown, which I do not mind, only if Aloy was not so slow.Another problem with the combat, is the terrain. Unlike the first game, Horizon Forbidden West have a lot of complex terrain and environment, that makes it easy for Aloy to get stuck during combat or the camera could be awkwardly positioned. It is because of this and the slowness of Aloy, that got me killed a couple of times so far. As for the exploration, it is obvious that Guerrilla was inspired by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with the useless collectables and mundane side quests. There is a lot of collectables in this game, but unlike Horizon Zero Dawn, I have no interest in getting these collectables as they are SO BORING TO GET. Some machines are locked behind the story. So, if you want to be an early bird and fight some of these machines for components, you would need to progress onwards in the story. Some of the machines are Stormbird, Dreadwing, etc., and these are usually the machines you need to defeat to upgrade the top-notch equipment.For example; the Relic Ruins. My god, who the ♥♥♥♥ said this was an amazing idea? It's like Guerrilla wanted to pack so much into their game, to the point where they wanted to stick illogical ideas into the game and stick them with a tape. Relic Ruins are a part of a collectable, that consists of platforming puzzles. The annoying part of this is that; there is  ONLY ONE SOLUTION. You have to go through the puzzle linearly (as there is one way to approach the puzzles).It doesn't stop there. Most of the Relic Ruins are powered by a sexy obstacle called "Panels"  that are often locked behind a "numerical password" that you have to find by using your Focus to scan for any important message logs or what not. These panels allow you to go through the doors to get an object to give to someone, who would give you a legendary weapon after providing all of these specific objects to them.The same applies with the side quests and errands, but it is quite important to do them for the skill points (as there are significantly more skills to get). There are a lot of boring side quests and errands that aren't worth your time to go through unless you want to unlock the skills.In Horizon Forbidden West, there are a lot of skills to get. You also get new skill types like Weapon Skills and Valour Surge. Those are typically okay-good, however, they and other normal skills does not make much impact on the fights you have with the machines. With human enemies, the game pretty much forces you to fight them in close combats with your spear. The spear combat and combos are better, but the input to perform certain combos is a bit wonky.Finally, let's talk about the equipment - pouches, weapons, and outfits...Pouches are the same, they require you to hunt for animals, getting their feathers, meat, carcass, etc. That's okay, I got no complaints aside from the rarity items I get from the animals being simply annoying.Now, for the rest. Somehow, the devs decided they want us, the players, to waste our lives on this game. Instead of the weapons and outfits not being upgradeable in Horizon Zero Dawn, and are given to the player with their full potential/capabilities, this game throws that away.How? By introducing upgrades to the weapons and outfits. The problem is; the upgrade requirements are not optimised. It's rubbish, boring, and very grindy. You need to grind as if you have no life, just to upgrade high-tier equipment. This is much more true for legendary weapons and outfits, as you would need obscene amount of machine components.Also, the machine parts are a bit of a ♥♥♥♥ to get. Especially the machine hearts, and a few others, as they have a drop rate. By upgrading the equipment, the stats are improved and locked coils are unlocked (if they were any to begin with).Verdict: While I did enjoy this game a lot for what it has to offer, I can't help to feel annoyed and conclude that this game is very unbalanced. It's not polished unlike Horizon Zero Dawn that was perfect imo.I did find the story to be shorter, than Horizon Zero Dawn. However, there is a lot that can be done to make up for this. I'm not sure if it's just me, but that's how I felt. In Horizon Zero Dawn, the story was longer but lacked the side quests and other things that are more predominant in this game (although HZD was more balanced and fleshed out).My main complaints are the combat. It feels so unpolished compared to Horizon Zero Dawn. Despite this, I would recommend people buying this game for what it has to offer. I cannot wait for what is next for Horizon!

This is such a difficult game to review. There is so much that is excellent about it. But on balance I have spent more time irritated and angry than having fun.It's a wonderful sandbox, and there are amazing options to tailor the experience, but frustration is constant. It feels like trying to enjoy yourself while the developers constantly interrupt and undermine you. None of it is related to difficulty, but rather to enemy behaviour and the systems of combat. Enemies that psychically dodge and move based on where you aim, even from stealth. Enemies that move too fast to hit even in slow motion. Weakspots that are microscopic, that give only the mildest damage improvement when hit. A recovery animation that feels years long. Enemy AI that only makes sense if you take into account the fact it's cheating. The absolute worst point against the game is, by far, the story. There is nothing as infuriating as characters making deeply stupid decisions when we have to live with the consequences. Plot beats are so obvious you find yourself banging you head against the wall during cutscenes. By the end I resorted to skipping them, and trying not to be too demoralised by the painfully idiotic cliff notes. Plot twists may as well be marked with giant neon signs, erected three hours beforehand. Enemies you want dead dance around in front of you during cutscenes then escape through laughable plot contrivance. Character deaths may as well be foreshadowed with long speeches about being two days from retirement.  A wonderful sandbox spoiled by bad design decisions and simplistic writing. Not as easy to dismiss as a true bad game. It's greatness, but soaked through with mild poison. Over time you just end up getting sick.

Forbidden West suffers a bit from middle installment syndrome. The first game had a focused and coherent story, with well-paced, incremental revelations of what the heck is going on and of Aloy's origins. Aloy's character arc was especially well-drawn, I think.This game is necessarily less focused. It has more ground to cover, narratively, though to less overall effect. For one thing, the key revelations don't have anything near the same punch as the revelations in Horizon Zero Dawn.The middle part of the game is a too-familiar three-extended-fetch-quests structure, though at least those quests are interestingly varied and bring their own revelations and interesting set-pieces (like the bit underneath the ruins of Las Vegas.)Some of the narrative mechanics have become more erratic, too. The brain/heart/fist dialogue options which were peppered through HZD show up only very occasionally in HFW, and don't show up at all when you might think they should.Also, HFW makes (so far as I've seen) only one attempt to the player the chance to make a consequential choice (regarding the Desert Clan of the Tenakth), though its consequences are really only very slight. Where there are really consequential decisions to be made the story is entirely on rails again.Aloy does have something of a character arc, here, though it is less focused and coherent than it was in HZD.Still, as a whole, I've found the game pretty enjoyable, and it's actually a lot of fun to learn to take down robot animals more efficiently.

Horizon Forbidden West makes a number of changes to the formula, similar to some sequels like Borderlands 2, the game retains the spirit of the original, but completely changes the feel. So much that adjusting from HZD can be extremely difficult at first as the changes to mechanics, and new mechanics take some getting used to.Some changes to the formula are really good: being able to dye your armour. Apply facepaints (if that's your thing). Apply other armour looks to the armour you want without losing the stats of the good armour. The shieldwing glider was a great addition (although it does mostly completely take away tension from climbing sections, since falling has little consequence aside from time lost). The grappeling hook adds a lot to the movement toolkit. New interesting mounts have been added (especially the new flying mount that you unlock late in the game.). New weapon and ammo types allow for new strategies. And a whole bunch of new enemies and enemy variants fill the maps.Now we get to the bad stuff:... Aloy has been nerfed SIGNIFICANTLY. Her movement speed has reduced, her recovery time has increased, she now has a host of new debuffs applicable, her dodge roll has been greatly reduced (to the point where the devs had to introduce I-frames to it and some other moves just to make the game playable). Climbing mechanics became more complicated (which creates more times when Aloy simply will not do what you want her to do, between refusing to climb on certain things, to moving in a different direction to where you are intending). These problems also extend to moving around the world (Aloy frequently gets stuck on terrain, which can result in stunlock when fighting enemies, her slowdown has increased so when she tries to shed speed, she often overshoots which can result in unintentionally running off ledges, especially in ruins). The new shieldwing often disables prematurely if you get close to, but not touch geometry while falling (This can cause huge damage or instant death if you cannot redeploy it in time). Having an abundance of weapons does have a downside, it can be difficult to find the right weapon for you, and even harder to find good coils for it (stat increase items). Hacking machines, which was a staple of the first game has been basically ruined, with the exception of mounts (the only class in the game that remain permanently hacked), as every hacked unit only stays hacked for a very short period of time, I really do not understand the reason for this, they already added Apex and corrupted units (unhackable units), so we can have situations where we can't break the game balance. Some enemies do not make a return (For some this makes sense; the Sawtooth was just a worse ravager, the Deathbringer didn't really have a place, both the Strider and Broadhead were too similar to the charger so they were scrapped, the trampler has had a lot of its mechanics given to other new machines, but I was genuinely surprised that they removed the watcher from the game (its literally the mascot of the first game and its the perfect tutorial enemy, easy to understand and defeat, however they did bring back the red eye variant much later in the game). The under water sections are just annoying, they are forced stealth sections where you are completely helpless (you cant even use your spear for some reason), they drag on, are disorienting, and generally just not fun to play, plus until you get a certain piece of equipment from a certain quest, most underwater sections are actually impossible to play.Now given the wall of text on bad things this game has, you'd probably think my overall review of the game would be negative. But no, the game is good, its fun, the world building is still top tier, the characters are mostly well written. And despite everything I absolutely recommend the game. It has some really good moments throughout, the ending is really good. And aside from the negatives above, and the amount of mid game grind, there is little to fault the game on.

Only play this game if you have already played Horizon: Zero Dawn for two reasons:1. You will understand what's going on much better. While the story is explained briefly here, it is nowhere near as in depth as playing the first game, and honestly, the experience of figuring out the story of the first game is absolutely worth it. If you have even a slight interest in good storytelling in games, don't even launch this game until you have beaten the first one.2. Horizon: Zero Dawn is a great game itself. The game play experience the first game offers is like nothing I have ever really experienced before, and it is easily one of my all time favorite games.If you have played Horizon: Zero Dawn, then you absolutely need to play this game as well. This game takes everything the first game does, and does it better. New machines, improved and new mechanics, including a glider, grappling hook, and a lot more upgrades, better inventory management, which makes exploring a lot more fun, and a great story that does an excellent job at continuing where Horizon: Zero Dawn left off. While $60 is certainly a hefty price, it is totally worth it. The amount of content you get is incredible. I've currently played the game for about 36 hours, and have just completed the second major story milestone in the game, with there being at LEAST 4 more. All of the side quests are interesting, and even the fetch quests don't feel bad to do since they give you an excuse to run around the incredibly immersive world the developers have created. Speaking of which, the graphics and lighting are just as beautiful, if not more so, than the first game. The world itself is packed with things to do, from machines to fight, to side quests to complete, to ruins to loot and collectibles to grab. The in-world lore items found with the focus do a great job at expanding on the world building set in the first game, and they are everywhere. It is painstakingly clear that the developers of this game placed every rock by hand, and left nothing up to chance when creating the world. Finally, the music is incredible. As an aspiring video game composer, I can confidently say that this music is some of the most touching music I have ever heard. I am constantly getting goosebumps from the beautiful sounds the composer brings out. The battle music is upbeat, doing a great job at combining the sounds of flutes, hand drums, and other early instruments with more mechanical sounding synths, perfectly representing the intertwining of the machines with the less technologically advanced civilizations that have settled the Earth. A good game with a continuation of the first's great story, characters, and world/lore but with some caveats I've noticed while playing. This is just a critique of what I think are the game's weaknesses but I still enjoy it and recommend it as a whole. Several aspects of FW's gameplay mechanics are, for lack of a better way of putting it, outdated. The focus on crafting, RPG stat elements, over-abundance of worthless loot, etc are all stale and tired mechanics that hold this game back. I read in another review that someone recommended turning the combat difficulty down so you don't have to worry as much about build optimisation and loot quality and I've found that does indeed make the game more enjoyable. Taking a detour away from a super important story quest to kill some random machines or wild animals to improve basic gear was a complaint people had with the first game and it continues here, if not even moreso. Horizon takes too many notes from other loot-choked games like Assassin's Creed instead of forging its own path. My inventory and stash are an overflowing mountain of random crap that I have no idea the function of and I frankly couldn't care less. Turning down the difficulty a smidge so I can focus on other things has helped. The beautiful world and story are FW's biggest strengths and these mechanics are bloat that weigh it downCombat remains good and felling machines feels as satisfying as the first game, although I found some of the new machine designs difficult to parse. If it wasn't for the massive glowing weakspots I would have no idea what does what. They range from being mildly obtuse to being absolute fusterclucks of greeble and particle effects that I can't even tell what animal they're supposed to emulate or what. There are not enough visual cues to tell, at a glance, what part of a machine is important or a possible threat. And no, stopping mid-fight to read a machine's user manual in your notebook is not a good alternative. Additionally, Cauldrons also share this issue and are a visually incomprehensible mess. More than once I've had to look at a tutorial just to figure out what the hell I was looking for. I know they are, as per the lore, not supposed to be human-inhabitable places but this is a human-playable game and it still matters.Climbing/parkour has been improved and Aloy can scale a lot more than she could in the first game. Most rocky surfaces can be climbed (with or without visual assist from the Focus) or you can bunnyhop your way up in many cases. There is still quite a lot of jank though, as it is difficult to tell when Aloy will snap onto a climbable object or sail right past it. I have failed a lot of jumps because there was no indication if Aloy was going to attach to the thing I was jumping towards and I wasn't close enough by a few centimetres.The game also needs a bug squishing pass... or 3. I haven't had any issues with essential quests yet but I have encountered several side quests that required a save reload or I had to walk away from entirely because they are impassable. I have also had Aloy get stuck in walls or under objects and have had to reload for those too. Also a few strange visual bugs like physics objects on Aloy's outfit twitching and flapping erratically.Lastly, and this is a minor quibble, but way too many quest have an annoying "twist" to them. It would be nice to have more quests where Aloy goes to a location to do something and just does it instead of needing to do extra busywork like rescuing someone, tracking a machine, doing an additional quest chain, etc. Sometimes it makes story sense but sometimes I can tell it was done to pad length and it can be quite tedious. This could perhaps be included in the game having tired, outdated design choices as other games of this genre have done this too.

As every single person in the review page has already said this game might actually be ground breaking from the technical perspective but I want to focus more on the world and the actual narrative of the story.Starting with the negatives I was disappointed with how unrewarding it felt to explore the world outside of the mission areas. Some places where rich with history and didn't necessarily need any more text logs to understand what happened or who was involved but it was nice to know that there were actual people living in those horrific times. Other places felt empty and as if there was alot missing there just to end up learning that those locations were either side or main mission areas with nothing to find there unless you have a specific mission active/unlocked. I got to say that it felt like the only good reward you can get after exploring areas that are not specifically marked on the mad, was greenshine. Even though it says that you'll need it in the later game, I barely used any of it so I felt like I was collecting resources just to have my stash full of it.I enjoyed the story but I do wish that some characters that were very interesting and had alot of history behind them would be more important to the plot.The ending of the main is the main thing that really stuck out for me. Again comparing to Zero Dawn, after defeating Hades we had a whole emotional scene with Elisabeth which gave me some breathing room to feel like the antagonist has been defeated and now the main character can relax for at least a few hours before revealing that Sylens is up to something again. In Horizon Forbidden West the ending doesn't really give that satisfaction but instead goes straight into "oh yeah we gon make a third game, deal with it" mode. Besides that everything else in the game was truly an amazing experience. Combat was fluent, bugs were nonexistent and the cutscenes felt so realistic that you start to think that those are actual people speaking to each other. Characters somehow felt like they were in-depth than in the first game, everyone had history, everyone had their own culture and that culture was truly unique.Overall - good game, me like, recommend.

Definitely some of the best content to come out of the triple-a sphere in a loooong time.Most of the technical issues I can forgive, both for the hardware quirks as a result of this being a ps5 port, and from seeing what it's able to pull off while keeping a consistent frame rate (shoutouts to burning shores). I have an i5 11400f/3080 and kept a modest ~70-130 fps depending on how complex the current area was with everything on low/medium (definitely think I was cpu bottlenecked tho).Gameplay-wise its HZD but more developed. You have far more variety in weapon and elemental types, ults and stamina-based skills are now present, far more things to choose from as consumables in your hotbar, etc. I do have a few complaints regarding combat and such, but keep in mind this is without me restating everything I liked about HZD, so if it seems negative it's mostly because there's not a ton to say; it's good for the same reasons HZD's combat was. These are moreso things I hope get tweaked or addressed in potential future content. I also played on hard for the duration of the game since difficulty might affect some of the things I'll mention. This isn't so much a review to inform a buying decision as it is just me critiquing what I played. I enjoyed this game.-The quantity of items you can have on the hotbar gets dangerously tedious sometimes. There's something like 20-30 items you'll have the ability to equip to a hotbar and cycle through, and it can be tough to figure out which ones to take. Top-tier traps are expensive, but mid-tier may not do enough late-game. Not all elements are available as traps or spear canisters, meaning you'll want a couple of both. Do you take shields and such with you, etc. Equipping everything and cycling through it every time has definitely gotten me killed a few times, and getting in that tedium range is fairly easy. By the end of the game i think I only had around a quarter or so of my options equipped, which sometimes didn't feel in the spirit of Horizon's "use everything" gameplay loop. A few more buttons to use items from, or even just a simpler way of managing hotbar slots would have been nice.-Heavy weapons felt effectively useless. Between long pickup animations, dropping them when dodging, and the lack of especially significant stagger on enemies unless you can get a good sustained fire going, they often felt more detrimental to pick up. The only real exceptions to this imo were the explosive weapons like thunderjaw disc launchers and clawstrider bomb launchers. I appreciate heavy enemy stealth strikes no longer being tied to a skill, though. I think they reduced ammo quantities for them as well, but I don't feel like it really mattered, and I like that more machines have more quantities of useable weapons.-Most machines don't have an animation of them dodging away from you. HFW feels a bit more soulsy than HZD. There's a new "stumble after three dodges" mechanic, and an incentive to keep some machine parts intact to loot resources from, giving machines a wider moveset. Components feel harder to take off even with tearblast arrows, and cansiters now often have armor of their own. There's a lot of machines with very soulsy feeling melee combos with specific dodge patterns. I love this, it puts more emphasis on genuinely learning machine movesets and not just blasting off every component and moving on, and I like that it's not just a copy of souls and has its own identity (consistent dodge quantities over stamina bars, far more directionality in dodging with sweeping lasers and combos that can only really be avoided by dodging underneath and away, etc.) It can, however, lead to some issues with machines getting a bit stuck on top of you. In HZD, you could usually just pick a direction and spam dodge until you were clear, in souls, bosses of all sizes often have one or more moves where they put distance between you and somewhat reset their position in the arena, which isn't especially present here outside of flying enemies. It can make for a few unfair-feeling deaths where you can't really see what's going on and only realize once you die and the camera zooms out that you were pinned against a wall, but I ultimately prefer the direction they took. There's a lot of potential ways to address this, from nerfing armor stats and making component tear a bit easier, to increasing dodge capacity, but I feel the "get off me" animation is the simplest practical fix.-Animations feel a bit more unstable than HZD. As with that game, everything here is reliable. You won't find yourself missing a stealth strike or getting stuck in terrain, but there's a point where it gets a little immersion-breaking. Out of all the stealth strikes I've performed in this game, I'd wager to say less than half of them saw my spear actually making contact with the enemy. Machines can get a bit jittery on uneven terrain, which can make hitting shots weird, too.-Potion capacity felt too small. Entirely possible this is just a skill issue, but while I found the concept of a much more limited potion capacity really neat, in practice it usually just meant me using exclusively cleanse potions and large health potions. Overdraw and stamina potions just didn't feel useful enough to sacrifice a slot.-Upgrading started feeling pretty grindy late-game. Pretty self-explanatory, I feel like the costs for some of the later upgrades should have been toned down a bit. Even with my obsession with making sure every machine I took on saw its upgrade-relevant parts harvested, I rarely had enough on hand to casually upgrade anything. It was always a dedicated effort to find the parts I needed, which got tiring fast. In the end I beat burning shores with a barely half-upgraded purple outfit, and an even number of purple and blue weapons, with only the blues fully upgraded. It's honestly for that reason I've avoided touching on damage and health bars since I think that's precisely why things started to feel really spongy and deadly near the end, but I just wasn't that interested in hunting upwards of 30 to 40 individual machines to fully upgrade everything I had equipped or wanted to use, and that's just to fill six slots. Getting all elements covered and multiple outfits probably would have been more.Again I'd like to restate that not only did I enjoy this game, but I definitely think it's superior to HZD. I'm hoping these little nitpicks and such get addressed in the next game, because I'm pretty sure the game would be a quick 10/10 for me then. Loved my time in this game.

I played this mostly because a) I came in interested and b) my partner became Really interested as she watched me play, which is of course the single most potent motivation for an adult gamer to binge a title.I have to say, this is the most impressive game I've ever encountered. Taking the crown from games like Witcher 3 and maybe TWWH2, what Guerrilla have done here is really hard to describe.The detail, the scale, the scope, the content, the characters, the variation, the gameplay, the combat, the difficulty, the depth, the controls... It's all top of the range. High class, high polish, high ambition, high execution. Console warriors managed to make this game essentially a 50-50 deal with regards to how loved it is, but it's total BS and I hope the PC version can allow non-PS users to see how damn good this game is.I wasn't prepared to give up entire months of my life to this game, so I passed over all side content except what I needed to get to main quest recommended levels (which usually worked out as being the story-relevant quests of the side characters, or the cauldrons which are highly profitable time sinks) so that means one day I'll be able to drop back into the world and go find any of hundreds of side quests - all of the ones I've actually completed having been pretty unique and worthwhile - to explore.Early on you complete the opening area and are presented with an inviting gate out into the new zones, but if you hold off a bit and talk to a green question mark nearby you'll save a man from execution, track down remnants of the baddies from the first game and, later on, wipe out their tenuous presence in the new lands - a delicious full stop for the pricks who rained on your parade at the start of the first game.The main story, however, can carry this game on its own - it is long, twisting, full of intrigue and wonder, with excellent, hackle-raising villains and viscerally satisfying triumphs alongside memorable allies - in the face of genuine mechanical difficulty. Characters, old and new, are excellently balanced and very well written. Factions are distinctive and easy to root for and against.Other good things. The fast travel system is acceptable. Go anywhere you've been before from campfires, or burn a travel pack thing for a random one. You'll still have to go on - and I can't overstate this - epic journeys many times in pursuit of the ending. The music is epic but not overly intrusive, and nicely various. The graphics are exceptional, in a game this giant a few areas are bound to be slightly lower res, but the body of work that the game artists have put into what you're exploring subsumes even these moments to a wider, wondrous whole.There are areas to question - nathan drake-style parkour for all? I didn't ask for this. Ways to boost your character's combat expertise and make fighting less repetitive? Hard to parse until you've accidentally overlooked them for a few hours. Aloy's schtick starts off tiresome, to the point that most of the plot is at least in part a process of almost literally locking her in a room with her friends and being prodded to actually be friendly to them.But these are all very nitty nit picks. The kinda things that occur to you every 8 or 10 hours of gameplay after you've been distracted from the great content you're consuming.Are games ever worth the full price? Well, after playing this one I think I must say that they CAN be worth it, but the bar has been set pretty high.9.5/10

Incredibly well optimised with a good selection of settings to tweak based on your hardware. Visually it's one of the best looking games available to date, with stellar facial animations and full mo-capped dialogue sequences. Landscapes and weather effects are wonderful, environments are varied and detailed, it's hard to fault the game both visually and technically. Sound design too is superb, with great use of spacial audio and excellent mixing, machine (enemy) sounds are gritty and attack sfx help make abilities feel like there is weight behind them There is a fairly engaging collectables mini game in the form of 'Machine Strike', think Chess but with more unit specific abilities and environmental tiles. It's up there with Gwent, although it lacks some feedback polish, collecting and adding to your unit roster is a nice side activity.Combat is a big step up from the original title, the enemy roster is massively improved, larger and contains many more variants for each machine. Melee combat has been tweaked and overall feels tighter. The terrible floaty feeling of ranged combat is gone, and the new bows feels far punchier.The inclusion of weapon specific abilities and special attacks help round out the combat which all and all is a big step up from HZD. There are some usual open world traits such as map collectables that I expect will start to feel like busy work after a while but so far each of these have been tied into narratives that keep them interesting enough. There is machine strike, fighting arena's, hidden caves and dungeons, enemy bases, towers, puzzles etc. If you enjoy side activities you will have your hands full.Voice acting is also very well done. Armour design, enemy design are all excellent. The main story narrative has been enjoyable so far, impressive set pieces and surprisingly well written dialogues with interesting characters but as I have not completed the main quest I can't say how this holds up later on. Overall this is a solid port, a really well done experience. Take note Capcom.

Sometimes she even offers you advice on how to solve a problem that you have literally already solved. "Maybe you should shoot the antennas off those scroungers" she suggests, while you are literally at that moment holding the freshly shot-off antennas in your very hands. The whole time you are taking out a bandit stronghold, she keeps saying, "I need to take care of these bandits" every 30 seconds, even though that is exactly what you are doing in the entire scenario.Sometimes she will even tell you things that are patently false, like telling you that you failed to shoot a particular part off of a machine when you are in the act of picking up the part that you did in fact shoot off. Having just finished the main campaign after 75hrs i figured i'd write a short review.My rig is: i7 13700k, TRX 4090, 64GB RAM, game run off of a fast 7GB/s NVMe drive, 2560x1440 monitor. Played using keyboard and mouse.Technical stuff:The game runs like butter with all the bells and whistles on, loads up very quickly especially after fast travel. We are talking 3 or 4 seconds most of the time on fast travel. I have had no bugs, no crashes, no floating textures/items as I have seen some reports of when it first came out. This is a fantastic console to PC port on the performance front.It looks amazing and the fact that you can see any changes you make happen live on the graphics menu screen is they way every game should be. There is a bit of pop in at long distances when flying with standby models updating to the full detail ones but there is zero pop in when on the ground.This super detail can, at times, make the screen look a bit 'busy' and could be distracting, but it is rather realistic no matter what.The menus are excellent, easy to navigate, informative and allow for full key rebinding. It also shows in the list any conflicts so you don't spend ages trying to find what else is bound to the key you just used.nixxes have done a brilliant job.GameplayIf you liked Zero Dawn you will like Forbidden West. They have expanded the melee combat from just light/heavy attacks to include combos, specials and power attacks. No parry or block though. Well, not for Aloy...the human enemies get to block! MELEE COMBAT WHINGE:: Personally i hate combos and timed strikes etc. especially when the timing indicators are a subtle glow appearing on the spear and  quiet 'bing' in the middle of a fight. Combos with pauses where the pause length indicators are the glow/bing make the game way less fun for me especially when lots of the enemy attacks knock Aloy off her feet where she takes what feels like half an hour to get to her feet. You WILL find yourself stun locked and flung around like a rag doll against the bigger mobs. The ranged combat is just as good as it was, by far and away my favourite part of the game!The open world is fun to explore, as it was in the first game and although the climbing is slightly more 'free' than in ZD the fact that not everything is climbable is very disappointing. You can scan with your focus to see what things you can climb (they get yellow lines and crosses on them). You can even put this on permanently but there are just too many places that look identical to climbable places that you can not climb! You get the yellow pained bits on buildings but you can't climb the walls or scaffolding or statues or trees. Only the rocks the devs said you could climb. It should have been more like Assassins Creed: Odyssey to enhance the fun. You can still cheese some none climbable bits by jumping like a madman but come on, let us climb the rock that is identical to the one we can climb but you didn't tick climb=true.You have a glider vis a vis breath of the wild which does add some enjoyment but it does seem to be artificially limited to glide rate in certain places aka you get a waaay bigger than you would expect vertical drop rate so you can't go as far horizontally as you'd expect to. Plus it handles like you are drunk if you try to do anything but straight and level flight!You have a huge selection of weapons and armour which can be upgraded though 'crafting' and adding booster coils (like +5% to impact damage etc). This is where i both love and hate the game. I like the idea of upgrading for better protection or more damage or more coil slots etc but it is the GRIND to get the damn reagents that make this a huge pain at times. An upgraded blue may be significantly better that the stock purple you just bought.....grinding time!! Just let a blacksmith upgrade them for shards ffs! (note: you can make a 'job' to locate the drops for the next upgrade level on the map but only the next level and you can only make the job at a crafting table)Some of the best weapons and armour (legendary 5 upgrades required!) are locked behind the arena (enforced machine combat in  a small arena so something I really don't like to do as I prefer ranged stealth so I never even bothered to try this) or combat pits where you fight human enemies (again, something I didn't bother with as I really dislike the melee combat).The hunting grounds are still there and just as annoying as they were in ZD but now they also have mounted races! These look so awful I wouldn't touch them with a barge pole as the mount handling is terrible!The story line is quite a good one. It was always going to struggle when judged against ZD as that was an excellent exploration of what was happening and why. But it holds its own for the most part. The end is a bit weak compared to the build up but it does set up a 3rd game quite well. There are loads of side quests, errands, salvage contracts etc. I still had loads to do when I decided to start the final quest at 73 hrs. They are varied enough and a lot of them link together into some nice story chains. I'd say I could have passed the 100hr mark easily if i'd wanted to.All in all i can recommend H:FW.TL:DR+great port+lots of quests+enhanced melee combat options+looks beautiful+key bind heaven-crafting weapon/armour upgrades as a grind-melee combat sucks-climbing artificially limited-can be stun locked by bigger mobs-mount races/hunting grounds/arena limit access to some weapons/armour

A technical behemoth, forbidden west is ambitious at every thing it tries to do and is flawless in virtually every aspect. Do you want a good story, with rich lore, interesting characters and beautiful fantastical places to visit? You got it. Do you want to skip the lore  and just have fun with the main story? You got it. Do you want to exhaust not only the main story but side quests and world activities? Forbidden West got you covered with quality side content that feels just as good as the main stuff... Do you want variety of weapons, mechanics and enemies? Horizon has it all. I have never played any other game that is so technically perfect in every aspect I can think of... Not only that, but the game is fun as hell. I played it on the ps5 and have been dreaming ever since to play it on pc on native 4k and 120 fps. My dreams has come true. What a masterpiece.The game also runs very well. Nixxes did a great job again.Tips: use a dualsense controller if you play with a controller, but also use with a cable to have its full functionality. In the settings, select auto pick up and thank me later.Avoid using fast travel, as the world is filled with interesting activities and they are usually very rewarding. Don't start a quest that's above your level. I recommend at least 2 points above the recommended level... Doing so will be easy, though, as there are plenty of activities for you to chose from. Try out a few, pick your favorites and go for it.Have a different arsenal of weapons. I know it might be tempting to just use bow and arrow because some of weapons take a while getting used to, but trust me, mastering those weapons will be the difference between fighting a boss for 3 hours or 10 minutes, I'm not even kidding. Overall another amazing game in the series. Everything that was great about the first is in this one and often expanded upon like new weapons, "special" items, transmog, and even a flying mount. Really the only big issue here because most other things are either minor/optional but this is unavoidable and a constant annoyance. They added too many different weapons and armor that need upgrading often just to unlock an ammo type. This is just bad design to artificially inflate game time with grind and it's just not needed with how much content is already in the game including a NG+ and DLCGauntlet races. The horse races they added are awful. Just awful. Easily the worst part of this game. Way too much rubberbanding. It's not a race so much as "beat the ♥♥♥♥ outta the other people while mashing shift and hoping you cross the finish first".Machine strike. It's not as bad as gauntlet racing but suffers from the same bloat as the rest of the game and it's made worse by the fact that there are many mechanics that are never explained. If you're going to make an in-depth minigame, you have to give me the tools to play it properly.Parkour. It's still a mess a lot of the time, especially with keyboard and mouse. It's serviceable but they lean on it hard in some segments and the controls are clunky and sometimes outright buggy.Melee combat. They added all these cool new combos and even a pit fighting activity but melee is still just not viable in the game when you're getting flanked by 5 different machines that will break any combo you try to start. Some of the new stuff works well in tandem with bow attacks but melee itself is still just meh.Mounts. They will too often get themselves killed and force me to go get another. Just let us dismiss them. Also the controls for ground mounts are still pretty bad and they get caught on every little pebble. And I'll never forgive them for adding a friggin' velociraptor mount that tops out at 8 mph. It literally has "velocity" in the name, guys. Writing. Some of the dialogue is immersion killing. It's often pretty good (if cliche and predictable), but having a tribal warrior in the post-apocalypse say he wants to find his dead comrades to "bag and tag them"? What bag? What tag? Just bad writing at times.Environmental "puzzles". More a comment on this kind of game design but they are prevalent in ZD and FW and I hate them. A puzzle is something that requires logic, critical thinking, and often spatial reasoning to solve a problem (Baba is You is an amazing example if you actually want PUZZLES). A game should not try to emulate the feeling of looking for your car keys but this one does it constantly. There's some decent puzzles in this game but way too many consist of you knowing exactly what to do within 30 seconds but spending 5-10 minutes looking for the tool you need.Overall, still a great game. Like the first game, probably in my top 10-15 games in recent history but I feel like they went a little too far into "quantity over quality" and it shows in a lot of the little things. Everyone should play this game at some point so you can be equally annoyed by the issues and amazed by all the great parts.
