As someone who LOVED Zero Dawn on the PS4, I actually bought a PS5 with Forbidden west bundled with it because I just couldn't wait 2 years for a PC  release. This was a HUGE mistake. of course -- I don't think I played this on PS5 for more than 2 hours before giving up on it. While the PS5's performance mode I'd guess top out at 720 to 1080p fsr upscaling at 60fps, -- a terrible look for my living room oled, and since it's not the 1980s anymore I refuse to play games at 30 fps. This new PC port by Nixxes, on the other hand, hits 115 to 160 fps easily (on my 4090, so, take that with a grain of salt and keep expectations in check) with DLAA enabled on my 1440P IPS monitor (that's NOT DLSS upscaling BTW, just DLAA) and with every graphics settings maxed (except for motion blur, depth of field, chromatic abberation, bloom, or lense flare, because Forbidden West is a videogame and was not filmed on video equipment for the cinema, Now, Granted I've got a decent rig -- a 4090 and a 5800x3d, but even if I were limited to 60fps at 1080, the mouse aiming and higher FOV ALONE, not to mention the DLSS upscaling, would make it more than worth it,  So if you've got at least, say, an r5 r5600x and a card with 8gb of videoram, the same should run well enough to justify purchasing it over the PS5 version, if only for the QOL improvements. FW on PC might just be one the best looking (and best feeling to play) video games I've ever played. The higher FOV, raw mouse input (that I was able to set to my preferred 360/cm sensitivity for both aim and camera mode within less than ten minutes -- which, if you're a mouse and keyboard nerd like and you've been using the same sense in Counterstrike, Valorant, and every other FPS for decades now, you know how important that is. On top of that, no cashes, fast loading, and not a single stutter or egregious frametime drop to speak of. There's a short shader comp now and then, but otherwise, it's smooth as butter. On top of that, despite using Frame Generation, a long as I force my refresh rate to a few FPS below my monitor's refresh rate in NVCP and enable Gysnc, along with Ultra Low Latency mode, plus reflex + boost in gamer, latency is  a non issue. I know Frame Gen gets a lot of hate, but I'd recommend trying it -- worst that'll happen is you'll turn it back off if you hate it. I tried both, measured a good ten or so extra milliseconds, (comparable to the 16.6ms you'd get at 60 fps, though sometimes dipping into the single digits-- if you've got a good VRR display, the consistency is MORE than fine,) And I mean, it's for a single game that's already running at in the low to mid 100 FPS, at 4k with DLAA, maxed graphics -- and we're still talking less than 40ms, MAX. This isn't counterstrike and valorant, and IMO, the graphics tadeoff is worth it. But if you'd prefer to go without FG, the game easily hits 165+ fps on a 4090 at DLSS quality -- with, as far as I measured, about less than 15 ms latency. I'm not lucky enough to own an ultrawide 1440p Oled PC display, sadly -- still rocking that IPS panel, but according to Digital Foundry and several others it's an even bigger visual treat. Even with it though, I don't think I can name many other current AAA titles on PC that look as gorgeous as this one. Maybe not on a technical level, but the Decima Engine's put to good use when it comes to the art direction. It makes Death Stranding and Zero Dawn ACTUALLY look last-gen, something that's not seen often this generation of gaming, Anyways, I digress. If you like open world adventures, especially ones with that gorgeous Decima Engine aesthetic, and if aiming/doging/setting traps/explpoiting enemy weakspots, twitch-style aiming at enemy weakspots (which the console version will always sadly lack), exploring caves, mountains, forests, and labs full of ancient technology, then you'll love this game. If you've ever dreamt of fighting robot dinosaurs, of course, this is your chance to finally live that dream. That being said, It's not a game for EVERYONE -- for me, though it's 10/10. And I haven't given a game a 10/10 since Resident Evil 4 Remake -- which, if you've played, should tell you enough about whether or not you'll agree with my review or not.  Before that it was probably Neon White (which is an underrated gem and if you like shooters, you owe it to yourself to play it.) Maybe Doom Eternal or Metro Exodus before that.

Navigating the middle ground between negativity and positivity on the Steam platform has long been a vexing challenge for me, especially as a fervent Steam reviewer. Among the myriad games I've delved into, none have exemplified this struggle more than Horizon Forbidden West.At its core, the game shines with substantial new content, doubling the offerings of its predecessor. The introduction of aerial mounts for traversal and a range of new combat abilities add a touch of excitement, despite some flaws in their execution. Moreover, the sequel boasts a stunning visual upgrade—character models are impeccably sharp, environments are rich in detail, and the overall graphical fidelity rivals that of Hollywood productions.However, these advancements are overshadowed by significant drawbacks that mar the experience, at times rendering it frustratingly close to unplayable. Chief among these issues is the persistently problematic camera during combat, an oversight carried over from the first installment that remains unaddressed. Combat encounters are marred by the camera getting stucked on walls, terrain, or even fixated awkwardly on the sky, disrupting crucial gameplay moments. Moreover, the quest design suffers from excessive bloat and convolution. Questlines often meander through a labyrinth of tangents—whether blocked paths, locked doors, environmental hazards, or fetch quests that feel uninspired and repetitive. While there's no shortage of side quests, most feel like filler content with characters lacking depth or significance. Only a handful manage to engage and resonate, while the rest blur together in a tedious cycle of formulaic tasks.Horizon Forbidden West's new skill tree system is imbalanced and slightly pointless horizon forbidden west, you barely have to make tough decisions on which skill tree to max out, because you get almost all the necessary skill points to upgrade every skill tree. While it undeniably elevates the franchise with enhanced visuals and expanded content, these strides are undermined by persistent quality-of-life issues, lackluster quest design, and other critical shortcomings. Horizon Forbidden West builds on the amazing mechanics and gameplay that we saw with Horizon Zero Dawn. The good:- Improved climbing mechanics so now you can free-climb on a lot more surfaces than with the last game. This was one of my biggest complaints with Zero Dawn. It's better but not completely bug-free and still far from perfect. - Much better movement and maneuverability, with exciting new items that open up entirely new ways of traversal in the open world and in combat. - Super rich story-telling, with meaningful side quests that leave you wanting to go for a 100% completion. - Improvements to crafting - if you are stuck trying to find that one elusive resource to craft an important upgrade for your bow, just keep playing through and eventually you will find some vendor somewhere in the open world that sells precisely the resource you need. - Improved skills. The skills in Forbidden West have better progression and allow more customization to play style.The bad:- As of writing this review, the game is still buggy. You will find yourself in situations where a machine you killed falls and creates a barrier between you and something you needed to pick up to progress your quest far too many times, requiring you to restart the game from a save to reset the machine's position. - The game will get stuck loading shaders occasionally causing the game to completely crash in the middle of gameplay. - The chess-like machine strike mini-game they added to Forbidden West is bland and even after spending enough time to become a master player, the rewards seem bleak and you will probably find yourself just ignoring this mini-game completely. - Collectibles are challenging and time consuming to acquire, with most requiring equipment that you wouldn't even get until you are almost done with the main story. Even with that the rewards for getting these collectibles are pennies in shards, and you wouldn't see anything meaningful until you complete entire sets. With all that said, it is definitely a game I would highly recommend for the amazing RPG that it is. You will constantly find yourself wanting to uncover the next chapter of Aloy's story and you will actually end up wanting to listen to every dialogue rather skip through. The puzzles are more challenging and also more fun; the quests are way less repetitive and actually seem quite diverse. Even the most repetitive quests like "Climb the tallneck" from Zero Dawn are actually completely different with each tallneck in Forbidden West. If you've played Zero Dawn, the storyline builds extremely well from where it left off. If you haven't, then I do recommend playing that first, but the game does try to give you conversation opportunities to recap what happened in Zero Dawn from time to time if you haven't played it.

Spoiler-Free review!Continuing on from the state Zero Dawn left the world, Horizon Forbidden West takes place immediately after the first game's ending. Horizon Forbidden West (HFW) is a great game, and one of the few great sci-fi series that I would say has high quality of a novel.ENVIRONMENT: First of all it's beautiful, just like Zero Dawn was. The environmental storytelling is turned up even more in this game, with much more ruins from the old world. I appreciate this as they expertly show the passage of time and decay. Really, this game shows the decay of buildings and objects better than anything else I've seen; it's so interesting to look at, and emotionally evocative to see what was and is.MUSIC: The music is so SOO good in this game, it brought out my emotions continuously. Ambient music evokes a sense of place, calm, and peace, in some areas the loss of what once was, and other varied themes. Powerful enemies also have their own exciting and powerful battle themes.DLC: The DLC, Burning Shores, adds a good amount of content, music, and culminates in something I was not expecting, that's so SOO good!The game is great. Keep that in mind for the next section.WANTED IMPROVEMENTS: I like HFW and recommend it, and will describe in detail some things that I hope can be improved for the next game, in this series that I love so much. There's only a few things I don't like about HFW, and they have to do with combat.Getting Slammed Around: My number one peeve with this game is how much it knocks down Aloy. Enemies hit very hard, quickly, and often, with attacks that are a mix of dodgeable and undodgeable. They put Aloy on the ground a LOT, taking control away from the player, and it's extremely frustrating. When enemies group up, you're on the ground getting attacked, and can't do anything but get knocked down, and hope you have enough healing berries to tank it. When in these battle situations, health potions are hit or miss if they can be activated while getting slammed around. Part of the problem is hitboxes. I've had arrows go right through enemies, but enemies can hit you while clearly missing. It seems the hitboxes don't match up with the models, or aren't synced with the animations (the animations are excellent, btw!). It wasn't unsynced in Zero Dawn. There are also a few very annoying enemies that never stop attacking, have an enormous range, and constantly throw things at you. I don't view that as fun, just annoying.Weapons: In HFW, weapons are nerfed quite a bit. They're much weaker, to the point where I feel they're underpowered, even with a few of the late-game weapons. Just like in Zero Dawn, coils can be obtained to increase power, decrease reload time, etc. But even with multiple coils, I feel the primary damage-doing bows are weak.For example, the "main" bow is a Hunter Bow, which fires regular arrows. But quickly it doesn't keep up with the medium and difficult enemies in terms of damage output. Even the high-end Hunter Bows aren't good for damage. I started using Sharpshot Bows instead, which do about triple the damage, but the reload and draw speed is sooo slow. Even with coil upgrades, it's slow. I eventually got 3 purple coils, and it made my Sharpshot Bow bearable, but still low in terms of damage output versus enemy health.In the middle to late game, "Apex" enemies appear, which have much more health than the normal variants. Damage done with any bow is minuscule compared to their health. Of course, elemental combos help a lot, but the only elemental combo that's worth it for most high health enemies is freezing with chillwater ammo, then peppering with arrows from Sharpshot Bows.There are also a *lot* more weapons in this game, which multiple upgrades each. This isn't a bad thing, but makes getting upgrade ingredients for them a chore, since there's so many weapons and variants. The only way I was able to upgrade the ones I wanted without excessive grinding was to turn on "Easy Loot". Easy Loot lets you loot all of a machine's parts that aren't completely damaged in battle; basically Aloy takes the whole machine instead of a few parts, lol. This can be done by setting the difficulty to Custom, which makes the Easy Loot option changeable. I recommend turning it on early, after getting used to the game mechanics.The spear I never use except for Critical Strikes against downed machines, which are fun. However in the late game even Critical Strikes do hardly any damage against stronger machines with lots of health.Melee Pits: Introduced in HFW, Melee pits teach you spear techniques. Again I never use the spear much, as I prefer ranged combat, but still wanted to enjoy this content. But I found melee pits literally impossible to complete, due to precision-timed moves that must be completed perfectly, or the trial fails. I frustratingly got through most of the melee pits, but the last one I found impossible to time correctly, even with a video guide open. There was even one that puts you against 2 enemies that can attack and stunlock you before controls are enabled, that I had to cheese by placing bombs on the field beforehand, lol. I've given up on completing the melee pits.CONCLUSION: The game is great and definitely worth playing spoiler-free. But there are some needed improvements discussed at length, because I love this series. I look forward with much anticipation to the 3rd installment in the series.RIP Lance Reddick.

Overall, a decent FPS/TPS RPG.  70/100 in my book.Basic details on eval:- Playing the game on PC (keyboard/mouse).- Playing game as casual gamer, with a lot of time playing FPS/TPS shooters and top-down RPGs.- Playing HFW with the Burning Shores expansion (although exp. not complete at time of review).- First playthrough on Normal diff.  Did not run NG+ on this game (and will not do NG+).Abbreviations:HZD: Horizon: Zero DawnHFW: Horizon: Forbidden WestOne key caveat: while the overall HFW gameplay loop and many features of the game are similar to HZD, this game feels way worse in combat.  I'm marking "Recommend"; but note this is conditional.----Story / World: 42/50As a sequel, the studio did a good job from a story view.  The game feels like a good sequel should; it adds more story/lore, without either significant immersion breaking or overuse of lazy variety-stretching (e.g., re-skinning) to justify the new game.  Like HZD, HFW builds on a very detailed world, and adds nicely to the lore.  Characters new and old are pretty well done.  Backstories and such are just as detailed and thought through as HZD.- From a story angle, I definitely like the fact that both the machine and tribal diversity has improved.  Just makes good overall world sense, and done well.- I don't like the real-world location references (specifically cities/city names).  While it may help explain some of the ruins, it highlights the weird compression aspect of the world.  HZD tried pretty hard to keep these references vague; HFW would have done better to match.- The gender-power imbalance is still very pointed in the game.  I noted this on my review of HZD; still holds true for HFW.  No change there.- Would have preferred the Burning Shores content be more integrated with the standard game flow, rather than the way it is now (strictly a post-game expansion, on separate map).----Gameplay: 28/50Graphics / Smoothness of Play: 8/10Roaming Mechanics / Puzzles, etc.: 15/20Combat: 5/20The studio effectively had a good system with HZD.  Then they made some changes to it.  HFW is a similar-looking game, but it balances differently.The free-roam aspect is one area I feel was improved.  Core world movement and travel mechanics are effectively the same, with the addition of three major tools: glide-flight, deep-dive swimming, and true flight (with the Sunwings).  Also, with many of the world's cliffs now having significantly more holds, traversing the world is much easier in general.- I did not like the increase in difficulty with some of the building scaling (specifically with high rise type buildings), and increasingly exaggerated complexity on jumping.  Where integrated as part of puzzles (e.g., ruins, or story travel), this got to be quite irritating, especially with an increased chance to mess up / fall.The reworked combat system specifically ruined the game for me.- The core problem, is that it feels like the devs tried to "spice it up" by adding things; and went a bit too far.  They changed core combat flow, and focused too much on "showier" visuals.  More weapons, more tricks, more moves - and all of this, adds very little that is useful to / usable in the game.  Most are hard to use, and slow the player's combat pace (which is typically fast), so don't be surprised when you get punished for trying to use the new stuff.  I had to reconfigure the controls, working away from the new features, because they were mostly getting me killed.  Other than the warrior bows, and the spikes (javelins), I pretty much stayed away from new gear.- They compounded this change, by also making the new enemies in particular, MUCH harder.  Human opponents are not bad (only scary one is the new champion melee type).  But the machines are way overtuned.  When fighting the new machines, expect more aggressive diving / dashing, sweeping AoE melee hits, compounded by much more accurate ranged fire (with multiple projectiles or explosives/AoE).  Machines anticipate dodges as well, and slide into strike range with melee attacks, so if you commit too early to a roll, you get hit anyway (and the dodge has no cancel).  And machines hit hard.  Against most, expect to die within 3 hits (worse if underleveled).  Standup animation / stun effects, generally last longer, and are more prevalent.  Expect to get knocked down or stunned in chains, especially against groups of enemies.- Over-leveling helps; but even being 2x+ the machine's level is NOT safe.  Many large and mid-level enemies have big attacks that can do in excess of 400 damage a hit (note: max HP, at max LV, is 800).  This is on Normal - the game's recommended difficulty.  I ended up playing about a third of the game at "max level" (60); and even now, with end-game gear and upgrades, I still struggle with some of the harder single enemies.- Enemies to watch for include: Leaplashers, Rollerbacks, Clawstriders (esp. Acid), Clamberjaws, and ALL of the large boss-type machines (old and new).  The old large machines often had blind spots and angles of attack that were safer (e.g., Thunderjaws); new machines often have turrets / missiles that cover 360 (Shellsnappers / Tremortusks / Slaughterspines / Dreadwings), or large 360 AoE spew / thrash that punishes the player at melee ranges, and stay on top of the player (Tiderippers / Slitherfangs / Bileguts).- Upgrades for weapons, armor, and pouches are harder to complete.  This means less ammo, less healing berries, more crafting of arrows mid-combat, etc.  Coils and weaves are weaker, and harder to equip to armors and weapons (typ. less slots).While HZD hunter bow spam was kind of "button mashy", it was enough to get me through a first pass on HZD.  They broke this in HFW, pushing this in two separate directions: the warrior bow class (rapid, but shorter range, and WAY less accurate); and a slow down in the hunter bow class rate of fire.  This doesn't really work.  The warrior bow range is way too short (the arrow vanishes at medium range), and the slow draw time on the hunter bow makes kiting impractical, as everything can catch you.  Combine this with more damage taken overall, and the early game grind hurts.  This also makes it hard to get experience to level to a better state.  End-game gear helps improve this some over time, but it is never as effective as in HZD.The "bullet time" (concentration / BT) effect, with its zoom / accuracy improvement, is practically required to make meaningful hits.  I "tap" this into effect per shot, which uses less bar, but this gets disorienting, zooming in and out every 1-2 seconds.  In HZD, I could engage weak enemies without BT; in HFW, I cannot engage most machine enemies without this, as many simply move too rapidly, and/or have more effective armor coverage.In total, combat feels VERY different than it was in HZD - because of all of these changes together.  Harder machines aren't as bad with better engagement distances and long range hard hits.  New, special weapons would have been far more exciting and usable if machines were easier to engage.  The skill tree revamp and Valor skills are okay, but I'd much prefer HZD's setup to this.Story mode might be easier.  But considering I'm no newbie to the game, and I'm playing on the recommended difficulty, the overall balance of the game seems unnecessarily punishing.  I don't think the lower difficulty will fix core combat mechanics; and because of this, except for getting killed less often, I don't think the game will actually get that much easier.I just barely squeaked through the end of the base game on Normal.  I'll probably complete out the expansion, if I don't lose patience with getting jibbed.  I am NOT doing NG+.  Once is enough.  HFW's story is fine; but I had to put this one aside several times before I could make it to the end.I enjoyed HZD.  I tolerated HFW.Your experience may vary from mine.

Another instance where a "yes" or "no" isn't really ideal, but if you love HZD and are on the fence about HFW at full price -- I say wait for a decent discount. HFW isn't a bad game by any means, far from it, built as it is on the backbone of everything that made HZD cool -- but HZD, for my money, has a better designed and spaced out world, and certainly a much more engaging story, along with a more natural progression into the mechanics and breadth of its world. HFW's early hours feel cramped and samey and sort of overstuffed in a generic way that reminds me of Ubisoft games. I felt compelled to actually pay attention to conversations in HZD, whereas in HFW I find myself just button-mashing through them all. None of the characters are particularly offensive but nor are any of them very interesting, and in the early hours, their passive-aggressiveness about your need to get on your way is actively annoying. The combat in HFW is less forgiving than HZD, which may not be a bad thing depending on your preferences, but for me the difficulty of HZD felt more natural. Graphically, I also (to my surprise) like HZD a little better -- you'd think the newer graphics would inherently be superior, but not necessarily. Both games look amazing, but I think the art direction and lighting in HZD feels more painted and inviting and awe-inspiring, whereas a lot of HFW feels grungy and dusty. I even like the map UI in HZD better. HFW does offer some admittedly refreshing quality of life improvements -- gliding, visible climbing points, etc. make it generally a little easier to get around -- I just wish I could port them into the original HZD. There's more weapons and abilities in HFW, but I dunno -- the fundamentals are the same, and the combat doesn't feel as thoughtful to me. Fights feel a little more frenzied. Every weapon and ability in HZD felt useful and kind of fun to me, whereas in HFW it just feels like a bunch of stuff with a lot of overlap, with too much time spent switching between what weapons are in your active inventory. Again, both games are marvelous gorgeous open worlds full of things to do and machines to hunt, but HFW has made me pine for the experience of the first game more than inspire me to dive deeper into its own world. I think it's definitely worth getting, but maybe wait for the discounted prices if you're on the fence.

Played for a few hours at this point and I am enthralled! The game is absolutely beautiful, the music and writing are fantastic and I can't keep the smile off my face.The game will be familiar to those who have played the first. It looks similar at a glance but the lighting, and density and detail of the game's world so far, are a vast improvement over the original. Denser foliage and a massive step up in texture and quality. New water simulations I found sorely lacking in the first game are now here and they look amazing.I'm only just barely scraping the surface of combat at the time of this review, but there are so many different moves and combos (and enemy types) I will be able to fight and unlock in the future, that I am *almost* overwhelmed. The variety of what you can do is going to make people very happy and keep people entertained for a long time.The game is drop dead gorgeous and the cinematics / facial animations are certainly top of class. Aloy's character movement has a bit more weight to it than the first game, and animations are fluid.Now lets talk performance.My expectations are blown away and the game is butter smooth. I don't have what people would call top of the line hardware anymore, but I will list my specs so that you are able to compare how the game may run on your system.- RTX 3090 24 GB- Ryzen 9 5900x @ 5.0 ghz- 32 GB 3600 mhz ram- m.2 NVME SSD 2 TB- 3440 x 1440 resolution.Like I said, the performance has shattered my expectations, I was hoping to play at high settings 60fps. ( like most of us, I'm sure, we were bracing for another god awful launch) However I have found that the game is most playable at max settings on my hardware and resolution.With DLSS Quality enabled I am getting 80 to 120 FPS. With DLAA or TAA instead, I still get a most agreeable 60 - to 90 FPS, which is great, as I have always preferred high resolution and fidelity in story games over what upscaling has to offer.That being said, this implementation of DLSS is quite good, it seems to lack the smeary feel found in other games / versions, but still suffers from noisy crispiness from sharpening. The amount of sharpening is adjustable to your preference however. DLAA is black magic and the best AA option at the moment, IMO.With patches, this will only get better.The graphics, gameplay and accessibility options available are vast and comprehensive. However there are some options lacking.The Bad:Even with the expanse of options available to the player, there is no Gama slider available. Fellas, it's 2024 this is basic stuff.Secondly, there is no UI scaling option, (which correct me If I am wrong, the first game had) meaning that fellas with ultra wide monitors cannot adjust UI elements to sit in the corners of their screens. This is a minor annoyance, but again, should be a bog standard option for PC games in 2024. (I turn most of my HUD off anyway, in games like these.)Third: While player and NPC animations alike are MASSIVELY improved from the first game, and I do mean massively, (characters are so much more life like now) there is just the slightest touch of jank to Aloy's climbing animations, and often your character will clip through objects when climbing.And, that's actually all the bad I have to say about the game so far. The game is great, the performance is quite good and I am actually very excited to dig into it.Thank you Sony, thank you Nixxes and thank you Guerrilla, Keep em coming!

Damn it's a complete masterpiece and a massive level up in every way imaginable compared to the original. Oh how I sincerely hope that games with this kind of production budget and artistic quality and value will continue to be created for a long time to come, even though it's obviously becoming ever so challenging with the industry being in the state that it currently is. If it ever comes down to it, I believe that for games like Horizon: Forbidden West we should be willing to pay a hell of a lot more than what we were able to get it for. Starting with the good:This game is beautiful. The texturing and art design is impressive, so bravo to those artists. The added gameplay elements such as the glider and swimming mechanics are a much welcome improvement.Now the bad:Post process effects. They are all absolute GARBAGE. Thankfully the folks at Nixxes gave us toggles to turn all that crap off. Only two of these effects are useful but majorly flawed; these are Screen Space Reflections and Ambient Occlusion. I highly recommended turning off SSR as this is one of the first games I've played where fidelity is lost with it on - it blurs and undulates across reflective surfaces with a grainy smear masking the efforts of the texture artists. Ambient Occlusion here is a necessary evil. It's poor quality and floats around Aloy like black smoke. Post process effects feel like they were slapped on last minute.Gameplay is a mixed bag. Ranged combat is okay but doesn't feel as satisfying as HZD. Melee combat is downright awful. They have changed this mechanic to a brawler style button sequence making you have to remember a series of timed presses to engage unlockable melee skills. I personally don't like brawler fighting games. Fortunately, you can beat the game mostly with ranged combat. The skill trees just feel uninspired. The climbing mechanic is glitchy and all to often leads to small frustrating moments that break up enjoyment, especially during main quests. There are also a few minor texture bugs yet as well as a handful of places to get stuck inbetween geometry and crates under the ground or floating.The story is pretty B tier. All the side quests are forgettable. The main story however is interesting but, some of the scifi elements are poorly realized and not portrayed in a satisfying way. The way Faro was handled left me very disappointed. Between all the side content and the main story line (as mediocre as it was), the experience got monotonous fast. As someone who likes big open world games with lots to do, I found myself surprised to feel blase. Excited to see the conclusion of this story I was again disappointed by the ending, which was clearly setup to allow for a followup installment. I just barely started the DLC but plan on taking a long break. Possibly not even returning to it. If I want to adventure with Aloy again I'll just play HZD instead.WARNING:To normal common sense players who want to avoid the ever present woke nonsense that seeks to perverse our entertainment and media these days. This game although not overtly in your face preachy (though you could interpret some instances as such), it does contain elements of the alphabet cult influence in some side quests and a face paint option. Also, a disproportionate number of the main NPCs are gay, however this can be "dismissed" as this is mostly limited to inconsequential dialog. Since these things aren't front and center the game's core can be "enjoyed". But, now that these devs are bending the knee to this cult I will be very wary of future releases from them - this title likely being the last I purchase.

I finally found a game to surpass Sekiro as my favorite singleplayer game of all time.A perfect mix of gameplay and aesthetic presentation, with neither detracting from the other, but let's start with aesthetics:The setting and story progression are extremely good, forming one of the most engaging narratives I've seen in media. There's a lot of cool sci-fi "what ifs" to pick your brain over, but beyond that the characters are well written and their voicelines/delivery are superb, with the Decima engine being phenomenal at facial animations and expressions. But there's also so much detail in settlements and the world abroad that make the game feel so immersive and cohesive. The studio went out of their way to script Aloy's dialogue ( or monologue because she's constantly talking to herself) to be organic, no matter what order you decide to approach the massive open world, she will react appropriately to what she sees.There is a huge emphasis on exploration, and a massive part of that is discovering enemies for the first time, often through story events before they can begin appearing in the open world, ensuring that they are presented for maximum effect. I can't tell you how many times I found a machine for the first time and just hid in bushes for minutes in awe of how it moved and functioned.Graphics are generally not something I look for when picking up games, but this was the first game that I went out of my way to pause the action and take awesome screenshots in Photo Mode. It is hands-down the best looking game I have ever played. Everything about the art direction is incredibly polished, and the music is great too!On to gameplay, there were a couple of systems in Horizon:Zero Dawn that felt a little bit undercooked, but were much improved in this game; its a straight upgrade in every way. Especially in the melee combat department. The way that inventory, weapons, and armor function in this game is so much better, and offers so much versatility in playstyle and builds. It can be a little grindy to try to fully upgrade the highest tier of armor and weapons, but if anything that pushes you to improve your gameplay and try out new methods of killing enemies quickly and efficiently. And there are a LOT of different and fun ways to achieve that with so much build variety. I am looking forward to starting new playthroughs and emphasizing different weapon types.The tactical depth to combat is very deep, and I've spent many hours watching Arktix videos and the like to understand the strength of weapons, weaknesses of enemies, and optimize my playstyle. In particular Shredder gauntlets and Spike throwers are SUPER fun additions.The skill tree is a bit daunting but gives you a lot of room to try out new playstyles, and decide whether you want to move on to something new or invest further with Valor Surge upgrades and the like. Because otherwise everything is so good, I'm going to list the few criticisms I have.1. I would like better potion management, something similar to the potion crafting interface where I can drop/send to stash any potions I don't need. Its frustrating to be full on potions I wouldn't normally use when I need to craft a cleansing or stamina potion, for instance. And the auto-restock from stash doesn't seem to work ideally.2. I don't mind listening to Aloy talk to herself most of the time but sometimes the hand-holding for puzzles and the like feels just a bit too much; a slider to choose how much she guides you would be nice, or a button prompt for a hint might feel better.3. There are too many gelatinous animals in the game, please let animals drop both bones and skins, not just one or the other (or none).4. This is personal preference but hotswapping outfits in the middle of combat seems a bit too strong? There's no penalty to just switching to armor that gives +Silent Strike, +Critical, +Resonator for the respective damage boost, and then immediately taking it off after the damage registers and back to your general combat equipment. It just seems a little silly is all.5. A way to replay story quests would be really nice, ffs let me replay the final DLC mission again without having to trek all the way through another playthrough. It does give me something to look forward to in the future though. I suppose it may be too strong for farming materials, but just make it work like the arena where your resources revert back to what they were previously.

Horizon Zero Dawn is a game where some redhead born out of a mountain shoots down robot dinosaurs with a bow and arrow. It's a pretty wild premise. I won't dwell on it. Because the protagonist surely doesnt. There's a cutscene early on where that guy from the first game I wouldn't have remembered had I not been replaying Zero Dawn in New Game+. He's the son of a warchief who's really gruff and tough and never smiles. I don't remember her name, but she's cool.Point being, that guy goes ''old on, why do you look exactly like some long dead scientist''. At which point Aloy, our protagonist, explains how she was born of a mountain with the purpose of giving life back to the earth. And the guy goes, that sounds like some spiritual ♥♥♥♥. At which point our protagonist gets annoyed because, as a pariah within her own religion and a well educated person about the true nature of technology, she's become kind of an atheist. Which is interesting.Now, I'm only like two hours in as of writing and one thing I can say is that the game is gorgeous. It might, in fact, be the most gorgeous. It kind of has a cartoony vibe to everything, but, if pixar level graphics is your standard for visuals. This is one of the few games to truly deliver that. People make a fuzz about her peach fuss. But it's for good reason. I was replaying the older games and, during conversations, people really have this smoothness to their skin.Adding that layer of grit to the face really makes them seem that much more real. Now, one thing I heard is that the first 10 hours are set in the old game's map. Which is kind of a reverse of red dead redemption 2, if you think about it. I have this distinct memory of peering into the horizon in the first game, seeing the whole expanse of the map and thinking to myself. I'm going to have to walk aaaaaaaaaaaall across this over and over, arent I. I remember simply wanting for my life to be over at that point.Ok, so I ended up getting a refund on Forbidden West because the performance was just unbearable. The first two hours or so of the game run fine. But, as soon as you leave that linear prologue area, and get back to the larger open world, the game just started constantly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ itself. With certain scenes going as low as 10 frames per second... And that's with frame generation.Mind you, I have a 4060 ti, which is roughly equivalent to a 2080 or a 3070. Its biggest limitation is VRAM, but the minimum specs seem to say that the game will run on graphic cards with as little as 4gb of ram. And, I'm playing the game at 1080p, not 4K. Vram shortage wouldn't explain such catastrophic framerates anyway. It would create stutters and texture issues, not slowdown.It should be said that I am pretty much reaching the reccomended specs and beyond. I have the exact recccomended CPU for this game. But, yeah! That's my review of Forbidden West cut short...

Absolutely stunning!The music was epic, a literally watched the titles until the very end because I didn’t want to miss a second of it! The world sounds were also amazing.The variety of machines was awesome and I would actually jump sometimes during particularly realistic battles. Special kudos to the creators of the monkeys, I developed serious hate for those creatures by the end haha The story-writing continued to be unbelievable, with even more twists and turns until the very end of the main story arch. I love that the story uses modern events to build on top of, so much fun! Technology and science were well researched and totally believable. The scale and beauty of some scenes was insane! I would catch myself gasping in disbelief. The characters were beautiful! And cinematic cut scenes added yet another layer of immersion to quests, interactions with NPCs and of course, the epic battles.  When I got my flying mount, I literally just flied it around for a while, enjoying the view from above. It was also very cool to get a selection of different tools to use in different situations and each one was bad-ass in its own right. I enjoyed the addition of the ruin puzzles, they were fun.It was awesome to get companions, I personally really liked that. It reminded me of the original Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic, in all the best ways. And because each tribe in the world has such beautiful, unique character, values and culture, it was very cool to have them all united in protecting the world. I thought each tribe was very poetically written, I really enjoyed the costumes, the speech patterns, things they valued, and many more little things that were some masterfully thought-through. I am an explorer-collector player type, so crystal caves were pure dopamine. I could use much more things like that, but I know they are not for everyone. For my taste, there could be more relics, shiny artifacts and finds in places in the world where many people wouldn’t think to go. I like when games reward curiosity. I have been thinking for a while why is it that finding things in this game doesn’t feel good and I came to an odd realization – I don’t like that the inventory icons are so uniform. I an embarrassed to admit, that I was on the other end of the exact same decision many years ago, in pursuit of branding consistency.  It’s kind of shocking to realize that I myself don’t find to be satisfying. Again, being a collector, I like to admire all the different things in my inventory and their colorful different icons. On the other hand, I really appreciated the improved inventory mechanics (stash), so you don’t lose any of your gathered goodies. I also liked improved crafting. It still made it possible to make things and modify/improve gear, but it was easy and out-of-the way, as long a you had resources. Which I always do 😃 Overall I loved the game and I hope there will be part 3 coming!

TL;DR: This is a fantastic PC port, as well as a fantastic game. I would highly recommend fans of Horizon Zero Dawn to play this. There's some issues with performance that can come up on mid-range hardware (at least, there was at release) but not too many.Here's the longer version:- Fantastic game overall- Engaging story, with characters introduced that don't feel shoehorned in- Graphics look fantastic, and they take better advantage of hardware than the previous port for HZD- Controls feel far better compared to HZD once you adapt to them. Very intuitive after this many hours of gameplay.- Progression system overhaul makes it feel like there's a point to level after beating the game- Collectibles now have a point, makes for good endgame content- The map is HUGE and feels super expansive, also the change to fast travel is very much appreciated- Weapon upgrade system feels very nice- Various changes to the weaves and coils system that make it VERY nice to upgrade/change weapons- The graphics can be a bit hard to run on lower end hardware, even with DLSS I noticed some SEVERE frame drops in the early game cutscenes, down to 24 FPS even on medium settings with DLSS set to balanced.- Game graphics settings needed to be set to low/medium in order to maintain stable playable framerate 90% of the time, still noticed some drops here and there- Some in-game models seem to not render correctly at mixed low/medium settings, particularly around the neck-to-torso transition area. At lower settings, a gap in the model is visible. Unsure if this shows up on higher settings, as my hardware doesn't allow me to go any higher than what I set it to, while still maintaining playable frame rates- TOO MANY TOOL TIP POP UP MENUS - By this I mean whenever a new ammo type got picked up it would pop up a large menu about it in the middle of the screen. Got to be kind of annoying after this many hours of playtime.- LOTS of collectibles/activities, so little time: I found that during the main campaign and a lot of the side quests, I skipped LOTS of the other activities available such as Machine Strike, just because of the size of the game. At time of writing, I only have ~54% of the main game completed. I'm still working through everything.Buy this game. It's fantastic. Your hardware should usually be able to run it, but it will require some settings tuning. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but it's worth considering if you are on an older/lower-end machine. Personally, my rig is a Ryzen 7 7700X with a 3060 Ti 8 GB (not the best CPU/GPU combo, I know, but I'm planning on upgrading it).

This game took most of what made the first one good and threw it in the bin.TLDR for those who do not like reading long reviews:1. The story is badly written. No mystery anymore and probably the worst antagonists in gaming history I have seen.2. Combat felt better, but the talent tree, weapon variety and armor choices were awful.3. Side questing is lazily written, and constnatly requires you to backtrack. The rewards aren't really rewarding either.4. Minimal innovation. Lots of old systems recycled and lots of open world filler content without any real value.5. Shallow characters and an obvious woke and misandrist tone to the entire game.The story is abysmal and so incredibly far fetched I barely managed to stomach it. The writing was often done in a very childish way leaving lots of plot holes, questions and giving unsatisfying answers. A vast amount of the encounters in this game feel like an interaction between toddlers. Also the attempt to make this game "more woke" is obvious. I wish they focused on making well written characters, rather than taking a very bland chartacter and making them a minority who is also female who also had the hardest upbrinding all while her potential was strangled by men all around her. They didn't even hide the misandry. Aloy is also a PHD in electronics all of a sudden because the way she throws terms around that should not be known to her is really immersion breaking. When she starts talking about overriding the mainframe to melt a cpu core and engage the ram blah blah blah... It's not a direct quote but summarizes the problem well. No matter how much time Aloy spent playing around with her focus there is no way she actually learned those terms and what they mean so it just felt unnatural.The combat feels like an improvement over the first game. I must admit I did have fun fighting the machines. Though the upgrade systems for gear and skill points were a total downgrade. Upgrades were expensive, armors barely felt like they made a difference in my playstile and 80% of the unlocks on the skill tree felt like they didn't really give me any meaningful advantage. In the first game I would try and get the skill points so I could improve how Aloy fought, while here it was like I was getting and spending them on the tree that made the most sense without any noticeable improvements. Also the way I went through so many side quests and so many merchants and still ended up with 4 of the same bows on my weapon wheel which were too expensive to upgrade, just so I could have different arrow types (50% of which overlapped btw because it's fun having 3 corrosion bows!!!!!) was pretty disappointing.The ruins are the same as before, except now you know the actual story so the mistery is gone. They didn't really do anything innovative here. Just copied everything you did in the first game. It honestly was kind of disappointing because I was hoping we'd get to experience something new.Overall I feel like this game could have been much more but ended up being a basic open world game for the sake of having a sequel.Do not recommend if you want to keep your good memories of the first one.

Horizon Forbidden West picks up about half an year after the events of prior game, Horizon Zero Dawn. Both take place in post apocalyptic North America, where animal-shaped machines are main threat to technology-augmented tribal humanity... or so they thought.The game is beautiful open world with RPG elements (gearing, talent tree, questing) and good story. The combat is what really shines - it's dynamic action packed, as you have to avoid massive machines attacks, while getting to know their weak points and use them to your advantage, manually aiming with weapons like bows and fitting ammunition. While bows are somewhat the main weapon, there are also other weapons, including melee spear, stealth combat (to a lesser extend that previously), traps, slingshots with explosive ammo and more.Comparing to the first game, Horizon Forbidden West is improved visually, especially in the parts where it lacked previously - NPC interactions. Gameplay wise, new machines/enemies, weapons and minor features were itroduced, while some of the old changed or removed. While the game is still good, I think I liked the previous game more in overall, especially regarding combat. I played both games on maximum difficulty, starting with stealth combat in first one, which seems not viable at all in this one. Machines are also more annoying than difficult, especially Burrowers, who take role of the Watchers from first game. Elemental and situational ammo seems less impactful than previously, especially Tearblast Arrow - previously overpowered, now useless. Nonetheless, Forbidden West also introduced some quality of life changes, like summoning previously overwritten mount, no matter where it was left out.Tech wise the PC port by Nixxes is very good from day one. Performance is good and I haven't encountered any major problems, latest upscalers and frame generation (DLSS 3+, FSR 3.1, XeSS) are available, NVIDIA Reflex, FOV slider and some more options. I still had muscle memory after Zero Dawn, so I found it weird that the default controls are different, though over time they allowed rebinding some of them. There's even light-weight old-school launcher that allows you to change some setting before starting the game itself.I recommend playing the game, but would suggest playing Horizon Zero Dawn first, especially given the "remaster" is around the corner. Both Zero Dawn (non-remaster) and Forbidden West don't require PSN account as of writing this. There is some telemetry you can't opt-out from though.

Horizon Forbidden West is an open world, third person action game which continues the story of Horizon Zero Dawn. The world’s biosphere is collapsing which could lead to another extinction event, and Aloy must find an artificial intelligence to heal the world, while some powerful villains have other plans.Zero Dawn was one of my favourite games from the last few years, and Forbidden West combines good gameplay with an excellent story and high quality technical performance, but unfortunately there are lots of little annoyances that often get in the way of fully enjoying the game.•	Combat is challenging on normal difficulty, and becomes more enjoyable as you progress further into the game, acquiring better weapons which allow you to take advantage of each machine’s elemental weaknesses.•	There are several new machines to fight against, which have interesting designs based on animals and dinosaurs, including some huge bosses. Something about the animation of Human enemies makes them much easier to headshot, and therefore less annoying to fight, than they were in ZD.•	In addition to the main quest, there are lots of side quests which have unique short stories where you’ll need to help villagers, usually by protecting them from bandits or machine attacks. The open world has several activities, including tallnecks, cauldrons, bandit camps, combat arenas, races, a turn based minigame, and multiple types of collectable items to find.•	Main story is very well written, and features an outstanding voice acting performance from Ashly Burch, while the rest of the cast, including Hollywood stars Lance Reddick, Angela Bassett, and Carrie Ann Moss, also do a great job.•	Cutscenes feature excellent lip syncing and facial animations, which helps you to understand character emotions in each scene.•	Using Digital Foundry’s optimised graphics settings I was able to get a very smooth framerate while playing in 1440p (i7-12700K, RTX 3080, 32GB DDR4). I think the key setting here is texture quality. I started with it on very high and I noticed some frame drops, but after changing to high, performance across the main open world map was stable with no noticeable loss of picture quality. •	In most areas of the world, the environment looks stunning, from snowy mountains to a huge desert, tribal villages, old world ruins covered in plants, and lakes where you can swim underwater.•	It took me 79 hours to complete the main story, burning shores expansion, most of the side quests, and the open world activities which I found most interesting, which is great value at full price.•	The game only crashed twice, which I think is acceptable for such a long playing time.•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.•	Aloy’s dialogue while exploring and questing is extremely annoying, because she constantly tells the player exactly where to go and what to do. This doesn’t just relate to puzzle solving, but also basic world navigation. Climb that ladder. Stand on that crate to reach the ledge above. That gap is too far to jump, I’ll need to glide. She’ll draw our attention to important objects the moment we step into a room, before we even had a chance to find it for ourselves. She’ll constantly remind us about using the focus to look for hidden items, even though that’s a basic gameplay mechanic that we have to use in almost every quest. To be clear, I like Aloy’s personality during the story cutscenes. I just wish she’d be quiet while exploring the open world. I don’t need my hand to be held every step of the journey. Let me figure things out for myself.•	The first major area of the open world (after the tutorial), at the far east of the map, is spoiled by a high volume of dust particles in the air. When running around the open world, these particles fly at the screen like stars zooming past the USS Enterprise at warp speed. During cutscenes, having dozens of huge white dots floating around the whole screen was extremely distracting, and at times I struggled to concentrate on the dialogue. I spent about 10 hours completing quests in that area, and there’s no option to disable or reduce the effect. Thankfully, as you travel further west, the air becomes much clearer in most areas, although the dust particles do come back occasionally (seems to be worse when there are lots of trees nearby).•	Aloy’s focus has a green flashlight, but the player has no manual control and she hardly ever turns it on. There were several occasions, either in caves, or just exploring the open world at night, where I was struggling to see. My brightness settings are perfect during the day. The game really should have had a flashlight button.•	Crafting feels too grindy. Every weapon, armour, and ammo pouch has between 3-5 tiers of upgrades. Even machine overrides, its not enough to explore the cauldrons, you still need to actually craft each override. Every upgrade needs a specific component from a specific machine or animal, and they don’t always drop from each kill, so you’ll need to either spend hours trying to farm the items, or save up thousands of shards and just buy what you need from traders.•	Climbing controls lack precision. There were many occasions where I had to press the jump button 3-4 times to get Aloy to move up to the next hold point. Sometimes she’ll either yeet herself off a ledge in a random direction away from where you want to go, or do a small jump and fall short of the next platform.•	Even using optimised settings, the Burning Shores map had frame drops in some areas.Horizon Forbidden West is a good game, and its definitely worth playing if you liked Zero Dawn, but it could have been so much better if not for a few poor design decisions that frequently undermine the fun parts of the game. As this is a direct sequel, you’ll need to play Zero Dawn first to properly understand the story.

I loved Horizon Zero Dawn on PS5 all the way until I had to aim my bow on a gamepad. After that I switched to a PC version and had an amazing time with it. The optimization of HZD was a bit rocky at first but by the time I played it (a few months after PC release), it was basically flawless. I got Forbidden West for PS5 for about 8€ and the same thing happened. I had a great time until they gave me a bow and tried to teach me to use my right thumb for accuracy, which is impossible. So I waited for the PC version instead and I'm glad I did.Technical side:Horizon Forbidden West skipped the rocky start and its PC port is already flawless on release from what I can see. DLSS with frame generation works wonders to keep your framerate in triple digits without any input lag or any UI issues if you have a system that supports it. Ultrawide is perfect. No notes. This is how you do ultrawide. Everybody please learn from these guys. Your UI is in the center of the screen and you have the option to turn off letterboxing during cutscenes, so the game is as cinematic as it can be at all times. I couldn't find anything missing in the options menu. FOV slider, Accessibility settings to remove DOF, camera shake, motion blur, colorblind settings and more... All there. If TotalBiscuit could see this release, he would have a huge smile on his face. This is just the way we PC players like it. I can't really comment on the performance side, because it's smooth as butter no matter what with a 4090, but your mileage may vary. From what I've seen in Digital Foudry's technical breakdown, it looks like most PC players will have a good experience no matter the configuration unless your PC is over 5 years old.Story and gameplay:Loved it. I got super invested in everything Aloy goes through. The world building in this gorgeous post-apocalyptic civilization is second to none. Voice acting is fantastic. Ashley Burch is always fantastic and I'm glad Lance Reddick would be really proud of his legacy. And that's just scratching the surface. This game has a stellar cast. Carrie-Anne Moss, Angela Bassett, Noshir Dalal (although it would be weird if a AAA videogame came out today without him in it), nobody phones it in, which means you'll really get immersed in this beautiful world. Progression is great, because the skills you unlock are actually interesting and meaningful and not just lazy "+X damage dealt" or "-X damage taken". The open world and the side quests are almost on CDPR level and the combat is varied depending on what you are fighting, especially with the whole weakpoint system on different enemies. I really have almost nothing bad to say about this series. Maybe it can get a little bit repetitive as all open world games tend to do, but there's always something interesting or challenging to do no matter what phase of the game you are in. Maybe it could get boring if you go for every single side activity? I don't know, I didn't get that far, but Forbidden West never got boring for me and I did a lot of side activities, so I expect more of the same and from what I've seen, even the side activities are fun. Also even if it did get boring, I would just follow the main storyline and finish the game, which would still take dozens of hours, so there's really no issue here no matter how you slice it.I'm super happy that these amazing Playstation titles are coming to PC and I'll gladly support all of them with full price, because PC will always be the best way to enjoy them and I'm glad we don't have to rely on shoddy emulators anymore.Also there's no micro transactions or any similar predatory system. You buy this Complete Edition and you get the full game with its DLC. That's the way it should be with all games, none of this live-service, pay 70€, get 30% of the game bullcrap. No. You pay 60€ and you get everything the game has to offer. Thank you for this, devs/bigwigs. We see you and we are very grateful.

The visual quality is perfect and highly immersive. 10/10The game delivers a diverse array of biomes, each beautifully rendered and distinct, enhancing the exploratory experience. 10/10This aspect is more complex. While the game features various impressive locations like tribe capitals and scenic vistas, these often lack lasting significance or practical uniqueness. Unlike GTA V’s memorable locations with unique functionalities, many sites in Forbidden West, like the Golden Gate Bridge, feel underutilized. The uniqueness in , exemplified by Meridian’s diverse vendors, is missing in most of Forbidden West’s settlements, except for the Arena. 6/10Enemy placement is generally well-executed, though it occasionally lacks the interactive elements that could enhance the experience. While some enemy positions are excellent, others fall short, leaving a sense of imperfection. 9/10The game excels in enemy design, offering varied movesets, behaviors, and a wide range of adversaries. Boss monsters are particularly well-introduced, with iconic battles in memorable locations. 10/10The weapon system is disappointing. Although there is variety, each new weapon starts at its base level, requiring significant grinding to upgrade. The pacing and introduction of weapons are less effective compared to , and overlapping arrows add to the frustration. 5/10The combat is decent, though slightly more challenging than in .Without revealing spoilers, the storyline is subpar, particularly marred by the ending dialogue of Burning Shores. The narrative pacing is also poorly executed, detracting from the overall experience. 6/10The side missions are a mixed bag, with some being good but most falling into the average category. 7/10While  excels in graphics and enemy design, significant flaws in weapon progression, narrative execution, and the lack of practical uniqueness in locations make it a less compelling follow-up to .

I recommend this game; it is an amazing and memorable experience.I also recommend that it is played on PlayStation if possible, despite the lower frame rates and fidelity, at least for the moment. I hope that some of the issues with the PC version will be addressed, but I do not think they all can be. I originally completed it on PS5 when it came out.Story:I recommend completing the first game before playing this one, although it is not necessary, you will get slightly more out of it if you do.The story is not great, its not much of anything really, just a reason for Aloy to go on a quest.That is fine with me but it would be nice if it was at least on par with the first game.I would say that it levels itself out to a neutral level of being neither good nor bad.Graphics:The graphics are amazing, it has some graphical bugs and limitations not present on the PS5 version. Such as the dust devils looking weird and some flashing textures etc. It does not ruin the experience but it is a little disappointing.Overall it is still fantastically realised with a great art style and incredible fidelity, especially at higher resolutions.Audio: Most of the audio is great, the sound effects are crispy and the soundtrack is very good.I found the audio in 7.1 sounded more like 5.1 and the voices always play from the centre channel which can be confusing. There are occasional bugs that make some sounds not play.General gameplay:The open world is an amazing place to explore, there is always something interesting to find, but the number of collectables is overwhelming. If you like that, then its fine, if you can and want to ignore it, then it is also fine. If you have OCD it might trigger you somewhat. By the end of the game, I grew fatigued from doing the same things repeatedly, it stopped being fun and became a chore. Traversal:Some other games could learn a thing or two from this game’s traversal mechanics. That said they are not perfect; one issue is the jump problem, there is no indication if you will auto jump or you must press the jump button. This can result in you thinking that it will auto jump and just running off a high platform to your death. Alternatively, if it is an auto jump and you press jump then Aloy will auto jump then jump again casing you to fall to your death. Aside from that, the cliff climbing can be a little weird having you dancing around a ledge that you should be able to just climb up.Mostly it is a fluid and enjoyable traversal system, I enjoy the new zip mechanic and the variety of mounts.Combat:The combat system is robust and has a good level of variety, it can be hard and does require some experience and study of each enemy to “get gud”. There is a wide assortment of weapons to choose from and they can be further customized with addons. So, you are sure to find something that appeals to your fighting style.I would not say that the skill ceiling is high, you can change the difficulty at any time, if you get stuck you can temporarily lower it. It has many levels of adjustment that allow you to customize the gameplay experience. The enemies vary a great deal in their difficulty, and for the most part you can choose your fights.There are some downsides to combat in my opinion. Firstly, I think that there is far too much “input reading”, if an enemy launches itself at you and you dodge, they will defy physics to redirect towards you in mid-air, this also happens with energy or elemental blasts that will curve after being fired to track you.Secondly some attacks will “hit” even if the enemy fully misses you, occasionally by quite a distance. Additionally, you will sometimes be “hit” by something without any attack visibly taking place. Thirdly traps in the game have been highly restricted, with the max upgrades you can place maybe five traps? I’m not sure what the limit was in the first game but it was allot, at least ten to fifteen. I found this resulted in me ignoring them, except in some rare situations. Also, the enemies now seem to target traps shooting them as soon as you place them.Overall the combat is fun and rewarding, there is nothing like taking down a giant “boss” robot after many tries.Boss battles and story missions:I put this separate from everything else because they clearly are not the same in terms of gameplay experience, some of the story missions can be quite restrictive and pedantic about what you are allowed to do. Some of the story mission boss battles are badly done and not a fun experience. Mechanics like doors or other interactable objects only unlocking after a dialogue or after another discovery (like finding a data bank or voice message), ruin the immersion for me.Final thoughts:This game has a free roaming sandbox unlike any other, I love the world they have created, it is an absolute joy to play, with variety of game play that encompasses everything from super chill to very intense.There are issues that could have been fixed a long time ago on the PS versions that still mar the experience.Some of the story missions and boss battles are just objectively bad.

I really wanted to like this game. I loved the narrative of the first game, Zero Dawn and the gameplay in that was fine, not great. And that's where the problems begin for Forbidden West.There were no improvements from the first game. The combat system which had terrible hit boxes, and a rudimentary weak/strong attack system still has all the issues, but now they tried to build a combo system on top of it. However the combo melee system is nearly pointless because every enemy machine is so aggressive that they will attack straight into any combo and interrupt you. So basically the entire combo system was put in just to fight other humans' which is at most 20% of the game as far as I got.Because of the 'improvements' to the combat system the sneak attach system has been severely neutered, so now half the enemies in the game have so much HP that a sneak attack will only do 30-50% damage basically forcing you into janky melee combat system to finish them. Unless you want to constantly use smoke bombs to re-enter a hidden state.One good thing was having to shoot off components for upgrades from enemies which actually made hunting enemies funner...but...again the combat was so janky that I eventually said 'Ok, I'll set the game to easy and just enjoy it'. Well then on easy every enemy just drops every possible item basically mocking you. So the one good improvement ruined.Packs of enemies would overlap, so you if were lucky enough to eliminate 3-4 in a group, then when you got to the last one and got spotted suddenly more run in from seemingly nowhere.They took the worst mechanic from DA: Inquisition where you use R3 to 'ping' and highlight lootable items nearby, So you're constantly running around R3...R3....R3. Then, with the focus scan it always had trouble marking/targeting animals, and again, no improvement. You try to target a bird while in focus mode (or anything small) it's a complete guessing game whether you need to center it, or have it towards the bottom of the reticle, or the right side.IMO climbing took a step backwards. Now there are dozens of small crags when climbing so Aloy just seems confused to which one you want her to grab on to. And then when you reach the top the character often has a hard time pulling herself up over the final ledge.Lastly, they added a cooking system for food and dye system for armor which I don't think anyone wanted.I freely admit I didn't use the elemental advantages or traps because I feel like if the game gives you different play styles they should all be viable. I wanted to know what happened and that drove me forwards. It was a bit ubisoft-esque, but offered enough to keep me playing.What happened in Forbidden West that made me dislike it?- They nerfed the hunting gameplay. You can only use around 5-6 traps pretty late in the game if you heavily invest in that skill and gear, making that gameplay style obsolete (most of the early game you can only use 3). On top of that, enemies are made more spongy. This causes the combat to be a chore instead of a nice challenge. This ruined the gameplay for me.- The story is a mess. Cartoonish villains, one-dimensional characters and Aloy, oh Aloy. Everyone has to tell you she's awesome, because in the cutscenes she isn't anyting like that. Instead of the veteran warrior/hunter she should be (and she is when you're in combat), she is one of the most uninspiring whiny temper tantrum throwing characters I have ever seen in videogame. This ruins the story even more. All side characters are one-dimensional predictable dullards. I didn't care about any of them.- The world is way too big with too much generic samy content. It's as boring as the most boring ubisoft games, maybe even more so. It's very pretty looking, don't get me wrong, but it's all just a facade to hide the incredibly boring reality.I tried so hard to like this game and hoped it would get better. With over 50 hours I really feel I've given it a chance, but now I wish I could have this time back. It's such a shame as the developers are clearly very talented, the games feels polished and looks amazing, it's just so boring and Guerilla Games really needs a good storywriter, because that was just terrible. Beautiful game, and I enjoy a lot of the exploration on offer here.  It misses the mark in a lot of other ways.  The lighting engine usually creates beautiful vistas, but it's very unrealistic looking at times.To preface a negative review, I do want to say that the tallneck cauldron was probably the moment that made me remember what I loved about the original.  Interesting, unique experiences that are designed to reward you in ways that only this world can.  Once you get unlimited swimming, the underwater sections are woven in well with exploration.  I really enjoy wandering around the world and unlocking points of interest.  The world is still one of the best designed ones in all of gaming.  I like the base where you can talk with the NPCs you have relationships with (although those relationships don't really develop at all as you progress).For the things I dislike, the first one is that I'm not a fan of the climbing changes - what is climbable or not is impossible to tell from a distance, and then once you're there, you have to ping it to paint the surface with yellow lines that don't mesh with the environment, making it feel like a minigame.  You have to ping the area constantly while exploring (as opposed to the previous entry, where you only pinged to search for loot).In several areas, noticeably during the prologue, I was regularly getting caught on edges of the maps with things that look explorable and are climbable/mountable, but then Aloy falls off or floats on the edge.  Janky jumps and climbs are pretty common throughout the game, and there's a lack of polish here overall.Combat feels off - traps are expensive and slow, the tripcaster is nerfed, and I find that I have to rely on the spear way too much.  The minute you break stealth, you have to roll constantly because the enemies are relentless with both melee and ranged attacks.  The roll is nerfed for spacing, and enemies don't stagger, almost ever.  A lot of fights are about defense and how many herbs you can stuff in your mouth between rolling to avoid attacks and taking pot shots, and even elemental attacks are less useful vs a heavy break weapon and a lot of concentration.The weapon grind and abundance of weapons with very slightly different uses is bad - getting a new weapon feels like a chore to grind it up to make it a slightly better option than what you've got, and many weapons just sit in the bag for the entirety of the game.All the blocked passages with keys + locks are unnecessary.  There are so many spots where you have to open a blocked passage by using a grappling hook or a special module on your spear instead of blowing it up with explosives.  It's immersion breaking that I can't just blow up a wall with the bombs I'm using against enemies - I have to target these blue brackets and yank real hard, or shove my spear into it, or hit it but only after an upgrade.  The first ruin you come across involves a huge amount of traversal and block pushing, when the thing you want is two feet away through an open window that Aloy could very clearly duck through.I think the sequencing with the Poseidon quest deserves a special call out for being awful - the need to swim directly towards a thing that is telegraphed to kill you in order to trigger a nearby interaction point is awful.  I wasted over an hour trying to figure it out until I found an old reddit thread about it.Sequels are hard, and this game suffers from the need to improve or change things that didn't need to be touched.  Probably still worth a play, but not worth full price.

The game runs very well 1440p high settings, but for me because of the case design, the gpu was running at 74C and 82C hot spot, so I tuned it down to 1440p medium with high level detail + DLSS quality, and it's at a happy 55C; 66C hotspot.POST COMPLETION EDIT:When I posted my initial review I was only 7 hours into the game and my thoughts about it haven't changed. Superb AAA game. Visually stunning. The acting, performance capture, and character models are all top notch. I bought it hoping for an iterative improvement over the first game in the franchise, as I really enjoyed that game, but it ended up being far superior in virtually every way. The game is however much more of an RPG, whereas the first game was much more of an action game. The story and cinematic sequences are quite extensive (most are very easily skippable for repeat playthroughs). The crafting and upgrade system is more extensive and more difficult. The side quests feel much more important, both to the overall world and story, and to character progression because they all award skill points. The Focus/scanning aspect of the game is more detailed and important, as many upgrade parts you have to shoot off machines before you kill them or they get destroyed. The skill Tree is much more extensive and has a greater impact on how you choose to approach most combat situations, especially the first half of the game where you don't have enough skill points to invest into Ranged, Melee, Survival, and Overrides so you have to pick 1 or 2 to focus on. You can't just mash potions to heal through anything like you could in Zero Dawn, you have to actually use positioning and dodging to avoid attacks unless you're playing on normal/easy difficulties. If you enjoyed the first game, or you enjoy open world RPGs or action-RPGs, you will enjoy this one.
