Really good game. It is pretty fun, improves a lot from the first game and kinda makes a few things worse than the first. But overall pretty good though. In more detail: - Looks gorgeous - i mean of course - The combat is still fun. Although it feels a bit less fun than the first. The combat in FW is more complex, is more rich, gives more options on play style. But in their attempt balance the combat properly (and you do not steamroll the whole game with all the new options) they kinda used annoying ways to keep the difficulty up. Do not get me wrong: they really nailed the difficulty curve (on normal at least the challenge is ideal). But they did that with lots of crowd control on attacks, long stunlocks, restricted dodges with few invul frames and very high density of attacks. Makes many of enemy attacks feel unavoidable and many fights just end up just a simple exercise of taking the damage and overhealing. Combat is still fun but when ZD was fun 100% of the time FW is like fun 80% of the times with a bit of annoyance in the other 20. - Melee combat is much improved and actually usable. But has no defense or block options. So it is not very useful in practice besides a few fights and the arena duels. That is a shame. They made a whole revamp only to make it less useful by not giving some defense features. - Improved writing but a lot. ZD had great lore but the actual plot and characters were forgettable as hell.  I could only really remember Sylens' name at the end of ZD, the only interesting character. But in FW. The plot is much improved and the characters , old and new, are actually likable and have arcs and evolution. Especially the new characters. Even Aloy finally had a character arc (no she did not have one in ZD - leveling up is not an arc). The plot still suffers from way too much talk and not enough show. And the Villains are basically forgettable generic Marvel villains number 3354 to 3502. At least the story setpieces are visually really good. They have a good plot finally in this game. But they really have to work on how they are presenting it. - Side quests (the actual ones not the open world busy work) also very much improved. They have at least some nice story behind them even if repetitive.-  Open world busy work is actually kinda worse than the first game. The first game had the typical Ubisoft game busy work but had the correct density. Just before it becomes too much. But FW is so dense it is actually annoying. Just throwing everything on it. It is just too much and kinda boring. But also easily completely ignored. Only did the big side quests and only a few of the busy work and ignored the rest and was always overleveled.- Very good port for the Core game. Everything worked great and had good performance, except the expansion area. Performance in the Expansion completely tanked. I had to reduce details a lot to make it playable and even then it did not performance as well as the core game. I want to appreciate the increased fidelity in the expansion but if i have to reduce details for it it kinda defeats the purpose of the improvement in the first place.

Gameplay - The gameplay is extremely solid. There's a much larger emphasis on melee combat (which I enjoy even though I don't really partake in it) but the combat overall is rock solid, I feel like it stands up to the first game. I'm not sure how much more I can say about the combat. Exploration was nice, varied environments were nice, but something I felt it was missing was the initial sense of wonder the first game had after leaving the Nora lands. The first game made such a big deal about it, that when you finally got turned loose everything was "ooooooo aaaahhhhh" and here' you're just seeking permission to go deeper into the map. That "barrier" felt more like an annoying obstacle than something that needs to be there, like how the Nora refuse to leave because they need to protect their sacred land.Graphical Fidelity - The game looks amazing. There was a much larger emphasis on water in the later stages of the game and in Burning Shores, so the water physics were on point. Rivers flowed and reacted to rocks in them, the underwater portions of the game were well constructed. Being underwater looked as good as being out of water. It was all very very visually pleasing. The lighting was fantastic and the clear nights with the moon lent a very strong feeling of dread when sneaking about in the overworld, not knowing when I was going to stumble into something I shouldn't. The effects were nice as well. Overall, the game is eye-candy.Audio - The sound overall is good. Sometimes too loud but this can be adjusted. The soundtrack is really good, some tracks give off a witcher 3 vibe, but not many, maybe two. Sound effects are very crisp, and the 3D spatial audio is on point.Nit Picks - These are things that I personally look for that make a game good or bad. Foliage occlusion is a huge plus for me. If I am stalking through the grass, I want to see the grass move. The water has this particle effect in it when you're under water. This is also something I look for when there's any sort of underwater element to a game.This review was written after the completion of the Burning Shores DLC. After careful consideration I feel like I can recommend this game, but cautiously. There's a lot of kerfuffle about Aloy being a manhating girlboss, but honestly it's no worse than the first game. The only thing that's different is in Burning Shores, when she seems to warm up to one of the NPCs in a way she's avoided opening up to everyone else. While I don't feel like this is consistent with the way Aloy was initially written, it's not outside of the realm of possibility for Aloy, an outcast herself, to seek companionship in another outcast. Especially since the events of Forbidden West reminded her that life is fleeting. Being staunchly anti-DEI is becoming a huge thing now, and people are taking a much closer look at the social messages their games are pushing, however I don't think this game falls too heavily on the DEI side. Aloy is a bit sharper towards males in this game, and many of the men in the game are written to be less competent, there are still plenty of strong, competent males in this game. A lot of the "Aloy is better than the men" sentimentality seems to be a side effect of the main character syndrome Aloy exhibits because, well, she IS the main character. So, naturally, she's always going to win, and always going to bail people out. These people are men and women alike. For that reason, I can't say I feel like she's "girl bossing".

tl;dr - Its a "meh" game following one of my favorite games of all time: Zero Dawn. Steam really needs a "meh" recommendation option. If I hadnt played and loved Zero Dawn, I probably wouldnt have bothered with this game. My complaints about it?Stealth is pointless considering how much effort you have to put in to pull it off successfully. The whistle ability made stealth easy, sure, but now its not easy and a waste of time. Plus enemies spot you from a mile away if you so much as fart in their general direction, making stealth even more pointless.Having to override a new mount every time you lose your current one is incredibly tedious. Sure, its more realistic than just pulling out a new mount from my bum whenever I want, but I dont play video games for realism over practicality.Melee is useless because its basically impossible to reliably knock down enemies and does ♥♥♥♥-all damage-wise. Sure, its more realistic than stabbing a giant, two-story tall robot dog with a stick and having it fall over, but...well, that "realism" thing again. All this leaves without stealth is just shooting dudes, which removes the natural flow of combat from its predecessor.No, you cant stun them, but they sure as ♥♥♥♥ can stun lock you! Even the lowest level enemies can knock you on your ass just by looking at you funny. And these guys are RELENTLESS! Zero Dawn's combat feels like the enemies are working together in such a way where you figuring out their attack patterns makes combat feel strategic and rewarding, like you arent just boomer shooter aiming and shooting. That combat style has its place, but its not here. In this game, dudes just lunge at you completely irrespective of what other enemies around you are doing, making combat with more than 2 or 3 dudes unmanageable since they can just all attack and stun you one after the other. Is the combat hard? No! Thats to preempt all the inevitable commentors countering this argument with such. No, combat is not hard, but feels very frustrating nonetheless.Yeah...out the door with new ability unlocks that felt good to unlock a new substantial ability, in with marginal boosts that feel meaningless and overwhelming. Many core concepts preserved and extended nicely; somewhat over-complicated in other areas, losing some of the simple appeal of the original.  The drop back to starting level is handled... acceptably (eg some things that were skills to pick up in HZD just come fitted, others Aloy has somehow forgotten).  New skills system looks like it ballooned out of control.  Guerilla - learn when to stop adding things.  Graphics still gorgeous even on an older PC.  New plots, new drama - story carries on, so we lose some of the aspects of first-time wonder, but there's plenty of delightfully bitter commentary on the nature of humanity.The added complexity both opens up tactical options and I think goes a little too far, meaning you probably pick your own subset of mechanics and stick to them.  The multi-key combos feel like a consolization thing; hint, these things work better on console controllers, where the different keys *feel* very different, vs keyboards where they don't.  Controller ergonomics is a well solved science, so be wary of converting that straight to keyboard (don't ask me to swap to a controller though, mouse aiming is always going to be easier).Minor quibbles aside, HFW is still shooting robot dinosaurs with bows and remains better than it has any right to be.  It benefits from the superb backstory of HZD, though I think coasts a little more in terms of storytelling.  If you are going to do H#3, put your back into good story, it's what made the first one so special.In summary, HFW is excellent, and the quibbles come entirely from the comparison to HZD which was absolutely amazing.

Horizon Forbidden West is an excellent sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn that successfully improves upon and adds to the world of the first game, taking you to new and interesting locations in western North America. I rate it 9.5/10 with details below, and I highly recommend you pick this up if you've played HZD.Pros:- Facial animations look much better when compared to the first game thanks to the use of motion capture. Aloy's face looks different as well, but I had no problem with it.- There are so many new machines: Ferret, Kangaroo, Monkey, Pig, Birds, and more Dinosaurs. New varieties of mountable machines are also among the number of added critters.- The story, while not having the same charm of being unique like HZD, was well-written and had me invested the whole time.- Combat has been changed to give players more options in melee with dedicated combos instead of the simple system of HZD. New types of elemental damage have been added along with the return of some flavors from the first game. - All gear can be upgraded, with weapons and outfits being the big-ticket items. The coil/weave system still exists, but now along with the potential to improve gear. There are also additional weapons to play with.- The Burning Shores DLC unlocks after completing the main game quest line, and it's a worthy addition with content you won't want to miss.- There are loads of other things added in this sequel but I'll leave it to you to discover them for yourself.Cons:- Aloy has this awful habit of immediately providing hints to puzzles. Given how many more puzzles are scattered around the world, it's very noticeable.- The downside to the upgrade system is that you have to go to machine hunting grounds and hope for a specific part to drop. I felt like it was a grind.

First, if you haven't played Horizon: Zero Dawn, you really should play that first. ZD isn't as good as this one, but it's still pretty good. It should sell for a lot cheaper when on sale and will introduce you to how the battle mechanics go. More importantly, it does all the world building, and it does it very well once it finally starts clueing you in on how an advanced society is reduced to tribal bands and machines that seem to think they are cows and eagles.The biggest problem, at least for me, with Forbidden West is that it can't build the world again. We certainly do learn more about the world in this game, but nothing like going from a clueless kid to enlightenment. Balancing that, though, are the side stories - something Zero Dawn didn't do so well, and something you'll spend far more time doing in Forbidden West.What FW gives you over ZD is... extensive.  Here's a partial list:If all that is just too much, the difficulty levels will help you out.  The only problem with not taking advantage of everything is that Aloy won't be quite as powerful as she would be otherwise, which you can counter by simply lowering the difficulty level.  Find the level you are comfortable with, and away you go.  If your build is terrible in small spaces and you find yourself in a boss fight in a small space, just drop the difficulty for that one fight and then bring it back up.The game autosaves pretty often and retains the last 10. It will make a special 'boss battle autosave' before fighting a boss, too. Quick saves and manual (permanent) saves must be done at campfires, which are plentiful outdoors but won't be found in "dungeons." I think there's a limit on the manual saves, but I had 25+ of them and didn't hit the limit. Saves execute VERY quickly - so fast I that I don't notice autosaves happening, much like in Cyberpunk.Not all is perfect, naturally. The voice acting is better for the minor characters now and they animate better, but they are all acting as if on a stage and they want to make sure the people back in the cheap seats can feel the emotion. There are lots of head nods, and arms flailing around, and wandering about as they explain (by getting some separation, they can flail around without injuring anyone).More worrisome are complaints about stuck quests. I did run into a couple of spots where the quest requirements were  unintuitive, to say the least, but I never had a quest get stuck. There were other people on the forums complaining about a few, though, so I expect there are some freaky situations than can break them. If you see something weird happening in a main quest, for pity's sake don't try to leave the quest and go play sidequests for another 40 hours hoping it will work itself out, because often times the only fix is to go back to a save from before the quest started.Oh, and with 145 hours under my belt, I've had 0 crashes. Nixxes is really good at what they do!Overall, this game is one of the greats! Zero Dawn was good stuff but, with Forbidden West, the Horizon games get fleshed out into something truly top level. This is what AAA should be!

I'll just get the negatives out of the way right off the bat.Yes, most cutscenes have weird FPS drops. No, it's not nearly as bad as people make it out to be.The biggest issue I have with the game is crafting. A lot of the endgame armor and weapons require an unreasonable amount of grinding big machines which is not always super difficult, but becomes tedious. It's unfortunate, because the machines lose their menace and mystique when you have to kill so many of them. The second issue I have is the minigames. None of them are very interesting or fun. In addition to the frenetic hunting challenges, we have a couple of new ones. Machine Strike is a tactical board game that's way too complicated to learn in the little time it gets. Melee trials are mainly just quicktime events, and duels that scale into high heavens on higher difficulties. And finally, the Arena that rewards all the best gear, but features timed fights against multiple machines.My favorite way of playing, stealth, isn't supported in any of the minigames, and it's hamstrung by other design choices. Mainly it's just that you can't one-shot enemies, so they can alert other enemies, which leads to a lot of waiting. My first playthrough was 161 hours, and I hate to think how much of it is just sitting in the bushes, either observing patrol patterns, waiting for an opening, or waiting for the guards to go back to their business.The new antagonist caused a bit of whiplash at the start, but overall it serves a story so good that I can't really complain.The loot is scattered into too many boxes, and they usually blend into the landscape.And that's all the negatives I can think of. It's really minor stuff. The rest is just great. It's a lovingly crafted open world, with lots of things to do, and almost all of it feels engaging (looking at you, Cyberpunk 2077). The story is actually good, with a few surprises, and has a good message. The protagonist is an interesting character. Most of the NPCs are fun to interact with.But make no mistake; this is not a roleplaying game. It's Aloy's story, and you're there not to take it in wild directions, but to help her realize her destiny. And I have no problem with that.In a nutshell, despite its flaws, I don't think I've had as much fun with a game in years.

TLDR: Good combat. Amazing story and world and characters that gets way better if you play the first game. Needs a good computer. It is a massive game so it comes with problems most of them have. Horizon Forbidden West is a great sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn and thus if you have not played HZD the early parts of the story may feel strange. And so if you want to enjoy one of the best parts of the game to its fullest I recomend playing the first game. The story is one I belive is best enjoyed blind, it has some of the most tuching moments I have experinced in gaming. Sure there are things that may feel strange if one skips large amounts of side content. I also have to say that the voice acting and mocap work is fantastic. The combat is quite good, very similar to HZD but with a way better melee system, the amount of new elements, coils, weaves and skills add a good degree of customization. I have only played the game on Ultra Hard (the hardest difficulty) so I can only speak on the challenge it provides. It makes it so that at anypoint in the game without a dedicated tank build you will be oneshot by enemies. It also makes things like stealth and melee really strange as without a dedicated stealthbuild, stealth is only useful earlygame. Melee feels only useful aginst human enemies, but since you cannot block combat, and the fact that enemies can block you attacks if you spam. Melee combat can feel quite passive,  but with all the cool combos taught to you by the melee pits it can feel quite fluid. But it is weaker than ranged combat by a decent margin. HFW strong points are the world and it's story, and the way they are integated into each other. Now for the bad: The game needs a beefy computer, and even with high specs you can sometimes experince viusal bugs. From my experince this gets worse with New Game+. Due to how long the game is, it can feel grindy and drawn out at times. Especially for farming late game components. I also have to comment on the ending, there seems to be wery mixed feelings on it trought the community. While I enjoyed it, there are problems with it. There is one potentially game breaking bug I have encounterd, one that makes it so that you are unable to hold down any mouse button for a long time. So I can't charge any weapon, making combat almost impossible. The bug does not trigger every time you hod down a mouse button but it gets worse over time. I solved it by loading a older save that did not ahve the bug and enntering combat. (It gets worse in combat). My main complaint with combat is the fact that you can get knocked down and while you cannot take damege in this state you have to suffer trough the animation of getting up and being unable to act. Not only is is simply just a anoying part, but it can put you in a worse situation being uable to doge another attack. There are also timed events , Hunting Grounds and the Arena and I have lost those challenges by laying on the ground for tens of seconds in a singel fight. Lastly there are a ton of content to do, and some of it gets really repetetive and boring after a while, mainly the Rebel:Outpost. I uninstalled it. Here's why.Initially, I fell absolutely in love with the game. I had to do a serious graphics upgrade in order to run it, and when I finally opened up the game on PC, I was in gamer heaven. I loved the new mechanics, the new weapons, and the new story. The Focus works better and more efficiently, underwater exploration is VERY cool, the Shieldwing is awesome (GOODBYE FALL DAMAGE), and eventually unlocking the Sunwing mount ability makes it a WHOLE new game (so um...Aloy can fly...how come, though, she never figured out how to ride Glinthawks...just sayin). HowEVER.The "new and improved" was eventually too much. What's the saying...if it ain't broke, don't fix it? Adding a zillion new elements and machines wasn't necessary. Not only do you have elemental attacks from blaze, corruption, chillwater, etc, you ALSO have plasma. Acid. Purgewater. Cottage cheese. And each machine has an elemental variant, so it doesn't matter if you learn how to insta-kill a burrower, because there's still FIFTEEN MORE TYPES that you haven't discovered yet. I missed the originality of the HZD machines. There were a couple here and there, but somehow this Forbidden West is ALL new machines and ALL new experiences. Would have loved to see a little more of a crossover from the first game. The weapons sucked. There were too many. Too many options and not enough input on what weapon is good for what purpose. Just...too many weapons. And the new upgrading system is weird. You need shards and machine parts to upgrade your weapon, but then you use a bunch of parts to upgrade only to come across a trader who has an even better weapon, so you buy that one and waste a bunch of machine parts and shards to upgrade it, until you find the next better one...can we just stick with modification slots? And can we not LOCK them?The best of the armory, also, isn't unlocked until the VERY end of the game, when you start the DLC. And then you gotta do the find-all-the-bluegleam thing, except it's not bluegleam, and by that time you might as well just complete the DLC and wait till ALL campaigns are done to play with the cool toys. Overall, just a little bit much, as far as the gameplay is concerned. This is also coming from a dedicated Horizon Zero Dawn vet, so I assume I'm not the only one who was a bit of a snob when Forbidden West came out.****SPOILERS AHEAD****The story was lacking, mostly at the end. I get how the point was that Aloy doesn't have to save the world alone anymore, and I kinda liked that, but Varl's death was anti-climactic and unnecessary. Aloy's once-chummy relationship with Erend is stressed, until later in the campaign. He was the BEST side character in the first one, change my mind. Having the Zeniths come into the story and having another Elisabet Sobeck clone was pretty awesome...so, overall, story not too bad, but it was the ending that made me go crazy. You get an exTREMELY frustrating boss fight, only to have the story end with "well, the threat is still coming and there's nothing we can do about it. But HEY, we killed the deranged lesbian lady!!" I expected a MUCH more resolved story arch after all that work, and basically, the news is, we didn't solve the problem. Finally...I'm a pretty conservative gamer. I'm a Christian, in fact. Maybe you didn't know we Christian gamers exist, but we do. I was VERY upset with Aloy's lesbian character arch. I heard the news about it shortly after the game came out on console, but my understanding was that it was a very minimal part of the game, and that it wasn't even a choice that players had to make. Come to find out, the developers, in their attempt to cater to a MINORITY, decide to make the O.G. Aloy, or Elisabet Sobeck, part of a homosexual relationship with the "protagonist" Zenith. So not only is that an unavoidable part of the campaign, Aloy's lesbian character arch comes at the end of the DLC, and no, the player does NOT have a choice in the matter. No matter what response Aloy gives to her "true love", their conversation ends with a very intentional homosexual energy to it. Once I found that out, I stopped. After the ground-shattering success of the first game, with none of that woke crap whatsoever, the developers decide to cater to a minority. If you're gay, I don't hate you. But I hate how society bends over backwards for you. So yeah, I uninstalled the game and I'm now starting a new game save on Horizon Zero Dawn on Ultra Hard mode, to redeem my experience with the second game. Watchers can kill you when you do that, by the way. And Corrupters suck. Anyway. Have a good night.

I've been completely immersed in Horizon Forbidden West—it's an incredible experience from start! Horizon Forbidden West, the highly anticipated sequel to 2017’s Horizon Zero Dawn, is nothing short of phenomenal. Guerrilla Games has masterfully built upon the foundations of the first game, creating an open-world experience that captivates players from start to finish.The Good:Engaging Combat: The battles against elaborate robotic foes are as thrilling as ever. Aloy’s arsenal of weapons and tactics keeps combat fresh and exciting.Stunning World Design: The Forbidden West is a visual feast. From the overgrown remains of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge to the eerie animal-like machines, every corner of the world is meticulously crafted.Compelling Characters: The game introduces a host of characters, each existing in the gray area between friend and foe. Their stories unfold in surprising ways, leaving players guessing until the very end.Deep Lore: The lore behind Horizon’s universe is rich and rewarding. Uncover hidden secrets, explore ancient ruins, and piece together the history of this post-apocalyptic world.The Not-So-Good (Minor Quibbles):Old Habits Die Hard: While Forbidden West improves on many aspects, it occasionally falls into familiar patterns. Some of the exposition-heavy moments could have been streamlined further.Lengthy Playthrough: My relaxed playthrough, including side quests, took around 32 hours. While this provides ample content, some players might prefer a shorter experience.In summary, Horizon Forbidden West is a tweaked, enhanced, and confident sequel that delivers an open world full of compelling characters, an intriguing story, and yes, more super awesome robot dinosaurs. If you loved the first game, prepare to be blown away all over again. And if you’re new to the series, buckle up for an unforgettable adventure.Rating: 9.5/10

I am in the minority and actually preferred HZD. Don't get me wrong, Forbidden West improves on a lot of aspects over the original, but it does suffer from a bit of bloat.Pros: The world is big and beautiful with much more variety than HZD. The new machines are fantastic. The melee system has been vastly improved. The side quests are really good. Climbing has been massively improved in the open world.Negative: Perhaps my biggest gripe is the new weapons and extra elemental statuses. There are a ton of them, and it is difficult to build a load out that satisfies all situations. In HZD a typical load out included a DPS hunter bow, an elemental hunter bow, a sharpshot bow, and the 4th slot was flexible. In HFW you have 6 slots, but need a dps bow, 2 sharpshot bows if you want tearblast + armor piercing + adv precision, at least 2 weapons to cover all the elements, and one extra slot. In reality, the best bows have 2 different ammo slots of the same type, meaning you would need 3 weapons to cover your elements and have no extra slots for things like boltblaster, ropecaster, etc. So in the end you have a super cluttered weapon wheel that actually leaves you less room to experiment with non-bows.Tl;dr; if you loved HZD, you'll love this. If you haven't played HZD, play that first.

Forbidden West is an amazing sequel to Zero Dawn, and improves on everything that game had to offer. I've put about 175 hours into Forbidden West on PS5 and couldn't wait for it to be ported to PC. The PC version of this game is as flawless a release of a game as any other I can remember. I have experienced zero bugs or performance issues. I haven't had one crash or any stutters. The game is absolutely breathtaking and all of the characters have a level of polish and development that is truly amazing. Aloy is more mature and believable as an actual person, rather than a typical protagonist of a video game. For those people who love getting lost in an immersive open world with much more than typical open-world filler, this game is for you. The side quests are nice additions to the game and many develop their own mini story-lines and other minor characters to the game. The only detraction I can see for some people is that the map is absolutely massive. For those of us who love this series, it's a blessing, but I can see how some will find it overwhelming. If you liked HZD at all, you should definitely play Forbidden West. I would not recommend playing this game without playing Zero Dawn as the story is a direct continuation from the first game and does not do much in terms of introducing players to the essentials of the original story. I also play this game on my Steam Deck while on break at work and I can usually get around 40 FPS with reasonable settings with FSR 2.2 quality mode. There isn't a major drop off in terms of visual fidelity that is can be seen with FSR implementation of other games. The game is very CPU intensive so more aggressive FSR settings only hurt performance on the Steam Deck as too much of the game is taken away from the GPU.  I cannot praise this game enough. The story isn't held back by performance bugs and the characters are solid. The voice acting is top notch and the porting to PC from PS5 was incredibly well done by Nixxes Software. I'm currently running the game on a 7900 XTX and 7800X3D and at 1440p max settings, I average around 160 FPS with 1% lows around 135 FPS. The VRAM requirements aren't absurd and I usually find that I'm using about 11GB. Hope that helps!

There are many reasons this game is amazing. As a big fan of the first one, being totally caught off guard and it turning into a true gem, and 100%ing it, this game offers everything the original did, and so much more. Before I even get into the pros, it has to be said: this is perhaps the best dialogue animation I have ever experienced in gaming. The motion capture and expressions achieved in this game were captivating like nothing else I have ever experienced. It really felt as if each person was a unique character without a script. Props to Guerrilla Games for this achievment. It truly helps escalate this game to greatness. The passion put into this title is on full display in cut-scenes and dialogue interactions.- Including the facial animation and detail, the graphics of this game are also just breathtaking. Foliage, ruins, water, people, armor, structures, and even the more fantastical machines and technology all seamlessly blend in. I even tried to look at often textures where game developers prefer to cut corners, and I failed to find much. Other that some remote rocky locations, I was always impressed with the graphics around me. Some people mention there is some yellow light filer in the game, and theres already mods to remove it, but I felt it was fine as is.- The graphics are good, and the optimization on this port, like most other Sony ports, is very well done. I have a very good setup with a 1440p monitor and a 4090, and I run pretty much maxed out natively around 110-135 fps. Other than some slight visual bugs when first engaging in dialogue scenes, Im 35 hours in, and havent noticed anything off.- Combat is like the past game, but better. As you would expect, bigger world, more variants of both weapons and machines, more ways to tackle them, more gear, more in depth skill trees, new abilities, verticality of movement, etc. The devs really just threw in whatever you could want. On normal or easier difficulties, most fights arent too bad, and you dont HAVE to invest much time in going out of your way to upgrade, but I just know it will be mandatory to have builds ready to go for harder difficulties.- The story in this sequel builds off the first one, and constantly raises the stakes. You learn SOOOO much more about the world, its history, and its future. - While the world is bigger, there are more things to do, and a lot of them being interesting, as someone who enjoys a good open world game to get 100% in, Im 35+ hours in, just beat the main story, and going on to the DLC, and I will admit, Im not sure Im all that into 100%ing this title. There are SOOOO many things to go do that feel like are either checklists, or just kind of pointless. Feel like its either the amazing and captivating main story, engaging side quests and exploration, or shopping list grinding. There is a very sharp fall off in enjoyment I believe when transitioning into the tertiary content this game has to explore. I guess I will see, however, as I still have many more hours to go into this title. If I change my mind, I will come back and adjust this review.I am glad I waited to play this masterpiece on PC. This was a beautiful, immersive, breathtaking, technically impressive, expansive, detailed, and just all around amazing experience. I look forward to playing this passion project from the developers more and seeing what else this game has to offer me. I look forward to seeing where Guerrilla Games takes their talents next. I will be waiting.9/10

*SPOILERS IN THIS EDIT BLURB* Edit: After completion, I still feel this review stands. While the game introduces a little bit of QoL in the last 1/4 of the game (SPOILER: flight), it just makes me think that the game could have had some better pacing on top of my other critiques. This QOL makes grinding and powering up so much easier and I think my frustrations around combat and player power would have been alleviated had I been able to go off and farm components easier, earlier in the game.***ORIGINAL REVIEW***I've played this for 82 hours and I think it's time for a review. I'm still not done with the game but I've made my mind up on it enough to post a review; I don't think the last part of the game will sway how i feel about it.I played the first game, and loved it so thought this would be a no brainer, which is why it sucks to be posting a negative review about a game I can tell had a lot of love put into it.***Let's talk about what's good first.-The graphics really well done, beautiful game, I've taken so many screenshots and really enjoyed some of the exploration around forbidden west.-The storyLike I said, i'm not done with the game but i've enjoyed the story so far, I'll update my review should I feel this will change but given where the story is headed, I can safely say this is a positive aspect of the game.- Things to see and do the game has lots of different side missions, quests, mini games, puzzles, etc and I feel they are spread out enough to make the game interesting.- The stamina systemLove the ability to swap different firing modes for my weapon and having that controlled by stamina, this just felt like a better version of the valor system.- Quality of life featuresInfinite inventory, things going to stash when my inventory is full. Nice quality of life feature.- The mapThe way the map looks and displays information is better than any video game I've ever played, the little 3d effect and uncovering parts of the map was super cool.***So why a negative review? What was so bad that graphics and good story drove a thumbs down?- The combat I don't know what happened between this game and the first one but something dramatically changed in the combat cycle. I went back to try out the first game to see if it was just me, but no, the machines feel have so much more armor.The game leans on much larger machines, that are much tankier and difficult to deal with, the machines move faster and are overall much more aggressive.Many more AOE knockdown mechanics, or machines screaming to make your character dazed, you spend much more time on your butt than in the first game.The melee combat in this game and the melee fights was just... horrible. Learn this entire system to do a handful of fights, you'll never use this against machines because they'll constantly stun you if you get into melee with them.- The weaponsFor some reason, the weapons in this game don't feel as impactful as the first, for example the ropecaster in the original game felt like it was useful enough to tie one machine down, however in this game it feels like i need double the shots to get the machine into a tied down state and then have only half as long to shoot before the effect wears off.Status effects expire much quicker meaning you have less of a window to do things in.Bolt blaster vs rattler is feels like a downgrade.Warrior bow is terrible. RIP War bow which was great for elemental infliction.Blast sing feels all around less effective.Shredder gauntlet is fun but hard to use well against the large machines.Spike thrower is pretty neat but is really hard to use against larger machines.So where does that leave you? Hunter bow, hunter bow, hunter bow, hunter bow. The first games weapons felt impactful and strong, but if you're not using a bow like a lot of the combat guides on youtube show up - you're gunna have a bad time.- The skill treeJust like the first game, the skill system is definitely the worst part of the game. I think the game would have been so much better if aloys overall ability was higher without the need to invest skill points.There are so many options, so many choices that as a player, I feel overwhelmed with choice but when i actually get into the talents, they aren't that interesting that it could have just been baked into the characters core power rather than this bad talent system.The trap skill tree sucks btw.- The valor systemI really dislike the valor system, investing skill points unlocks these power up modes that make Aloy do more damage, have better tear damage or whatever but honestly, having to see a cut scene for a quick power up is so so immersion breaking. This is honestly the worst thing in the game, again - why do I need yet another button to press.- The notebookWading through a giant notebook for a quest objective was infuriating - why make me look through this junk to tap in some code when you could literally say "aloy knows the code now, when the player goes to the door she taps it in" why do i have to sift through a bad menu system to find some junk code to punch it in, not an interesting gameplay mechanism, just annoying.- The game lacks "soul"I don't know how to put this and the first game was a little bit guilty of this too, but sometimes zero dawn feels like it's missing that little something that makes it special. This is probably a me problem because I think the new Zelda games have the same problem despite them being acclaimed games.*** OverallA game with many cool things about it but the core combat loop system lets it down, I find myself being frustrated with having to fight machines and than my weapons often suck and I need to lookup a youtube video to figure out where to go and get some better equipment. The game is bloated and gets in its own way with way too much random stuff to do that feels mandatory as I'm constantly underpowered for the task at hand. My talents don't feel impactful nor do my decisions.5/10. Sometimes less is more.

Providing a stash for organizing excessive items, weapons, and resources to get around a carry limit, all new vertical traps and other tools for setting up traps and crossfires, all new skill trees with surges to change the tide of battle. Melee was completely overhauled with an entire skill tree dedicated to it and made it actually viable in combat. Pretty much every aspect of the game gameplay wise felt better. Scanning machines was easier with a single button press cycling between parts, it just really felt like the devs put a ton of effort into taking the series to the next level. Animations were miles better, with facial animations being a major flaw of the first game. Aloy's face conveys so many more emotions in Forbidden West and it really feels like a next gen visual performance.Combat was fluid, if not even more chaotic with the addition of new bigger machines. Some of them were easy to handle with certain elements and some like the new Shellsnapped would put you in a body bag and absolutely melt you if you weren't on the top of your game. Much like the first, I loved how every machine has strengths and weaknesses, which meant that you couldn't just use the same 2 arrow types the entire game. I spent a lot of time planning out attacks and placing traps to turn the tide and the game really rewards you for smart strategies. Of course you can still use unoptimal strategies and plink down machines for 20 minutes from afar, but the possibilities are really endless. When it came to story and writing, Forbidden West is a bit of a mixed bag. The story isn't bad by any stretch, but its not quite as good as Zero Dawn. Like a lot of other games, it suffers from the constant battle between "youre on a timer, the world is ending!" and "hey lets go explore and talk to everyone and solve their little squabbles and problems". Side quests feel more in-depth when it comes to writing and dialogue, yet there's a ton of filler open world fetch quests. Many are simple "go to area, use focus, follow track, fight machine you've fought plenty of" quests. That being said, the major story points and voice acting performances of the characters are phenomenal. Ashly Burch once again shines as Aloy and the late great Lance Reddick puts on an absolutely steller performance as Sylens to create a truly interesting and captivating character and foil to Aloy. The new characters introduced in the game are strong in their own rights, combined with everyones favorites from Zero Dawn being just as great and making their returns. Despite the not as exciting ending, the action picked right back up in Burning Shores. Making it a perfect 2/2 in the series, the Burning Shores DLC was fantastic. In some ways(especially the ending) the condensed storyline of Burning Shores outshines the base games story, with an absolutely mammoth final fight that felt like straight out of a Mission Impossible movie. The new villain is ruthless and hateable paired perfectly with your new sidekick(and possible love interest if you so choose). It was the perfect wrap on the game after 80 hours doing pretty much everything in the DLC and base game besides collectibles. Could some of the fat and filler been trimmed off? Sure it could help, but even with that Forbidden West soars to the upper level of games I've played in the last 5 years and if they come out with a 3rd one to complete the trilogy I will definitely be there to play it.

TLDR at the start hereAmazing game with incredible visuals, improved-ish combat system, great story and phenomenal character roster with great mocap and voice acting. Solid 10/10Now for more a more detailed (spoiler free) reviewThe combat system in this game is both a massive jump forwards when compared to Zero Dawn and equally more frustrating and overly complex.  It took much longer for me to properly grasp how you can best use Aloy's abilities to move and fight more effectively.On the topic of combat there are some new weapon types, these include Shredders which I found marginally useful, Boltcasters (think automatic crossbow) which are fun but heavy weapons that I got some good time into using, Sharpshot, Warrior and Hunter bows all make a return but sadly the Tearblaster doesn't (big sad) I like that the game tries to make all weapon types viable depending on your particular build that you run, changing weapons on the fly is certainly a good tactic and one I used multiple times.There are some negatives with the combat though (as previously alluded to), the biggest one for me was the removal of the "long dodge roll" which was a really good move in Zero Dawn that allowed you to dodge AoE or large slashing attacks more consistently, I wouldn't mind the removal of this so much if the game didn't have a greater emphasis on melee attacks and combos, personally I didn't use them outside of when the game forced me to and the rare time an enemy snuck up behind me.The skill tree is massively overhauled with more skills to learn in more branches, most have a good use and the valor surges are fun to use, on future playthroughs I'm going to take a deeper look at which I should use.Moving on to enemies and the world in general.The amount of machines has been hugely increased, with Corrupted/Daemonic machine variants replaced by Apex versions, personally I prefer this system as unlike Corrupted/Daemonic the weaknesses generally don't change and aren't set to "only fire can really harm it" which adds more diversity to the options you have when engaging them.The new machines are both great and small, with a large portion of the machines from Zero Dawn making a return, my slight gripe is the first machines you meet in game (Burrowers) cannot be oneshot to the eye like Watchers were in Zero Dawn, this may be a deliberate choice to get the player used to using melee weapons (like previously talked about with the slightly reworked combat system) but I found it slightly discouraging, not the biggest issue though.  The new large machine types are a barrel of fun to fight, I loved figuring out the ways you could most effectively take them down and how to maximise damage while avoiding as much in return, and the design of them is top notch as well just like Zero Dawn.The world, map and places are incredible, Guerrilla Games really hit the nail on the head with this one, each new area is visually stunning with a distinct style and aesthetic, I loved exploring the different Tenakth tribes and how they're all so unique but related in subtle ways.  I'm genuinely impressed with how well they do this.  Then you have the later groups that appear towards the end (I won't name them here for reasons) which continue the distinct and inspired visual style which is so recognisable and incredible to look at.The story is well done, although like Zero Dawn I do feel like it takes a bit of time to truly kick into gear, and it's not until about 20 or more hours in that I felt like I was really starting to progress through the set pieces of the storyline, that being said that is most likely my fault for sidequesting so much.  After then I was really captivated by the story, learning and observing all the different emotions, interests and goals combining and clashing with the various factions at play.Speaking of, Characters time, Aloy returns in full form, watching her grow throughout the game was amazing, going from someone who works solo to embracing the team around her and truly having friends, the new and old side characters that are brought back are intriguing and just as well written, with some moments between them being highlights of the game for me.And lastly I'll briefly touch on the finale for the main story (excluding Burning Shores, just the main game), very well done, with a somewhat predictable move from one of the characters, but after what had happened just before you start the finale quest watching a scene during the finale got me hyped, it was almost cathartic watching the scene play out.Anyways, yappathon over and here is my final verdict:10/10 overall package, can't wait for a sequel (also looking forward to the Zero Dawn Remaster)

A very, very good game. If you liked the first one - get it. Otherwise here is some more details.The gameplay:Fighting machines is awesome. This game improves in pretty much every way - there is more weapons, more fighting styles, more elemental reactions. I would say it's better then the previous one at making you use the weaknesses of the machines - weak spots and elements both - without them fights are drawn out. Generally even late game (depending on difficuluty) you will still have to be putting effort in.Human combat is... well. They attempted to improve it and there are combos. They rarely work. Humans are best dealth with from stealth, that has not changed.At the base setting the game can be grindy - particularly when it comes to upgrade materials, because some of them are specific machine parts that you need to remember to shoot off the thing before it dies (or they apparently disappear forver) or not shoot because they'll get destroyed. Yes, you'll get confused. You can also go to custom settings and disable the first part of it and loot it from machine corpses which I edned up doing - yea, immersion, something, I do not have enough patience. But since there is a setting to circumvent it - it's fine.Exploration is amazing. On foot, on variety of mounts and then you get to fly. With the added bonus of being able to throw yourself off cliffs very early in the game (fall damage who?). Climbing got expanded as well and you can climb to most places.We get some nice customisation option of outfits - the favourite "apply look of another outfit that's cute but has damn bad stats", as well as dyes and facepaints, so we can look stylish while we get thrown about by giant machines the size of trucks.The lore and plot:I'd say a tad worse then the first installment - partially because we cannot replicate the sense of wonder and dread at finding out what happened, partially because the Main Baddies are not really utilised to their full potential and some get comically evil. On the other hand we get more npcs to interact with regularly who are decently written and a very nice plot of your friend attempting to coach a socially inept outcast into how to maintain relationships with people. And while I say the main plot wasn't as good as the first one - it was still really well done I think and kept me engaged.New tribes are interesting and distinct from previous ones so it's fun to explore them (though due to location change we pretty much stop seeing any Nora, Carja or Banuk which is sad).Music and graphics:Amazing. Really. Just so pretty to look at. I will keep staring at it.Overall - a reall amazing game. Sure, it has its issues, but a lot of them stem from comparing it to the first one. And human combat sucks, but who would want to fight humans when there are machines around. Haven't run into any noticable bugs. A polished huge open world game with a solid linear story.

Hello there! o/ Has been a while since I made a review but let's take a look at Horizon Forbidden West..What did I like about the game or not and how my experience went during playing the game.Horizon Zero Dawn was an amazing game by its own right. Good storytelling, great graphics and despite the relatively linear gameplay, it felt balanced enough to be a fun experience and I personally had a blast going through that one from start to finishSo how Forbidden West did fare? It's very important to mention that before you play Forbidden West, I strongly suggest that you play Zero Dawn first.While both are different games to their own right, they are very much connected in terms of the lore. so in order to understand Forbidden West, you have to play Zero DawnThe gameplay loop and world design has been expended from the first game by giving the open world more of a purpose to go through and learn more about it. the side story quests + the world itself being larger pretty much reflect that.As for the gameplay? Forbidden West does introduce more weapons and armor sets to play with and giving them a larger role during the playthrough. as a result, if you are interested in maxing out the game. the grind becomes considerably longer. As far as the combat goes? Forbidden West does move away from the simple system in Zero Dawn and instead encourages the player to use their tools more effectively and pay attention to the boss fights for their respective weakspots to do the most effective amount of damage.While I do respect the combat being more challenging, It also had the side effect of making the game feeling more clunky and in some instances.. irritating would be an understatement.Story? As I did mention earlier, Forbidden West continues from the same point we have left off in Zero Dawn. So if you got along with the previous game in that aspect then you will be familiar with the story. Speaking of which? the story itself is interesting and does have solid merit to it but it does suffer from terrible pacing issues at the beginning of the game. the first 2 hours show it really well and most people do off around at that and you will feel like that you are forced to go through in order to enjoy the game.Graphics? Zero Dawn looked amazing and very pleasing to look at and Forbidden West is no different from that. The game looks great from the perspective of models, textures and vibrant colors combined with the open world and other effects like weather changes to polish it up.And since we did brought up models as well. was there any reason to change Aloy's face to have more "fat" to it? as aesthetically, I couldn't find any real reason to justify such changeBut overall, 7/10 in terms of the rating. While the story does have its merits and genuine interest in it. the pacing does hurt and makes it very hard to get into the game if you aren't interested from the get go and while combat has been expended on. It also made the game more clunky within that aspect which does hurt the experience
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys adventure with a bit of danger added for fun.

A great game, good story line, epic graphics fidelity, intuitive mechanics, huge open world map for exploration, GENERALLY very fluid battle experience. It carries over much of the Zero Dawn's feature and expands upon it, making it a very familiar platform for players coming from the previous title. -It is still primarily a bow and arrow game with additional range weaponry added into the arsenal, however the melee combat doesn't quite sit right in this game in my opinion. Sure you can "Make it work" but this is no Souls game, you only have a spear and most enemies have range attacks. It is like bring a knife into a gun fight.-It seems like much of the elemental damage has been significantly nerf compare the Zero Dawn. Fire damage barely tickles enemy, and Shock Ammunition, at least the decent ones is not accessible until very much further into the game. I genuinely though the ideal of these elemental munitions, aside from doing more damage to particular enemies, and being able to detonate elemental canisters, is to enhance your combat power, to kill the machines faster, but sadly it is not the case and it makes me wonder why go through the trouble of drenching enemies in a particular element when it does not enable you to kill it any faster? Why introduce new elements when the old ones frost/shock still triumph above all else? -The Skill system has been revamp and split into different play style categories rather than utility. Though weapons specific skills are tied to a specific skill tree, they generally work hand in hand. I do wish the weapon skill would give you more information on the damage buffs it provides, even it if is just a rough estimation because I for one have been mislead to believe these skill would do a lot more damage, but ended up disappointed. These Weapon Skill are very resource intensive for the amount of damage it delivers. Additionally there is a weapon stamina feature to gate keep the frequency of which you can use these skills during battle, which make me wonder the point of all these nerfs for a single player game? -They added a pseudo Ultimate Skill call Valour which enhances your experience with its respective skill tree. It require combat to build up and upon reaching a threshold you can unleash it for an extremely limited amount of time. Its mostly boost damage capabilities which I personally horde onto this commodity because it is too valuable to be waste on non-boss fights and ended up being a vanity skill that just sits there for the greater part of the game."Our Heroine has found a new World Ending Catastrophe and is out saving the world again!"-Its disheartening to praise a game for not crashing/ rarely crashes which sets precedence on how bad some AAA games is during this day and age. Fortunately Horizon is amongst the better ones.Surprisingly I did not encounter any of the following issues when I played this game on my PlayStation. I wonder if these are PC specific bugs.Other than some well know bugs and glitches, these are the ones that I have experience my self thus far. Note that restarting the game can alleviate most of these issues.-Human Enemies which heads are impervious to all damage. "yup, his head is tougher than Woverines Adamantium Skull"-Quest Characters that you are suppose to follow but their pathing got block by another NCP so they just gave up. Happens often enough for me to take note. -Cover plates for canisters on machine that is unbreakable. -Some open world plants and ancient chest that are stuck beneath/within objects and terrain making it inaccessible. It is not game breaking but it would be nice if it is absent.

A breath of fresh air from "modern gaming". In my opinion it's not as good as the original is some ways (story, atmosphere, progression), but overall it's still a good game.The game just works. And it runs very well on maxed settings @ native 1440p without any upscalers. It's silly that these days this is something that needs complementing, but given how atrocious a lot of big budget game releases are these days I felt that I should point this out. No microtransactions as well, however it does have analytics.The graphics are very good, even though not the best, and most importantly the game is crystal clear. No forced blurry TAA. You can actually see details in the environment.Not much to complain about here really, a very solid port.The bad:* The game  discourages exploration in the first . A lot of collectibles and stuff are locked behind story progression. It's very frustrating, and it made me really not care about collectibles at all.* The main character never shuts up. She will explain every puzzle solution 2 seconds after you reach the puzzle, even with "exploration mode" setting. She will try to fill silence at all times, even when standing still in a bush waiting for enemies to pass. And there's no setting to tone this down* Movement, especially climbing is not as solid as it should be. You just can never be sure whether the character will grab a certain ledge or land on a beam, or just fall to her death for no reason.* The glider mechanic is also unreliable, sometimes it will just not activate because it's a "hold to open" action, not instant on key press, sometimes the grappling hook will activate instead because they are bound to the same key.* Ammo type variety is vastly expanded here, but it feels too extreme. There are so many special arrows and I don't even know what most of the non-elemental ones do. On normal, the default Hunter bow did 90% of the job for me. The first game required me to use a ropecaster to take down stormbirds, made it a lot easier, but here it seems to not really do much.* Outfit and Weapon upgrades are straight up just worse here, especially the higher rarity items. The problem is that they require specific machine components that you need to manually shoot off of enemies and that gets very tedious when enemies are quite slow to kill. Some of these items are entirely RNG based, and each weapon requires a decent amount to upgrade. There are a lot of weapons and weapon types, and upgrading them each to test what you prefer is just not viable, so I ended up just using 1 weapon for most of the game, compared to 3 or 4 in the first game.* Traps are still largely useless, at least on normal. More so than the first game even. They are not very strong without upgrades, have weird limitations and are slow to place, and there aren't many situations where you know enemies will walk towards you so you can prepare.* The game felt kinda too long. This may be a good thing to some, there's undeniably a lot of things to do, but far from every quest is compelling.* Some keybindings are weird - fast travel is right click, world interactions are sometimes via a "use" key and sometimes left mouse button. Stopping a playing audio log is E, and so is "pick up item". Map panning is very slow for no reason.The good:* They removed annoying inventory limits that were present in the first game* A good amount of accessibility/difficulty settings* A lot more fights alongside friendly NPCs* Each Cauldron and Tallneck feel very distinct from each other compared to the first game, they are not just different parkour paths, there are actual different gameplay elements involved* There are also no long overdrawn animations in the UI, everything feels snappy, as it shouldThe overall story is a mixed bag. The best part of the game is still the world building in my opinion. The first half of the game is kinda cool and there are lot things that happen that make sense, which I liked.But the main villain(s) () are not really fleshed out and therefore are not really interesting, They feel like generic bad guys without any logical motivation for their actions. The last few missions of the game feel kinda rushed, and the conclusion is not really satisfying, but I guess I don't know what I expected.I also didn't really like how they handled certain character(s) from the first game here. Burning Shores DLC is not much better. The main villain is just as generic and uninteresting as the main game, and I really didn't care for the the seemingly forced in romance subplot, it just doesn't feel believable. The only saving grace is that the final boss fight is pretty cool, probably the best between the 2 games.

Another quite generic AAA open world game, just as the first one. Must be one of the safest sequels to a game I have ever played. Really does nothing new at all except for the phenomenal visuals and animations, but the first game looked great already. Everything is basically the exact same or sliiiightly improved except for the story which was a bit more interesting in the first, but that is understandable as the universe they were setting up was completely new back then. The only things that I actually do not like are the really repetitive and bloated dialogue scenes with not much substance, constant looting/crafting, the climbing and getting knocked down in combat. Sometimes the dialogue works, but most feels quite bland and as one who is interested in the lore of this universe it became kind of a chore to try and learn more. May or may not be mostly my fault though for pursuing it that much, but I still thought it was difficult to be interested in what was going on, especially in the stuff beyond the lore. I found the story kind of lame and I felt barely anything the whole way through (mostly due to the characters being pretty bland and that "emotional scenes" barely affected anyone) but it was not bad, just kind of bland. A decent ending tho, but a bit too focused on setting up a sequel than finishing off the current games story in a satisfying way. Aloy has an arc which is interesting in itself, but it is just not that convincingly told imo and could have been way better. She basically only has one mode and that is to save the world, and barely develops any sort of relationship with any other character which just feels off. Climbing manages to feel both too precise and imprecise at the same time and also way too scripted and "stop and go" feeling. There is no real momentum in your movement. Also the grappling hook is a dull gimmick and you will never use it in an interesting way. There is way too much junk to constantly pick up (you can set certain things to be picked up automatically without an animation which is a plus) to marginally upgrade generic tiered gear which kinda sucks. The combat is great except when you get knocked down. I have no problem with the concept itself, but the time you are knocked down is just way too long and machines often resets before you are even up which may cause a constant knockdown loop which is just not that fun. Keep the mechanic but shorten the get up animation a bit. But as I said the presentation is stellar, love that everything is performance captured, really cool universe/lore/worldbuilding and the combat is great (against robots, humans are slightly better than the first game). Basically just like the first game except the performance capture part.It was kind of jarring for me to go between this and Ghost of Tsushima, as that one manages to feel quite special and like they are trying and succeeding to achieve something a bit more than just another product to consume. Kind of like how Disney movies generally feel today compared to (mostly) non Hollywood. Sure, GoT is not the most special game ever, but it is nice to see something with that high of a budget strive and succeed in something more. Also easy to compare as they are from the same publisher and competing in the same open world market. I just find this series kind of lame and I still do not really understand why this series keeps receiving the really high praise it gets, but the games are definitely not bad and deserve to exist just as much as any other. I get that people may get easily attached to it as it is very safe and comfortable, which is completely valid. Probably just is not really for me which is fine. It is hard to be bad trying to appeal to as many as possible, but it is also hard being anything above just decent if that is what you try to do. This sequel is especially "frustrating" as it seems to have taken almost no inspiration from other newer open world games throughout the 5 years it took to develop making it feel a bit dated in some of its design, especially compared to a certain one that released at the same time as the first. I just wish the game and franchise was better as I can see that there is a lot of passion and love behind it. Still, I am having quite a lot of fun though, especially as I was kinda craving a "fast food game" at this moment-7/10Burning shores: More of the same, but it is more accepted and expected when it comes to dlc. For once in this game (was handled pretty well in ZD from what I remember, mostly because everything was new to both player and Aloy) there is a relationship/friendship that is actually convincing and Aloy manages to be more expressive because of it. Actually showing a personality beyond "basic hero". The person is even more present during missions instead of just sitting at the home base as a living info dump. Not amazing and a bit rushed, but a welcome change and pretty good. It almost feels like they knew there was a problem with Aloy in the main game and they desperately had to make her interesting. Story was way more focused than the main plot which made the pacing feel better. The final setpiece was also very impressive, probably more impressive than anything in the main game actually though more so in visuals rather than gameplay. I even liked the ending more here as the main games ending was a little bit unsatisfying. Pretty good way to finish off the game.

I 100% completed Horizon Zero Dawn.I didn't even finish Forbidden West.While the good parts of Zero Dawn are all here, all the worst parts are also back, and unfortunately worse and more present than before.  My main gripe with this entry is the amount of insane grinding you need to do for even half-decent equipment.  When you buy gear, you need to trade specific machine parts along with scrap metal to get what you want.  Not bad.  I can deal with that.  Ok, now if you want to upgrade that gear you have to grind even more machine parts.  The higher the rarity, the more pieces you need, and the higher difficulty of machines you need to kill.That sounds pretty annoying right?  Now let's throw in the "Apex" machines.  You'll end up needing parts from Apex versions of different machines.  They are not confirmed spawns.  You need to go to machine spawns at night and hope they spawn.  Sometimes you'll need several of the same Apex machine.Half of my playtime (or maybe even more) was spent running around grabbing parts to make my weapons even usable. And why did I need those weapons to be good?  Well in order to get better weapons of course.  And what did I need to do to those weapons?  Upgrade them.  Grind, upgrade, purchase, repeat.  Holy ♥♥♥♥ I can't do it anymore.  The amount of snoozer platform puzzles around every corner was extremely annoying as well.  Ever ladder was some kind of gimmick.  Every bridge had to fold or collapse followed by Aloy shouting "Welp!  Looks like I'm not going that way!" Can a man just run around and shoot robots without having to pull switches, dump flooded rooms, and kick ladders every 5 minutes?And last but not least, the arena.  Oh man, the arena.  I'm all for doing some sort of robot killing challenge to test my skills.  A timed challenge?  Ok, annoying but fine.  How about every single arena stage being timed and it costs scrap to retry?  Who in their right mind thought this was a good idea?  Obviously I'm just going to reload the save if I fail, which only makes it take longer.  This adds absolutely nothing to the experience other than frustration.If you can get passed this, and you enjoyed the combat of Zero Dawn then I say go for it.  As for me, I couldn't go another minute in this game without losing my sanity.

Every detail, from the wind, the dust from the ground bouncing as Aloy runs, from sea waves and the incredible simulation of sea swells, this game left me with my mouth open every 2 minutes, it's something out of the ordinary.I liked the first game, although it wasn't anything great. This one, while it improves on many of the aspects of its predecessor, doesn't improve the combat in my opinion. However, the story had a continuation that you don't see much in games nowadays, in which it maintains past and new characters, and tells a story that leaves anyone with a feeling of addiction.But what I think, where the game shines, is in its exploration of the world, in the detail of each area visited. Every puzzle in this game is done in such a relaxed way, but at the same time, it requires the player to use their imagination and curiosity. It looks like Lara Croft had a child with Nathan Drake, for me that's the end result of this impressive game, one of the best audio visual experiences I've ever had as a gamer.I think, however, that the game's progression was not thought enough by level designers, as any player who wants to play secondary content is almost 95% of the time forced to continue playing main missions, took me around 15-20 hours to unlock all different gadgets that blocked progression. I found myself with 90% of the map uncompleted at first, because most locations required gadgets locked by main missions. Gear management for me got worse also, in zero dawn you had a bow for humans and another for machines, they all had if recall, shock, fire and normal ammo, the other had precision arrows and against armor ones, this time around you got all these 6/7 types of weapons and for me it makes no sense as most of them as rarely used and why having fire bows, cold bows, electricity ones, why not have all elements in the same, aloy changes arrows, why carry 5 bows, they are all made of wood, they're not special, but well it is a video game, but i think zero dawn kept it simple and nice, not that i dont like the spike thrower for example, but makes 0 sense having so many effects at once in a bow, simply put it only in other types of weapons. Having to deal with humans in this game is a pain in the ass, i loved outposts in the previous entry but now i mostly try to avoid it as you can no longer 1 shot humans anymore, you can only stab them stealthy now.Alas, i do think Horizon Forbbiden West is a 9.5 out of 10, and i do think combat got worse somehow, some machines are way overpowered and some of the game mechanics like dodge at times feel completely useless in some situations, but it may be me that am not good enough. 50 hours, i am yet to complete half the map, yet to start the expansion, and i have not finished the story yet, huge game, an almost perfect game, with amazing parkour sequences and that continues the story of aloy, a very believable character, with a very charismatic personality.

Horizon: Zero Dawn - 8,5/10Horizon: Forbidden west - 7/10In detail: (Spoiler warning)Overall, a good game, worth buying, enjoyable, though nothing extraordinary.played on normal difficultyStorytelling/Lore: 9/10 (major factor for me)Graphics: 9,5/10 (minor. sadly high HW requirements)Combat: 8,5/10characters/NPC: visually 8,5/10 ; personalities, interests: 4,5/10 (most of them very uninteresting, but there were great exceptions)Machines design: 10/10Side quests (everything - side, errands, camps,...): 4/10. (same as with NPCs)Skills: mmm... 6/10. Havent used 80% of them, used mostly passive ones for dmg or concentration boost.Gear: 7,5/10. Good, but a bit over-done. too much combinations to find the one for your playstyle.Voice acting: 9/10Differences between ZD and FW:pullcaster - pointless "improvement", climbing could have been done very well without it. And the pulling beams or vents was pointless even more so.Free climbing - mmm... I would say needles as well. I understand why you put it into the game, but it was super glitchy (especially with vents in the cauldrons) and often handyless. Like when you jump aside in the middle of a fight and you latch yourself onto the mini-boulder nearby, getting hit three times before you manage to get yourself loose.focus activation/pulses - usefull, good idea. the need to scan your target several times during a fight to reveal again and again his weak spots was annoying, but other then that it was a good addition.Cauldron and tallnecks variety: good idea, to make cauldrons less monotonic.Stash - great addition. would have been even better if there would be "sell from stash" option.A few more positive things from me:I love Sylens'es design. His voice acting, presentation, calmness, stoic expressions.I was very intriquided by the Zeniths and their design, as well as by the mystery around them.Machines are designed very well. I enjoyed every single fight. Especially the Slitherfangs were fantastic!Graphics, even though I have played on the lowest possible settings, were spectacular.Lack of swearing. I do not mind occasional F-bombs or Sh-words, but it is good the game went through mostly without any of it.Tennakth and Quen design was interesting.A few more negative things from me:Arena - The whole game is turning around you fighting machines on almost every step you make across the map. And as a bonus, to get the best gear in the game, you have to fight even more (a lot of!) machines to get them. As if there wouldnt be enough of it everywhere else on the map.Cutscenes where Aloy is useless. She can take down Thunderjaws, Tremortusks, scorchers without getting hit, but when she faces Erik she is COMPLETELY without wits or strength, being held under neck and flailing helplessly.I was VERY disappointed how the rebellion got its conclusion. Vast majority of the game, the rebellion is viewed as the main things, but the crescendo of it is basically whole skipped to your fight against Regalla herself... I felt a great amount of pity for her after she was defeated. I understood her too well, and I really wished she would have some kind satisfaction in the end...Utaru design was dearly uninteresting. (though Zo herself was cool, in her way.)Conclusion: Worse episode then Zero Dawn, but still pretty enjoyable and worth buying and playing. non-proffesional advice: spend less money on graphics developement and throw more into quests and character design.Looking forward for another episode, though a bit less then after ZD.Thanks for the game!

It's a very young-adult story over a somewhat cool videogame. If you're in your teens or early 20s, you will probably find a lot to like, here.Much older, and you'll have seen these story beats many times before. Also, the perspectives on offer will feel flat, obvious and underdeveloped. Aloy's a lady who needs to learn the value of friendship. She'll turn down help like she's allergic to it. Someone will tell her "hey don't go out there yet; the other nations will get the wrong idea and we'll have a war." She'll respond "screw that; you can't tell me what to do" and then run out and accidentally start a war. She won't ever reflect on that.Then, her friend will say "I came out here to help you" and she'll respond "GOSH DARNIT Varl I told you to stay in the DAD-GUMMED car!" And she'll be an entire character arc away from realizing how hypocritical she is. But we see it right away.Also, for what it's worth, I really don't understand why she hates Sylens, so much.  He's not really getting in her way. In fact, he's inviting her along to learn with him. She'll mutter "that blasted Sylens" and I'm sitting here "what problem exactly is he causing, right now?" But that doesn't really matter. Aloy straight up fires Lance Reddick the actual actor in the beginning of the game, so that Sylens dynamic is abruptly cut short.Bad guys are punished for having unchecked egos and control fetishes. You'll read a bunch of text logs by and about Ted Faro. They are all various versions of "muah ha ha haaaaa" if by him or "Ted just yelled 'muah ha ha haaaaaa' in front of everyone," if about him. All other villains in this story are the same thing.This one also continues the sort of half-attempted perspective on gender roles that the first one started. Men are one way. Women are another way. According to this story, anyway. That perspective seems interesting when we're young, or when we're watching standup comedy specials from the 1980s. When we're older, attempts to classify people so rigidly seem childish and lacking wisdom.It's a very long game, too. I'm bee-lining the story, but I have to step outside the path for long stretches in order to find upgrade materials for my armor and weapons. Long stretches of time. I need an apex thingy heart to bring my bow to level 3/5. So I go kill some apex thingies and hope the dice roll in my favor and a heart drops. I've got 46 hours so far, about to start the final stretch.I'm not really sure why I stuck with this. That probably says something about it. I've put Skyrim down 100 times since it first came out due to boredom. I'm bizarrely compelled to finish this, though.
