After finishing both the main and dlc quest, I have revised my review to a positive. I have also added a few additional notes. I have also bumped my score to an 8 out of 10 from the previous 6. My pros and cons:PROS - Dialogue camera is so much better. Instead of two characters just standing idly and moving their mouths, all dialogue has been given a unique scene. Makes it more dynamic. - Memorable characters. Some new some old. Still keeps with the same pace of personality that makes them so memorable. - Advances the story in interesting ways. - I like the new skill system and giving most weapon three special moves is pretty dope- Tons of new machines. Very nice. - I like the verticallity in exploration. - There are numerous sidequests that lead to another sidequest, tying together the world. - There are also numerous sidequests that affect the world, it's really nice to see that your actions can be seen in the world you're exploring. - Since the game wants you to complete its main story first, I do love that they added in additional dialogue from most, if not all, sidequests that address the main story. MIXED- The new weapons are awkward to use and most of the times you're just going back to your trusty hunter and sharpshot bows. - The intro is pretty long. I remember getting into the world of Zero Dawn in 10-20 minutes. Here it felt longer. Maybe it was just the cutscenes? That's why it's mixed. - There are times where I felt brute force is the only way to beat a machine instead of comboing different weapons to work with each other.- You need to finish the main story before you go exploring or sidequesting. This may sound restrictive, and it is, but the game does compensate for it in many ways. See the positive note above. CONS- The direction in cutscenes is horrendous. Too many times Aloy is just watching as something important unfolds when she's perfectly free to do something about it. At least give her something to do during those moments to excuse why she's unable to stop it. - They gave melee depth, but it's terrible. They introduced Fighting Pits to teach you how to melee, but in all honesty you will quickly forget about it. - Human enemies are insanely strong. It comes to a point where humans will give you more trouble than machines, which is dumb. - Player Direction. The game loves throwing stuff at you, but they never tell you how to get it. Aloy will constantly say stuff she sees, but you'll be scratching your head to see what she's talking about. The game also loves to remind you how to do stuff when you don't need it, and then it stays quiet in times where you do. This is the game's biggest flaw for me. You can't say ♥♥♥♥ like "I should do X" and not at least tip us in the right direction. I'm not asking for hand holding, I'm asking for consistency. - Machine Strike. They introduced a new minigame, a board game where you have little pieces representing machines with each having its own stats. You then build your own set and fight against other players. Let me tell you something, the only time I had fun playing this minigame was the very first game after tutorial. The AI is ridiculously one sided in strategy that you're FORCED to cheese to win. No fun at all. - Much of the extra dialogue leads nowhere or adds too little. At times it feels like they're padding for content. - Camera work needs improving. You often run into rubble, trees, stones, etc. because the camera is too damn close. - Like Zero Dawn, this game has low replayability. Once I finish this game, I don't think I'll be touching it again until a new game in the franchise is available for purchase. 8/10 overall.

This review is about the game itself, not the PC port. If you played it on Playstation and just want to know if the migration to PC is worth it, I'd say yes, it is. The frame rate is stable, what few bugs I encountered were annoying but easy to fix, and the whole thing generally feels polished.Now to the game itself.I'm sad to say that after the awe and wonder  inspired in me,  failed to elicit the same emotional response. I normally spend a bit of time with introspection at this point, trying to pinpoint where exactly the game dropped the ball, but in this case that's unnecessary for it is blatantly obvious.First of all, technically the game is great. Graphics have been improved even further, the world is gorgeous and lovingly crafted, the soundtrack is really good. The new machines are all incredibly impressive, well-animated and a whole lot of fun to fight. Well, most of them, anyway (damn Clamberjaws...). That gets us to the gameplay, the first aspect where cracks began to show. It's safe to say that  is peak 2020s gaming, and I don't mean this as a compliment. Whoever designed the gameplay seems to have tried to cram absolutely every tired old open-world and action RPG gameplay element in the book into this one game. Grappling hook? Check. Pointless food crafting for temporary buffs? Check. Convoluted yet utterly pointless melee combo system in a game that's 99% ranged combat? Check. About twice as many mostly pointless collectibles as in HZD? Oh, you bet. Incessant internal monologue by the player character clearly meant to make sure even the dumbest player can figure out the game's simple puzzles? You guessed it, check. I could probably list another dozen examples, but you get the gist of it. The only gameplay element in  that's actually fun and somewhat unique to engage with is fighting the machines. Everything else has been done a hundred times before, with next to no innovation whatsoever. The next thing that put me off was the completely uncalled-for overhaul of the weapons mechanics. Veterans of the first game will remember how it used to work: hunter bows dealt physical and fire damage, war bows covered most of the other elements, sharpshot bows launched my beloved Tearblast arrows, and so on. Each weapon class had four to five models that differed only in their base stats, growing stronger as you progressed through the tiers.Well, in , every weapon is pretty much unique. You can find just about any element on any weapon, in random combinations that inevitably have massive overlap. The tier system still exists, but if you grew attached to a particular weapon, no exact equivalent on a higher tier exists. Why would it? That would be way too easy and convenient. I found it incredibly frustrating to try and recreate the HZD weapon roster I was used to. In fact, it's pretty much impossible on a first playthrough. For instance, the one high-tier sharpshot bow with Tearblast arrows in the entire game can only be acquired in a New Game+ campaign, basically forcing you to play about 100 hours without it. The game seems to try to compensate for this with more slots on the weapon wheel, which does functionally work, but it can't do a thing about the fact that all this extra gear needs to be upgraded separately.And oh boy, the upgrade process... I can't begin to describe how incredibly grindy this part of the game is. You'll spend hours upon hours upon hours just getting a single legendary weapon or armor maxed out, and there's scores of them. True, you won't need most of them, but still, it's tedious AF.Now that my gameplay pet peeve has been adressed, let's get to the main reason why I can't in good conscience recommend this game, and unfortunately, it's part of the peak 2020s gaming mentioned earlier.  is by far the most misandrist game I've ever played, or even heard about. About 70% of all named characters are women. Almost all the game's movers and shakers are women. If a villain is female, they'll turn out to be of the tragic sort that usually can be redeemed. Conversely, all male villains are absolute monsters without even a hint of redeeming qualities. All the game's most powerful fighters are female. One of them, and I kid you not, is an old woman in her late 60s who swings around a giant sword that looks to be heavier than she is, and this granny is the Forbidden West's officially recognized, undefeated arena fighting champion. Let that sink in for a moment. Every other sidequest is given by, or involves, a woman who was or is being kept down by men, had her revolutionary invention stolen by men, had to go on the run so she could escape the oppression by men, or just wants to take revenge on some abusive man. If a quest involves searching for a group of missing persons, the one survivor will almost always be a resourceful woman, or a meek, useless excuse for a man who survives only because Aloy bailed him out in time.Speaking of male characters, they're almost to a fault either useless sissies, stupid jerks, or allegedly badass warriors who still exist only to enable and praise Aloy every chance they get. None of them shows any noteworthy amount of agency. Probably the best (or worst) example is Erend, our favorite Oseram Vanguard captain from HZD. He's back, and literally his only contributions to the entire mainquest are 1) gushing over how badass Aloy is every time they talk to each other, and 2) carry something heavy during the final quest. That's it, that's everything he does. What a disgrace.Aloy herself has also taken a sharp turn for the worse character-wise. After taking much of the first game to learn that she can't - and doesn't need to - save the world alone, she apparently forgot all about that in the few months between the games and is now back to pushing everyone away, only to then complain about how lonely she is. Yeah, no s***, Sherlock. She's also frequently one of the worst offenders in terms of how men get treated in this game, often displaying stereotypical girlboss behavior to a degree that would be comical if it wasn't so offensive. Apart from that she's turned into a downright Mary Sue who can do everything, knows everything, is instantly better at everything than any (male) expert with decades of experience, is never wrong, can bulldoze through any and all established laws and customs without suffering any consequences, and can bully everyone into doing what she wants without anyone holding a grudge over it. Now that I've finally gotten all this off my chest (I've been waiting to do so for days because I wanted to finish the game first), I want to make one thing perfectly clear: I absolutely enjoy well-written strong female characters in fiction, and I'm a sucker for strong women in real life. I want equality and fair treatment for everyone regardless of gender, sexual orientation, or whatever else they identify themselves through. What I do take offense at is this insane school of thought among modern-day writers that a character can be written as strong by portraying everyone around them as irredeemably evil, weak, or stupid. That's not how that works. A D grade in school doesn't magically become a good grade just because everyone else in class got an F. Applying this to  makes the whole thing especially frustrating because it was absolutely unnecessary. Aloy proved her strength in HZD while paired with, or pitted against, mostly competent sidekicks or enemies. This switch in characterization only weakens her, denigrates everyone else, and thus creates nothing but a lose-lose situation overall. It's just sad, and it makes me worry about how the next installment in the series will approach this issue.

Played HFW and Burning Shores to completion before writing my review. I won't keep you in suspense, the game is an interactive novel! I absolutely loved every aspect of the game: visuals, fluidity, depth of character, story and lore, and the world is so amazing, I'm blown away at the artists ideas, and programmer's ability to bring it to life. I can't say enough good things about this game, and highly, highly recommend it! There are, however, a few things that rob it of having the "Perfect" title. 1. Mount Control - Land mounts are easier, but flying can be irritating when you're close to things. Basically, you have to aim your pointer in the direction you want to go, and move forward only, it seems. I wish you could get closer to things when flying, but it is what it is.2. Dismounting in the air - This was dangerous, and frustrating at the same time. So many times I wanted to dismount, and glide, but would keep reattaching to the bird. I would either have to look straight up/down to not have the option to re-grapple the bird, or fall uncomfortably far before gliding.3. Swimming - Probably my biggest complaint about the game. Never really got used to it, and no matter what, she's crazy slow. Pressing to go a certain direction is sluggish, and she doesn't spin before heading a direction other than straight forward. Caught under things so many times, it was annoying.That is actually it. Those 3 frustrations are minor, and don't dampen my appreciation for the game at all. However, another item I find a bit annoying is the very obvious shift in, how can I say this...gayness. I don't care if a company wants gay characters in the game. It isn't the inclusion of gay characters. What doesn't make sense is the hard-turn shift between HZD and HFW. All of a sudden, nearly every character seems to be gay. Helping a trans troop leader find a Sky Clan guy who went to get a flower on a snowy mountaintop, the two Quen navigators you help at Landings find gear to get back home. Eventually you find out the Diviner you help out is gay, and then of course the finale that, unfortunately, Youtube spoiled for me on a suggestion feed. Not to mention the Sky Clan colors (which were pretty cool with the thick-haired armors), and the "pride" face paint "special" option. It was just so much all of a sudden. It honestly felt like pandering.Again, if a company wants that element in their game, fine, but it just felt rushed, like a quota was needing to be met, and so they just dump a bunch in all at once. There is so much character development in HZD, and it's awesome, and then HFW comes along and we're introduced to all these new characters that are gay. I laughed at how gay the game was when I realized Las Vegas/San Fran/LA were the ruins...lol. Honestly, my biggest problem with the gay aspect in this particular setup, is the setting in which it's occurring: small tribal populations looking at impending global destruction. Especially in Burning Shores. They lost most all their people, and are stranded where they are with no contact with the mainland. Again, it just felt rushed, and out of character for the rest of the fully-developed characters in the game. Outside of some gameplay aspects, and what felt like rushed-demographic appeasement, this game is one of  my top all-time favorite games ever, alongside God of War, and Legend of Zelda. It plays like a novel reads, and leaves you wanting more. It always stinks having to wait for the next release, but usually winds up being worth it. HFW was an awesome follow-up to HZD, and I can't wait for the 3rd installment. Take all the time necessary to make it perfect, please. Note for readers of this comment: This is my honest, long-thought review after over 200 hours of deep play. I did nearly 100% of the game, and loved it. I say that to say this: if you can't get past my slightly-negative take on the injection of gayness from HZD to HFW, just move on to the next review. It's okay to disagree, and move on.

Arrrrghs!!! Why did they add a cool feature that was sorely missing from HZD like the arena but make it so terrible? It's the WORST! Each level progression can only be completed with a fixed loadout battle which provides a bunch of weapons I hate and never use. Just let me use my preferred weapons! I pretty much only use bows. I use hunter, longshot, and warrior bows. All the other weapons are trash. I get that the fixed loadout makes sense in the context of a leaderboard. But the leaderboard is clearly nonsense because the top players have negative times recorded. I absolutely hate online features in single-player games. Usually you can just ignore them. But not for the arena. If you want to progress to the next level, you have to complete the leaderboard battle. Why didn't they just make the leaderboard battles a separate category so it doesn't affect the regular arena progression? I'm changing my vote to thumbs-down entirely because of the arena leaderboard battles. Why can't single-player games just be single-player?Even though I really like HFW overall, I don't get how they implemented an expanded melee combat system that is so very bad. Aloy has no block, parry, or counter abilities even though every human enemy has those. I'm guessing they started developing a more comprehensive combat system but couldn't bring it together so they backed it out. Dodge is the only defensive ability she has. But even that is flawed. The success of a dodge is mostly based on timing it correctly. But you also have to get far enough away from the attacker otherwise you still get caught by the tail-end of his attack. The dodge should either be timing-based or collision-based. It should NOT be both. That is a very poor design! It is extremely rare for me to purchase games on release day. But HZD is one of my all-time favorites so I wanted to show support for the HFW port. I figured there would be some issues and some patches to come. I'd just patiently wait for those before really digging into the game. However, the PC port seems, as far as I can tell, pretty close to flawless. I haven't had any issues other than the slightest of frame-drops during a particularly intense machine battle. I'm running it on a 3080 at 4K with mostly high graphics settings. That seems more than reasonable. So many kudos to Nixxes for the quality work they did.As for the game itself... I have mixed feelings. I tend to prefer the more simplified, projectile-oriented combat of HZD. I pretty much only used the various bows and sometimes the ropecaster. The spear always seems like more of a backup weapon. And the slings, rattlers, and what-have-yous never really appealed to me. That being said, I don't  the new combat schema. After all, if you just want to use the bow, they don't strong-arm you into other combat modalities. They did improve some things I disliked in HZD. For example, if you tell your mount to go a specific speed, it will continue going that speed indefinitely. You don't have to continuously prod it to keep its speed up. It's a minor thing but I found it very annoying so I'm glad they fixed that. The overflow inventory management they added is pretty great. Each unique item has its own capacity rather than a shared, global capacity. I really hate inventory management so I'm very pleased that I haven't been forced to do that. And they added all sorts of nifty options like auto-pickup items that are not currently maxed-out. Players who really enjoy the immersion of commanding Aloy to pick up every little stinking item still get their fix. But I'm able to avoid that tedium. I'm a big fan of options. I never understood why developers have historically been unwilling to add these kinds of quality-of-life options that allow individual players to maximize their enjoyment. I'm guessing most players never bother to change these options. But I know there are plenty of people who want these options because so many of the most popular mods you find for games are geared towards providing them. So why not just bake them into the game as native features? Finally, I'm a pretty big fan of the HFW Focus improvements. I like that you can now tag individual components. Not only that, you can tag components on each individual enemy. How great is that?!Overall, I'm extremely satisfied with this game. And it's very refreshing to play a new PC release/port without any major issues. If more game releases went as smoothly as HFW, I'd be more likely to buy them sooner rather than waiting a year or two for a Steam sale.

tl;dr Horizon Forbidden West is a good game, but IMHO it's not as good as Horizon Zero Dawn.  If you wanted HZD but more, of everything, then you'll love HFW.  I certainly wanted more of HZD, just not more of *everything*...I've played HZD through fully twice, so a lot of my perceptions of HFW are based on comparisons to the first game.Story - The storyline is great.  It was interesting and compelling and it kept me wanting more throughout the main story.  The hub is good, but could have been used to do more.  More companion quests, for example.Fighting - The fighting mechanics are as tight as HZD and a great deal of fun.  There's still nothing quite like taking down a Thunderjaw!Inventory management - This has been streamlined a lot, and I liked the stash mechanic.  Not as much as infinite inventory, but better than nothing!  Managing which potions you were carrying was a little irritating, which would have been helped by having a "standard loadout" setting somewhere.  Having more weapon slots is good, though not really necessary for my playstyle.Graphics - Nothing to say here, really.  It's a very good-looking game, and animations are extremely good.Sounds great, right?  So what do I find wrong with it?Keyboard controls - I hate poor keyboard control implementation.  I bounce off Cyberpunk because of the awful control set-up.  I felt a lot of that in HFW as well.  In HZD TAB brought up the weapon wheel.  In HFW it is hardcoded to bring up the inventory/journal/map overlay.  So you need to use one of the other, limited in number, easy to access keys.  In HZD shift-click to heavy attack.  Which is not possible in HFW (can't have multi-key combinations at all) so it's tied to a key/mouse button.  So I virtually never heavy attacked.  Just a terrible PC port, as far as control scheme.  And there's no good reason for this - it's just lazy porting.Inventory capacity crafting - I just didn't need 3 times the wildlife variety (probably more than 3 times...), in order to upgrade pouch size.  It's a lot of wildlife farming to get everything upgraded.  In HZD I remember the hours of farming racoons and salmon to get those final upgrades.  In HFW it's worse.  Much, much worse.  It ends up being too much busy-work/grinding for something you really want to be getting.  Especially for sharpshooter bows, where the max capacity is massively reduced compared to HZD.  Weapon/armour crafting - Being able to upgrade weapons/armour is a good idea, but the way it's implemented really adds to the grind, thereby devaluing it.  Being able to create jobs for finding crafting items is a lifesaver, but I feel like it's more patching a bad system rather than being a positive thing to add.  With the need for niche machine parts, it's just a bit of a slog.  You spend so long upgrading that armour you have right now, and then you get some new cool armour.  Which is an upgrade, but tier 1 of the upgrade armour is a downgrade on your fully upgraded set.  So you're left with a choice of spending several hours getting the items to upgrade it or just continue on with your armour as is.  So I completed the game with some rare (blue) armour that I got quite early on in the game.  Finishing the legendary armour quests turned into disappointment rather than an exciting upgrade.  In effect, by allowing item upgrades, they devalue the progression of items being better as you move through the game.  A mistake, I think - they didn't really need to allow item upgrading, that's what the mod coils/weaves are for!Weapons - In HZD there was a clear set of attributes for each weapon set.  War bow was the element bow, hunter bow was your daily drive mid-range bow and had things like fire status, sharpshooter bow was your damage dealer & tear bow, and so on.  They went in a completely different direction in HFW.  Now, war bow=short range/fast speed, hunter=mid-range/medium speed, sharpshooter=long range/slow speed.  OK, you may think, seems reasonable.  But then the status effects are completely random and scattered.  Which, again, affects upgrades.  "Hurrah, I've just found an epic (purple) bow, fantastic.  I can replace this rare bow, finally.  Oh, but the arrows it fires doesn't include fire, which I use a lot.  Also, I need to spend 3 hours getting all the upgrade materials.  Maybe I'll just stick with the bow I've been using."  So, again, I just stuck with rare hunter & sharpshooter bows since I found ones that fit my playstyle relatively early on.  The same goes for the other weapon varieties as well, with an almost random set of ammo types for each one.Hunting grounds - Not my favourite mechanic in the first place - I prefer more methodical play compared to "rush this in 60 seconds" challenges.  However, there was an obvious benefit to this in HZD.  You end up with a core set of late game weapons(and armour? I forget :)) that carry you to the end-game.  As any final reward for that grind to get full suns everywhere in HFW would likely end up not being that much of a reward, I completely ignored the hunting grounds.Collectibles - There's a lot.  It's just too many.  HZD had quite a few, but I never really felt like it outstayed its welcome.  I did find the story locks irritating as well.  Needing late game equipment to get at something in the starting area, is frustrating more than anything else.Which is a good note to end this on.  HFW starts to outstay its welcome and the things that might have kept you pushing onwards in HZD just aren't in HFW.  The rewards don't exceed the effort.  HZD is 60-70 hours to do a 95%+ run.  I spent 76 hours in HFW, haven't done the DLC, and skipped a huge amount of the side quests.  It's odd to say this about open world games, but it feels like HFW lacks the focus of HZD.  Sometimes less is more...!  Something the games industry really needs to learn.All in all, it's a thumbs up, but only just.  If there was a sideways thumb option, I would be using it.  It's a good game, but I would recommend people play HZD over HFW, if they haven't played either.

tldr: This is a really, really great Ubisoft gamelisten, it's fine, but it feels like a step back in most ways. The saturation undoes all the understated realism from the first games visuals, but I have to say, some of the "gameplay additions" are just really bad:- number code doors: is this really a fun addition? safe codes? really?- "grapple debris" doors (hold trigger + triangle then pull): just complicate opening the doors a bit for fun- "fire doors" hold button then walk away: find yet another way to add a step to opening a door- "find the power cell and put it over here" doors: this felt like such a hit feature for boring sequels latelynone of these are fun, they are tedious. which brings me to climbing. Climbing was always boring but cmon;- grapple points that serve as very slightly higher jumps: this isn't fun, its more tedious. This is just a extra-step jump.- grapple points to unblock another climbing point: this is even more tedious, but at a whole new level of annoyance.I'm worried each "legendary item" I unlock is just going to keep adding more annoying steps to the worst parts of gameplay. They add nothing whatsover, no depth or excitement - just extra steps to already mundane or okay systems which kinda just makes them worse or more cumbersome to useThe game plays far less fluidly, and has some weirdly ancient designs like "move the crate around this room to reach the second floor". I'm going to leave a negative review for now and update it later. This game is cheap and it is very early access and a lot of my issues with it can be fixed however I can't recommend it in the state it is currently in. Now:The gameplay loop is fun. You buy items, you repair them, you sell them. You go to auction, you buy items, you repair them, you sell them. H o w e v e r, that is also the problem. You have to repair 9/10 items if you want to make the most profit and repairing takes a full day. That's not sustainable when I have 10 items that need to be repaired and some of them even take 2 days. I end up just wasting days in my shop declining most people to make sure I have enough money for rent. Is repairing 100% necessary? No, you can sell broken items. But the cost effectiveness far outweighs everything. I had one item go from 4000 to 12500. I don't know why the developer put in that you can change your bed sheets, but not that you can upgrade the repair machine to take less time or at least do multiple items.The customers. I know I can buy a cleaning robot, but every single customer leaves a piece of trash? Really? Either that or I had terrible odds and the drop rate needs to be fixed because I spend a lot of my time going around and picking up trash at the end of each day. Also the stats when buying or selling to customers seems to mean nothing, I had more than a few customers with high greed and low knowledge seemingly know the exact price of the item and would barley budge, or high greed and high knowledge take over 100 less for an item worth 500. There is also many days you can go without selling things. Customers just don't want to buy from you. I got so desperate at one point someone gave me the exact value of the item and I didn't even haggle I just took it because I needed the money and couldn't take the chance they got offended and left.The auctions. It's been said, but I'm saying it again, the auctions are honestly horrible. 1, I have no idea what's in any of the boxes so no idea if anything is worth it. "That's the point of an auction" this is a GAME. I should be able to either upgrade so I can scan a box or two or the boxes should  be more distinct per object. 2, I assumed as each planet opened it would be more expensive but the jump is so far. It goes from most garages between 500-1000 then on the next planet I'm seeing prices of 15000. Cut it back, there needs to be an inbetween.Heists. The thing that made me leave this review. Heists are AWFUL. To start with, the explosions can kill you through the wall. I died way more times to that than anything else. Also, there was more than a few times the blaster shots also went through the wall. Next, the enemies. They shoot at you before you enter a room. They are constantly shooting at the door making the first issue much worse because you can barley enter a room without losing far too much health. I find sprinting through the door helps but it can only help so much. Now onto the point of the heists. The money you get from them is decent sure but the items? Unless there is some massive item at the end I haven't got, it doesn't even seem worth it to go in. I got all the way to what I'm pretty sure is the last room, and I found around 3000 and 1 oil slick. That's it. The first time when I died, at least there was a safe key to presumably a safe somewhere. But this time? No. Nothing. So why would I even bother going in there? As well as that, I have no way to regain health. There really needs to be something. There also needs to be a warning BEFORE you go into the heists that it will take your money and items. Luckily I already assumed it would take items so I didn't take anything in, but I wasn't expecting to lose over 1000.All of this to say I think it CAN be great but I think it should not have been released in this state and it needed more time in the oven and it needed more, or any, beta testers because a lot of these issues feel like they would have been spotted very quickly by even one person who wasn't attached to the game playing it. You can see my playtime is under 2 hours and I have all these issues that could have been fixed before early access.

I really praise about this game, or rather this demo:What I find less good about this game:Since this is a demo, I'm sure that my review as useful feedback will help the developer release a pretty good full version of this game. Not often I leave reviews, but I am too excited about playing the game when it comes out, that I had to share some thoughts;I am admittedly a sucker for proper pixel-style graphics, but I am impressed by not just how Signal & Echo captures an authentic style with clear limitations, but also is able to create an original own art style that is simultaneously familiar. I do also find the music to be quite effective, offering calm melodies that are reminiscent of lounge, yet still diverse enough to be stuck in my head. I was admittedly confused at the lack of sound effects and even jumped when I checked the dumpster at the end, but it was not a big issue as I was still immersed.Though the gameplay is what I was enthralled by. It is somewhat odd to play a point & click where the main protagonist is not a huge cleptomaniac with questionable mortality, but this restriction really paid off. I love that I have to examine the environment even further and take notes on what I discover. (Also, loved the clever joke on why I would need a pen and paper)The intro was also great for setting up how this game was to be approached, while not letting any of the tutorials be a bother to veterans. The latter is something I find often being a problem in newer games to the point of me questioning if I want to continue, so happy about that!I was also surprised by not just how important putting clues together would be and being thorough with your notes, but also that the concept of original point and clicks (writing in commands), was implemented here in conversation and searches with nouns. I really enjoyed it and felt rewarded for seeing that I had the solutions already written down by simply being a notetaker!Though I do wonder if certain words could be added? Perhaps it is my poor English, but I wanted to point at the "poster" hanging on the chip store, though had to write "notice'". A varied assort of names without going overboard I believe could help. However, I do understand that words like "Principal" would have made certain sections too easy, so maybe just alter some wording there to make an excuse in tone with the story?Overall though, I was engaged in finding clues on what was going on, immersed in the presentation, and loved how the simple gameplay demanded me to pay attention and actually use my noggin ^.^ Cannot wait to play the real thing <3

TL;DR - The game is fine, has a bunch of issues, but is overall passable-to-enjoyable. 6-7/10Imma preface this review with the fact that I played the entire 14 hour (possibly +1h of demo, Idk if it counts) experience in VR, and I have done so across multiple 1-2h sessions within a single week. I think on the surface, the game is very good, with an interesting premise, story, and mechanics. But there is a lot of problems under said surface.To start off, a lot of the VR content is less immersive than you'd think. The world is empty because everyone is in Augmented Dreaming version of reality (AD), but AD is only available in limited areas, and you have to go out of it to travel between the main areas. And while moving outside of the AD boundary smoothly brings you back to the real world, leaving/entering manually is associated with added wait times whereas it could've been a really cool smooth transition.And this isn't a standalone issue. Every time you enter a scripted dialogue scene your character blinks which freezes you in place for the duration of the dialogue, until you blink again, which either frees you or jumps to the next scene. There is a lot of waiting, and even characters running away from you will wait for their queue, adding to the feeling that you're going panel by panel in a 360-degree virtual comic. Overall fine, but occasionally very awkward.This is accumulated by a host of other small issues that plague the game. Some animations play off the center of the playspace, other off the presumed head position, others still off your actual head position. Letting go of an item returns it to where it originally was, so you better not accidentally weaken your grip for a single frame while carrying something, or you have to do it again. Some items are both collectibles and memory triggers, so you need to pick it up to trigger the memory, and then pick it up again after memory is done to collect it. And memories themselves will sometimes require you to replay them (at least once, sometimes multiple, especially if you make a mistake) but they don't have a fast forward button, so you're just waiting there for the characters to get to the point.As a cherry on top of all those issues, resident consolation minigames start as a nice change of pace from the Detective Visual Novel gameplay bits, but they quickly turn into distractions away from the game, making for awkward pacing in tenser moments, especially given you need to check (nearly) every room you enter for the patients if you want to 100% it. And even then, I somehow only got ~60% of all patients. And frankly, the very simple Simon Says is the most challenging part of the game. Everything else is quite linear, and if there are parts where playtesters got stuck, you can bet that the game will beat it over your head what you need to do.Finally, there are the accessibility features, or lack thereof. I have no idea why there is no height controls for a VR title, or a way to recenter the playspace. The game would often throw the place where it thinks I am in a corner of the room, and because you get transported during a blackout, I could never know if me not going out of it is intentional, or if the game put my head in a middle of some object or just outside the area I'm intended to be in for a certain interaction. There is also some moments where your controllers vibrate, and mine did so at full power every time. They vibrated so hard for so long, that I could see the tracking accuracy degrade in real time. My controllers were vibrating so loud it drowned out in-game sounds. I'm all for adding a kick with vibrations, but when it feels like I'm holding a pair of drills in my hands, I'd like the ability to tone it down or disable entirely. And it's strange, because the game seems to do a lot to accommodate VR so that it doesn't seem sickening, and can be very comfortably played in a seated position (probably better than standing for majority of the game tbf). But it still has some problems, some of which can be fixed easily, others not so much.And yet... despite all that wall of text, this review is positive. Why? Story.While all the issues above bogged down the experience, they didn't ruin it. The story carries the game real hard. It's by no means perfect - the main gimmick is a bit contrived, and the further into the story you go, the more you need to suspend your disbelief to not notice some issues. But it's a good story, with interesting twists and turns. Again, the format tries to bring it down because everyone that matters has a face, and everyone that doesn't don't, which makes the pool of suspects and major characters very small. But still, the web of interactions is very tangled, and untangling it is a pleasant journey that you go on alongside your character. Him lacking his memory is a fantastic empty vessel for the player to slot themselves right into.There are some issues here still. VA occasionally falls off, Elaine will often sound as if she's a robot, and while I think a lot of the VA intonation choices were intentional, I don't think they always hit the nail on the head, but I think the protagonist is at least very well voiced. Varied, with mostly correct emotion and responses to the events happening. You spend the most time with his voice, so I'm really glad its of good quality. Same for our mini sidekick, even if people might find her a bit annoying.And in the end, I'm really happy they went with a dual edition. Even if it makes both the PC and VR version slightly worse than had they kept focus on just one. I think a minor sacrifice of quality there is worth bridging the gap that VR games tend to have And it means you can play it in VR, and when you get tired from standing around with some goggles on your head, you can take them off and still continue enjoying the story on a flat screen. Even if I purposefully didn't use this feature, there were definitely times where I would've had I not been going for a full-VR run.So yes, game has issues. It aint perfect, far from it. But it's a solid story across a good amount of time, so I think it's worth a recommendation.

Let me begin by thanking Izanagi Games and MyDearest Inc. for bringing this game to the world. Playing through this story was like riding a roller coaster of emotion when diving into it. I will not be going into too much detail regarding the story to avoid spoilers but can I just say that the events of this game really get you thinking. I was even up till 3 am one night trying to wrap my head around some of the how and why things happened the way they did, and what could have happened had they unfolded differently. As the name implies this version of the game features both a desktop and a VR mode so that players from both sides can experience it, those with both could take it for another spin to get the full experience looking for things that they could have missed on their initial play through.You begin your investigation in Astrum Close, the city where murder is supposedly impossible and the citizens of the town are connected to the network. You as the player assume the role of Hal Scion and with the help of your adorable partner Lilly will you be able to solve the case in time? You must remember though Lilly is here for you! If you need something to do while thinking about the task at hand, how about giving her some head pats?  This story as mentioned above is quite the investigative experience, yes it feels as if it's holding your hand for some of it but once you get into it you don’t really mind it at all. Even if your hand is being held or you're stuck between two points you can still easily miss things, or even overlook something entirely. You have to be sure you're paying attention to what is said to you by the NPCs! They could be telling you that you're near an easily missable collectible or even an achievement criteria, anything is possible.In terms of how smooth the gameplay ran on my rig, I was amazed at the quality of it. I find it rare to get a buttery smooth 60fps in a game nowadays but Dyschronia was like I got you! The game was running at around 60-65 fps on my system and aside from a few moments in the story it just flowed from point A to point B like a boat sailing downstream. What about the bugs or glitches did you encounter anything major? Yes, I did encounter one thing that could be considered major during the events of Episode 3 in desktop mode. While you are attempting to go through two past interaction puzzles the screen will remain black without even a dialogue box during the post-scene that says you won or failed. It only happened during two specific puzzles. Once again thank you IzanagiGames and MyDearestInc for bringing this story to the world. The events of this story hit me in all of the right places, and it left me with a strong desire to playthrough again. For those of you who enjoy a solid investigative adventure novel experience give this a try it has a demo! The Key for this review provided via keymailer.

You can view my full review & gameplay here: This is a very solid VR adaptation of a narrative-driven adventure game (some may call this a walking simulator). Technically, there are some puzzles, but they're not that difficult and most of the challenge here is just listening and being observant to find the correct objects, along with some dialogue choices to be made. The hardest thing so far is just the memory mini-game that you play in the alternate dream reality. The game sort of feels like a VN, but there's not that much reading involved, since it's mostly voiced (unless you choose Japanese audio & English sub-titles, I have it English audio, no subtitles). It feels like you're inside a crime-thriller manga (detective mystery).Story is pretty good, if you enjoy manga story-telling. There is a small girly assistant (Lily) which some may like and others may find annoying (she acts like a little kid, but does give useful hints). The main concept here is that you can control time and go back and change some things in your investigation or see hints from the past with your special powers. You're investigating a murder mystery in the future where technology is prevalent, but where the citizens are seemingly willingly controlled by a device that has reduced crime to be almost non-existant. So there's a lot of intrigue, not just about the crime your investigating, but about how this new technology is effecting its citizens and about these kids with special powers.Game is running on the Unity Engine. On my RTX 3080, I was getting a steady 72 fps (Q3 default). You have full / smooth locomotion available, along with smooth or snap turning (speed of turn / degree of turn). You can play comfortably seated as you have button crouch and magnet hands. Most of the interactions are of the point & highlight variety. Overall, I have enjoyed this experience & recommend it. It took me about 16 hours to complete one play-through. If you enjoy mangas, I think you will enjoy this experience. If you're not used to reading mangas, the experience may be a little bit difficult to get into due to the cultural differences. However, it's a nice introduction into this specific genre.

Boreal Blade is a fun little sword fighting game that really exceeded my expectations.Overall it is pretty similar to games like For Honor, Chivalry, or Mordhau if you’ve played any of those.You have your character and by default you only have this long sword unlocked. And how the combat works is that you press the left mouse button to attack and you will attack in which ever direction you are holding your sword.And you can change that direction by holding the right mouse button and moving it in different positions. And this right here is the bread and butter of the combat. And that is because there is not a designated block button. Instead you block your opponents attacks by moving your sword in the correct position to match how they are attacking.And there are a couple of other important features like you can kick the opponent to try and disrupt their attack or you can hold a special block button that heals you a little bit if you get a successful block while holding it. There are also fainting attacks that allow you to try throwing off your opponent. You also have a berserk meter above your health that you charge up while fighting and I believe it makes you stronger but also when it is max you can throw your weapon and depending on what weapon you have it does different things. So for the longswords you throw them like spears and it instakills the opponent if you hit them which is crazy satisfying.There are also hundreds of different weapons, armor, and cosmetics that you can get while playing and you can also apparently sell and buy them on the steam market as well.And so all these different weapons act completely different from each other. You could have a spear you try to stab people with or you could have a shield and another one handed weapon.One concern I have with the game is the playerbase as it is kind of low right now but there are enough players to find some games in the server browser. Also the game doesn’t have dedicated servers. It only has peer to peer.But overall I would highly recommend getting this game. Normally I would worry a little bit about the player base but as of right now there is enough people to be able to find games for and since it is only $4 if you get the game and play for several hours and then the game dies I think it would still be worth it for those several hours of gameplay. And who knows this game just came out in early access and its made by the devs that made the Trine series so I could see this game getting tons of updates and getting a small but loyal player base.

Watch my video review here -OR-Read the review below. Thanks!     The kind people over at Frozenbyte sent me a beta copy of Boreal Blade on steam, which just opened up to beta testing today, November 12, 2020. Boreal Blade is a team-based melee fighting game with a focus on player vs player combat. From what I can tell, this game aims to simplify the controls of melee fighting, while still keeping the mechanics complex.      So on initial launch everything seemed to work fine. While I would like to see “advanced”  graphic options instead of just basic presets, the game isn’t exactly a graphical marvel, so it’s not all that important. The game runs just fine, didn’t crash once during my game play, and doesn’t have any frame rate limitations either, so all is well on that end.     The game gives you the option to do a quick tutorial, and it will teach you the basics, and really only the basics. Once you get past the beginning stages of learning how the swing mechanics work, the tutorial is over, and you are left to read how the rest of the mechanics work on your own, instead of guiding you through the rest of the learning process. This is an example of telling rather than showing, something I think a lot of tutorials make the mistake of doing. I am hoping that this is something that gets expanded upon in the future.To make matters worse, the guidebook that you need to refer to doesn’t specifically tell you how to do the moves it is teaching you, or in some cases explains things so vaguely, it can lead players to have false impressions of how the mechanics work.For example, the tutorial guide literally says “there is no need to block enemy attacks intentionally” in the blocking section, but in the very next section under “Focused Blocking” it states “If you block an incoming attack while focusing, your health is replenished, and the attacker is stunned for a short while”These instructions are vague at best, and literally do not tell you what buttons to press to perform any of the actions. In order to figure this out, I had to go into the controls to see that there is, in fact, a block button. Only upon going in game and having someone explain how blocking actually worked was I able to figure the game out and move on from there. Not a very smooth introductory experience in my opinion.    The developers over at Frozenbyte have come up with an interesting combat concept in this game. Attacking is only done with the left click, but that does not limit you to 1 type of attack. When holding Right Click, you aim your attack, and the UI on screen shows you the arc you are going to be swinging, allowing you to attack from a very wide variety of angles, without over complicating the controls. You can fake or “feint” an attack by right clicking mid attack, allowing you to change angles mid swing, parry (which I haven’t quite figured out yet), and dodge. Blocking is actually by far the hardest part about this game. You have to match the incoming attack with your own sword positioning on defense, and there is no UI to tell you which way the swing is coming from, only the visual cues of the enemy swinging his weapon. This is similar to For Honor’s blocking system when set to the hardest difficulty. Honestly, If For Honor and Mordhau had a baby, it would end up something like this game’s combat.    As it currently sits, this game has game sizes as low as 2 players, and as high as 8. There are 2 game modes, Team deathmatch and Deathmatch. It does not have any single player content besides the tutorial and the practice hall. The game does offer character customization, but as it sits, the options are very limited. You earn more costumes and cosmetics and you progress in level, however I do not see a way to purchase anything, or a way to see what you are unlocking next. One real nice feature that I always love in any PvP oriented game is the statistics page. You can see the basics like kills, wins, losses, and all that, but you can also see some cool ones like “throwing weapon accuracy”, or your average lifespan. Definitely a cool touch.That being said, as someone who is a big fan of games like For Honor, Absolver, and Mordhau, there is one flaw that really For a game aiming to be as reliant on timing as positioning as it is, having peer to peer hosting at times just ruins the experience for me. Even when I sorted my games by lowest ping, and I was still over 100 ping about 50% of the time.Players would hit me when they should not, I hit players when I should not, and it made the game confusing. Most of the time I couldn’t tell if I was making a mistake, or if it was just lagging.While I understand that this game launched originally on the Nintendo Switch, I think Steam users will have a very different standard of performance, and I hope they do some work on the net-code, because that is a deal-breaker for me.

This game is pretty up my alley, but I can't recommend it for a few reasons.1) hit detection is not the greatest on the sides of the swings. You swing in an arc, but it is not reliable that you will hit from the sides, even if the sword trail visually passes through them. In fact, it's not super great from the front against enemies that are backing up either. I assume this is due to latency.2) the mixup RPS isn't particularly fun or deep. Basically, you can do light slashes, which will beat charged slashes but are easy to block or chamber. You can do charged slashes which can't be blocked, but must be focus blocked (hold CTRL) and you can kick, which disarms people who are focus blocking. You can feint and change the direction of your swing, but the swings are so slow that it doesn't really accomplish anything. Also, focus blocking has a delay and doesn't feel very responsive, so it can be annoying to try to pull off.3) it's not that satisfying to kill people. The animations are weird and clunky and do not have much weight or viscerality.This game can be compared to Mordhau,  but Mordhau is much more responsive, polished and satisfying, with more interesting maps, better game modes, more features... I can't really think of a reason to play this over Mordhau aside from price. But you really are getting what you pay for with this game. Considering it costs less than a $5 Biggie Bag at Wendy's, that is not saying much.tl;dr, game has potential but is ruined by poor hit detection, clunky animations and unengaging mixups

WEdit: I wrote that because I kept trying to post my review, but I thought maybe it was too long or something so if I would just type something short it would post then I could edit it later, but then it didn't work, but I guess it did.Oh my oh my oh my.  The beta was already super promising. Sure I didn't get to play much in the beta since they weren't many games running, but it was a blast. And I was expecting to pay $20, and then it's $4, but then on sale for 10% because why not, and, and less than one 5th of the price, and, and... Oh yeah I have to talk about the game. Alright, well, Boreal Blade is a 3rd person melee combat game (besides the throw mechanic which I'll get into later). Instead of just pressing a button like in Chivalry, or moving in a direction and pressing a button to change the direction of your swing (only game I can think of off the top of my head that does this is Clone Drone In The Danger Zone), you hold right click to change the position of your sword, which changes the direction you swing. This is also used to block alongside the focus block by placing your sword where the enemy's sword is (or teammate's, you never know if they're going berserk),  with the focus block being more of a defensive parry that also gives you health when used correctly. Now I cannot stress enough how cool it feels to combine all these moves (there's more than this too, like feints, countering fully charged attacks, dodging etcetera) and annihilate your opponent without taking a single hit. But there is one mechanic that can be a bit frustrating, which is throws. Now I miss mine almost every time, but there is this Goldilocks zone to where the enemy is not close enough to cancel your attack (if attacks are to close they don't go through), and they aren't far enough away to have a bunch of time to react to the sword traveling, and since there aren't dedicated servers even if they do react in time they're probably going to die anyway (the sword through is a one shot, unless you use I think it's 1 handed weapons then it becomes this spinning blade that deals 50 damage). Good thing is, you have to charge up a meter which I think blocking helps it go up, so at least it's rewarded to defensive players. Something I feel this game nails is this feeling of being unstoppable. Even if there is 4 other enemies, it still can be possible to win (maybe besides on the smaller maps, which is why I don't like them as much). I think this is partially do to a little mechanic called team damage. Without this, 4 people could run at you and just start slashing away, and I'm pretty sure there is no change. It's just like an enemy (besides not being able to get health from like focus blocks and stuff but that makes sense).I think my main issue with the game is the lack of dedicated servers, although I've gotten pretty lucky when it comes to ping, but there is still host advantage, and there is still the 500 ping guy that brought a sniper rifle to a gun fight.I definitely think the game needs to explain the mechanics more. I  don't think I covered everything, and I'm probably going to be like, "Oh yeah gotta add that to the review". Luckily I got a head start since I was able to play the beta, but I was still confused about some things like how armor works with the like green arrows and stuff, and I'm still a bit confused (they should really show that in THAT menu, unless they did and I'm blind, but I think the only way to see the tutorial stuff is in-game at this one dude that's in the corner of most or all maps, or in the training hall).Despite the issues, I definitely recommend this game. For $3.59 or $4 if it's after the sale, that's an absolute steal of a price. If you're like me, and you like Chivalry, and probably Mordhau, and maybe for Honor, you'll (probably) like this.

I seriously cannot suggest this game enough, it is an absolute blast. But at it's current state, you really need to get a few friends together for it, and the more the merrier at that! it's 4 bucks, which makes it super easy to convince people to get a copy.If you don't have friends to play with, it's a bit rough, the fan base is clearly spread out quite a lot, and servers are pretty rare, but if you do have some friends and your playing the game with them, you should make the servers public with some space for extras, i can say from several points of experience it can be really fun having strangers fall into your game from nowhere and either be just as new to it as you are, or seem like total experts who can take on you and all your friends at once like a boss battle.Combat feels great, it's easy to figure out, but you still feel like your getting better and better with every play session you have. Shields can feel really Bullsh!t a lot of the time, I've certainly gotten mad at them more than a few times, and while I have nitpicks with them, I don't feel like their totally overpowered or anything. When you're first learning to use spears they can feel useless and weak, but the more you use them and the better you get at them, the more often you'll be able to kill an opponent in two hits before their anywhere near you, and feel like a god of death.Kicks against people in light/medium armor should have more knock back in comparison to the non that they currently have. A lightly armored person can stand hovering over an edge, and need to be kicked three times in a row before they fall off the cliff.The combat can sometimes feel janky, especially when latency issues are added in, but they never have the level of insane jank that Chivalry has, and the fights certainly feel more engaging and rewarding than Mordhau and For Honor.The variety of weapons is insane, and the variety of armor is wild. You can look super unique, and your personal character design can really empower your play. Not to mention how unique and honestly GREAT the art style of this game is.The thing i'd like to see more than anything in this game is bots. Not like the PVE functions that i've seen other people beg for, frankly that sounds terrible to me. But not having anything to practice against is pretty tough. There's an npc in the training hall who just stands there blocking, but fun fact they won't pick their weapons back up, so if you want to practice disarming opponents, you just gotta wait for an internet vagrant to join your game. Some sparring bots could really improve the game in my eyes, they don't have to be complex, just one who attacks you so you can practice blocking, and one who blocks so you can practice faking and disarming.I'd love to see more about the world design, perhaps in the form of more flavor text on weapons and armor about the nations we see referenced by them, or about the legendary warriors who've wielded them in the past. Perhaps having NPCs who show up in your training hall as you level up, wearing the full armor sets of their nations, in the proper colors, who can tell you a bit about their homeland, and about how the warriors of their land fight. So as you progress through the game you might find yourself Identifying with a nation who fights the way you like to.All in all I've had a lot of fun with this game, and I hope beyond hope that it gets more popular in the future, cuz it deserves to be. I give this game a 9/10, as you can't rightly fault a game for not having enough players yet, and aside from that there a no major flaws and few minor ones.Please please give it a shot! And if you do, I hope to one day see you out there!

Boreal Blade is an intriguing melee combat game that excels in delivering a rich, tactical fighting experience. Players can choose from a variety of weapons and fighting styles, each offering unique advantages and requiring a different approach to master. The intricate controls allow for a high degree of customization in attacks and defenses, making each duel feel intense and rewarding. The medieval Nordic setting is beautifully rendered, creating an immersive atmosphere that enhances the overall experience.The multiplayer aspect of Boreal Blade is particularly compelling, encouraging players to hone their skills against others in intense, competitive matches. The community-driven gameplay fosters a sense of camaraderie and competition, as players can form teams and participate in various modes, including deathmatch and objective-based battles. The game's emphasis on skill over randomness means that victories feel hard-earned and satisfying. While the learning curve can be steep, the depth and complexity of the combat system make Boreal Blade a standout title for those who enjoy thoughtful, skill-based melee combat. With its engaging gameplay, stunning visuals, and robust multiplayer options, Boreal Blade offers a unique and rewarding experience for fans of tactical fighting games.

Boreal Blade is a team-based melee fighting game, similar to Chivalry and Mordhau. If you like that style of games, you'll love Boreal Blade. It's clunkier (because it was never finished) than the "bigger" brothers, but still extremely entertaining. Unfortunately, the game is abandoned. No player base, and no support from developers. Going free-to-play could help, but it will probably never happen. Right now, the only way to play the game is to beg your friends to buy it and then do some duels. As much as I would love to, I can't recommend the Boreal Blade. The online population is dead, so you won't be able to play without your own crew.No story mode. Tutorial and Training Hall are the only available offline modes. The tutorial itself is super short and barely teaches you anything.Combat, the most important thing in every fighting game, is good. It lacks polish (especially animations) and has some problems with hit detection, but it's still enjoyable. You can attack from any angle. To block upcoming attacks, you must position your weapon in the same place where your opponent swings. You can do power attacks, kicks, fake attacks, throw your weapon into the opponent, and much more.If you want to do well in duels, it's important to find your favorite combat style. Heavy armor will slow you down, but it will let you tank more hits. To be mobile on the battleground, light armor is the way. Every weapon is slightly different, so it's good to be versatile to counter your opponent. There are some customization options that you can unlock by leveling (aka. playing the game). It's a bunch of cosmetics, but also some functional items, like armors and weapons. Basic options, like gender or your looks, are free, but there's not much to choose from.Maps are a little bit small, but they are fairly well done. The visuals are simple (lower poly), but the game looks rather pretty nonetheless. Stylized textures are doing their job.Great music, solid sounds, and even some voice-acting in the Tutorial (it's not good quality tho).Fairly good performance (stable 144 fps), with some rare drops (from 144 to ~130).Spelling errors in the Tutorial. Animation bugs while using certain weapons (like an invisible spear).Lack of dedicated servers. This is a big issue because user-hosted games are highly unstable. They can randomly crash, and there are serious latency problems when a person with a slightly higher ping joins your match.No bots, so you can't even have some fun offline.

I really wanted to like this game, in fact, for the first few matches, I actually enjoyed what little I was able to play. I liked the way the world looked, I liked the soundtrack, and I liked the gameplay. The combat system has roots in a Mount and Blade sort of system, and it takes that same formula and adds a few more mechanics to it, so you can do things like dodge or throw your weapon at people. It took me only a few minutes to get myself familiar with the controls, and I was already able to take out a few players in my first few minutes playing the game. For a moment, I was actually having fun.Unfortunately, that only lasted for about an hour, and every subsequent match since then had been ridiculously laggy. Since the population is so low, the only servers I found were far away from me, making the experience twice as bad as it already was. I'm not talking sort of rubberbandy, but I mean people would moonwalk in place and then a gush of blood and everyone was dead two seconds later. Counting as of right now, I saw 2 servers with a grand total of... 7 people across them. That is really, really, really bad for a multiplayer only game. There is no single player, and there are no matches against the AI of any sort. I get it, making AI is hard. But starting at the main menu and hoping for a match is also hard to justify to a consumer.My other concern that I will address is the progression system. When you start, you have a very, very limited selection of what weapons you can use. In fact, you actually just get ONE weapon when you start, and you have to play for a bit before you get the rest. I honestly don't care much for the cosmetics. Sure, make cosmetics the incentive for playing matches, you should have a starting weapon of every weapon type at the very least. It isn't just that either, there's also throwables that you can unlock, but it takes long time to get the healing one, which I have seen everyone use.You cannot have important bits of gameplay locked behind a progression system when there is almost no one to play. Players will not get to experience all that your game has to offer if they cannot move forward.There's also a Steam market tab for the game, and I'm not sure why, but it certainly rubs me the wrong way.1) You like Mount and Blade's combat ( or another similar title )2) You have several people you can play with who also enjoy that same style of combat.3) You acknowledge that there may or may not be anyone to ever play with and that you may be wasting your money.I took one final look while writing this review, and there is a grand total of  available servers online. I hosted one for a few minutes, but then I gave up as I sat alone for a short while.It is a shame, because I know that I would have enjoyed this game otherwise, but even at $4.00 USD, I think there are still other games you could try, especially when those games are on sale.

Fun game. Matches go pretty quickly, so it's something you can play a few rounds of whenever you have some time to spare. Very cheap price ($3.59 at the time of posting), I got my money's worth in the first day.Combat is sort of a hybrid between Mount&Blade and For Honor, but a lot more free-form than both. Attacks and blocks are directional, but there is no fixed left/right/up/down attack positions. You can attack from any angle. And to block an attack, you must position your weapon so that it get hits by your opponent's swing. There is a "Flick Attacking" option that makes attacks work based on your mouse movement, and is very similar to Mount&Blade.There are a lot of customization options. Lots of cosmetics, and lots of functional items like armor and weapons. These are earned randomly as you play and level up. They go into your Steam inventory so you can trade them with others or sell them on the community market. There are also weapons of each type that you are guaranteed to unlock at certain levels. You can play well with just the default sword though, the loot drops are not necessary to be good and every piece of gear has a trade-off.Different gear changes the way you have to fight. Heavy armor will slow you down but let you tank an extra hit or two. Some weapons are better at offense, and others help more with defense. You will probably swap gear between rounds to counter whatever your enemies are using.As for negatives... no dedicated servers makes it a little annoying getting into a match. Fighting players with high ping can be frustrating. And I would like to see bigger match sizes (5v5 or even 6v6) on bigger maps.

You play as one of two detectives investigating a murder in the city of Antioch. Interestingly, and perhaps uniquely in the genre, Antioch: Scarlet Bay is a co-op game. One player plays as a fresh-faced, young police officer, investigating their first case, while the other plays as the grizzled veteran one day from retirement. The two players communicate through asking each other questions, proposing actions, and interrogating suspects and witnesses together. As much as Antioch: Scarlet Bay is a game of solving a mystery, it is also a game about building a relationship with a partner and learning more and more about who your character is through their interactions with their partner. The world provides an avenue not only for resolving a story of a corrupt world, but a voyage of self-discovery.Antioch: Scarlet Bay’s gameplay is almost entirely text-based, with players selecting dialogue options and destinations from a basic map . The only way to move forward is not through any particular gaming skill, but through conversation, deduction, and some degree of teamwork. However, to say that the focus is on the mystery misses the greater story Antioch: Scarlet Bay is telling. The mystery itself was fairly easy to solve (my partner and I figured it out within an hour or so). The difficulty is more in finding the correct evidence and following the correct conversation trails. The joy is in the paths those conversations take and what they reveal both about your partner’s character and your own.For games that rely on their writing to convey their story, it’s obviously necessary for that writing to be effective. Antioch: Scarlet Bay’s writing is a baffling hodgepodge of poor translation, grandiose worldbuilding, and moon logic. In any given conversation, I wasn’t entirely sure what I was actually meant to be learning, and was never quite sure if this was due to a poor translation or the particular person I was speaking to not actually having any idea what was going on. This is not the first poorly translated game I’ve played, though. A poor translation, even in a game where subtle slips of the tongue make all the difference, isn’t enough to stop me from enjoying the game. Indeed, at multiple points, the writing made me laugh unironically as I enjoyed the characters’ various quips, snide comments, and the way the story was being told. However, the writing was not mine to meander through on my own. Antioch: Scarlet Bay is a co-op game, with both players engaging in conversations as they investigate the mystery together. These conversations are not separate. Instead, they happen simultaneously, with one player tracing their line of question, potentially in an unrelated direction from the other player.  This leads to absolute madness rather than a coherent line of questioning. Indeed, if one line of questioning ends before the other, the player with no more questions can find themselves forced to do or say things that make no sense for their character, just so the other player can continue their potentially more fruitful line of investigation. This ultimately creates a story that is less the story of two detectives solving a mystery together, and instead creates the story of a straight man gradually losing it as their partner dives headlong into utter madness.It creates Disco Elysium.Much like Antioch: Scarlet Bay, Disco Elysium follows a detective investigating a murder in a world just around the corner from our own. It, like Antioch: Scarlet Bay, has a living and dynamic world filled with characters who are simultaneously compelling and archetypes. It presents the player with the option to have absolute madness conversations as they tug at the threads of their own mystery, and it encourages introspection and self-discovery. They’re both mystery games, heavily reliant on their text. One key difference, though, is in the player experience. Disco Elysium, like nearly every mystery game, is a single player game. The player plays as Harry and chooses how to approach the mystery on their own. However, Harry is accompanied by a straight-man partner named Kim Kitsuragi who provides a foil to Harry’s more outlandish moments. Together, they work to solve the mystery.The comparisons draw themselves, but only in the fact that all mystery games must have some commonality. The commonalities between Antioch: Scarlet Bay and Disco Elysium are the commonalities that are likely anywhere in the genre. Instead, I’m bringing up Disco Elysium because both games share the dynamic of working alongside someone else to solve a mystery, and of having the option of bouncing off someone else to be able to do it. The important distinction is to what extent that bouncing and foil ultimately succeeds. In Disco Elysium, Kim Kitsuragi becomes a deeply compelling character in his own right. Though only viewed through Harry’s eyes, Kim is built up and characterised so completely that he feels as whole a character as the Harry the player has built for themselves. In Antioch: Scarlet Bay, there is no such opportunity. Because the dialogue options are so muddled and crossed, it’s impossible for either player to actually build a character for themselves, let alone understand who their partner is. Instead, the partner dynamic becomes one of insanity as one partner desperately tries to stretch out their end of the conversation in the vain hope their partner might gain something. By having both players draw from the same pool of conversation options, conversations cease to be conversation, and become mindlessly clicking with the occasional giggle at a particular line. This is not to fault Antioch: Scarlet Bay for not being Disco Elysium. Disco Elysium is a modern classic, and each game should and must be its own enterprise. However, it is telling that the element that seeks to set Antioch: Scarlet Bay apart - the fact that you play alongside another human - is so fundamentally flawed in its design that a character wholly pre-written is more human than the one controlled by a person. In trying to create a system where two characters can interact with each other, Antioch: Scarlet Bay instead succeeds only in creating disjointed one-liners and a pair of detectives so incompetent, it’s a miracle they can successfully buy a box of doughnuts.And yet, I can’t deny I had fun. I played for roughly three hours before I got to an ending. I felt satisfied by that ending, where even the fail state felt like it fit within the world the game had created. The art is beautiful, and the music creates the perfect atmosphere. I sat beside my partner, absolutely engage for those three hours, having a wonderful time of laughing both with and at the game. As flawed as Antioch: Scarlet Bay may be, and as much as it fails to accomplish what it sets out to accomplish, there is  a lot to love. It is an adventure in patience, and an exploration of a world that aches to be explored.
