So, my friend and I did a playthrough of this game today. While there were some negative aspects to it, I would say that overall, we had a good time.I'll start with the negative aspects. The English translation is....mediocre at best. A lot of the times, the characters don't feel like they're talking to each other, and are just spouting nonsense. There's also a lot of spelling errors (like spelling "traffic" as "trafffic"), naming errors (sometimes, a character is called Blanche, and in other scenes she's called Bianca, or Jackie suddenly being called Jacq), or simple grammar mistakes (something like "do not you think so?" or wrong forms of verbs). These errors happened often enough that they were very noticeable, and while my friend and I weren't too bothered by them, we did sometimes lose track of conversations because the sentences just wouldn't make much sense.Another negative aspect is a major glitch that happened while we were in an area called the "Tribunal Archives". Without spoiling anything, the script there got completely mixed up. We'd choose text options that turned into whole other options once we clicked on them, and my friend (who was playing as the old cop) would even get prompts MULTIPLE TIMES that were just the voicelines of the NPC present at the scene. The entire script got jumbled at that point, and while we could laugh at the sheer ridiculousness, it was incredibly distracting and we lost our way there.A final smaller complaint is that at certain points (especially at the end) it's unclear what you can do and where you have to go. We ran around like headless chickens. While that has some appeal and incentive to make notes of stuff yourself, there's literally no way to check all the information that you've gotten in the game, and you get a LOT of it.All of this being said, we still had a really good time. The 2 main people, while you have a certain control over their actions, are very stereotypically old-day cop-like. This made the investigation feel realistic and authentic. Even the racist comments they sometimes made, while kind of uncomfortable, added to the real feel of the game. The entire vibe of the game is very nice. The artstyle is really good and the music, while there doesn't feel like there's a lot of variation, did add to the whole detective vibe. That saxophone was amazing.The story really felt hopeless a lot of the time, which is a good thing. Most characters do not want to help you, and a lot of them actually do not help you. There's a lot of fake leads in this game that lead nowhere, but you often couldn't tell beforehand if a lead was gonna be helpful or not. There were also a lot of moments where both my friend and I had moments where we'd figure out plot points, that made us feel really accomplished.The game can also be pretty funny at times, and I can say with confidence that your actions in this game have a lot of consequences. I'm pretty sure we got a certain character killed because we made the wrong decisions, and that riled both of us up to not wanna ♥♥♥♥ up like that in the future. It's also possible to completely work against each other, which is what we sometimes did. I won't spoil the results of that, but those moments made the gameplay more interesting. The story was good enough to keep us interested and guessing throughout.tl;dr: Despite the fact that the game has a lot of polishing it needs to have a proper English version, my friend and I had a lot of fun with the game and would definitely recommend it if you and a friend want to solve mysteries in a very intriguing setting.

OK, hear me out.This isn't a great game.  It's not even good.  The English translation is simply terrible.  The story is convoluted and incomprehensible.  Consequences are harsh and unpredictable; mistakes cannot be repaired and you can ruin your chances of getting the best ending right at the beginning of the game.  If you miss a critical clue it is gone forever.BUT.  The design concept is fascinating.  The co-op integration is wonderful.  The banter is charming.  The atmosphere is brilliant.  The tone is almost* pitch-perfect.  (*There is some racism and sexism that I could have done without.)With such a small team, I'm honestly impressed that Midnight Mood Studio made a game that is functional, beautiful, and can be played from beginning to end while maintaining the complexity and depth of its original vision.  And I'm glad that even a suboptimal ending finishes on a hopeful note - my friend and I failed to close the case but the finale gave us hope of redemption.Will you love this game?  Moment to moment, there is a lot of frustration and a lot of confusion.  It's hard to feel a sense of control or agency as you play it, even as you make disastrous choices with severe consequences.  But I cared about the characters, it was a bonding experience with my co-op partner, and I will remember the game and its vibe very fondly.So I don't know if you should spend $5 and 5 hours on this.  That's a question you'll have to answer for yourself, detective.

I used to love all those seek and find books when I was a little girl and so these HOG type of games scratch a little of that nostalgic itch for me. I'm going to copy and paste this review for all the commissioned games I've played so far cause this is my whole opinion and thoughts on the Bees 0, Bees 1, Bunnies, Cats, Dogs, Frogs, Ladybugs. I would have to say I love the different types of art by various artists and because of this all the objects that you are trying to find will look slightly different, I like some of the music but not all because when I play HOG games I like soft mellow chill music playing in the background and not every song was this way but there is settings in the menu to where you can turn the music and sounds down or off. There is also other settings such as making the screen brighter and making the window full screen and such which I much appreciated. My favorites so far out of this series would have to be the cats, dogs, frogs, and ladybugs. I really like how you can zoom in and out on the art work if you're having trouble finding an object because some of them can be very tiny and extremely hard to find. I also liked how these games had a couple items to find and not just 1 thing. The games that I did play ran great and I didn't experience any bugs or glitches, the Steam achievements work too in case anyone is wondering about that. Negligee: Spring Clean Prelude is a visual novel that has you running a lingerie store, aptly named, Negligee.To preface, this is the first game I've played in the series, and I've probably botched the order in which I should play the games, so take what I say with a grain of salt.Follow Hannah, her ex-boss Karen and her employees, Charlotte, Jasmin and Sophie and make it their mission to run a successful lingerie store!This game is quite unique, having you play in multiple perspectives, picking between the main five girls in certain scenarios. Most choices revolve around you picking lingerie for either the customers or the main characters. The options being, nice, naughty or neutral. There is a correct answer each time, so you have to analyze and choose wisely each time as to pick the appropriate lingerie for the occasion.The game has different paths you can go down, and successfully completing a path awards you with a card collectible of the character featured in the path. Quite different, but a very neat little feature.In the prelude or demo, there's three paths to choose from. Though they aren't very long, they give you enough of a glimpse to see what the full game has to offer. There's also a bunch of art, displaying the large cast of colourful characters available in the full game. There's no crazy NSFW scenes as I'm sure some of you were hoping, but that's why this is just a demo.The game has a pretty nice soundtrack too, I enjoyed it thoroughly, and it felt very fitting for the environment I found myself in.Overall, though this game probably isn't the first in the series, it is a pretty decent gateway into the series. It has more than enough content to potentially convince you to buy the full game and well, it's free! So there's no harm in trying! Absolutely recommend if you're into these sorts of visual novels!

I didn't know much about this game besides the demo that came out a year ago, nor have I known much about the developer besides that pig-mask game (?) I saw a playthrough of. So I mostly went into this game kinda blind. Needless to say I was pleasantly surprised.Survival horror is a tough balance to accomplish. You don't want the game to be too hard because it goes from being scary to just irritating and frustrating. You don't want to manipulate the player into  there's danger when there isn't, because when that happens, the player knows they have nothing to worry about, the game has no challenge, and the horror is gone. This game (mostly) does a good job of keeping that balance. If enemies spot you, you can flee from them and/or hide. You don't die instantly if you take damage, and there are health pickups scattered about in case you get injured. The game gives you a sawn-off shotgun (and an optional silenced pistol), but with limited ammo, so you can't go around just blasting enemies. Also it takes a  to reload your shotgun, so you best be damn sure you don't miss. Also something I'm incredibly happy about is that the player can sprint for quite some time without getting tired, unlike other games () where you can only sprint for a few seconds. There's no battery mechanics or lighter fluid mechanics either, so you can use them as light sources indefinitely.The voice acting was fine for the most part. A couple times it sounded like the Protagonist is a little bored, but nothing terrible. It's clear many of the voice actors and actresses know what kind of game they're in and they ham it up with their performance, especially with how smug the Faceless Speaker can be.The graphics seemed good for the most part, albeit at times it lagged a bit during the more chaotic cutscenes and sequences, but that's probably more a case of my PC specs and not the game itself. Nevertheless, some glitches do occur; one part of the game had an enemy and his dog spinning around in a circle indefinitely if you alert them, and a cutscene doesn't contain audio for the Faceless Speaker shortly after the Bob's Big Boy fight.Plot's fairly straightforward. You're stuck in a police department full of masked killers. Get out. For a game like this, the plot doesn't need to be super in-depth. My only issue is that after you beat the game, it feels like the story of a second game is about to start up, but then it ends. I'm assuming(?) a sequel or DLC will be released in the future, because the game has intriguing world building (which I'll get to later).The gameplay is quite fun once you get the hang of it. You have a sensor that monitors where the killers are patrolling, and you have to decide when you do or don't move, if you should distract them, if you should kill someone, etc. Most of the game is spent solving puzzles that are secretly codes for a keypad to unlock a door, finding fuses to activate generators, that sort of stuff. Collecting two film reels that both reveal a four-digit code and can only be obtained by solving two cryptic puzzles is much more engaging than simply walking into a room and finding a key or finding a note that says "This is the door code."By far the two best levels in the game are Toxicity and Darktooth's Lair. Toxicity is entirely polluted with lethal gas, so you have to spend the whole level wearing a gasmask, meaning you can't use . You have to rely on being stealthy and peeking around corners so the gasmask killer in the same area doesn't see you. Darktooth's Lair, meanwhile, is incredibly dark, has no candles, and has the chainsaw-wielding Darktooth wandering around. You gotta choose between getting three fuses and evading him the entire time, or whip out your shotgun and kill him, then get the fuses. Again, reloading your gun is , and Darktooth does not go down in one hit, so if you ♥♥♥♥ up, you're gonna die.There are also three other bosses in the game--none of which make any sense compared to Darktooth, who is more in line with this genre. All of them are ridiculous in the best way possible. I'm not even gonna spoil what they are or how they're supposed to be defeated, because when you get to them, you have to simply embrace what is happening and go with it. Overall, I was having a blast playing this game and it actually left me unnerved on multiple occasions.And then Episode 3 happens.And this is where it feels like the developer ran out of time or budget or just got tired of the game. Because most of the levels can be summarized as "Run down this dark corridor and go through this door." That's it; that's the whole level. The very first level of Episode 3 is just a cutscene, you picking up a key, you solving an (optional) puzzle in a basketball court, and then walking through a door. The level right after this is just wandering through a giant dark area with a flashlight, finding a door, and going through it. And then there are the Numb Bodies, who are basically blind zombies. They're very easy to maneuver around and even outrun, but some of them have an annoying habit of camping in front of you, forcing you to kill them or to get caught and bolt. I don't know if this is a glitch or if they're supposed to do that, but it's annoying. What they are or who they are is never explained. It's jarring that the game went from evading killers to just easily walking around discount zombies.And then you fight a giant...thing that walks around in a park but won't directly harm you. Then the game ends. And I was just...confused. So much of the game and the plot led into one another and flowed naturally, but Episode 3 feels like an "And Then" plot. And then zombies appear. And then a giant  is released. And then you gotta destroy it because no one else can aim properly. And then the game is over.  Did I miss something? Where was all this before? Who were those soldiers? How many of those giant things exist? Where did they come from? How did the Numb Bodies become a thing? Certain elements were implied, but the game never confirmed anything until it happened.So yeah, overall I had a great time with this game. The combat was realistically clunky, and hiding and fleeing from the enemy was difficult, but reasonable. The game is more tense than scary, but that doesn't detract from how much fun I had--especially with all of those bosses. Really my only complaint is that Episode 3 as a whole was disappointing and felt very rushed, especially after how Episode 2 ended.Other than that, game was very enjoyable.

An departure from Vincent Lade's normal style of horror & storytelling games, but it still packs in interesting game play via stealth.To be perfectly honest, I'm not sure i fully grasped the story on this one. However, my basic understanding is: you play as a character that is part of a gang. You are tasked with stealing from a local police station that has thought to be abandoned by a rival gang. However when you arrive, you find out not only is it NOT empty, but has been taken over by the infamous (and strange) Jawbreaker gang. You become trapped inside the building and are forced to sneak your way out to escape.I personally despise sneaking games except for the MGS franchise, but I managed to get my way through this one without too much issue. You really have to pay attention to enemy pathing or you'll be dying a LOT.I do recommend this game, however if you're wanting a game with spooks, significant quantity of jump scares, and action - this is NOT your game. This game was much longer than I expected, so prepare for a sneaking ride through a very massive police department.PROS:* Controller capable (used 8-bit Pro Duo)* Simplistic controls* Banger soundtrack (SO GOOD)* Creepy atmosphere (even if it wasn't "scary" per say)* Cute and creepy collectibles to find* Amazing voice acting from all characters (even NPCs)* Very basic puzzles (not overridden with complicated or convoluted puzzles)* Standard collection box at various checkpoints to store items* It has a map and I'm on the fence if it's useful or not.* Linear gameplay (I like this)CONS:* No manual saves, only autosaves at the beginning of each section - meaning if it's a long section and you die, you have to start that section completely over* Story is very lack luster and is not engaging* Boss battles are a series of trial-and-error until you figure out the mechanic and what is going on. I found it challenging to figure out what I was even needing to do (and had to look at YouTube walkthroughs to see what I was supposed to be doing).* Pick up-able items could be highlighted better for accessibility* Guns are essentially useless except for boss battles that require them* You can't pick up bodies to hide them from other NPCs (causing other NPCs to become aware of your presence)* You essentially have 2 HPs (even though your UI says 3) because after two hits you're dead (could be a bug?)* Inventory screen is a bit funky with sorting, combining and moving items around* Hiding locations rarely worked (enemies have a very strict seek mechanism) - easier to run around corners until you're out of line of sight and hope for the best, or die and start over

This problem is that ammo is so rare you basically can never use your weapons. So, the game becomes almost fully a stealth game with poor stealth. And when I say poor, I really do mean the most frustrating trial and error sort of stealth. Enemies can easily see you, and you basically can't escape them once detected. You can't hide either, because you can't hide if you have been detected for some reason (not to mention that hiding hampers you because you can't use items that help you see enemies, like motion trackers). So, you might as well let them kill you once you've been caught. Then it stops being a horror game called Jawbreaker and becomes a rage game called Spiritbreaker. The first encounter of the game is just brutal, and it honestly doesn't let up from there.Ammo, as I said before, is stupid rare. There are only about 6-8 shotgun shells in the game from what I've seen and read (up until close to nearly the end of the game, I believe, but I didn't get that far), and you use 2 shells when shooting the double barrel shotgun. So, if you stick to using the double barrel, you end up with maybe 4 shots at most. You end up saving it for "when you need it" then the game ends. Each and every encounter is frustrating and tedious, made even worse by this.So, what all this means, is that most of the game is either puzzles, walking, or these awful stealth sections. The best part of the game is the confusing boss fights.It just isn't worth it. Without the cheap deaths from crappy stealth the game would 4 hours long and it would pretty much just be a walking simulator.

It's not a complete trainwreck, and I hate to be critical of a small solo developer, but "Jawbreaker" completely lost me after about 2 hours of gameplay. When I got the double barreled shotgun, I realized two things:1/ Stealth is most likely going to remain a trial-and-error affair until the end. As a matter of fact, the shotgun feels like a 'one up' item that can help recover if you made an error and got caught. It doesn't seem like it was designed for combat.2/ It's a nitpick, sure, but it's also the detail that finally broke me: Upon firing the shotgun for the first time, I realized that one blast consumes 2 rounds of ammo. It's seemingly impossible to shoot just one barrel at a time. So it's really a one-shot weapon, even though nothing about it indicates that's the case, and also, well, it feels counterintuitive and wrong.Being instantly detected in the second or third larger stealth section, I decided that's enough.I think the right way to do stealth in horror games is closer to "Amnesia: The Bunker" than "Jawbreaker" or "Outlast". As a developer, you probably should want the stealth to be relatively easy. Getting mauled because of a single error is frustrating, and frustration kills the fear. If the player is able to just barely avoid the stalker, even to the point that they can't see what the enemy looks like - this builds tension. Getting killed releases the tension. Or at least so I think. That said, there's audience out there for games like Outlast, so for all I know, I may be in the minority.

Good but could be GREAT! (Minor Spoilers)To begin, I must commend Jawbreaker for its striking style and menacing atmosphere. From the outset, the game exudes an intense vibe that immediately drew me in, prompting a desire to uncover why the world had descended into such devastation and how gangs had risen to dominate it.The art and atmosphere captivated me from the start. The thought of navigating this bleak scenario, surrounded by unpredictable psychopaths with no hope of rescue, sent shivers down my spine.However, while Jawbreaker excelled in many areas, there are a few issues I encountered that detracted from my overall experience:Firstly, the inclusion of larger bosses like the tank and robot felt unnecessary and disrupted the game's pacing. I found myself longing for more encounters akin to the chainsaw guy, which felt better integrated into the immersive world without compromising the tension.Regarding weapons, I understand the emphasis on survival horror and stealth gameplay, but managing ammunition became frustrating. Despite having two shotguns, I often found myself with as few as six shots, and there were instances where the inventory displayed loaded bullets but the gun remained empty, which was disorienting.Additionally, the decision to send the protagonist out unarmed in a world where gangs rule and violence is rampant felt implausible to me. It broke immersion and raised questions about the game's narrative consistency.Furthermore, while the "true ending" provided explanations for broader aspects of the game world, it neglected to shed light on our own bunker where the radio transmissions originate. This omission left me feeling disconnected from potential other survivors and the larger context of the story.Lastly, I felt the coin system for purchasing items was superfluous. A crafting system tied to looting locations such as police stations or military bases would have made more sense thematically and gameplay-wise. Crafting ammunition and health items could have added a strategic layer to resource management, enhancing the survival experience.In conclusion, while Jawbreaker excels in creating a chilling atmosphere and compelling premise, these gameplay elements could benefit from refinement to further elevate the overall experience.

This is probably one of the best (if not the best) "action rogue-like" I've played.  Most games in the genre just have swarms of enemies that may have different sprites but functionally are all the same; they either move in a line at you or they hang back and fire some ranged projectile at you.  That's basically 99% of rogue-likes and its pretty boring.  Cellfish actually has a variety of enemies that engage in different ways and force you to adapt.  It also does an excellent job with both visual and audio cues for stuff like dash cooldowns or other in game timers.  Everything about this game seems designed thoughtfully and well executed.  Each ship functions in a different way and forces a different playstyle; I had one ship with a strong recoil on its shot that I would use to help me maneuver and one that would lay mines behind you which required serious mental adjustment (especially when most enemies come at you head on).  I've played Vampire Survivors, Boneraiser Minions, Slime 3k, and probably more I can't remember right now.  Cellfish and Halls of Torment are on top in terms of enemy design and to me that makes for more engaging gameplay.

It's incredibly realistic that those who graduate with degrees in paleontology (and archaeology for that matter) can't find work and either need to do something else, or just take a chance to pursue their dreams. Yes, there's still some optimization that needs to be done and some of the controls can be a jittery at times, but I don't think it makes the game unplayable by any means. I look forward to seeing how the game progresses and I hope to see more content in the future.

Dinosaur Fossil Hunter calls itself a simulator, but it's far too casual to be one. Or at least a good one.What's the first thing that comes to mind when you think of finding fossils? I'm going to take a guess it's the process of very gently brushing and cleaning fossils. In Dinosaur Fossil Hunter, there is never a need to be careful. You can throw those fossils around all you want without penalty. There's no need to gently brush them clean, you just swing your mouse wildly until the progress bar hits 100%.I wouldn't recommend Dinosaur Fossil Hunter, and I'm not sure if I'd even recommend it for young kids. The game is in a weird spot where it's far too casual for people who could understand and handle all of it's mechanics, but also likely too difficult for kids who would be fine with how casual it is.The developers tried biting off more than they could handle in regards to the amount of mechanics/features/minigames included here, and as a result no single part of Dinosaur Fossil Hunter is done particularly well. Finding fossils is dull, repetitive, and the ground deformation while digging is obnoxious (I frequently got stuck and had to reset my position). Fossil-cleaning is monotonous, and like I mentioned above it requires zero effort since you don't have to be careful with them. Driving feels awful and having to frequently clear obstacles off the roads is annoying, leading you to want to abuse fast travel. The on-foot movement, like driving, is . I can't think of the last time I played a game where the act of just walking down a hallway was a chore thanks to the feeling of slipping around on ice.The only parts I enjoyed were putting together the miniature models on hard difficulty (otherwise it just tells you exactly where to put each piece..) but there only seems to be three of those (?), and the museum-decorating part of the game, but that seemed pretty basic. Additionally, the game only has one mouse sensitivity slider, and while decorating the museum your sensitivity is incredibly slow, to the point that I couldn't rotate the camera unless I wanted to swipe my mouse 20+ times across my entire mouse pad.This game also suffers from the . When you move around, it feels stutter-y and all objects around you look blurry. I very much doubt this or any of my other complaints will be fixed since the last patch was almost a year ago.

I am writing this today, 5/26/22. The game was released, full release. No early access build, where we expect to see most of the negatives I bring up below, and hope they get looked into. Fun for the first 10 hours, after that, it became a chore.Tutorials - 10/10Graphics - 6/10Sound/Music - 6/10Controls - 4/10Game world - 5/10Gameplay - 6/10Replayability - 3/10So first off, the tutorials tell you all you need to know to learn how to play. They continue throughout the game as you play, even into the late game where you find your first collectible. So 10/10 on tutorials.Graphics are about what you expect. Nothing to write home about, but certainly not horrible. 6/10Music is fun and relaxing. The sounds are good, again, nothing amazing, but I wasn't expecting amazing here. 6/10Controls - Here is where I give my biggest complaint. When you are cleaning dino fossils, the controls get really horrible. You are too close, too far away. This became more clear when I was working on the triceratops head. After this, I gave up cleaning any fossils myself. Controls at the dig points were good. Really, the only time I had issues with the controls were in cleaning/assembly mode, or the exhibit design. Controls there are also really bad. Flying the drone felt natural though, I intuitively knew how to fly it. 4/10 ControlsGame world - It is empty of all living things. The museum is empty of people. You have workers, but you never see them. In a game where you are finding long dead things, it may seem weird to want a living world, but I do. 5/10Gameplay - Overall, the game is fun for what it is. You dig up fossils, you clean the fossils, you assemble the fossils, you exhibit the fossils. It got really repetitive pretty quick. 6/10Replayability - Other than a DLC or large updates, I can't imagine playing this game again. The gameplay loop got old at about 10 hours, so I started using workers/drones for everything. I have 1 more dino to find, then I am sitting on this game in my library forever. PROLOGUE REVIEW:A fun and relaxing game of dinosaur fossil hunting, which brings back childhood memories of searching the local outcrops for tiny shell-like fossils left in the shale rock.  I live in the Ottawa valley in Ontario, Canada which was once a large sea that left layers upon layers of sediment which became a perfect fossil producing substrate.The Prologue gives you plenty of things to do in various areas, from the excavation site, to the museum with it's various sections for receiving, cleaning, and displaying your dinosaur finds.  The Exhibition Room is where you show your dinosaurs in different poses, with decorated environments, along with the room itself.At the end of this Prologue, you find yourself as a post graduate Paleontologist, starting out with very little prospect oF work.   You help out your Grandfather to clean up his garage and make a special discovery, which ends the demo but leaves you wanting to play the rest of the game.I know I will be purchasing the full release of the game when it's available.POST-RELEASE REVIEW:I'm totally enthralled with the different aspects of being employed at a local museum of Paleontology, which gains prestige as you obtain the rights to work on even more fossil deposits throughout North America, which promotes the museum to become a State Museum, followed by a National Museum.Finding a complete set of fossils for a new dinosaur is quite exciting, including all the work associated with finding, excavating, preparing, and finally putting it up in your museum exhibitions.You have a number of off-road vehicles to carry all your gear and supplies to a new dig site, which I find a bit difficult to operate due to the view options and the terrain.  You'll have to use quite a number of tools to find and prepare your specimens for transport to the museum, including advanced technology such as drones.Overall, the game is well done and totally worth getting if you have the slightest interest in either dinosaurs, the career field of Paleontology, as well as the outdoors type work.

An appealing and certainly unique concept quickly turns into a time killing "simulator" from hell. The game starts well enough, with narrative and some basic structure, which you presume you will be following (while listening to supremely cheerful and grandiose sounding music, which I had to turn off, because it kept playing when nothing was happenning). However, few hours in, you start getting into the "really obnoxious, time consuming, but never complex in any way" stuff, which has no skill involved, just takes a lot more time, because you will be putting together 100 little bones, you will seriously question whenever this game should even exist. It's not fun, and it has nothing to do with real life, because I can imagine restoring bones in real life being time consuming, but fascinating, however, in a game, simply clicking on pixels over and over is anything but that. And it will take considerable amount of time. You can't avoid it. You just keep clicking or moving cursor around and things happen. From the beginning to the end, no matter what you're digging out or assembling, it's the same, increasingly tedious busy job. If I wasn't listening to the videos on the side, I would've uninstalled the game long ago. But eventually, I just couldn't take it.Perhaps the grind wouldn't be as bad if simply moving around in the game wasn't a chore as well! Basic movement isn't smooth at all. Your character likes to get stuck at everything. There is a jump button, but it's a dice toss whenever the game will respond or not - maybe you'll jump, maybe you won't. The whole game doesn't feel right, as if everything is jittery, even if steam shows me 144 FPS, it feels like the game runs below 60, it's just weird. And where walking is bad, driving is the worst. Cars are annoying to handle, and the camera is painful - if you're driving down the hill, you can't see in front of yourself, because the stupid camera is angled in a way that doesn't respect elevation! You literally cannot see where you're going. There is no first person camera. Your car can hit a pebble and randomly flip over - if a game has a dedicated button for resetting a car, you better believe it's there for a reason. Also, if you're like me, you will forget to bring tools to set up new camps, so you will waste even more time - you will get warned sometimes, but that happens automatically, regardless of what you have loaded in your car... Devs should've just throw a reality aspect away here and make it less tedious for players. You will eventually unlock fast travel, but I will argue that most of these upgrades should've been there from the beginning, as they improve restrictions imposed by the developers, which just make the game more annoying.Aside from the overall shoddiness, game is also buggy - several bones got stuck and I was prevented from cleaning them, had to send them to the automated workers, because couple of small bone fragments simply didn't fall to the ground, like they're supposed to. When you fast travel with the car, you can't unload the boxes with bones at first, you need to get out of the car and back into it, only then they become interactive and you can actually unload it. There was more stuff, nothing completely gamebreaking, but just more sloppy stuff.Add few other things, such as unintuitive UI, or lack of the advertised storyline - the game description lies. You get couple of cutscenes at the beginning, and then, absolutely nothing, it's all just an endless grind to excavate all the bones and put them together - that's the game. What seemed cool at first turns into mindless routine that has absolutely nothing to it. Due to how bad the movement and driving feels, I had zero desire to explore the maps - for what? Few collectibles that add absolutely nothing? If the gameplay was wrapped into an engaging story that it seemed like it was trying to set up, maybe the game would hold up. But that's not what you'll get at all. You will spend time sitting in that dumb preparation room, driving around, mindlessly digging in the groundI honestly question whenever games like this should even be made - what's hiding underneath an unusual theme is yet another game about killing time, where you end up doing mindless busy work that is simply no fun at all.I didn't even talk about the museum part, because it feels depressing - you have rather extensive customization for your exhibits, which nobody will ever see, because this game didn't have budget for any audience of this part of the game - you're a manager, but you do no managing, that's not in the game. Oh, you can visit other people's museums I guess, but I couldn't care less about some random person visiting my stuff, especially now that nobody plays the game. In my eyes, that is the most pointless part of the game, because there is zero impact to something that should be a strong moment.It's not engaging, it's not challenging in the slightest, all you're focusing on is completing checklists without anything driving you but your own will and how much obsessive you can get. I've played too many games with these kind of design practices and I'm sick of it. The gameplay is bad, and there is nothing holding it together in any way to make you want to continue. Perhaps the developers got too ambitious and time got in the way, or they aren't experienced enough, but regardless of what caused it, the result is a bad game.

Do you have a great passion for dinosaurs or have you always found it interesting how they carefully excavate, restore and set up excavations that are millions of years old?Then Dinosaur Fossil Hunter might be for you because here you will have to go through areas where you will have to dig up fossils.Check out my first gameplay as a paleontologist here: The game will start with excavating personal collections of found fossils, which you will then clean and keep neatly, but all this will evolve into keeping and maintaining a complete museum!The game consists more or less of a few parts: excavating, preparing and displaying the fossils.With the excavation you go with your vehicle to different excavation sites,pay attention because the route you have to follow is not always that comfortable, but with a little technique you will occasionally be able to find a daring shortcut that will save you a minute or two of maneuvering ;)You will also need to operate a device with a sensor that detects rock under the ground.This way you will not have to dig endlessly with a shovel and pickaxe, but you can work more focused.once you have the stone you can check with a radiation meter whether the stone contains fossils.If the stone does appear to have a fossil, you will have to pack the stones with a field jacket, just like real paleontologists do, this also prevents damage to the fossils during transport.When you eventually keep a museum open, you will also have to deal with new tasks such as preparing a complete skeleton,when you do this in-game you will quickly notice that there are a lot of sequential steps involved and that it doesn't just take a minute to complete, but that's actually pretty accurate with how these things are prepared in real life, so it's it's also a simulator of course.

[Edited, previously did not recommend]There was recently a large update which broke much of the functionality, but the devs have fixed most of it and the game has returned to a playable state and I can give it a proper review,Overall, this game is a wonderful paleontology experience! As a student I don't get many opportunities myself to go on digs, so I was hoping this game would give me an experience close to what a dig would be. While nothing comes close to the real thing, Im pleased to say this game strikes a great balance between a real experience and game mechanics.The digs take what would normally take hours or days and an entire team with heavy equipment, and breaks down all the important steps into a job and time slot that a single person could accomplish. Sifting through stone and dirt to find the target stratigraphic unit and locating fossil rich stone. After you find the target units you take those stones and clean them up a bit to see if there is any fossil material, and if there is you plaster it and get it ready for transport. This is overall done very well and presents all the steps of the dig process in a condensed manner. My only complaint is that you should actually know what units you are looking at. Inspecting stones should tell you what formation and time range they belong to, not just whether or not they contain a fossil, and you should have some information somewhere telling you what formation(s) you are looking for. Other than that nitpick, digs are fun!Then there's the preparation. This is where I have the most experience irl, and aside from game limitations this process is also presented very well! It walks you through all the steps from dusting to cleaning, and the only real issues I come across are trying to handle really small or thin pieces, such as carpals or ossified tendons. Because they are small, its hard to get the tools to clean them properly. I dont have many suggestions other than perhaps allowing some panning during the assembly process, and bring the bones closer to the camera when cleaning. Minor technicalities.The last part, the museum showcase, is where I really begin to have issues. First I would like to say that the displays themselves are marvelous! I've always wanted to assist in designing museum displays and this is as close as I've ever gotten! Everything from foliage decor to water, posing and positioning specimen, and even sizing the size of the display itself, you can create some astounding displays! It's honestly my favorite part! There are an ok selection of decor, and there isnt much space for too many displays, only a handful, but it goes without saying more space will be added later. That's a given.My main gripe with this game, actually comes from the descriptions of the dinosaurs that are present ON the displays. Some displays include information that is misrepresented, mistranslated, or outright disproven. As an example, the Triceratops fossil appears to be T. prorsus, but the descriptions labels it as T. horridus. On top of that, the description is full of grammar issues, and mentions Triceratops frills may have had an acoustic function? This is simply incorrect, and while Triceratops is the worst, it's not the only description filled with poor grammar or false information. While a minor part, this game has been super accurate up until this point, and it could pass as truthful to someone who does not know better.I don't believe this was done intentionally, and is simply mis-translation. I for one would be excited to help transliterate the game in english, but I'm sure there are also better candidates out there. All I wish is they find someone who is better able to translate or transliterate these description to make sure these animals are presented correctly.Overall, Dinosaur Fossil Hunter is a joy. I can see myself pouring countless hours into it's many different aspects, and I am more than excited to see where it goes from here! The developers have shown to be patient with the community and dedicated to this project, and I'm looking forward to seeing what else they have in store for us!But please, update the descriptions :')

Dinosaur Fossil Hunter is a simulator game at its core. You're doing tasks related to fossil diving, recovering, and displaying. But you're also doing a lot of the in between stuff like driving vehicles and removing debris like logs and stone. You're driving forklifts to transport crates full of fossils. The game has a cycle of pretty much traveling to different maps, scanning and digging for fossils, and then transporting them back to the museum. You then prepare the fossils with an extensive cleaning process taking multiple steps before putting bones together into various dinosaur models. Then you have great freedom to set up the exhibits. You can pose the models and change the habitat decorations up. You can even change up the texture and design of the wallpaper, ceiling, and furniture. It does take awhile to obtain and start showing off your goods but it's pretty satisfying once you get it just right and walk through your own exhibits. I recommend this game, with a caveat.It's janky. A lot of the controls are floaty and don't feel great. Driving is as much of a mess as the other people are saying. It's not well optimized and a lot feels unpolished. The tutorial is also a little frustratingly slow.However, I still very much enjoy it and recommend it to anyone who loves paleontology and is willing to look past the issues. It has a simple yet overall satisfying gameplay loop for someone who is interested in paleontology, dinosaur fossils and skeletons, and who enjoys games in a similar vein as Powerwash Simulator. The overall process is truer to actual paleontology than anything else I've seen to date, and you can tell that these developers are really trying to make a game grounded in actual science.For me, while the core gameplay loop is nice and relaxing, the real treat is the exhibit decoration. There's a surprisingly robust exhibit creation system that allows you to create some interesting and compelling scenes throughout your museum. Choosing biomes, skeleton posing, water and stone features, and manually placing foliage is very satisfying and I thoroughly enjoy it.I haven't yet played the painting DLC but I'm curious and hope it will add to the experience of exhibit creation. I will update later once I get a chance to try it.To summarize, I wouldn't recommend this game to the average person. It's targeted towards a very specific brand of nerd. But for those nerds, this game is an absolute gem and 100% worth it. Now if you'll excuse me, it's time to research what sorts of paleoflora grew in Alberta during the Late Cretaceous so I can plan my next exhibit...

A fun and fluffy metroidvania with plenty to discover!Among the graphical design of the scenery is a lot of texture in addition to chic backgrounds. In a similar vein the character designs are colourful and cute with a lot of character as one would expect from furry characters. There is some clear heart and effort that has been put into this game including but not limited to the graphics of it.The sound design is also well done albeit nothing that felt too out of the ordinary. It works quite well in establishing the atmosphere and is pleasant to listen toThere are plenty of biomes and mechanics unique to each one making this a very solid metroidvania. Additionally over half of the abilities you get have both a use in platforming as well as in combat. The one thing I would like to change a bit is the map by giving it a bit more detail with for example markers for some additional quality of life, but that is about it.Bossfights are fun and require you to learn the pattern, which can be said for the regular enemies as well on a smaller scale. Overall the fights are balanced well so that you might need a few tries with the bosses or a particularly difficult room but it doesn’t become frustrating. Plus you save every time when entering a room, so there isn’t really a long walk back to a difficult spot.I played on the Hard difficulty which is decently challenging yet not overwhelmingly so, though if you prefer focusing on the exploration and story without having to mind combat so much I’d definitely recommend going with the Easy difficulty.Most of the story is in the collectibles, various descriptions and a big chunk towards the end. To not spoil anything it is nothing particularly new, but still very nicely executed. You do get some hints to it in the environment as well.The translation is serviceable, you can understand everything well enough however you never forget that it’s a translation either. Additionally there are a few lines that are not translated at all though those seem to be of no real relevance, so nothing is really lost there.As Doge is a good girl, so is this a good game for free, which I can certainly recommend as a solid metroidvania with good graphical design.

A very good indie Metroidvania that should take most experienced players between 6 and 8 hours to 100%.I would recommend that those experienced with the genre play on Hard Mode for their first playthrough, as the game is incredibly forgiving of deaths, auto-saving after every room transition. This allows the game to have several challenging but not infuriating boss fights and some complex platforming and puzzle rooms.The majority of the sprite-work is very appealing though in one area of the game, the dead forest on the right side of the map, it can sometimes be difficult to differentiate between platforms and background elements. The map itself is filled with unique room layouts and landmarks, so at no point did I ever feel lost or unsure of where to go to progress and secret areas can be identified very naturally, at no point did I have to bomb every wall in order to break a seemingly normal wall tile.While I did enjoy the game, it is not without flaws. As the game was made by a small team who all speak Japanese as their first language, there are many minor translation mistakes and typos and there are even a couple of very minor characters who's dialogue is still in Japanese (however, this specific text is not relevant to the plot or any game play knowledge and can be ignored by the player without consequence.) Due to the game's relatively simple plot, these translation issues do not make the story hard understand but they did cause me to have to re-read several lines in order to understand what they were supposed to say.The game also has several bugs: item pickups can sometime get stuck in the ground. Twice, I encountered a bug where I was unable to enter a door with the W key and the only fix was to return to the hub area or close the game (this was only ever a minor inconvenience due to the game's frequent auto-saves.) One time, the game crashed while transitioning through a door, this had no affect on my save data and I have seen reports from some players that only certain controllers are supported. However, I would recommend that players use the keyboard and mouse anyway, due to the game's simple control scheme. One more gripe I have is with the final boss, which is mostly fine with one exception, which I fear may lead to some players not understanding how to defeat it:This is incredibly unintuitive for the player.Despite the previously listed flaws (which I have no doubt most will be resolved in a patch), I still believe Garm Ruins to be a fantastic effort at a Metroidvania, with great music and cute characters. Once the game is polished some more, I would not blame the dev team if they were to charge $5 for it.

I bought this game yesterday, and I'm already 14 hours in. My friends keep asking me "what's this game about?"Basically, you just build and manage a cat colony. As you progress through the levels in the campaign, you get access to more jobs and buildings. Such as a farmer in level 2. I haven't even been able to get past level 2 yet. There is a variety of challenges such as making sure you have enough food and housing for everyone in your village, to completing the goals in each level, facing off against hoards of rat thieves and other baddies, and making sure your two starting cats don't die. If they do, you have to restart the entire level over again. Unless you have a recent save you can load into. So save OFTEN. Imagine if animal crossing met Minecraft. This game, however, focuses on prosperity, progression, growth, and of course, management. But the cool thing is, is that you can go at your own pace. So while you still get the options to let one cat befriend another, the interactions between player and NPCs isn't deep at all. However, the relationship with one cat has with another can determine certain aspects. In my experience, if one cat doesn't like one of my Knights, for example, that knight cannot take that cat on as an apprentice. I am not too sure if relationship dynamics branches out beyond this, such as two cats refusing to share a house together. There are some aspects to this game where players are left confused and wondering what they need to do in order to complete goals and requests made by other cats. The building mechanics are a bit funky too. It took me a while to understand how building the bridge in level 2 worked, but I was able to get it. As far as finding player guides and walk-throughs for this game, I wasn't able to find much, so as it stands right now the player is left on their own for the most part to figure out the game. I haven't played much of sandbox mode to give a decent review on this, but I once I play it I'll come back and edit this review to include sandbox mode. I recommend the game because it's challenging, it has a casual feel and play style to it, your cats CAN and WILL die, you can build and upgrade. Overall, this game feels like your classic MMORPG you'd play back in the early 2000s, but with a cute and casual spin, tailored specifically for the player's personal preferred pace. You can speedrun or you can take your time and build the biggest and coolest town. There's no pressure.

This gives it more direction You train your cats in various specialties, and eventually take on enemies who will try to loot and pillage your growing city.  You grow your village to produce food and resources to either use to feed your cats and grow further or to sell for gold to use on other things. The game has a perfect balance of laid back casual with strong strategic hardcore strategy elements peppered in to keep direction in your gameplay.   It is rare to see a game strike this balance so early in it's early-access run, and it includes a difficulty selection to allow you to select the balance right for you.Who will like it:Do you like cute cats?Do you like laid back slow and steady strategy games?Do you enjoy games where you build cities?Well you'll like it.Does anything that isn't a blood and guts ego shooter make you puke?Do you like your games ultra-hardcore competitive like DOTA?Do you prefer games you can play in 5 minute sessions?You probably should look elsewhere. Adorable game with incredible potential. Having a lot of fun recruiting and controlling all of my little cats in my little colony. That said, in the current state of the game, I would not recommend it. This game has a crazy amount of bugs. These are bugs that have been brought the the dev's attention years ago that still haven't been addressed such as cats with the clumsy trait completely disregarding tasks given to them once they fall over. Bed assignments mean absolutely nothing because cats will not abide by them (earning you lots of negative buffs) and cats in combat will continuously run to attack spawn even after you've told them to retreat back to base. Also, items up high do not fall to the ground so dropped equipment such as bows cannot be gathered and certain missions (such as keeping a cat up all night) do not work and will glitch out before it completes. Game also needs some AI fixes that are tolerable initially, but, in the later stages, quickly become irritating. These are things such as cats not automatically drying off after taking a bath (You have to manually tell them to dry off each and every time. No problem in the beginning when you only have 3 cats. Not manageable anymore when you have 15 to manage). Cats also either stay on a task too long and wear themselves out to the point of exhaustion instead of automatically maintaining a positive status when resources are plentiful, or they won't do anything at all and require you to micromanage every action (won't continuously gather nearby supplies despite having nothing to do). Finally, tutorial is a bit lacking. Game doesn't explain the roles clear enough and the tips and advice on where and how to do certain actions (such as how to equip accessories) are on the loading screen that is so quick it's impossible to read. Also, you cannot report any of these bugs or issues in-game. The bug report form in-game doesn't work. I'm pretty sure, based on the discussion forum, that this game might possibly be abandoned and won't ever come out of early access which is shame because despite all of the issues I listed, it's a wonderful game. Just needs a little more love and polish.

So, you have no idea how disappointed I was, when I realised (pretty early on into playing it) that Catizens was NOT the  that I wanted it to be, and in fact, it's a pretty bad game as well. Cons:  No functioning sandbox mode (you know the mode, where in Sims4 you can spend 400hours+ on a single map? Well, this game doesn't have that. The mode that the game DOES have, is broken and explaining WHY it's broken would take up a page on its own, so you'll just have to trust me on this). The game is designed to ALWAYS give you flawed cats. You ALWAYS get cats with at least 1 'bad' trait. The AI of the cats are flawed. Your cats will often do needless BS when they SHOULD be picking up materials on the ground or resurrecting a downed cat. The game un-pauses itself CONSTANTLY. The class system (Knight / Architect) is convoluted and unnecessary. Your cats will sometimes sleep outside, instead of sleeping in a house, which makes no sense (and no, this isn't due to any 'sleep related' talents). The cats just ignore your instructions sometimes... like I would right click, and it won't even load the instruction into the cat's queue. The game MASSIVELY lacks transparency and tooltips. You aren't told what the differences are between 'easy' 'medium' or 'hard'. You also aren't told what 80% of the talents do.... it just says "increases your happiness" or "increases your armor", BUT BY HOW MUCH IS IT INCREASED?!?! Creating a road that is 1x1 costs 1stone, but creating a road that is 50x1 also costs 1stone. Where's the logic? The game has no FPS cap option The game has no v-sync optionTime will tell if the devs can turn this into a playable game (it'll take many years, but it's possible). But as for right now, I simply can't recommend it. Posting this because every other review I saw was positive. Sadly, despite the cutesy theme, good intro and fun concept, the game is bloody awful. So many glaring problems.Imagine Rimworld, but you have to manually tell your colonist to chop down every individual tree. The micromanagement is endless. Your cats will wander off into enemy bases, drop what they were doing mid-task because they decided to go bath or sleep, run away from combats they can win and forget what they were ordered to do without constant interference.The aggressive fog of war is HORRENDOUS. Basically if you don't have a cat or a building near an area of the map, it will fill in with full opaque fog. Exploring doesn't reveal the map - instead you have to re-explore every single time you want to move somewhere. It's annoying both for having no idea where to click to make your cats move, and for having to re-explore just so you can build things there. Now, you might think that the game is a cutesy city builder. You could not be more wrong. The game is actually mostly focused around combat. Enemies will continually attack your city from level 2 onwards, and they get tough fast. The combat is bad and annoying to control, with cats fleeing combat when they should stand and fight, with AWFUL pathfinding that results in your units getting caught on each other if you tell them to attack the same target. Even if it all works, the combat is just... bad. It's simple "you hit the enemy, the enemy hits you" with the only real 'strategy' being exploiting the terrible pathfinding and rotating whoever the enemy is currently targeting with their attacks. The only upside is that things die quickly. This also means your cats die quickly too, and it's annoyingly easy to have a cat stuck in the wounded state near enemies that you can't beat, so they just bleed out and die.At least by level 3 (last level of EA) there were no walls or turrets, so enemies can just run into your base and start stealing things. That's IF they run - I've observed them literally just spawning in my base and walking into my storage area to start robbing me. So much for the aggressive FOW meant to hide stuff like that. By level 3 I had a minimum of 4 trained knights + a ranger to beat most enemies, until I approached the final area of level 3 and watched as my army was instantly killed by the undead archers, who are incredibly OP. Losing any soldiers is brutally punishing as they have a gold cost, a food cost and an extensive training time. Think more like losing a well trained fighter in Rimworld than losing a unit in Warcraft 3. Oh and you lose the game if you lose a starting character.Despite all of the above being a problem, the biggest problems are with the controls and UI. The UI tells you nothing. All cats can only do certain jobs. What jobs can they do? ♥♥♥♥ you, figure it out yourself. Want to build multiple buildings in a row? Far as I can tell, you can't. Hope you like clicking the button every single time. Want your cats to focus on something specific? No button or command for it, you just have to keep shift-right clicking the things you want done and set the task. The controls are atrociously bad. You right click to do most things in the game. Except you ALSO right click to move the camera. If you right click and move the camera at all, even just a tiny bit, the order you were trying to give won't be given. That means I often found myself right clicking 3-4 times to get a cat to do a single task. It is ridiculously frustrating.Oh and it's buggy. Perks don't do what they say they will. Loading a save game didn't work for me until the second time I played. Give the game 1 to 2 years and it might be worthwhile.

I really enjoy this game; it is like the Sims but actually has a survival method to it. The game is very fun and engaging, because you want the wellbeing of your Catizens. If you neglect them: they may die or you'll lose Catizens, and if you lose an important character to something like death, the game is basically over.The game is coming from the ground up and finding a way to thrive.Pros:- Engaging- Interactive- Allows for creativity- Cute design, good graphics- Buttons and controls function well for the most part.Cons:- the easy and normal setting are anything but easy and normal, they are hard. Catsual (easy) says it is focused on the wellbeing of your cats, but I had a save where enemies basically spawn killed me.- Knights (the hunter cats) are the ones who fight. If they are unconscious, they can either die or everybody else is screwed, and if they are screwed, they can't revive you, thus death.- Food is so incredibly scarce. The game loads you with an architect (whom I've named Weed Snorter) and a knight (Crack Drinker). Knights can gather meat, but architects basically mine and build. If you really want food, sell everything you have just for a bundle of 3 bread for 5 coins. If you spawned with a gluttonous cat, good luck. Finding meat isn't as easy as it should be. As far as I know, wolves and boars dropped meat, but that meat is quickly gone. By the way, there is no farmer. You can hire a farmer but you won't be able to afford them because you don't have enough money because you need food. Plus, you'd need to learn how to be a farmer from the guy. So send your own infantry on a gold hunt.- Saves are incredibly broken. The game constantly auto-updates, but let me tell you this: if you load a save file, it deletes every other save file except that one, and you can't go back on your previous save.- Merchants are stupid. If you want bread because your town is going through a famine, and you might have 10 million gold laying around, if the merchant is NOT around then that sure does suck for you.- Cats are so autonomous unlike the Sims, but they are also disobedient and mischievous. It's frustrating working with these cats.At the moment, I am not far in the game. I love this game too, but it needs serious work. I can't find a guide for this game, and I'm not aware of cheats to remedy the suffering of this game. The Great Depression is real and lives on whenever you play this game.Nonetheless, overall I recommend the game WITH reservations. I must admit that when first playing the initial release of this game I was rather surprised to only see a total of 5 stories up until I opened the first one and found that these indeed appear to be much longer than older installments for both this series and Gay Furry Shading respectively. Being an avid fan of Furlough's franchises this game has indeed filled the gape I had when virtually begging for a continuation. I will admit that it has been close to a year now since I last penetrated the immersion of a Furlough title and I've found my time playing SATFT3 to jiggle my joy receptor and satiate my cravings. However I may be a bit ashamed to admit that it was also very thrilling to have the game bend me over a couple of times as well with certain levels which led me to think more carefully about every move and when to use power-ups. In all honesty I was highly esteemed to see the Isabella, Judy, and Elliot love triangle persist throughout the games and am all for this being done with other characters as well. (BRING BACK ROBYN I'M BEGGING YOU) Through my time playing I had encountered a few bugs although minor in nature that didn't really affect the flow of the experience too much. For example there had been several times where there were no more possible moves on the board and the game wouldn't reshuffle until a power-up was used to disturb it again, as well as the opposite happening, when the board would refresh even though there were still options or while pieces were still falling. Though problems like this on the initial launch are to be expected and I believe they'll be resolved not too long in the future. I'm just so proud to see the feats those at Furlough have achieved thus far and still continue to look forward to the future for what's next in store. SATFT3 as much like many other experiences created by Furlough   has reminded me of a bigger purpose in life, a battle of resilience, perseverance, and even more so and most important of all, love. Now well of course those first 3 are fairly obvious when it comes to experiencing this game. The levels provide hardship and critical thinking, lots of planning and luck that go into every single one of your valuable turns. Some levels end up being FARRR easier than others, and oftentimes the levels can take 10 to 30 minutes depending on how you're using power-ups and your own intellect. Though I believe the one thing to take away from this is the implementation of unlimited moves. With infinite turns it makes moves lose value as you mindlessly swipe, just like the hundreds of hours spent scrolling away on apps like tiktok. The unlimited turn button can be best described as a needy ex-wife, at first you think it sounds cool at first, y'know just to try it out and all, but then you'll soon come to find that all it was ever good for was being a little wallet wart. Apparently our friends in this game weren't the only ones sucking, because my word does that button know how to suck the life and joy out of the experience. Just like Rebecca. The skip button is there as a test of mental fortitude and endurance as it dangles what is by far the biggest, juiciest, bodacious free-bee right in front of your gaping mouth as it teases you to take a bite. However you may be mistaken, for though it may seem so easy and appetizing to take the easy way out and essentially give up on what could’ve been a very pivotal point in your life far beyond the reaches of the game, it is important to battle off and overcome the urges of temptation as it builds character and resistance to a hit of quick dopamine. It shows dedication and even pride in what you're doing and you should be proud of yourself choosing not to. Matter of fact I strongly know that the game objectively rewards you more if you choose not to use this option and I strongly suggest you find out for yourself. The challenge is and was intended to be part of the fun, so it’d be absolutely moronic and downright idiodic to remove that experience from the game, because what’s a bit of fun if it isn’t rough with you? Speaking of rough, I strongly encourage you not to give up or be discouraged by how difficult this grueling journey may seem at times, I find it important to farm money so that you may use it all on bombs and needles as needed. The levels are not at all shy about wanting to bend you over and rip you a new one and they absolutely will when given the chance, a lesson of mutual exchange if you will. The hours spent matching various shapes will be ones spent with sweaty, tearfilled, sticky steaminess while staring at your screen. Patience is a virtue and the contents of these levels are its gospel. SATFT3 operates at such a higher plane of existence and being that it often toys with you without you ever noticing. You’ll go through the game for quite a while thinking that you’re in control of how fast or slow you finish, however the entire time the levels decide when you do. You’re always following their pace and in turn are their pet, now of course you’re given treats every now and then, those being one of the various ‘scenes’ you may encounter in stories, or even the money required to buy your power-ups and safeword boosters. SATFT3 operates with something close to a soft dom mentality, and by that I mean that it allows you free reign to do whatever it is you desire: (ie.playing the game the way and speed you wish to, or rewatching your favorite scenes just to get your fill out of them.) only to remind you who’s in charge by slapping, scratching, smooching you and smooching, splurging, and spewing all over you just to remind you who’s in charge and put you in your place. I mean, it can leave you begging to go easy on you sometimes am I right? But when the time finally comes, and SATFT3 permits you to, then you’ll be bestowed upon with a rush and wave of ecstasy and pleasurable relief that fills your body and breaks your mind with dopamine as you’re glad it’s over and you’ve reached such a ‘satisfying’ conclusion. Or, the alternative, you could’ve used the unlimited turns and given in to your temptation and sloth for an easier way of chickening out of the full experience, preemptively draining yourself of all the joy you could’ve had while doing it legitimately. Sure you’ll reach your climax, but much faster and with a lot less impact as there was hardly any buildup or anticipation that had gone into it, “this game blows” you’d think to yourself. Nah, only you did, and far too early. You’ll sit there in not a puddle of pleasure, but in one of shame and humiliation. You’ll sit there regretful as the cold painful rod of disappointment is inserted in you, you’ll ponder on what could’ve been, yearning for so much more, and feeling so full of regret and such a fool for making the active and premeditated choice of literally scamming yourself out of such a life-changing experience. If anything it shows signs of what already is or what is soon to be the symptoms of addiction, you’d see such a quick rush of dopamine and satisfaction and do anything to reach it as soon as possible. It shows impulsiveness, and most of all weakness, as you allow your genitals way you down from climbing and soaring to new heights in life. SATFT3 is a life changing experience and honestly for the better, it’s something very big on aftercare and teaching you valuable lessons about more than just matching 3 puzzles and clapping furries. It teaches you an important lesson about self control and most importantly working for what you want in life, and learning to appreciate what you’ve already done so far and the progress you’ve made, instead of always dreading what’s left to do and never wanting to do it because of that. Overall I strongly recommend that you try out this experience for the humble price that it is, and most importantly, take away the important lesson it’s trying to teach you all along the way. “Edge as much as you can, it brings you a sharper climax to your journey.” XOXO

Being stuck in the warehouse sucks... Time to move some boxes out of the way and get out! A kind of vertical sokoban, you have to rearrange boxes to reach the exit. This is an enhanced remake of the old Block-Man game, with a lot more focus on level cleverness than just moving boxes.Grid-based movement, you can move left or right on a straight path, fall down edges, and climb up only one step at a time. You can also pick up and carry one box at a time, only if there is enough space above for the box to fit. What makes this super hard is that you can't just turn around to face the opposite way, so you can't pick up a box and just drop it on the other side. The game is super frustrating, but in a good way. You think you have an easy solution, only to find out that you can't actually do that, and you have to find an alternative path. Although there aren't that many levels, you'll spend a lot of time on each one.Two other elements complicate the levels: teleporters (called elevators, but I don't know of any elevator that goes sideways), and bonuses. The bonuses are a bit out of the way and usually require having a spare box, and they work both as a "skip level" token and for unlocking additional bonus levels. The teleporters are supposed to help, but more often than not they are actually another obstacle, since they automatically transport you when you step in front of them, unless the other side is blocked or you are carrying a box.For each level there are multiple goals: just finishing the level, finishing it within a good number of moves (par), and finishing it with a shortest solution. And, of course, collecting the bonus when there is one in the level. Moderate to hard, considerably harder if you want to get the optimal solution. 50+16 levels, for about 10 hours to finish and 30 to perfect. There is also support for custom levels, although not through Steam Workshop. Good. Very hard levels, with non-obvious solutions, and although there are a lot of moves to make, they don't feel like useless padding. Very good. Unlimited undo and mid-level saving (although it doesn't survive exiting the level), decent controls, multiple speed options, progress and skill achievements, decent settings, fast and responsive, level editor, manual. Yes. Frustratingly hard. Optimizing the score is frustrating, given that most levels require more than 100 moves, it's easy to make a mistake, and it rarely involves finding a shorter solution, but optimizing how you move many boxes from one pile to another. Not that much to complain about, just some nitpicking. Add Workshop support. Add volume sliders. Make controls rebindable. Add a story/cutscenes., very similar game, but with some special boxes., another good game about moving boxes around, but different mechanics.

I grew up with these sorts of games, so I may be a tad biased. I'm jaded by the hand-holding that many games these days do, and this one does not do that. It's much more difficult than I expected, which is a plus for me. The first row of levels does a good job of introducing the gameplay mechanics without having to resort to outright telling you what to do. The difficulty ramps up pretty quickly after that. I almost walked away when I saw that the game had hints added, but luckily they are not as hand-holdy as I thought they would  be. Essentially, they provide end-states for the boxes, similar to how a sokoban game plays. Even when turned on, the more difficult puzzles are still challenging, but I am leaving it off unless I get absolutely stuck.The level editor is nice, and I'm looking forward to come up with some ideas to upload, but the sheer number of custom level slots is overkill. It's nice to have plenty of slots, but I can't imagine any individual person making that many levels in the editor, and keeping track of that many would not be trivial. Also, while this game plays great with a controller, the level editor lends itself better to a mouse. Honestly, I'm surprised but appreciative that you implemented gamepad controls in the editor at all, though I think I will stick to mouse for level making.I think the bonus levels are my favorite part of the game. They are brutally difficult for the most part, which I assume is why they are separate from the main levels (granted the later main levels are pretty hard). The only bonus level I don't like so far is 10, that one is a bit tedious, to be frank. Otherwise, I love the bonus levels and wish there were more. Hopefully the dev is listening and will add more bonus levels in an update, or even a DLC level pack. In the meantime, I'll keep an eye on the community shared levels and try to make some of my own.Overall, this game is fantastic for oldschool puzzle gamers like me who enjoy thinky games. I remember playing something similar on my TI-84 in my college days, and this plays a lot smoother than that while not looking like a mobile game. I look forward to seeing what else this dev comes up with in the future.

Pros:- Nostalgic. Has retro graphics and plays almost identically to Blockdude which I played on my calculator about 15 years ago- Has two new additions that Blockdude didn't have: elevators and keys. These make levels more interesting.- You can undo your moves, and place one "save point" in each level.- Relatively high replayability: each level has a "par" and a "dev" score, that give you a number of moves that you have to beat the level in, in order to get a little icon on the level select screen and unlock some achievements. The "dev" score is often the fewest number of moves possible, or close to it, and the "par" score is a bit higher than that. Beating the "par" score on some levels is really challenging, and I have no idea how to beat the "dev" score on most levels.- Some levels have an extra object you can collect that unlocks a bonus level.- The levels are challenging without being too challenging, and there are a lot of them (66 total, much more than Blockdude). The first few levels are really easy, but they quickly get more challenging, and trying to beat the "par" and "dev" scores is fun.- There is a level editor with the ability to share levels with others. I haven't messed with the level editor at all yet.Cons:- The only negative I can think of is that it's the same background music and graphics for every level. Some variety would have been nice, but it's not that big of a deal for me.Overall, this is a simple but challenging puzzle game. Recommended if you like puzzle games.

Super Retro BoxBot is a delightful puzzle game on Steam that effortlessly combines classic arcade aesthetics with modern gameplay mechanics. It's a nostalgic journey down memory lane for anyone who grew up playing retro games, and it manages to capture the essence of those old-school titles while adding its unique twist.The game's pixelated graphics and chiptune soundtrack immediately set the stage for a trip back to the golden age of gaming. The visuals are charmingly reminiscent of 8-bit and 16-bit classics, which will indeed evoke nostalgia for those who spent hours in front of their CRT screens. The attention to detail in replicating the retro look and feel is commendable, making it a visual treat.Super Retro BoxBot's gameplay is where it truly shines. It offers a fresh take on the classic block-pushing puzzle genre, introducing innovative mechanics that keep things engaging and challenging. The core objective is maneuvering your pixelated character (the titular BoxBot) through increasingly complex mazes, pushing crates onto designated spots to progress. The controls are simple and intuitive, making them accessible to newcomers and seasoned gamers.In terms of content, Super Retro BoxBot offers a decent number of levels, ensuring several hours of gameplay. In conclusion, Super Retro BoxBot is a charming and enjoyable puzzle game that successfully marries retro aesthetics with modern gameplay. It offers a satisfying challenge for puzzle enthusiasts and a heavy dose of nostalgia for retro gaming fans. While a more comprehensive tutorial would be beneficial, the innovative mechanics and clever level design make this title a must-play for anyone seeking a nostalgic, brain-teasing experience. Get ready for a pixelated journey filled with block-pushing fun!
