i now have over 2 hours playing A-tech. so,..i thought it would be a good time to write an early review.there are some things you need to know about this game. first off at this point if you are expecting a complete polished product...well this isnt it....Dont get me wrong this is a good game..the level design is topnotch...the monsters look great..the weapon modles are near perfect..the locomotion gives you both walking and teleporting in an excelent format using one hand to walk and the other to teleport...they set the mood of the game using first class skill...and i cant recomend  getting in on a project of this caliber enough..as early as you can for 2 reasons first is to fund the development...the dev teem working on this game is world class and it shows in their work..the second reason is you will end up with a AAA title for durt cheep in the end.I am running an I7 2700k (OC to 5ghz) ..an invidia GTX 1080 founders {OC +100mhz) and 32GB DDR3 @ 1600mhz with a raid-0 hdd array {2 x 7200rpm)the game loads quickly runs smoothly ..and doesnt tax any of my system resources more than 60% on max settings so it would probably run fine on a gtx 970.with all that there are some bad things about the game...the holsters are easy to miss..the health bar would be better if it was lower on the hud or even movable..and the voice acting is sub par but starting to grow on me..also grenades dont belong in your holster lol..so yes the good far out shines the bad...and the game is still in development so some of this may change..(for the better)...so yes i recomend this to evryone looking to get in on the next AAA title because this is it.

I've owned this game for a while, shortly after purchasing it I was hit with incompatible (out of the box) controller setup, it was looking for Index controllers and I couldn't find a way to change it. I knew I could work around it by mapping the controllers manually but the arcade-esque intro level and janky controls put me off.Well, today I was looking for something to play in VR and decided to  spend 15-20 minutes creating a decent controller profile for this.  I'm glad I did! The game-play is arcade like, you aren't getting a mil-sim here, but that is fine as long as you go in expecting this to be a fun arcade style action game you will get a treat. The environments are beautiful if a little repetitive. The enemies don't vary much but they swarm you in fair but challenging ways. The weapons are very satisfying, and the enemies respond to tactically placed shots. For example, on narrow walkways I got into a rhythm of saving ammo and shooting their legs out at the right moment, causing them to stumble and fall off. Head shots are good, but their brain is a non-vital organ so they will still come after you with a spurting stump between their shoulders.There are a couple of areas that were genuinely creepy, pitch black, you and a torch/flashlight surrounded by scratching noises and groans. I really enjoyed my 5+ hours in the campaign, the developers knew what they were making and executed it perfectly. Just like Zero Caliber, these devs are clearly working on a budget but they manage to get a LOT done with the resources they have.

This is the experience I had with with A-Tech Cybernetic. Every player will experience things differently. Also this is not my full review for A-Tech Cybernetic. The full review will be out after the full game is released. Now on to the early access review for A-Tech Cybernetic.Story: A-Tech Cybernetic is a game set in the future where mutated experiments escaped and killing people. You are....you...honestly nothing is known about you. You are just there with a voice in your head. The only thing explained is that the creatures are experiments that escaped. Your job get out alive. There are 6 or 7 chapters to the game making each can be played on easy, normal or hard mode.Survival Mode: (sure that is not the actual name of the mode but that is what it is to me, just survival) is a game mode where you just well survive as long you can through wave sections. Each wave mixes the different enemies to add a challenge. It has a buy item where you survive a certain number of waves you get to buy the next gun, There is also health, shield and slow-mo drops as well. This is okay but if you save the slow-mo enough you could slow-mo 2-3 waves and be fine.  The "checkpoint" system is complete crap. I died several times once I got a good chunk into the map & die to be brought back to the beginning of the level. The graphics look horrible on low & the game doesn't render in at long distance & with the in-game super sampling setting will help make the game look clear on low setting. On medium & high well those somehow causes me to have lower FPS & uses more CPU even though my PC meets the recommended requirements to play on medium setting. Other players who have better PCs then me compalin about the same thing of getting low FPS. The sounds are great I am constantly looking everywhere to find the source of the sound but the music was very loud, louder then the main game sound & there is only an "off" setting which doesn't work at all, the music still keeps playing regardless of it being off or on.There is an issue with this FPS & CPU indicator at the top middle of my screen that I can not disable at all. I tried looking in-game setting to find nothing. I tried STEAM setting to find nothing. I do not know why the developers added this to the game it just takes up more FPS & CPU to display that information while game is running. Controls are okay I was/am having issues with the snap turning. The snap tern is also the teleport button as well so when you use the snap turn, you may teleport as well. You can click the very edge of the button to do it but I some times still teleport. I would have liked to seen a move option so people can have 1 move system enabled instead of 2.Weapons are okay, mainly standard in games. The given pistol, the assault rifle and a shotgun. There are melee weapons and grenades as well but those don't do enough damage to the enemy. There is also dark weapons that acts...like a regular weapons but maybe a hint bit stronger. Also the ammo and weapons are placed way too much around the game. I never had to resort to a blunt weapon or my fists because the game just gave me enough ammo even on hard difficulty. However if you leave the game & come back for some reason it removes everything from your inventory & makes you restart collecting all over again.Creatures: There are multiple creatures in the game which make killing a bit difficult & challenging at times.Items: There are only 3 items in the game. Ammo, health and shield items.Logic: The logic is not that great in game. Like head-shots are not 100% instant kill. Throwing grenades are so hard to do (for me any ways). I activate it & then I trow its as if I never threw anything in my entire life, just goes not even an inch forward.  Immersion: The game has no immersion to it. There is no manual reload or double gripping. You never have to pick anything up by hand since the force grip makes it easy to do that. So what can I say about  A-Tech Cybernetic that makes it fun to buy.....nothing really. From my old review to this new one & posting issues to the community, it feels like once the game got a good amount reviews the developers just slowed down to a near screeching halt on the games development. The game feels worse now then when it first came out. So that puts the score for me at 5/10 score making it an average game. Its fun to play from beginning to end one time. There really isn't any replay-ability to the game & it just feels like the development hasn't been great. I can't recommend this game just due to its graphic issue. That is the Pony review for A-Tech Cybernetic

A-Tech Cybernetic VR: The Roger Corman of VR shootersThere was a famous filmmaker named Roger Corman who would rip off big budget studios films and create his own low budget version of it.  Even though his films were low budget he made some pretty interesting cult films and influenced indie filmmakers and filmmaking in general. Unfortunately this "game" takes that same concept and completely falls on its face trying to make a VR game. So what is A-Tech Cybernetic VR? Created by X-REAL Games, The makers of Zero Caliber, this game is a Doom 3 rip off where you have to deal with zombies and monsters created by ignorant scientists that have taken over a research platform on another planet. Sound Familiar? This game plays as a VR FPS shooter where you collect guns and ammo while clearing out rooms of enemies. Sound Familiar? Enemies include giant hulking brutes, fast zombies, zombies that shoot, zombies that teleport etc. Sound Familiar? This game just screams Doom as your playing it, but all it serves to do is remind you of how much better Doom is than this z-grade game. First the good:The only positive thing I can honestly say about this game is I enjoyed the narration. You are jacked into someone else's body and that person talks to you while playing. I thought the voice acting was good and the dialogue was funny at times. Yup. That's it. The bad:Besides what I have already said about this being a derivative low rent version of a better game, this game is a buggy mess. I'm going to list some of the bugs I encountered and discuss a couple game breaking ones including one that actually stopped me from completing this game. Bugs:Items including ammo and health will get stuck in the floor frequentlyIf the floor is even a cm off in a spot you WILL get stuckIf an enemy gets too close to you you can't move and cant shoot them because they are too close.Holsters are too far out from your body so you will accidentally draw a weapon frequently when trying to pick something up.Encountered game breaking bug at the end of chapter 2 where I died during a gauntlet after using most of my ammo and health so when the game reloaded my checkpoint, instead of starting with what I had at the start I started with NO weapons and 1/4 health during a gauntlet. I finally managed to beat it by running in circles around the enemies since I had NO health or weapons till the timer ran out and I could go to the next part. I don't think that's what the developers intended.The bug that finally broke me. I died in chapter 3 after making it through 90% of the level and when the game reloaded the screen it just flashed in some kind of epileptic nightmare and refused to load the checkpoint. The only thing I could do was replay the entire level. Nope not this guy. Congratulations X-Real Games! You did it! You finally broke and old school gamer who thought he could get over most bugs in a game. Faith in humanity gone...Do I recommend this game? Absolutely if you enjoy things such as splinters, sand in your underwear, pink eye or other such amenities of life. This game feels unfinished and in all honestly insulting to play. There are better VR shooters worth your time. Hell the DOOM 3 VR mod which is FREE is 100 times more polished than this garbage. Go play that instead.

The developers of A-Tech Cybernetic have stated that they're trying to create an unforgettable VR experience.I can honestly say that, with only two chapters out, they have succeeded a lot better than most complete VR games.The atmosphere and level of immersion are easily the best parts of the experience. It's very easy to forget you're just standing / sitting there playing a game. The screenshots above make it look like a balls-to-the-wall action / shooter. They don't really do it justice. The trailers are quite a bit better, but still don't quite capture the feeling of actually playing it. The actual game is a lot creepier and more atmosperic than they would lead you to believe.As far as the game itself, there's a lot of good things that can be said about it. Even the "zombie" type enemies are quite a bit more interesting as far as look and animations go. The controls are extremely precise, the guns feel great to use and the game preforms very well.It should also be said that this is exactly what an Early Access game should be. It seems to be in constant, very active development. I guess they've even gone so far as to completely revamp all the voice acting for the story mode, and completely rebuilt large parts of the levels because some people prefer walking to the standard VR teleportation movement. The devs seem very active in the community and very open to suggestions and discussion.Overall, I really hope more VR games turn out to be what A-Tech is becoming. If you're on the fence, you really should try the demo. I think there's a good chance you'll end up with the full game, especially considering how low the price is for what you're getting.

UPDATE 10 Dec 2018:I last played this game nearly a year ago. As per my original review below, I liked the game well enough, but didn't feel the urge to want to go back at the time.  Boy, have things changed, mostly for the better.Pros:- Nice control customization.  Being a smooth locomotion/turning kind of guy, this game had it all.- Nice weapon options.  The weapons this time around had a better distinct feel to them (how they 'felt', how they sounded. Handling grenades was a breeze.- Level Design was nice and varied; a mixture of indoor/outdoor levels kept in fresh.  I like how the outdoor levels gave a better sense of elevation in moving around (compared to the indoor levels, which mostly felt like you were in a single floor. The outdoor levels had a really grand scope of scale, making me feel like a rather small person.- World Building: What an attractive world they built.  The colorful displays and types of machinery laying about.  I actually wanted to play with thie stuff in this world.- Story:  Through the tablets and voice overs, there was sufficient backstory for myself to give a solid idea of what was going on (I did wish for a cutscene here and there).- Immersiveness: At times this game would 'suck me in', and I would lose track of time (the ultimate goal of any video game, I would reckon).Cons:- Weapon management was confusing.  It was not inherently clear to myself how the weapon selector wheel worked.  I think any weapon you picked up got added to the wheel, and from that wheel you could select it.  But there were times where the weapons I thought I had were not available.- With such a visually rich world, what a shame it was mostly shooting things (no, plugging connectors into slots is minimal interaction at best).  That was so much else in the world I wanted to play with.- PC Requirements.  While my PC is mid-range (1070Ti, 16GB RAM, I7-8700), with the settings selected, there were times when there was reprojections, or slight stuttering when conducting smooth turning.  It wasn't enough to ruin the experience, but did make me aware of that joyous trade-off between visual and gameplay performance.- Game Crashes: I had 3 game crashes where I had to CTRL/ALT/DEL to get off of a frozen screen; this generally happened with an onslaught of enemies where I kept dying and selecting 'return to last checkpoint'.I had one crash where restarting the computering was necesary to get the game to work again.  This greatly annoyed me because, up till this point in time, this had never happened before, and on a game I hadn't played in almost a year.  Fortunately, it only happened once, but still.....- Checkpoint loading:  There were times where I started back way further than I think I should have.  To be fair, I was immersed enough in the game, to where I ignored any checkpoint/save point indicators. But in Chapter 4, after one 'reload checkpoint', I could sworn I had to replay the entire level.Overall, my enjoyment of the game was dimished somewhat by the technical issues I was having, or some lack of understanding of how the game was working.  But, in the end, there were more pros than cons. Original Review: November 2017In terms of atmosphere and mood, this game has what it takes to succeed.  It's a bit linear, in that aside from going up and down a flight of stairs, everything seems to take place ona level floor (kind of like Doom 1 & 2).  Having the ability to shoot from a different floor than what the mutants are on would be a welcome change.The controls are very decent as it mixes both locomotion and teleportation. What the controls lack (for myself) is the ability to smooth turm (instead you press buttons to rotate in 45 degree increments).The weapons, although pretty to look at, lack any 'oompf' to them; it just has no recoil/kickback to make you feel like  your handling a weapon that allows you you to go medievil on a mutant.  Whether you use the pistol or pulse rifle, it feels exactly  ther same.Melee weapons (pipe, crowbar) are as lethal as the guns, which should not be the case.  There were a couple of hordes to where only a crowbar was needed to get the job done.  The game also has grenades you can use, but I could not find a way to store them to use later, I just left them on the floor (the crowbar kicks butt).Overall, the default difficulty is very easy.  Only a couple of times did I take some damage, and at no time did I really feel threatened.  It took me around an hour to get through the level.While it seems all I've done is gripe, the overall presentation is solid, and I want to give the developer a chance with Chapter 2, before rendering a final verdict.  I see good potential in this game, I hope it gets there.

On paper,  sounds like a good game - a  clone in VR. In practice,  is a general mess.Taking place in the far-flung Future™, players assume the role of a space marine who, for reasons not really important to the game writ large, finds himself trapped in a cloning complex overrun by pseudo-zombies. The situation is complicated slightly by the fact that you have a voice in your head, belonging to an unwitting scientist who narrates your on-going journey with enough wry wit to supply the whole of the eastern seaboard. We'll... come back to that shortly.Mechanically, this game is about what you'd expect from an Id-like shooter, even if it is in VR. Surviving waves of enemies, both in arenas and in linear hallways respectively, you must manage your ammo and health to survive to each major setpiece fight. And, at first, the game is promising. The visual style of the game feels a bit too "Unity asset-y" at times, but it works well enough and isn't too taxing on your PC. What's more, you can cycle through your weapons at any time, once you've unlocked them, carry a variety of melee weapons,  even three grenades at a pop.The execution is... messier. Melee weapons feel weightless, something made all the more obvious by the absence of any haptic feedback, and while weapons have some satisfying punch, the actual act of crowd control is basically impossible. Enemies move around silently and, due to plot shenanigans, can spawn in any time, any where; in practice, this creates situations where you'll clean a hallway out, only for more enemies to pop up, eager to nosh on your fleshy bits. This goes from frustrating to downright unfair during major arena fights, where you have no way to keep tabs on groups of enemies all at once. Combined with the fact that the game just unceremoniously drops you both into the main menu  the campaign without any prelude or set-up, and it's hard not to feel like the game itself is unfinished.This is bad, but it's not the straw that broke the camel's back, that caused me to put the game down for so long before giving up entirely. No, that prestigious claim goes to the absolutely  writing. Look, the game is about shooting not-demons; I'd hardly blame it for wanting to lean into camp. But that said, camp is still something that takes a certain deft hand to tap into, and the writers of this game have all comedic grace of an upset neoconservative pundit. The voice in your head, bless him, is doing his damnedest to pull off a mock John de Lancie, but the script does him no favors; when you first find a crowbar in game, he utters, "Hey, pull out that crowbar, and let's get Free, Man!" This baffling  allusion, friends, is the  of the game's comedy, and it only goes downhill and gets more irritating thereafter.For all my complaining, the  of  is a solid one. The shooting feels okay, and again, the conceit of the game is actually entertaining. The problem is that it slips up in almost every single regard, swiftly overstaying its welcome... a tricky task for a game this short. It's not offensive by any means, but   neither respects you nor your time. Seek your virtual reality demon killin' elsewhere.

And they're weirdly quiet, so if one spawns in behind you you might not even notice until you're dead. 2. NO TOGGLE GRIP! You need to squeeze the grip at all times to avoid dropping your weapons. And in case you somehow didn't know already, it *hurts* to grip things tightly for long periods of time! Plus, holstering is finicky. I found myself dropping my weapons on the ground a lot - and on top of that, unholstering my weapons when what I *meant* to do was grab something else at waist height!3. Bad lighting. Playing on the Valve Index, , I found that some environments were very dark, and the flashlight provides no illumination. Not gamebreaking on its own, but there were multiple times I went into a dark corridor, found myself suddenly surrounded by enemies I could only see because of their glowing eyes, and died almost immediately. Watching the trailer again, it seems like the game should be much brighter all around.If you like zombies, try Arizona Sunshine. If you want action, try Doom VFR. But give this one a miss.

A-Tech Cybernetic is a frantic and fast-paced Science-Fiction/Horror-style shooter. Here at VR Galaxy we were granted the opportunity to play and review this game for Free. We though this game was a total blast and a lot of fun. You can tell that the developers put in a lot of time and hard work to create the environments and make the atmosphere feel spooky and tense. You really feel like you are on a Outpost or base in deep space or on another planet. The lighting, textures and sound design are all top notch. The enemies are creepy and they run fast. There is a nice variety of weapons to choose from, including a pistol, assault rifle, shotgun, special weapon, grenades, etc. I like how there is smooth locomotion and teleportation support, so people who are prone to motion sickness can still enjoy this game, but those who can use locomotion feel more immersed. Right now there are 2 chapters to the game and a Horde mode. We played most of the 2 chapters, pretty close to the end. This game offers a lot of fast action and immersion and does a great job of keeping you entertained and on the edge of your seat....even though you're standing! There are a few things that we would like to see chnaged or added into the game. We would like to see a faster speed of locomotion movement, because when there are a lot of enemies chasing you, they can catch you too easily, especially if you run out of ammo. Speaking of ammo, we would like to see more ammo placed around the levels. Often times, it feels like you don't have enough ammo and you just die, because you are overwhelmed by so many enemies all at once. You might want to space out the enemies a little more. At times it feels like there are no enemies in some places and then there are a ton, all at once. Also, the big doors always close on you after you press the button to open them. They seem to be glitchy and enemies sometimes get stuck in the environments and "clip" out. Overall, these are minor issues and we would highly recommend this game. It has the perfect feeling of action and terror, being stuck in space with a bunch of scary beasts and we think you'll love it!

This game had a lot of potential to be fun.  Lots of shooting, zombies, sci-fi--what's not to love?  Sadly, I found the game anything but fun.  The gun holster/drop mechanics are TERRIBLE.  When you want to holster your weapon, there's a good chance you'll just drop it--and seconds later, it will DISAPPEAR PERMANENTLY.  I've played other VR games where it's possible to drop your weapon (like Zero Caliber), and haven't had this problem.  Additionally, when you go to reach for something in the environment, there's a good change that you'll grab a weapon from your holster, instead (even if you're reaching out in front of you)--and subsequently drop it, losing it forever.  If it were possible to simply pick up the weapon reliably or even re-load the level and have all your stuff back, it would be annoying but playable; but when your weapon de-spawns and you re-load a level, you start with NOTHING.  That's right; you were doing well at the end of the previous level, full ammo, good guns, etc., and now you have nothing.  Sure, the game might give you an opportunity to pick up a couple guns with one magazine worth of ammo, for each, but you're going to spend it in the first fight, and then have nothing with which to defend yourself.  Game over.Needless to say, I threw in the towel in the second map.  I'm just done.  Would refund this game if I could, but for whatever reason, Steam isn't letting me.

I really like this game. I want to recommend it for everyone. However, I ran into some game-breaking bugs in story mode which you should be aware of before purchasing the game. The first big bug I ran into is that the game lost my saved file. I had to restart from the beginning, luckily this time I believe my saved file is still there so hopefully this issue has indeed been patched. The second bug I ran into, which is pretty big and still exists is that if you die in the caves and you checkpoint near the lava pit then you'll more than likely have to restart the level from the beginning (which is a major pain). This is a known bug which I have reported as well as another player. Hopefuly this gets resolved soon.The devs seem to be very active in supporting the game. They are active in fixing bugs and adding more content. As of today, there are still many planned chapters to be added to the game. So any review of the game currently is bound to be incomplete.This game is obviously an homage to Doom. It has cheesy, scary hallways filled with gruesome laughs. But don't worry, the game is not just one hallway next to another hallway that looks almost the same as we have seen in prior VR shooters. This game has lots of character and lots of variety in scenery and gameplay. See my photo below which is probably the best explanation of what you can expect. This game has great pacing. The narrator was nicely voiced and added to the game, versus distracting from the action. There is great use of lighting. The guns all felt differently. You can use melee weapons, though they are rare to find. My main complaint is that you currently one-hand everything. I also did not really care for how the grenades worked. It seemed that they never did the damage I wanted. Tossing them and timing the explosion just right felt a little too complex. Also, there are currently only 2 slots for main weapons and 3 slots for grenades. There is lots of health and ammo around. I was usually at full health just because you are a badass and the game plays like it. Usually you're only in trouble when you're swarmed by enemies. So there are sudden difficulty spikes in certain areas, which can be frustrating with the checkpoint system the game has. You'll usually restart near the start of the action, but sometimes with not enough ammo. Running out of ammo does happen often, so you need to be able to pickup ammo whereever it is, and it can be difficult when there's so many enemies around and the vacuum hands are not always reliable. You can also carry 4 weapons (2 in each hand & 2 in your holster) as a way to avoid running out of ammo.I used free locomotion. On the Oculus, you use the a or x button to turn, which was awkward. You do have to teleport at times to get out of the way of enemies or to get up to certain spots.I had lots of fun playing. I also had lots of frustration playing the game. I can recommend the game. But just beware that it's early access and still in development and it very much still feels like a beta. I can't wait to see the final release.

There also seems to be a locked level that unlocks when you reach a certain amount of points in first level, I haven't reached so far thou, so I dont know what the locked level is about yet.Anyway, the developers are promising both more levels as well as a story mode, more weapons and challenges coming up during april-may 2017, so I guess soon we really can see this games real potential. Because when playing this (and other titles), I can't stop thinking "teleporting could really use some tweaking to be as smooth as Alyx'".Which is a shame as this game is pretty damn good! Speaking of "damned", you'll be fighting space zombie mutants in a space station where research on human subjects too place. So far, so unoriginal, but in all honesty, so was A New Hope.The writing is suitably humorous including an in-universe explanation of WTF you are doing there. The rest of the presentation is suitably awesome. I've read someone complaining it to Doom and it certainly does have a certain vibe of Doom 3. Including tablets detailing the crazy stuff crazy minds in this lab environment came up with. Up to and including guns, of course. With a fast-firing SMG in one and a shotgun in the other hand, the zombie hordes are all but manageable. Needless to say, there's no wrist-breaking simulated recoil (I'm sure my controllers would break before my wrist does), the weapons are very satisfying to empty into zombie paunches & heads. Selecting them is a breeze so satisfying shooting it is.Then there's the occasional puzzle, nothing world-changing, but they do contribute to the atmosphere. As does the overall design.I'm not big on bona fide horror games, those generatic the horror mostly from you being neigh-powerless against the odds. I'm more into action horror, where you can handle yourself & said odds just fine, but the atmosphere got a way of getting under your skin & staying there (ironically enough, Doom 3 falls behind in the latter department by relying too much on jump scares). By that ruler, A-Tech Cybernetic is worth playing indeed.PS: I swear I've heard that upbeat voice actor playing the player's best friend in another game before, but I can't for the life of me remember where.

Subject to change as the game gets more polished.Allow me to start by saying that  is a worthy opponent for , and I have played the hell out (pun intended) of the latter. For being an Early Access VR title,  showcases a pretty polished experience in every single one of its gameplay elements and being the devs so responsive about their community feedback could make this title stand out among the very best of VR. puts you inside the body of a former scientist, and I mean that in a literal way. You will posess him, and he will complain about it being your "conscience", a voice in your head that will give you advice about your surroundings along with a balanced mix of complaints, humour, sarcasm, lore explanations, and sometimes 4th wall-breaking comments. Your objective is clear: Escape from the A-Tech facilities alive.Gameplay-wise, this game is reminiscent of how  should be if it gets a VR remake.  is a frenetic gun & run experience, something that  is not, and I like it because of that.  offers a slower pace version of its counterpart, where not every single room has to be a combat area. Also,  features a set of jumpscares and unsettling moments that will give you goosebumps at certain times. As I wrote before, it is an atmospheric horror shooter, much like how the original  was conceived. also features a nice set of different enemies and weapons. Each enemy has an attack pattern that you should learn in order to escape an ambush or a massive attack. Also, you will have a versatile arsenal that will make your life easier if you manage your ammo. Should you get a second gun because you have a lot of ammo, or maybe you will risk to take up a machine gun, despite its high-consumption bullet rate? Strategy is something to take in account inside a facility that is crawling up with monsters that want to eat your brains out.Graphics are gorgeous, even in their current state. Lightning and particle effects, combined with high-quality meshes and animations, achieve a futuristic, yet opresive atmosphere. Something that, for an Early Access title, is not an easy task.The sound quality is also pretty good. The ambience music and the environmental effects perfectly fit the dark sci-fi mood of the game, and I have to confess that I found myself turning around more than a few times because of hearing something at my back.VR-related, it features both teleporting and a locomotion system using one of the trackpads. You can holster two weapons and take another two with you in each one of your hands, although you will have to drop one momentarily to pick up any other item. To reload, you just have to move your weapons to the ammo belt, making it a fast and intuitive way of managing your magazines.  features close combat techniques and weapons, wheter hitting an enemy with your bare fists or with a metal bar is just a matter of choice. Finally, it also allows to launch grenades by picking up one, pulling out its ring and throwing it away, releasing a big ka-boom that might save your life if you ran out of ammo.I totally recommend this game for its current price, even being in Early Access. Remember to check playtimes of reviews. A chunk of the positive reviews that seemingly recommend this game have less than an hour play time in it. Not very promising when someone who apparently likes a game can't even get more than a couple hours of playtime out of it.Full disclosure: I got this with a very cheap bundle. The cost of the game for me was probably a dollar, and even at that price I cant recommend it. There are a couple of pitfalls that make it very hard / unplayable for me, and I suspect it's also a contributing factor to why so many of the people reviewing this have such little played time regardless if they recommend it or not. 1: Can't use both hands to hold / manipulate objects. This is a big one. Aside from it feeling unnatural, it's quite literally a massive pain in my wrist to rotate objects this way. The repeated motion of twisting your wrist -> setting the piece down -> picking it back up and repeating "X" amount of times to turn the pieces far enough is not only slow, but gets uncomfortable / painful very quickly. 2: Lack of snapping / easy way to align things. The game points out in one of the tutorials that the physics aren't entirely consistent. That means having a tiny gap or bump in the track can potentially throw off the way your entire build works, assuming you can even build for more than 5 mins with the wrist pain. Having absolutely no other way to line up track other than using your potentially shaky hands makes building significantly less fun. You sit there wasting more time on lining every piece of track up than you do actually building / enjoying the game.3: Very limited selection of items. People that like this genre want to build stupid crazy wacky machines. Unfortunately, the selection is very limited. Not to say you couldn't build something cool, but it would be better with a wider selection.The last update for this game was almost a year ago and the community discord seems dead. I can't recommend the game in its current state, and sadly I don't think there's much hope for an update that fixes the main 2 problems I have with it. If you want a really good marble machine game that has significantly more content / track snapping, look into Marble World. It's not VR, but it's at a lower price point, has more everything, and you can get really crazy with what you do in that game.

Do you like puzzles? Do you love science and engineering? Are you fascinated with Rube Goldberg machines and you always wanted to experiment with them and build gigantic Ruberg machines at home but couldn't do so due to lack of space? Do you dream of taking part in annual Rube Goldberg machine-building contests in places such as University of California, MIT, Carnegie Science Centre or The Science Olympiad?Well, your dream has come true, because thanks to modern VR technology and passionate and committed developers Metanaut's two years' worth of hard work, it's finally possible to build simple or complex machines of this kind at the comfort of your own home in Gadgeteer. The graphics is soothing, calming, appropriate and beautiful and so is the background music, so much so that I'm planning on buying the soundtracks in near future to use as a sleeping aid. There's a short yet polished and interactive tutorial that explains the mechanics, and it's designed in such a way that you will go through it only once and quickly learn all that you'll ever need to know to solve the puzzles or to build your machines in Sandbox mode. Out of the 60 problems I've solved only 11 so far and I'm highly pleased with how they start off very simple but then begin to get a bit complex as I progressed, and how even though it's in early access there's absolutely no bug to be found. One thing I'd highly recommend the devs is to implement Steam workshop integration as soon as possible so that the community could make more puzzles, environments, objects and gadgets and share them with each other. On top of that, may be the devs could even make more complex puzzles in future and sell them as DLCs at an affordable price? Just an idea! At £11.39 (15 US dollars?) Gadgeteer won't break your bank, and if you are worried about motion sickness then good news is it has absolutely none of that. Since it's possible to move forward, backward, up, down and snap left and right using your controller and grip buttons, it's entirely possible to play it while seated. A comfort vignette option is still available for those who really want it.I used to think Talos Principle VR was the best puzzle game ever for VR, but Gadgeteer has proved me wrong. Kudos to the developers for making this VR gem. I can't wait to see more content and features by the time the full version is released.

Gadgeteer is a fantastic physics based puzzle game that easily fits into my VR Essential list which is all about creating your very own Rube Goldberg machine without any of the frustrating clean up afterwards. Now how about we get right into the review beginning with objective and game-play.There are two modes to Gadeteer, the first is a puzzle scenario where it gives you a start and a finish to each level, it takes place in an apartment thats been sealed off various areas which all help power a machine leading to a very mysterious door. The second mode is a sandbox mode which takes place in the same apartment but with no barriers to go crazy and make the Rube Goldberg machine of your dream. Both modes use the same control scheme which is very intuitive and makes setting up your pieces easy. One hand behaves as a menu that lists all your pieces while the other works as a multi tool to select, copy, remove and freeze the pieces of your choice. Movement is done but grabbing onto the world and pulling yourself around and also allows you to lower and raise your height by using both hands to adjust your view point. The physics all feel realistic and behave exactly how you would expect them too. Next up lets discus Features and content.Gadgeteer features over 50 unique pieces to let your imagination run wild and offers 60 different puzzles to solve throughout its puzzle game mode. The game offers a great amount of content for its price and with the sandbox mode the possibilities are endless if your the type to enjoy creating its easy to get lost in. Its puzzle mode also serves as a great introduction into building Rube Goldberg machines and piece selection starts off simple and grows in variety throughout the mode and later on giving you multiple ways to solve a puzzle by giving you more pieces than needed to complete them. Now lets talk visuals and immersionVisually the game is has a beautiful design that is both simplistic and clean. Its very clear and easy to understand what everything is at a glance. Its also very entertaining to watch your creation come to life the moment you hit the green button to start each puzzle. Immersion is good as well with everything being very intuitive in terms of control I found the experience to be very calming and relaxing for the most part. I found myself easily getting lost in the game and losing track of time spent inside the game. My only knock on the game when it comes to immersion is that i did experience a slight stutter at times but the moments were few, for reference im running the game on an rtx 2070 and ryzen 2600x cpu.To conclude Gadgeteer is a really great puzzle game and if you like Rube Goldberg machines its a no brainer. Its puzzle aspect is very well done and i was able to get lost playing it. Its such a simple concept but one that translates so well into Virtual Reality, one that is easy to understand.  If your anything like me, you have loved the idea of Rube Goldberg machines but never felt like dealing with all the hassles it entails, life does not have a rewind button when you make a mistake but Gadgeteer does and that makes experimenting all the more worth while. The controls are well thought out and work great. The difficulty curve is also planned out nicely and encourages creativity, the visuals look good where they need to be and its entertaining to watch your ideas succeed or fail. So if you like puzzle games or ever wanted to create your own Rube Goldberg machine be sure to check it out.If you enjoyed the review consider subscribing for more content!

Wondering when will new DLC for 'Love is All Around' or 'Knowledge or Know Lady' ever come out? Fret not! Here comes 'Director Simulator' (a rare instance of an accurate/direct translation of the Chinese title), another romance FMV game with 6 female love interests. How does it fare compared to others in the genre?Warning: There will be some story spoilers below!Pros:- The overall tone and writing is quite over-the-top, which makes for a light-hearted and fun experience if you don't take the story developments too seriously from Su Yimo constantly pretending to be dead to get protagonist Luo Yu's attention to celebrity Ouyang Lu immediately becoming friends with corporate heiress Ye Wen after a game of volleyball. It's something out of a romance manga/anime!- The design of the choices buttons blend in very nicely and makes the experience less like a video game and more immersive.- Closer to the end of the story, your choices have greater impact like if you choose to take photos of Ouyang Lu despite promising to love and be with the youthful Lin Xiyan, she would get incredibly jealous and somehow overnight becomes a Japanese horror movie killer who either wants to kill Luo Yu or her love rivals (Which is well-acted as it made me very unsettled!)- The mini-games like taking photos of the various love interests and typing in questions into a Magic-8 ball style book add some variety to the game.- The consequences of some choices are surprising, like if you do not look at bodyguard Jiang Zhiwan's...ahem...goods during a gym session, she would feel uncomfortable at Luo Yu staring at her face rather than seeking a peak at her goods. I feel the developer did such choices to be cheeky and self-referential about this genre.- There are some sweet moments like when the fierce Ouyang Lu gets embarrassed and hides behind a curtain when Luo Yu shares directly his feelings with her. - The ending credits song/main menu theme is really catchy and good.Cons:- Although the over-the-top tone can be fun, but I must state it has its downs. Serious moments where I felt you got to see the various women open up to Luo Yu only arguably start to occur in Chapter 4, such as Ye Wen sharing her view of love not being just about being joyful all the time or Jiang Zhiwan sharing her admiration for Luo Yu to keep pursuing his film-making dream. This is past the story's halfway mark and makes the romantic developments feel less realistic.- The timing of these serious moments feels off due to the story's exaggerated tone and faster pace. In Ye Wen's ending, Luo Yu and Ye Wen have an argument that reflects their different social backgrounds that is an interesting point to explore, but it felt like it came out of nowhere and wasn't given time to develop. - As a Chinese speaker, I could tell the translation was done through a translation software without further editing to improve the English grammar and structure. Some nuances are missed like Ye Wen calling Luo Yu "Little Brother" (basically she becomes his Sugar Mama) or things are translated literally. - The mini-games, particularly the music one is more STRESSFUL AND ANXIETY INDUCING THAN ANY HORROR GAME! It's like the Teatime mini-game in 'Fire Emblem: Three Houses' where you have a limited time to click timed QTEs that appear all over the screen and the video content can make it distracting to click the QTEs. - In Lin Xiyan's ending, there is also a series of QTEs where you have to say romantic promises to her questions and you only have a few seconds to respond. Since it came out of nowhere, it really is too fast-paced for players to respond! - For the camera mini-game, there is no baseline  or clues on what makes an "average", "nice" or "perfect" photo.- The endings, even the perfect ones are very abrupt with no sense of what post-romantic confession is like between Luo Yu and the chosen romantic interest. I think 'My Destiny Girls', 'Tomorrow's Love Puzzle' and 'Love is All Around' does a better job on this.Random Tidbits:- The guitar instrumental music used in the scenes when Ye Wen leaves her company to be with Luo Yu and the indoor snow playground scenes with Su Yimo was also used in 'Tomorrow's Love Puzzle', specifically for gym instructor Wang Yiman's endiing. - Ouyang Lu's stage name is 'Xiao Lu', which although spelled differently from the popular 'Love is All Around' love interest, may be a reference to the character.Verdict:Although I put a 'Recommended' verdict, I would suggest only getting 'Director Simulator' if you enjoy a very over-the-top romantic comedy that doesn't take the story or romantic developments too seriously. But if you are like me and like a well-paced romantic story with a nice balance of comedy and serious romance, I don't think this will suit you and I would suggest exploring other entries like 'Charming Hearts' or 'My Destiny Girls'

Despite a bad first impression, Director Simulator manages to recover thanks to a strong finish.Initially the story is poor, because it is disjointed, illogical, and somewhat childish. Encounters with the admirers are coincidental and nonsensical. Inadequate reasons are made to get players to choose which admirer they want to spend time with. The narrative rarely makes logical sense. When you get a job for a boss admirer, you never do any work and she instead follows to random places. One admirer stays in your apartment and pretends to be dead every time you come home. Another is a gamer who seems completely aloof and talks in riddles.There is not much finesse to the romance arcs and scenes are thrown together at random to take you to places like an amusement park, aquarium, glass bridge, gym, school yard, boat trip etc. The only narrative thread that links it all together is the player-character’s desire to make a movie, but this is tenuous and might be near invisible depending on choices. Yet all the admirers eventually gang up together to make it happen (was done better in Love is all Around). Then, while making the movie, you have to pick your heroine from the group. It is a fairly shoddy main arc, when taken at face value.The other problem is the poor English translation. None of the phone text messages are translated and the only silver lining is there are not many and player interaction is never required. All of the player choices arelistedlikethiswithoutspaces, which is annoying, but the worst part is that many are vague in terms of what your character will say or do—thankfully the timeline can be quickly accessed to retry a segment.Somehow it manages to recover from these major blemishes at the end. When you pick your lead heroine, it begins the final romance arc for them. And here is when their true personality emerges, sometimes in crazy and dramatic ways that are memorable, funny, or poignant. It is almost like 2/3rds of the narrative work has gone into the endings. Failed romances are the default, so finding the good endings takes a bit of trial and error but generally rewarding. The finales are also multifaceted in ways that are hard to describe, and it is a case where those silly parts in the story suddenly make much more sense.There are some unusual gameplay elements but not much interactivity. QTEs associated with singing take a few tries to get a perfect score, and it is impossible to watch the performance and perform well. Photographs are regularly taken of the admirers, and you have to time your shots with poses, which is a little ambiguous but works okay; in a group setting, the one photographed the most gets an affection meter boost, which is neat and should have been used more. At times you can choose which order you want to visit them—demonstrating the game’s proclivity toward jumbled scenes—but this changes nothing in terms of affection.Completing one full romance (to credits) will take about 2.5 hours. There is maybe 5hrs more content via branching paths. If you only go through one romance and call it quits, then Director Simulator is hard to recommend. Only when doing 3+ endings do things actually fall into place, and while not the best game of this type, it manages to wipe away most of its poor first impression.

I wish I could recommend this game. I am in love with the artwork, atmosphere, and general concept of the game. It even has some great ideas like the burden system, where you choose powers that burden you, requiring a heavier burden for more powerful ones, but penalizing you for burdening yourself too much.Unfortunately, the game feels a bit light on content. With only something like 18 monsters, while extremely well designed, seems quite low for a game that's meant to be played over and over again like a roguelite. I'm not really sure you can call this a roguelite, however. Yes, if you lose, you must start all the way over, but there is no meta progression and the variety and amount of decisions is very low. After every fight, you get to choose a card, but your deck is very small and cannot go over that limit. After some fights, you get to choose an aforementioned burden or sometimes a vague choice between two options. Eventually you'll learn what those options offer you, but it's trial and error at the start. These choices can offer you ways to regain health, lessen your burdens, gain currency, etc.The small deck allowance I feel really lowers any potential to build truly different decks. Heck, when you look at the card library and consider it's split between three factions, the amount of cards are very low. You will see the same cards regularly, even in your first run. You're not going to get the wide range of strategies unique to each character like in the GOAT of all deckbuilders Slay the Spire. Seriously, it's getting sad how few games even manage to reach the quality and replayability of StS, and Acolyte of the Altar isn't even in the running.The balance also seems iffy. I have only done two runs in the game, plus one for the demo. The amount of unavoidable damage, particularly as the imp faction, seems way too high. I had a fight take 9 of my 20 health in the FIRST fight. My deck obviously wasn't upgraded because it was the first fight. I played every card I could on curve, but I simply could not avoid the direct and overkill damage. The imp faction has a lot of low HP creatures. Overkill is basically trample from MTG. My low HP creatures could not absorb much of the overkill damage, causing me to take tons of damage to my life point. On that same run, I managed to get to the last fight, but, despite taking every opportunity I could to heal, the amount of unavoidable damage made the last fight impossible due to the fact that it has an attack that does a whopping 5 overkill damage EVERY TURN.Even after all this, I think the game could be fun for some people. It doesn't offer the amount of variety and content that other games in the deckbuilding genre have, but it has a lot of charm and uniqueness that I could see it finding a home in some Steam libraries. The reason I can't recommend this game to anyone right now is because of how buggy it is.In my two runs, I have encountered two bugs that have locked the game up. In my first run, when I died on the last fight, the game simply would not proceed past the "you lose" screen. I was stuck there. In the second run, an beast got stuck on its turn and the game would not proceed, forcing me to reload the game. If I'm finding bugs in just the first two runs, some serious QA needs to be done on this game. This is also when I found out if you're in a fight and you exit the game and return, the fight will start over with completely different cards and you can basically retry the fight.I appreciate what this game is trying to do and absolutely love the world they have created for it. It's too bad the game itself isn't better and more polished. A novel idea, but wait for a deep sale and some patches.

A great idea executed terribly.Acolyte of the Altar implements an idea I have had in the back of my head for a while, and demonstrates that this concept does indeed work. It effectively places itself between derivative deckbuilder titles (9/10 copying Slay the Spire, let's be honest here) and a more traditional CCG format (i.e. Gwent, Hearthstone, Magic the Gathering etc); monsters do not rely on one or two gimmicks, but rather a small expanding set of abilities that gradually open over time. These effects synergize with one another in some way and need to be controlled by the player, lest they want to get overwhelmed. It allows for way more expressive enemies than e.g. Slay the Spire and more of a "puzzle" oriented approach.Unfortunately the game does not seem to recognize that if you design your enemies around some synergy the player is supposed to disrupt, you also need to give them the tools to do so. As a consequence Acolyte of the Altar is a hilariously flawed game, bordering on unplayable. The player will very frequently find themselves deadlocked because they simply do not have the cards to deal with the puzzle at hand. Other bosses are completely pointless due to how vulnerable they are to everything; essentially emulating playing aggro in any other CCG (put card on board, press face. Repeat 6x).This is a consequence of the way the game has progression laid out, and a primary reason I think it would be awful to listen to the other reviews claiming "we need meta progression1!". The whole premise of the game does not cater towards it; it needs to facilitate immediate options for the player to get access to the tools they need. The progression during the runs is way too limited to guarantee players do not get deadlocked.Even though a good amount of love was put into the game, with lovely artwork, a unique aesthetic and pretty good sound design across the board it unfortunately failed the moment the developers did not understand their own game. Acolyte of the Altar does not need "more content", it needs to actually function as a concept to begin with.

This is not the most polished of deckbuilders, however, it is still very enjoyable. I strongly dislike the delay when hovering over the abilities of the enemies as it interrupts the flow of game play. Since the layout of the beast's abilities so closely resembles weapon abilities in hearthstone, I may be simply be trying to adjust to a clunkier format. Card mechanics are still very fun to experiment with, but after only a few hours I feel like I have already found all the build enablers. I probably haven't, but it feels like there are only really a few cards you actually need to win. Because of that, I lost motivation to keep trying to find new strategies because I already knew there was one from each class that worked better than if you were to mix and match strategies between patrons. I played through the game 3 times with each of the classes selected as my greater and lesser patron without any extra burdens and did not die once. In fact I didn't feel at any point challenged, so after that I selected every burden to put it on "max difficulty" and still had no difficulty completing the game. Anytime a game has me decide how difficult to make it I lose interest, which is probably why I enjoy games like dark souls so much, as the difficulty is mostly preset. If you want to make this game difficult you will have to create those challenges yourself by intentionally choosing inferior strategies. If that's what you enjoy then this is a perfect deckbuilder. On a separate note, the art, lore, and overall texture of this game is fantastic!!! This is what will keep me playing this game even after I become a master with all patron combinations. Stepping foot into the path of the Acolyte willing to sacrifice themselves just to prove that their chosen deity is best suited to care for the world carries such a deep weight that you feel during a run. The breathtaking journey you undergo encountering all sorts of forgotten relics that are the beasts give the world a certain age that breaths of forgotten secrets and ancient wonders, adding to the fact that this world has lost so much and is down to it's last three gods. And you, the acolyte, seek to remove two of the remaining three, bringing an end to the chaos that has wrought the world asunder. Very well crafted! This is a good purchase for 20$, and I would recommend it more for players who enjoy the enjoy the slower turns of MTG arena, rather than the hundred cards a minute of slay the spire.

I do have to agree with a lot of the comments that the amount of content currently in the game is a little bit sparse, and that there are a decent amount of bugs to iron out. That said, I am far more understanding of that with a team of five who really clearly have good ideas and wanted to shake up the genre.Why should you play this game? I've never seen anything quite like it. This is a strange and beautiful mashup of roguelite card games (Slay the Spire, Astrea, etc.) and boss rushes. It's a very refreshing take on a genre where a lot of indie games seem relatively content to just make "Slay the Spire BUT"- not that that's bad, and many of those games are great, it just gets old at some point.In Acolyte, the game is completely asymmetrical between how you work and how the giant Beasts work. You have an almost CCG-style deck, with normal mana mechanics, combos, and creatures. The beasts, meanwhile, get powers to ruin your day. This asymmetry works really well, especially when cards begin to play off of the way Beasts work (lighting powers on fire or removing them entirely).Overall, I think the game is a very strong start. I wonder if many of the negative reviews would be different if this game were stated to be in early access (which, based on the fact that we already have a roadmap, may have been appropriate, I don't know). I just know that the complaints I have on lack of content are easy to remedy, and the things that the game does right are more than interesting enough to make me recommend it.

I held off on reviewing this title because it felt a bit content-light at launch.  Recently the devs have begun adding in new card variants that are unlocked at the end of runs, and this little bit of meta-progression really invigorated my enjoyment of the game.  Acolyte of the Altar is a game that oozes with style and vision.  Kudos to the art and sound design of the game, which completely immerses you into this bizarre alien world.  Everything from the card art, to the stone tablet motifs on UI and card frames is consistent and purposeful.  The soundtrack is haunting and dark but also full of bops.  After some balance adjustments, the game feels really great to play, and while some particular deck strategies are more powerful than others, there's enough going on that I'm tempted to explore other strategies even when they're less reliable.  I think this can only get better in time as more waves of card variants are added to the game.The battles in the game play out a lot like puzzles, but each feels unique and interesting.  Learning them over the course of several runs makes a big difference in your chance of success.  They're all various degrees of brutal, but they all feel pretty fair.  Honestly I've come to love this game and this weird world.  I'd love more, and hope the devs continue to add to the meta-progression elements to keep digging in for more runs.  Honestly would love more games in this world and in this style.  Hope Black Kite Games finds success with this.  Bravo devs!

Played extremely actively for a solid month. Here's my perspectives.Gathering hero's and building up your troops is fun for a while. Cool system with five hero's per troop set up. Decent to customize and counter your opponents set up. Increasing their strength is more than just gaining xp in fights though. You can gather spell books to increase the hero stats. 20 of each att, def, and command per hero. Sounds great, until your running 10+ troops with over 50 hero's. Who all need to hunt 60 spell books each to max out their potential.The city building is ridiculously grindy. As you gain levels you get the ability to have another town. At first it's awesome, and then by the time you have your main city, plus 10 more cities to develop the exact same buildings in. It feels like a punishment to get another town. Sure, having 10 level 20 tax offices, or warehouses, ect, increases your overall daily production and capacity, but it's the same buildings over and over again, and each new town starts off with nothing but a level 1 city hall. Essentially, you feel like you are starting over again, repeatedly. Ok, let's do this all over again for the how many times now?There are ages the game goes through, and if you didn't start at the very beginning, you will NEVER catch up to the players who did. The ages go fairly fast, and if you don't make this game a part time job, you will fall behind quickly. Or P2W.The community is actually friendly, even rivalry is generally communicated and organized. The community is very small though. About 30 active members on global server 1.The top ten players are so strong that they can basically take down miracles and monument cities solo or in a small group. That means, unless you are online when they do this, you will never get to attack anything fun with your alliance. They already conquered everything while you were sleeping. And that's the best way to earn Merit as well. An important aspect.You snowball as you grow and gain more and more because of your strength increase. So those top players continue to skyrocket with merit gains, while everyone snails. The distance and divide only increases.It's colorful and definitely a mobile game ported in. It does a few things better than most games of this type, but it is absolutely not balanced at all, it has a ton of bugs, actions and in game content locked behind certain ages, so even after my play experience there are some aspects the game still hasn't even let me try or learn about. And it gets really repetitive.I don't regret trying this game, fun for while. It would be nice if you got bonus' to your main city instead of a brand new identical, but bare city to build all over again. And then another, and another. It would be better if they balanced the game so 3 people can't run around the world taking over all of the special cities by themselves.It's not difficult at all, just time consuming and very repetitive. Anyway, thanks for reading my experience. Happy Gaming Everyone!

With the main issues from the previous review having been addressed, I feel like the midgame is now much more manageable and less frustrating. A small issue I have is that I ended up selling an event weapon I leveled to +8 on accident and there is no buy back system that I could find, nor the ability to lock a sell-able weapon. This is my own fault, but it's never a bad idea to idiot-proof things, especially when you have to spam-click to throw all the sell-able items into the inventory of the trader, and when you're on autopilot because it's the 200th inventory of loot, you could end up selling upgrade currencies, or event items like I have.----------------OLD REVIEWThis game has a great atmosphere and a fun progression system, requiring you to farm materials to upgrade your gear to a higher level.However, the farming once you reach midgame (photon-2 level 5 onward,) becomes tedious at best. From the world spawning metal and events in like an mmo so you have to both compete against allies and enemies, and with the fact that if you don't spot an enemy player before they spot you, you have a slim chance of winning the battle unless they are aiming with their feet.The PvP exists just for a progression wall, it serves no other purpose. Selling back bags is fine, as you can just get 15k for walking around for 3 minutes at the midgame base, The Bar. And boy, is The Bar something else. As a joint base for both the Bandits and Stalkers, it creates two glaring problems; The entrances and exits are too close to each other, and it concentrates the players into the one area.The Factory map that holds The Bar outpost is the only place to get a material, the Pickle. A mineral that is green and shaped like it's name, and is used for the many weapons, armour, and attachment upgrades. It is dropped by human AI, which can be neutral, allied, or enemy. If it's an allied AI, you cannot kill them, but you can take neutral or enemy AI for the resource. The problem is that the map doesn't allow for easy access, you need to either sneak around tens of enemy faction players, or blast your way through as there are only 2 pathways to the other side of the map where the camps can only exist, on the enemy side. Now, if you broke through that should be fine and dandy, you can get to farming. However! Now you need to deal with the fact that the enemy spawn is only 20 seconds away, and there is only a few pathways through that are visible from the enemy spawn. Any experienced player would be able to run out from spawn immediately after death to get back into the fight.How I would suggest to fix this is:Rework the map!-Make the joint base into two bases, one for each side of the factory.-Add neutral camps to the center of the map to fight over, adding some reason to pvp other than just killing for the chance to access the material.-Open up the center of the map, there is way too many chokepoints and crates for players to hide behind. Have overgrown foliage, trucks, etc. Not hallways of crates and boxes thrown about like a horror game filled with jumpscares.Add a PvP minigame (deathmatch, control, etc,) that can reward the materials you need!-Lets players scratch that PvP itch while allowing progress. I know I like to PvP, but the only places to do so are to camp the places people need to go farm, which causes that progression roadblock.-If you need to slow down progression, increase the money cost to getting the new items, or add another material. Artificial roadblocks through PvP and terrible map design does not feel good.I'm likely to continue playing this game because I'm a masochist, however I'll be taking a break for the time being. Hopefully some of these issues can be remedied by the time I get back.

STALCRAFTA really, really pretty game that gets the most out of its style of graphics to expand upon the STALKER lore and universe in ways that is fairly lore-fitting. I have so little bad to say about this game. Except for one *incredibly* major aspect of it.The game is genuinely really pretty. I have no complaints about that. The weapons look good for the most part; the story is a bit weird, and I haven't seen it all (for reasons explained later!) But the setpieces the game sends you to can be downright beautiful, and interestingly-designed! It's very much so fitting in that STALKER aesthetic with a bit more fantasy than before, but nothing that seems 'too' out-of-place.The story is serviceably good! I like that even in an always-online MMO they've managed to include some elements of choice that affects what characters are present for you down the line. I like that quest decisions are usually notable and not just 'which character do you bring X item to' or 'which dialogue option you pick at the end of a quest chain to get a different reward'. Real fun stuff! Nothing groundbreaking, nothing here is, but it's also not /bad/. Simple, fun, the game works well within its own scope!You pick your faction, which is Bandit or Loner; later down the line you'll have the option to pick between 2 subfactions exclusive to each faction. The main point of this is to decide which players you'll be fighting alongside and against. Bandits can't shoot Bandits. Loners can't shoot Loners. So-on-and-so-forth. This is also relevant to the /appearance/ of /some/ of the equipment you can access, along with the locations you'll visit and /some/ characters in the story. I expected the main plot to be more affected by your faction choice, but hilariously enough; the main quest NPCs are nearly-identical and standing around in both camps handing out near-identical quests with the odd location or side-NPC switched around. Not bad! And some of the major quests also let you make meaningful (I think?) decisions regarding which story-faction you side with (AFAIK, this has no relevance on who you can actually fight in PvP)Now, the unfortunate aspects. The game has grind. It's not actually /that/ bad. For the most part. The grind can be a bit of a headache, and it unfortunately leads to a very boring gameplay loop of picking up your daily grind quests in the hub, sprinting at mach-5 to the daily grind quest location, doing it, returning to collect your upgrade materials, then repeating ad-infinitum, all while grinding map-spawn enemy camps. But it's never an unreasonable amount of grind. If it was a solo game. You get a decent amount of upgrade resources at a fairly quick pace so long as you stay running and rushing your daily quests and the randomly-generated hostile NPC camps that, upon killing all its NPCs, will spawn a crate of upgrade resources and a few useful items. You also must metal-detect for certain parts later down the line.STALCRAFT is an open-PvP MMO. There are 'safezones' but those are exclusively restricted to the town/quest hub areas. Leaving them means you're open to being ganked by anyone in the opposing faction - Or if you're in a particularly late-game, high-level area, anyone whose not in your particular faction's subfaction. Upon dying, you lose everything in your inventory apart from major gear. Things like armor, gun, NVGs, metal detectors, those stay with you; instead suffering durability damage that needs to be periodically repaired for a steep price. You lose all your ammo, anything you scavenged during your time out, all your artifacts, any upgrade materials you're carrying, medicine, and some quest items (Depending on the particular quest and its item).For a person like me, whose not particularly good at shooters; this slowly led to a feeling of exhaustion and frustration, and a really horrifically boring playstyle. Instead of going out and doing a couple quests or camps at once, I'd run out of the safezone, do one, immediately run all the way back, store all the items in my stash, then run back out and do it all over again. More of my game, particularly as I reached the 'Bar' area (Of which I never progressed past) basically ended up being 80% running back-and-forth, 10% inventory management, and 10% actually shooting stuff/doing quests, and a miniscule % ended up being me actually progressing the main story.The thing is, this sneaks up on you. In the early-game, you're in the Swamps, which are a fairly open and expansive area with little chance for you to run into people that aren't apart of your faction. Occasionally the game would throw a quest that's on the enemy faction's side of the map, but those were far-and-few between. Instead, you might occasionally have a PVP firefight, but you can safely grind the PvE for upgrade materials and do the main quest at a reasonable pace barring an occasional death. You also require higher tiers of upgrade materials as you progress, which can only be found in later areas.Once you finish the Swamps, you're off to the Cordon along with its respective faction towns, which is a roughly rectangular-shaped area. This was exceedingly frustrating as a Loner player, less-so as a Bandit player. Because the game likes to do a lot more of the placing quest locations in enemy territory thing. Not only that, though; because of how the map it set up, in order to proceed to the next area, Garbage. Garbage has town and only one hidden safezone that's only used for a quest or two and is easy to forget about since it isn't marked on the map. Even then, the safezone doesn't have a stash function (As far as I remember), making it mostly worthless for anything beyond a quick break.This is where the grinding, upgrade materials, and unfortunate open-PVP all come together to deeply frustrate me. The Loner base is significantly further from the Garbage, which is where you get the Tier 3 upgrade materials. Comparatively, the Bandit base is right next to the entrance to the Garbage, and not only that; as a Loner, you're forced to either take a horrifically-long side-path to get to the Garbage, or you're forced to sprint through Bandit territory in the hopes of not getting jumped by some guy whose like, a fifteen second sprint away from their faction base. Then, you do the whole thing /backwards/ in order to get back to your respective faction town to deposit your upgrade materials and hope to God you aren't shot and all your progress reset.It really, really killed it for me. The late-game looks like so much fun! I just wish there was a way to either pick lower-pop servers, go completely solo/offline, or have an instanced worldmap that's only for you and your invited friends to be a little adventuring group in.TL;DR, a well-designed game with a ton of respect to the STALKER universe, ruined by the fact that it's an open-PVP MMO. If the game had a singleplayer/coop/limited PvP mode, I imagine this would be a VERY easy recommendation, but at it's current state; I'd recommend playing through the first two areas. They're real fun no matter which side you pick, but once you get to the Garbage, the game can sharply fall off in frustration.

I’ve invested at least 10 hours into Stalcare X, and I must say, it masterfully combines the best elements from the Stalker Series and Escape from Tarkov. It features a carefully designed combat system, a solid economy, and immersive gunplay. Moreover, if you’re fortunate enough to have friends who share your interest in this genre of video games, you’re in for a treat. You can explore the zone as a squad and undertake missions together.Stalcare X is a simplified and less demanding version of Stalker GAMMA and Escape from Tarkov. A standout feature is that you won’t lose all your gear and weapons when defeated by a hostile enemy or mutant. Instead, you only lose the loot that you’ve acquired during your run outside your headquarters.Unlike other games, enemies or any hostile entities cannot camp outside your spawn point in Stalcare X. This is because the headquarters have their own defense systems in place to eliminate all nearby threats.The gunplay in Stalcare X is straightforward. Unlike other games that introduce excessive recoil to simulate realism, Stalcare X strikes a balance. It provides just enough recoil to give experienced players an edge, while also encouraging newcomers to improve their skills and adopt a more cautious approach.There are numerous ways to increase your wealth in Stalcare X. You can hunt, discover anomalies, or undertake missions for a variety of different NPCs scattered across the zone. You also have the option to auction your valuable items, allowing other players to bid and potentially increase your earnings. Additionally, you can hunt other players to claim whatever loot they’ve gathered in the zone.Importantly, in my first 10 hours of gameplay, I didn’t get the impression that Stalcare X is a ‘pay to win’ game. Despite there being numerous ways for players to spend money to acquire better equipment, the game allows you to obtain superior gear simply by playing and progressing.In conclusion, Stalcare X is a game that successfully merges the best elements of the Stalker Series and Escape from Tarkov, while also introducing its own unique features. It offers a balanced and straightforward gunplay, a robust economy, and a variety of ways to earn in-game currency. The game encourages both new and experienced players to improve their skills and adopt strategic approaches. With its player-friendly features such as the defense systems at spawn points and the preservation of gear upon defeat, Stalcare X stands out in the genre. Whether you’re exploring the zone solo or with friends, Stalcare X promises an engaging and immersive gaming experience. Most importantly, it maintains a fair playing field, ensuring that success is determined by skill and strategy, not by financial investment. This makes Stalcare X a truly rewarding and enjoyable game to play.

But then again even though this looks super casual it is somewhat hardcore gameplay. Its a lot more fun playing with friends especially PVP. So initially, I had mixed feelings about the game. After a few months of playing i'm going to give my honest opinion. If you're looking for an online game set in a STALKER world, this is as good as it gets. The atmosphere is great, guns are well made and fun to use, the story is on par with the original games. It maintains the harshness of the original STALKER games as well, minus the super irritating and unforgiving bleed mechanic. The early to mid game content is well done and enjoyable, and forces you to be patient and work your way up the gear tiers. Fair warning, some of the ending story bosses are NOT for the faint of heart. Their mechanics are designed to punish you heavily for the smallest mistake, almost to the point of being flat out unfair in the final boss fights. All praise aside, the game is lacking when it comes to endgame content. The endgame consists of the same super grindy world events that you have no choice to do in order to get endgame gear. Players that already have endgame gear are also very irritating as the game funnels players into specific zones where pvp becomes more and more abundant, with more factions becoming hostile the further you go. If an enemy spots you first, its pretty much guaranteed death. The amount of resources needed in order to craft late game weapons and armor, combined with the monotony of grinding the roughly 5 different world event types makes for a late game experience that just isn't fun to play.
